body:
Would love to see this fixed!

Any URLs which have 127.0.0.1 in them will have it rewritten to localhost . This also includes query parameters, which we use on the Kick Public API when performing OAuth authorisation. For any applications which integrate with the public API, and use a callback URL with 127.0.0.1 as their host, it will cause authorisation to fail as we require redirect URIs to match as NextJS is modifying the query parameter. See https://github.com/KickEngineering/KickDevDocs/issues/211 for more info.

URL normalisation definitely seems to be the cause. If I set the `skipMiddlewareUrlNormalize` option to true in the Next config on the reproduction, it fixes the issue.

body:
I though I was going insane. We have an API that can request so-called service & network "instances" by their name and the name might be just an IP-Address.
We were baffled when requesting the instance "127.0.0.1" we received "localhost" instead.

Simple copy-paste reproduction:
- create a file `app/ticket-79182/route.ts` with the following content:
```ts
import { NextResponse } from "next/server"

export const GET = (req: Request) => {
  return NextResponse.json({ url: req.url })
}
```
- build the application in standalone mode and start it up
- Run `curl http://localhost:3000/ticket-79182\?name\=127.0.0.1`
- Response is unexpectedly `{"url":"http://0.0.0.0:3000/ticket-79182?name=localhost"}`

This issue does not happen in development mode.

Not sure what the appropriate workaround is (maybe encoding and decoding the `name`?).
I fear that `skipMiddlewareUrlNormalize` might have unintended consequences elsewhere.

body:
It's expected that `generateMetadata` is called twice here, because the server receives two requests (one for the even number, and the other for the odd number param after the redirect roundtrip).

`generateMetadata` function has access to params (see https://nextjs.org/docs/app/api-reference/functions/generate-metadata#generatemetadata-function), so you could shortcircuit the execution of `generateMetadata` by checking params in the same way as you did for the page component.

body:
It should be fixable by NextJS, but the core of the issue is not specific to NextJS's metadata system. You can see the same issue if you use React's native metadata hosting introduced in react 19.

I don't know how next's metadata system works internally, but it basically boils down to:
- react itself makes no attempt to reorder metadata tags, so they might be lost (upstream)
- when NextJS adds its metadata tags, it makes no consideration for their placement in the head, so they may be lost (next specific)

depending on how the NextJS metadata system works, a fix in react itself may or may not also fix the NextJS metadata system

body:
Hi @theroot79 --

What you're observing is a behavior that was introduced as part of [streaming metadata](https://nextjs.org/docs/app/api-reference/functions/generate-metadata#streaming-metadata) to improve page performance in 15.2. It seems that Lighthouse explicitly checks for metadata within `head` ([ref](https://github.com/GoogleChrome/lighthouse/blob/main/core/gather/gatherers/meta-elements.js#L21)).

With this feature, whenever metadata resolution would potentially block rendering the page, we instead defer it and stream it into the page body. Browsers are still able to interpret the `title` tag properly regardless of where it's rendered in the DOM. 

We have handling in place that will ensure metadata appears in the `head` for a wide variety of bot user agents, (which can be customized in `next.config` -- you can even disable it broadly for all user agents by passing a wildcard regex). Since Lighthouse runs using your regular browser's user agent, it's not detected as a bot.

We're going to work on improving our documentation & education material to clarify this behavior.

author: bernatfortet

body:
As per the documentation at https://nextjs.org/docs/app/api-reference/functions/generate-metadata#streaming-metadata

`Streamed metadata is appended to the <body> tag. Since metadata mainly targets bots and crawlers, Next.js streams metadata for bots that can execute JavaScript and inspect the full DOM (e.g. Googlebot). We have verified that these bots interpret the metadata correctly.`

I agree with other comments that metadata in the body may not be quite as guaranteed as Vercel imply, and there may be bots/scenarios it doesn't work as expected. One example is the `manifest.json` that Chrome doesn't seem to detect if it's in the `<body>` tag. For anyone struggling with this particular issue, the simplest solution I found was to go old school and just hard-code the manifest tag in the layout.js:

`<head><link rel="manifest" href="/manifest.json" /></head>`

...then you're not relying on streamed metadata and Chrome picks it up.

body:
You didn't set up a monorepo, that's why it doesn't work automatically. This is a git repository with 2 folders that hold their own application with their own dependencies and their own lockfiles.

During bootup of Next.js the root of the application is decided, for which we look for e.g. `package-lock.json` `yarn.lock` and such. Since in this case `next-app` has a lockfile it will use `next-app` as the root. Not the parent above it, as that is just a folder.

When setting up e.g. npm/pnpm/yarn workspaces that would correctly automatically detect the root of the application. 

If you don't want to set up workspaces you can also provide the `turbopack.root` option: https://nextjs.org/docs/app/api-reference/config/next-config-js/turbopack#root-directory with the directory. However not having workspaces but still importing code outside of the workspace will cause a lot of duplication as dependencies wouldn't be deduped by your package manager.

This is both a security and correctness feature, as you wouldn't want e.g. your private key in the user root to be able to be bundled.

body:
@abhi12299 thanks for the response — but respectfully, this is a Next.js routing issue when using the App Router with output: 'export' (i.e., for fully static sites or SPAs).

✅ What I’m trying to do:
Use dynamic routes (e.g. /organizations/[organizationId]) purely on the client-side, without any backend or pre-rendered paths, just like you can in React Router.

Here’s the official Next.js documentation on dynamic routes:
https://nextjs.org/docs/app/building-your-application/routing/dynamic-routes

Nowhere in the docs does it state that dynamic routing requires server-side rendering or static generation via generateStaticParams() — but in practice, it throws a build error:

Error: Page "/organizations/[organizationId]" is missing exported function "generateStaticParams()", which is required with "output: export" config.

This makes it impossible to:
	•	Build a purely client-side SPA using the App Router
	•	Use useParams() in page.tsx without backend involvement

👉 This is a limitation in Next.js’s App Router for fully static/client-side routing, and it contradicts the SPA-friendly design that developers expect — especially when switching from Create React App or React Router.

Please reconsider whether this limitation is expected behavior — if so, it should be clearly documented as a constraint for output: "export".
author: mikayel

body:
> When you don't know the exact segment names ahead of time and want to create routes from dynamic data, you can use Dynamic Segments that are filled in at request time or prerendered at build time.

This is from the docs for dynamic routes. When you specify a dynamic segment, that value is either provided during runtime or during the build time. If you don't specify the segments during build time (with `generateStaticParams`), how will nextjs know what files to generate during the static export?
author: abhi12299

body:
**It is called Dynamic Routing — the whole point is that the segment value is not known at build time.**

React Router handles this perfectly well in SPAs — and so does any standard client-side framework. You can see a basic example I’ve built years ago:
https://github.com/mikayel/React-Composite-View/blob/master/App.js

If Next.js now requires all dynamic segments to be known at build time (via generateStaticParams) when using output: 'export', that is not dynamic routing — it’s static generation with templating.

That’s fine as a limitation, but please document it clearly. Right now, the [official docs](https://nextjs.org/docs/app/building-your-application/routing/dynamic-routes) do not state that dynamic segments require predefinition in SPAs.

👉 If the Next.js team has intentionally removed support for dynamic routing in static-only apps, it should be:
	•	Explicitly stated in the docs
	•	Treated as a limitation compared to other SPA-friendly tools like CRA or Vite + React Router

Please escalate this to someone more senior on the team if possible. This is not a misunderstanding — it’s a fundamental gap in how Next.js currently handles fully client-side routing with the App Router and output: "export".

body:
@xuerzong it is worth noting that some known bots, crawlers, etc, will receive the content within `<head>`. In this case you, as a human page reader, see them in the `<body>`.

For example here, I simulate a user-agent, `Slurp`, requesting my streamed page:

https://github.com/user-attachments/assets/09a34af1-9f02-46a8-96a2-19e3446a002e

Notice how the `<title>` is within the head.

Now, see this, same app, no changes, but now I am just a regular browser:

https://github.com/user-attachments/assets/7554aa1c-6447-442c-b131-0844fda3782e

Browsers are able to find these anyway, so the title correctly shows in places like the browser tabs.

For a reference, on which user-agents trigger the first behavior, you can consult:

- https://github.com/vercel/next.js/blob/canary/packages/next/src/shared/lib/router/utils/html-bots.ts#L3
- Some user agents, considered bots, are known to execute JavaScript, those are here: https://github.com/vercel/next.js/blob/canary/packages/next/src/shared/lib/router/utils/is-bot.ts#L4

Last but not least, you can control this behavior from `next.config.js`:

- https://nextjs.org/docs/app/api-reference/config/next-config-js/htmlLimitedBots

As Zack said, https://github.com/vercel/next.js/issues/79313#issuecomment-2892288965, you can put a match all there, with the trade-offs implied by that. 

> We don't recommend modifying the `htmlLimitedBots` configuration, but the option is there. As noted below, a PR with new bot User Agents is preferred.

```js
/** @type {import('next').NextConfig} */
const nextConfig = {
  htmlLimitedBots: /.*/
};

export default nextConfig;
```

body:
The position of title doesn't matter for human users as it can still display properly by browsers. Streaming metadata renders metadata tags sometimes in body is more for performance improvement intention rather than an error. It only matters for bots where some of the crawlers are limited to parse the meta tags.

We have a built-in [default list](https://nextjs.org/docs/app/api-reference/config/next-config-js/htmlLimitedBots#default-list) of user agent that we'll serve with blocking metadata for different bots. If they're trying out any new bot/crawlers, they can PR to the codebase to add new ones. Adding `*` will regress the rendering performance that force metadata becomes blocking. We don't recommend to add any user agent for browsers that for normal browsing.

@bernatfortet Yes, I use Turbo. You typically add the `--turbo` flag to your `dev` script in `package.json`.

Could you try adding the following to your `Next.js: debug client-side` configuration and then run your `Next.js: Full Debug` config?

```ts
"skipFiles": [
  "<node_internals>/**",
  "**/node_modules/**",
  "**/.next/**"
]

This might resolve the issue you described under Behaviour 2. There's a lot of external code being pulled in during debugging, and excluding these paths helps prevent stepping too deep into irrelevant internals. That’s usually why you end up in the “cryptic code” you mentioned.

author: icyJoseph

body:
Hi @icyJoseph,

Thanks for looking into this! You're absolutely right about the DOM reference issue.

**Regarding Stonly test environment**
Unfortunately, Stonly doesn't have a public test environment or demo script that I'm aware of. However, I was able to reproduce the issue by simulating their widget behavior in the reproduction repo.

**DOM modifications by Stonly**
From what I've observed, Stonly makes several DOM modifications:

- Injects modal containers - Creates overlay divs directly in document.body
- Modifies existing elements - Can wrap or move existing DOM nodes when positioning guides
- Dynamic script injection - Adds/removes script tags for guide functionality
- CSS modifications - Injects stylesheets and modifies element styles
- Event listener management - Attaches global event handlers that can interfere with React's event system

**Investigation details**
I traced the `removeChild` calls and confirmed the issue:
```
javascriptconst originalRemoveChild = Node.prototype.removeChild;
Node.prototype.removeChild = function(child) {
  console.trace('removeChild called on:', this, 'with:', child);
  return originalRemoveChild.call(this, child);
};
```
The trace shows React trying to clean up elements that Stonly has already removed or moved - React components that were rendered normally but got caught in Stonly's DOM cleanup process.
The crash happens consistently on mobile because Stonly's mobile guide behavior is more aggressive in DOM manipulation compared to desktop.
This is indeed very similar to the Google Translate issue you referenced - timing conflicts between React's reconciliation and third-party DOM manipulation.

body:
NextJS [automatically injects the meta tag](https://nextjs.org/docs/app/api-reference/functions/not-found) for 404 pages to prevent them from being indexed.

```
The notFound function allows you to render the [not-found file](https://nextjs.org/docs/app/api-reference/file-conventions/not-found) within a route segment as well as inject a <meta name="robots" content="noindex" /> tag.
```

As you've created your own metadata implementation within the `not-found.tsx`, it's now duplicated.

It won't be duplicated if you remove the robots segment from your metadata implementation:

```
robots: {
    index: false,
    follow: false
  }
```

Thank you, I saw this on the docs but our SEO colleague asked for nofollow and I don't know how to say no, so is this a feature of Next.js and not a bug?
author: GreedyWhale

body:
Right now this behavior is expected and harmless: Next.js automatically injects `<meta name="robots" content="noindex">` for any route that returns a 404, including `not-found.tsx`, while your own robots field (`index: false, follow: false`) is also being merged in, which results in two tags showing up. From an SEO perspective this is not an actual issue because search engines like Google will simply aggregate the directives across both tags and apply the most restrictive interpretation, so your page is still treated as `noindex, nofollow`. If you only need the page excluded from search results, you can remove the robots definition from your not-found.tsx and rely on Next.js’ automatic noindex handling, which avoids duplication entirely. If you also want to prevent link equity from flowing through that page, it’s cleaner to mark untrusted links with `rel="nofollow"` rather than relying on a page-level nofollow, but even if you leave your current setting in place the duplicate tags don’t hurt—this is more of a cosmetic quirk than a functional problem.

Ref: https://developers.google.com/search/blog/2007/03/using-robots-meta-tag

In my case, both development and production mode work improperly. I didn't notice this in development mode only because it just accidentally worked.

In development mode, DevTools showed CSS layers:

- 4: implicit outer layer
   - 0: ui
   - 1: base
   - 2: features
   - 3: pages

In production mode:

- 4: implicit outer layer
   - 0: ui
   - 1: pages
   - 2: features
   - 3: base

However, both of results were incorrect. In fact, my SCSS defined:

```scss
@layer base, ui, features, pages;
```

Then, I removed the line of `@layer base, ui, features, pages;` and tried again. The results were still random.

I aggregated these tests:

| (`b`: `base`, `u`: `ui`…)                   | Development  | Production   |
| ------------------------------------------- | ------------ | ------------ |
| With `@layer base, ui, features, pages;`    | `ubfp`       | `upfb`       |
| Without `@layer base, ui, features, pages;` | `ubpf`       | `upfb`       |
| ***Correct result***                        | ***`bufp`*** | ***`bufp`*** |

All these cases were unpredictable.

---

I also tested `@layer` in a pure Sass (SCSS) environment. The result was that Sass left `@layer base, ui, features, pages;` as it was. The position also stayed the same, so everything functioned normally. So I can confirm this problem has nothing to do with Sass.

I know many of you are using Tailwind CSS. By putting CSS in JSX and switching class names instead of overriding styles, both #79531 and #83941 can be bypassed. Because removing unwanted class names and put in new ones naturally avoided CSS prioritization issues.

Hi, @poupas97, the reason why you see the 'Loading' text when navigating from root `/` to `/f1`/ is because you have made a component `loading.tsx` in `/app`. If you were to copy this same component to `/app/f1/` it would also display the loading screen when navigating from f1 to f11.

Without an explicitly defined `loading.tsx`, Next will render the next page while you wait on the current page -> in this case, it was rendering /f11 while the client is still on /f1. I hope this makes sense.

EDIT: I'm a little late but I hope this is still valuable :)

body:
> When reading the documentation I got the idea that if I had the `loading.tsx` file in `/app`, I wouldn't need the same file in the child folders. So I opened this issue.
> 
> Is it really necessary to have the `loading.tsx` file in all folders?

If you're using `loading.tsx` then yes, since it only covers the loading state of its own route segment. Another option you could use is to wrap your layout in `<Suspense></Suspense>` manually, which would then apply this loading state to all of your pages.

body:
Hi,

This is a bug with how the closure is captured to be re-used when the action is called. If you add `allData`, and `user` to the `console.log` you do, then it'll work:

```ts
          console.log({
            formData,
            myData,
            name,
            email,
            redirUrl,
            // add these two
            allData,
            user,
          });
``` 

- https://stackblitz.com/edit/github-9olvaijx?file=src%2Fapp%2Fbug%2Fpage.tsx

The team has already prepared a PR to fix the issue.

Though, the workaround you have posted, is the right way to go:

 1. filter the list based on user knowledge during SSR time
 1. the payload sent when submitting the Server Functions contains only the current user's data
 
And, even though, the closure data is encrypted, it is good practice to not include unnecessary data client side, even more, if this is potentially sensitive data.

In general, be defensive when passing data from Server to Client boundaries. Include only things that are absolutely necessary.

- https://nextjs.org/docs/app/api-reference/config/next-config-js/taint
- https://nextjs.org/blog/security-nextjs-server-components-actions

body:
We just encountered the same problem with Next.js version 14.2.32.

For us, our custom error page worked in dev mode but would not be shown for ISR pages after a `build` / `start` cycle, either locally or when deployed to Vercel.

Adding the legacy error page _/pages/500.tsx_ also worked for us. Thanks @scottlet for the work-around!

How could this still be a problem months later, and on the stable Next.js 14 version?
author: jmurty

body:
It may not be clear from the issue description, so I will note that this problem only occurs for ISR pages that have not been pre-rendered in some way.

If a page is pre-rendered at build time via `generateStaticParams()` or at run-time for a successful page visit, that previously rendered page is shown instead of any error pages when a server-side error occurs.

It is only when an ISR page has not yet been rendered, and there happens to be a server-side error that prevents it from being rendered for the first time, that this problem occurs. This situation is relatively rare for us so we hadn't noticed there was such a fundamental bug in the Next.js App-dir error boundary handling.

body:
Don't put `useReportWebVitals` inside the component.
What you do is move it outside and export a function called `reportWebVitals`, and Next.js will call it once per real metric.

Here’s what I use in `_app.tsx`:

```tsx
import "@/styles/globals.css";
import type { AppProps } from "next/app";
import { useReportWebVitals } from "next/web-vitals";

export default function App({ Component, pageProps }: AppProps) {
  return <Component {...pageProps} />;
}

export function reportWebVitals(metric: any) {
  console.log("NEXT CWV", metric.name, metric.value);
}
```

And the log looks like this:
```bash
[HMR] connected
[Fast Refresh] done in NaNms
NEXT CWV Next.js-hydration 165.1
NEXT CWV: Navigating to Page 1
NEXT CWV Next.js-render 155
NEXT CWV Next.js-route-change-to-render 193.2
```

```txt
  System:

    typescript: ^5 => 5.8.3 
```
author: DiegoDev2

body:
honestly, I get where you're coming from. I probably would’ve been confused too — your implementation actually follows the official docs, so it totally makes sense to expect it to work correctly.

The problem is, in the Pages Router, using `useReportWebVitals` inside the App component causes metrics to be reported multiple times on soft navigations. But that’s not obvious from the docs at all.

Exporting `reportWebVitals` outside the component (as a named export) avoids the duplicates, since Next.js calls it only once per actual metric.

So yeah — good catch. It’s not just a bug, it’s also a documentation issue.
author: DiegoDev2

body:
Hi,

Yeah, this is because the web-vitals library, reports available metrics upon subscription. And we subscribe when the function reference changes. One way to fix this, is to keep the reference stable. I've made some doc change suggestions.

body:
Hi,

We strongly advise against the suggestion that was provided in this article. By blocking static chunks, you're also effectively blocking Google from being able to crawl the site. Google uses Chrome to render the underlying website. By blocking Google from downloading the JS, if you ship any feature that is client-side rendered, then it won’t be indexed.

When deploying to Vercel, we highly recommend leveraging [skew protection](https://vercel.com/docs/skew-protection). This can prevent issues that may arise from chunks failing to load due to older clients referencing resources that no longer exist. If blocking chunks is "fixing" the issue, that suggests that a chunk load error could be causing Google to soft 404. Vercel recently updated the skew protection window for crawlers like Googlebot to be [60 days](https://vercel.com/changelog/automatic-mitigation-of-crawler-delay-via-skew-protection) to help mitigate this problem. 

You could also consider shipping an error boundary that will recover the server-side rendered HTML, in the event of a chunk load failure: https://nextjs.org/docs/app/api-reference/file-conventions/error#graceful-error-recovery-with-a-custom-error-boundary

Some more information can be found in [this](https://support.google.com/webmasters/thread/322653126?authuser=1&hl=en) Google thread, showing how this particular issue isn't framework specific, along with context on how Google will do two passes on crawling: retrieving initial HTML< and spinning up a browser to do the rendering.

body:
Hi @Gul7333, 

I see you're aiming for a full static export of your Urdu dictionary with 100k+ pages to host on GitHub Pages. That's a cool project!

The error you're seeing, `[RangeError: Maximum call stack size exceeded]` happens when Node.js (which Next.js runs on) tries and fails to handle an extremely large number of synchronous operations or very deep function calls.

When you use Next.js's static export feature by setting `output: 'export'` your `generateStaticParams` function is called to list all the paths that need to be pre-rendered.

With 100k+ paths returned, Next.js then attempts to "collect page data" and render each of these pages into static HTML. This involves a series of operations for each page. When done for such a massive number in a single build process, it can exceed the call stack limit imposed by the underlying Node.js environment. It works for 5,000 pages because the total number of operations stays below this limit.

### The challenge with `output: 'export'` for GitHub Pages at this scale:

GitHub Pages does not have a Node.js runtime, so Next.js features like Incremental Static Regeneration (ISR) can't be used because they require a server environment, and, as discussed above, the `output: 'export'` mode can struggle to build that many pages at once due to these limitations.

## What you could do:

### Use Next.js with a compatible hosting platform. 
Platforms like Vercel https://vercel.com/ (which offers a generous free tier) or other Node.js compatible hosting platforms will fully support ISR. Your site will still be served statically and be very fast, but pages will be built more efficiently. This allows you to keep your existing Next.js project and scale effectively.

### If sticking with GitHub Pages is a hard requirement:
This is more challenging with Next.js at this scale due to the build limitations.

Your workaround options are:

- **Manual Chunking:** You could try scripting multiple partial builds and merging the `out` directories. This is difficult to maintain.
- **Increase Node Stack Size:** Setting `node --stack-size=8192` in `node_modules/.bin/next` build might offer a temporary reprieve but isn't a reliable fix.


## Consider Alternative Static Site Generators (SSGs) 
If the workarounds are too complex and GitHub Pages is non-negotiable, you might also consider alternative SSGs which are highly optimized for rapidly building a massive number of simple static pages from data. Examples include:

### Hugo (Go-based)

https://gohugo.io/

### Eleventy (JavaScript-based)

https://www.11ty.dev/

### Zola (Rust-based)

https://www.getzola.org/

These options would all entail migrating your project's templating and data handling.

The Next.js team is always working on improving build performance, but for your immediate needs and scale, shifting your deployment strategy to use ISR on a compatible platform is likely the most straightforward path to success with your Next.js dictionary.

body:
Hi @Gul7333,

I get your perspective. I glimpsed at the code to understand how Next.js does stuff under the hood.

For context, with the way Next.js currently pre-renders HTML, they'd likely have to shift their process to be fully stream-oriented, or to use iterators/generators to process the massive list of pages in a way that keeps the call stack shallow and memory usage low. 

This would be a significant architectural change, and would likely cost a nontrivial amount of maintainability. Next.js has a complex build system that caters to a lot of different rendering modes (SSR, ISR, RSCs, static).

The current system already has chunking (in `export/index.ts` sending work to workers) and workers already have internal concurrency limits (as seen in `export/worker.ts`).

However, the `RangeError: Maximum call stack size exceeded` suggests that either:

- The main thread orchestrating these chunks/workers is still doing too much synchronous work over too many iterations. 
- Or, a worker itself, when processing its assigned (potentially still large) chunk of pages, has an internal loop that is too synchronous over too many iterations, leading to a stack overflow within that worker process.

So, more batching, or perhaps different kinds of batching (like yielding to the event loop within tight loops) might be needed. "Little optimizations" might not cut it if the fundamental issue is call stack depth over a massive number of iterations.

They absolutely could look at how tools like Eleventy, Hugo, Zola, etc., achieve their massive static build performance, but the challenge for Next.js would be integrating such highly specialized static-gen techniques into its much broader, more hybrid architecture without compromising its other features or significantly increasing complexity. A deeper fix to make `output: 'export'` as scalable as a dedicated SSG for hundreds of thousands of pages would be a much larger undertaking for the Next.js team with significant design and maintenance considerations, some of which might differ from where their current priorities lie.

Anyway, based on the current behaviour, I also opened a PR (#80037) to potentially add a more descriptive warning for this situation.

body:
Thanks for the detailed repro!

I dug into this. The root cause is Next.js's automatic Node.js polyfill for the client bundle. When client code imports `crypto`, webpack aliases it to `crypto-browserify`, and `vm` is aliased to `vm-browserify` ([packages/next/src/build/webpack-config.ts#L1899](https://github.com/vercel/next.js/blob/canary/packages/next/src/build/webpack-config.ts#L1899)). `vm-browserify`'s `Script.prototype.runInThisContext` calls `eval(this.code)`. Even though it's wrapped in a `try/catch`, the browser still fires a CSP violation and reports it via the Reporting API before the error is swallowed.

A few workarounds for now:

1. Disable Node polyfills entirely in `next.config.js`:
   ```js
   module.exports = { experimental: { fallbackNodePolyfills: false } }
   ```
   Then migrate to Web Crypto (`globalThis.crypto.subtle`) on the client.

2. Alias just `vm` to `false` via a custom webpack config if you want to keep the other polyfills:
   ```js
   webpack: (config, { isServer }) => {
     if (!isServer) config.resolve.fallback = { ...config.resolve.fallback, vm: false }
     return config
   }
   ```

3. Drop the `crypto` import on the client and use Web Crypto directly — the cleanest long-term option since real `vm` emulation in the browser is impossible anyway.

Framework-side, I think the right fix is to either default `vm` to `false` in the client fallback config, or swap `vm-browserify` for an eval-free stub, since `runInThisContext` can never actually work under a strict CSP.

cc @ijjk  happy to put up a PR if you can confirm the preferred direction (stub vs. default-off).

I ran into the same issue when testing this — the `Super expression must either be null or a function` error happens as soon as `<LineChart />` is used inside the API route.

Looks like the core problem is that `recharts` components expect a browser-like environment, and even though `react-pdf-charts` uses `renderToStaticMarkup`, it’s still running inside Next.js’s **Edge/server context**, which doesn't support certain DOM assumptions or class extensions.

I also tried adding `"use client"` in `MyDocument.tsx`, but yeah — API routes don't support that.

A possible workaround might be:
- Dynamically import a client-safe component only when needed (although tricky inside an API route),
- Or move the chart rendering logic into a **standalone Node script** and call it via `child_process` in the API route — basically offloading the rendering to a separate environment.

Would be great to see better error reporting here, or a way to opt a serverless function out of React Server Components entirely.

Let me know if anyone finds a clean workaround!
author: blaze-gold

body:
Thanks @5shine1 — really appreciate you digging into this.

Yes, I also confirmed that the issue originates from trying to render recharts (which depends on the browser DOM and possibly class-based components) within a server context that doesn't fully emulate the browser — even with renderToStaticMarkup.

A few quick findings and thoughts from my side:

The Super expression must either be null or a function error points to an incompatible class inheritance (likely LineChart or a related component relying on HTMLElement or similar), which isn’t supported in the Next.js Edge/Node server context.

The issue disappears in a regular Node script or plain React server environment — so it's definitely something specific to how Next.js bundles/runs API routes under App Router and RSC rules.

body:
@hood I didn't notice that in your comment, sorry about that.

I spent more time to investigate.

This is **partially fixed** by changing the default bundler from `webpack` to `turbopack` since https://github.com/vercel/next.js/commit/9ba29b4125bf368f92d36b34a5a34aa8dce0a8ce and `next@v15.6.0-canary.40` but another bug prevents the `compile` from working and fixed in https://github.com/vercel/next.js/commit/051351309f13215d80fb6aacab3bf6c7b0de5b03. So the lowest working version is `next@v16.0.0-canary.5` or `next@v16.0.0`.

**Workaround**
You can still make it work using turbopack in `next@15.3.3` too, I confirmed it's working with just `compile` no need for `generate-env` in`turbopack` mode:
```json
  "scripts": {
    "dev": "NODE_TLS_REJECT_UNAUTHORIZED=0 next dev --turbopack",
    "build": "cp .env.local .env.production && rm -rf ./.next/ && next build --turbopack --experimental-build-mode compile && cp -r ./.next/static ./.next/standalone/.next/static && cp -r ./public ./.next/standalone/public"
  }
```

However, webpack mode will not work correctly even in the latest code due to the `inlineStaticEnv` changes the js files but it misses the files in standalone directory.

I implemented a fix for webpack mode in #85262

(sorry for the multiple edits! was a bit confused about the issue)

This is not the same issue as https://github.com/vercel/next.js/issues/79195

We're aware of this Vercel platform constraint and are currently rolling out a change to eliminate it entirely. Once this is fully rolled out, you can include non-ASCII characters in response headers. And if Vercel Functions runtime finds non-ASCII characters, it will encode them accordingly (percent-encode, RFC 3986) instead of throwing
author: smaeda-ks

body: Thanks for the update! I also learned after reading your comment that non-ASCII isn't allowed in HTTP headers by default - so thanks for that too!
author: tom-sherman

body: I wonder though if non-ASCII is not allowed in http headers, should Next.js handle that itself? Because otherwise every provider will need to implement such a fix.
author: tom-sherman

body:
@tom-sherman This is a bit more nuanced, and I actually don't think other providers will see this issue. The issue was specifically with Vercel Functions runtime strictly (and unnecessarily!) checking the response header values, and this does not affect self-hosted Next.js apps.

In fact, the HTTP RFC 9110 spec does not prohibit the use of arbitrary non-ASCII bytes in the response header value, and it suggests that downstream systems treat such a header value as opaque data, but does not define implementation details. So in practice, user code can use any bytes, but that doesn't mean it won't blow up downstream proxies/middle-boxes with its encoding. Therefore, we (Vercel Functions runtime) take the safest approach and encode non-ASCII bytes using percent-encoding (RFC 3986).

body:
Thanks for reporting this — I ran into a similar issue when using the Prisma client generator in a Next.js 15 project.
After reviewing the generated code and build output:
- The error appears to stem from the **`createRequire(import.meta.url)`** usage in Prisma-generated TypeScript.
- During `next build`, this gets compiled/minified incorrectly — `createRequire` becomes `t(...)`, which results in `TypeError: t is not a function`.
Confirmed:
- The issue occurs consistently on:
  - Node.js 22.16.0
  - Next.js 15.3.3
  - Prisma-generated ESM code
- Build output shows the error during the **page.js** compilation phase (`getQueryCompilerWasmModule`).
Possible Cause:
- Likely a **transpilation/minification mismatch** between ESM modules and the way Next.js handles server code with Webpack.
- Could also be related to [#62953](https://github.com/vercel/next.js/issues/62953) or [#78267](https://github.com/vercel/next.js/issues/78267), but this specific failure in Prisma’s generated ESM client may require tailored handling.
Related:
- I saw you’ve also posted in [prisma/prisma#27343](https://github.com/prisma/prisma/issues/27343) — good call, as it may need coordination on both ends.
Let me know if there's a workaround recommended for this — or if this needs an upstream patch in Prisma or Next.js’s Webpack config.
Thanks again!
author: blaze-gold

body:
Thanks for the detailed breakdown, @5shine1 — I’m glad to hear someone else reproduced the issue. I agree that the problem seems to stem from how the Prisma-generated ESM code is being handled during the Next.js build process, particularly the use of createRequire(import.meta.url), which appears to be mangled into an invalid call expression.

Given that this doesn't occur during development (next dev) but only during next build, I suspect this could indeed be a Webpack-related minification or tree-shaking issue, possibly tied to how ESM modules are bundled on the server side.

I'll continue tracking the Prisma issue [prisma/prisma#27343](https://github.com/prisma/prisma/issues/27343), but it might be worth looking into whether Next.js can better support ESM output from tools like Prisma that use createRequire. If there's any recommended workaround — such as switching to CommonJS output temporarily or customizing the Webpack config — I'd be happy to test it and share results.

Thanks again for helping confirm this!

body:
Did/could you try using `next.config.js` instead of `next.config.ts`?

We came across this same issue when upgrading from `.js` to `.ts`.
My understanding is this is because of the following:

> When next.config.ts exists, Next’s startup order changes.
> 
> With next.config.ts, the process looks like this:
> 1. Node starts
> 2. Next bootstraps SWC
> 3. Next loads internal tracing / telemetry
> 4. Next imports:
> - http
> - fs
> - path
> - often undici / fetch5. 
> 5. Next transpiles next.config.ts
> 6. Next starts the server
> 7. Only now does instrumentation.ts → register() run
> 8. NodeSDK tries to patch modules
> 9.  Too late, the modules are already loaded
> 
> With next.config.js, steps 2 to 4 happen after the config executes, which is why it appears to work.

We couldn't find a workaround for this.

> But only works when you do this:
> 
> ```js
>     remotePatterns: [new URL("https://avatars.githubusercontent.com/u/**/*?v=4")]

This is expected behavior. In most cases, remote images don't have a query string so the new URL pattern does not assume its there. If you want more flexibility you can use the old object format and it will assume wildcards for anything omitted.

```js
remotePatterns: [{ protocol: 'https', hostname: 'avatars.githubusercontent.com', pathname: '/u/**/*' }],
```

Although for the example you gave, I think its best to use the `?v=4` in remotePatterns since its a constant.

Another option since this is coming from github and the version probably doesn't matter is to strip the query string before assigning the `src` prop.

body:
That seems misleading. The default behavior (when `search` isn't specified in the object version) is to allow any query params. The default behavior when using a URL (when no query string is specified) is to require no query params. This is also under a section starting with "If using a version prior to 15.3.0..." but still applies even on newer versions.

This is also explicitly called out further down on that page:
>Good to know: When omitting `protocol`, `port`, `pathname`, or `search` then the wildcard `**` is implied. This is not recommended because it may allow malicious actors to optimize urls you did not intend.

My point is that if you are updating your version to >15.3.0, you may see this section and think "Okay, I'll switch from the object version to the URL version". If your previous object version looks like this:
```js
remotePatterns: [
  {
    protocol: 'https',
    hostname: 'example.com',
    port: '',
    pathname: '/account123/**',
    // search omitted because we want to allow any/all query params
  },
],
```
...and you switched it to a URL like this:
```js
remotePatterns: [new URL('https://example.com/account123/**')], // query params omitted because we want to allow any/all
```
...then the behavior would change without a clear reason.

body:
This is expected.

- **Transitivity of `use client`**: Once a component is marked with `"use client"`, everything inside that module is treated as client code. For example, if `C1` is a client component and it imports/defines `C3` in the same module, `C3` is automatically treated as a client component as well, even if it’s not explicitly marked. That’s the transitive effect.

- **Composition via props**: Passing a server component to a client component via props (e.g. through `children`) is different from “owning” it. The client component doesn’t make it a client component — the server one still runs on the server. That’s why the “owner” terminology works here: ownership means being defined inside the client boundary, not just passed through it.

**TL;DR**  
`"use client"` is transitive within a module’s ownership chain. Components defined or imported inside a client module are treated as client components. But if you pass a server component in as a prop, the client component doesn’t “own” it — it still runs on the server.

body:
Not necessarily difficult. You just have to get the idea that Next.js tries to statically render as much as possible, and you can opt-out from that through certain mechanisms. 

In this case, you are not using any, so-called, dynamic APIs, like params, searchParams, etc, so with the information available, Next.js tries to pre-render.

You can force certain behavior, through `export const dynamic = 'force-dynamic'`, then Next.js will not try to pre-render this at build time. https://nextjs.org/docs/app/api-reference/file-conventions/route-segment-config#dynamic

BUT! That's still not correct in my opinion. 

When a request arrives to `Home`, we try to render a response, and hit the `api/search`, so we make another HTTP round trip, out to the internet and back to your project, in turn, that's likely gonna make further requests, so you are adding an additional round trip for no good reason.

You should just do the work you do in `api/search`, in the Server Component. At scale, you'd have a `lib/search` module that exposes the primitives to do a search from any environments, React Server Components, Route Handlers, etc... 

- https://nextjs-faq.com/fetch-api-in-rsc

As of today, in the stable releases, Next.js decides "what to statically render" at page level, but soon, this will be possible at Component level, sort of. https://nextjs.org/docs/app/getting-started/partial-prerendering


Last but not least:

> app router hard to use

body: Hi, I think you have to escape the `&` to `&`. ```ts title: "MD0186 肉【钟宛冰&苏语棠】", ``` See here, https://codesandbox.io/p/devbox/ekko-sitemap-forked-dhvklq?file=%2Fapp%2Fsitemap.ts%3A18%2C8 I should add that, it is the browser that can't parse the xml, because of the `&` ~ Next.js is responding with what you defined.
author: icyJoseph

body:
Hi!
I looked into the sandbox provided and just wanted to clarify the root cause for anyone else encountering this error:
This is a classic XML encoding issue — the & character must be escaped as & in any XML-based output, including when using MetadataRoute.Sitemap in Next.js.

Instead of hardcoding:
`title: "MD0186 肉【钟宛冰&苏语棠】"`

It should be escaped like:
`title: "MD0186 肉【钟宛冰&苏语棠】"`

For dynamic values, a reusable helper might help:
```
function escapeXml(str: string) {
  return str
    .replace(/&/g, '&')
    .replace(/</g, '<')
    .replace(/>/g, '>')
    .replace(/"/g, '"')
    .replace(/'/g, ''');
}
```
This ensures your sitemap output stays valid even with user-generated or special characters. Hope this helps clarify the issue!

body:
You're absolutely right — this is a known issue in the current behavior of Next.js (especially in canary builds like 15.4.0-canary.83) where generateMetadata is invoked eagerly when links are prefetched in the viewport. This happens even when metadata isn't needed yet, leading to unintended server load or data fetching — contrary to the expected lazy evaluation model of streaming pages.

## Explanation
In your reproduction:

```
export const generateMetadata = async ({ params }: { params: Promise<{ id: string }> }) => {
  const { id } = await params;
  console.log(`generateMetadata: ${id}`);
  return { title: `Page ${id}` };
};
```

When a <Link href="/your-dynamic-path/123" /> is rendered in the viewport, Next.js attempts to prefetch the route, and as of now, it triggers generateMetadata() during the prefetch, not when the page is actually rendered. This is undesirable, especially for large-scale apps with expensive metadata fetching logic.

## Expected Behavior (as you noted)

- **loading.tsx** should be prefetched.
- **generateMetadata()** should only run on actual navigation to that route.

## Workarounds / Mitigations
Until the Next.js team resolves this issue, you can:

### 1. Defer Metadata Fetching Inside the Page Itself

Don’t use generateMetadata() if the metadata needs expensive fetching. Instead, render metadata inside the component body using a client-side effect (not ideal, but safe).

### 2. Disable Link Prefetching

`<Link href="/dynamic-path/123" prefetch={false}>Go to Page</Link>`
This prevents generateMetadata from running until actual navigation.

### 3. Conditional Metadata Logic

Use headers() or other context-aware logic to bail out early if it's a prefetch call, though this can be tricky and unreliable across environments.

### 4. Track the GitHub Issue
Keep tabs on the [official GitHub issue](https://github.com/vercel/next.js/issues/80583). Vercel might offer a fix in a stable version soon.

body:
Don't mark the file as use server. Just import the functions from your server components and call them during rendering as you are now.

By marking the file (or the function) as use server, they turn into server actions and you use this, if you want to call server side logic **from the client**. You are only calling them from an rsc context anyways so you don't need the use server directive.

body:
@andrewgreenh Thanks for your response. However, I believe there might be a misunderstanding about the expected
  behavior of `revalidateTag`.

  My understanding was that `revalidateTag` would only revalidate the specific queries/data that are associated with
  that particular tag, not all queries on the page. If `revalidateTag` revalidates all data on the current route
  (including queries without the specified tag), then what's the difference between `revalidateTag` and
  `revalidatePath`?

  The whole point of having a tag-based invalidation system is to enable granular cache control. For example, if I
  have a page with:
  - User data (tagged with "user")
  - Todo list (tagged with "todos")
  - Health status (tagged with "health")

  When I call `revalidateTag("health")`, I expect only the health query to be refetched, not the user data or todos.
  This allows for efficient cache management and reduces unnecessary network requests.

  If the current behavior is indeed intentional, it significantly limits the usefulness of the tag-based cache
  invalidation system, as it essentially behaves the same as `revalidatePath` but with extra steps.

  Could you clarify if this is the intended design? And if so, what would be the recommended approach for
  invalidating specific data without affecting other cached data on the same route?
author: assa1605

body:
Ah no, I misunderstood you :)
Your desired behavior is exactly what I'm experiencing in my setup.

- Page A
  - data tag 1
  - data tag 2
- Page B
  - data tag 2
  - data tag 3

Invalidating Tag 1 should invalidate the Page A, so that it is re-rendered, it should refetch the data 1, but should not refetch data 2.

Invalidating Tag 2 should respectively invalidate the cache for page a AND page b, but the data fetches for tag 1 and tag 3 should not be re-issued.

What worked best for me to debug caching stuff is to setup a local proxy to really see what requests get issued to my 3rd party API.

body:
I think the issues is that in builds next and react use the StrictMode and RSC(react server component). 

When client-reviews.tsx which is a client component is mount or update it will render all the parts of it that part of the same render boundary even if the header.tsx is a server component. 

So when react do hydration or re render on the client, it may re render parts of both header.tsx and client-review.tsx, solution is i think try to memoize it or just isolate one of them. 

And also in next app router both Link and Image that in server component is re render for hydration purposes.

So the re render means that each node in the DOM are being evaluated during hydration.

And the re render doesn't mean your server side logic(if any) being re runs.

And also both Image and Link it self is internally build as a client component so it needs to re render if the parent tree updates.

is this a bug? No.
is it weird? Yes.

but it makes sense because the Image and Link rely on both routing and Image optimization.

:)

Hello @kayhadrin 👋

I’m running Windows 11 + WSL2 + Docker, and I’m able to run npm run dev without any issues.

Project setup

**NPM script**
```json
{
  "dev": "next dev"
}
````
**docker-compose.yml**

```yml
services:
  web:
    image: node:24-alpine
    working_dir: /app
    volumes:
      - .:/app
    ports:
      - "3000:3000"
    command: npm run dev
```
**next.config.ts**

```typescript
import type { NextConfig } from "next";

const nextConfig: NextConfig = {};

export default nextConfig;
```

**Important notes (WSL setup)**
Make sure your repository is located inside WSL, not on the Windows filesystem.
Steps I followed:

1. Open PowerShell
2. Enter WSL:
```bash
wsl
```
3. Create a projects directory:
```bash
cd ~
mkdir projects
cd projects
```
4. Copy your repository into ~/projects (or clone it directly there)
5. Open the project with VS Code
6. Install the WSL extension in VS Code
7. Run docker-compose up
8. Ensure WSL integration is enabled in Docker Desktop
9. Make sure your WSL user has permission to pull Docker images

With this setup, my repository is running Next.js 16 inside WSL using Docker Compose, and fast refresh / hot reloading works correctly.

Please let me know if this works for you as well.

### Why was this issue closed?

To be able to investigate, we need access to a reproduction to identify what triggered the issue. The bug template that you filled out has a section called "Link to the code that reproduces this issue", which is where you should provide the link to the reproduction.

- If you did not provide a link or the link you provided is not valid, we will close the issue.
- If you provide a link to a private repository, we will close the issue.
- If you provide a link to a repository but not in the correct section, we will close the issue.

### What should I do?

Depending on the reason the issue was closed, you can do the following:

- If you did not provide a link, please open a new issue with a link to a reproduction.
- If you provided a link to a private repository, please open a new issue with a link to a public repository.
- If you provided a link to a repository but not in the correct section, please open a new issue with a link to a reproduction in the correct section.

**In general, assume that we should not go through a lengthy onboarding process at your company code only to be able to verify an issue.**

### My repository is private and cannot make it public

In most cases, a private repo will not be a sufficient **minimal reproduction**, as this codebase might contain a lot of unrelated parts that would make our investigation take longer. Please do **not** make it public. Instead, create a new repository using the templates above, adding the relevant code to reproduce the issue. Common things to look out for:

- Remove any code that is not related to the issue. (pages, API routes, components, etc.)
- Remove any dependencies that are not related to the issue.
- Remove any third-party service that would require us to sign up for an account to reproduce the issue.
- Remove any environment variables that are not related to the issue.
- Remove private packages that we do not have access to.
- If the issue is not related to a monorepo specifically, try to reproduce the issue without a complex monorepo setup

### I did not open this issue, but it is relevant to me, what can I do to help?

Anyone experiencing the same issue is welcome to provide a minimal reproduction following the above steps by opening a new issue.

### I think my reproduction is good enough, why aren't you looking into it quickly?

We look into every Next.js issue and constantly monitor open issues for new comments.

However, sometimes we might miss one or two due to the popularity/high traffic of the repository. We apologize, and kindly ask you to refrain from tagging core maintainers, as that will usually not result in increased priority.

Upvoting issues to show your interest will help us prioritize and address them as quickly as possible. That said, every issue is important to us, and if an issue gets closed by accident, we encourage you to open a new one linking to the old issue and we will look into it.

body:
This warning originates from a deprecated usage of `util._extend` in the [http-proxy](https://github.com/http-party/node-http-proxy) package, which Next.js uses internally for handling rewrites and proxies. You can trace it to:
```
node_modules/http-proxy/lib/http-proxy/index.js
```
This is not coming from Next.js core code but from a third-party dependency that hasn't yet removed the deprecated API.

The warning is only visible in development (next dev) with rewrites enabled.
It does not affect functionality or production builds.

Node.js deprecated `util._extend` in favour of `Object.assign()`.

### **Fix for this:**
You can upstream a fix to `http-proxy` by replacing 
```
extend = require('util')._extend;
```
 with 
```
extend = Object.assign;
``` 
Once that’s merged and released, we can update the dependency in Next.js to eliminate the warning. Until then, this warning is safe to ignore.

body:
Hi,

Thanks for the feedback, we need to iterate the docs, so that parts like these don't rely on deeper knowledge of other areas.

I'd argue that not mentioning it doesn't mean it is prohibited, specially if the `generateMetadata` function resource, says that you can. 

However, I think I need to do some changes. Roughly the reason is `streaming metadata`.

`generateMetadata` or the metadata object, are used as part of rendering the route, so you can totally call `notFound`, `redirect`, cuz, you are within a server component. See I forgot `permanentRedirect` there.

But! After v15 there's something called `Streaming Metadata`. When you generateMetadata function has to await data (implementation details aside), Next.js moves on and renders the Page bits, and then the metadata is sent later to the client.

In Next 14, generateMetadata had to resolve before moving on. So calling these functions within `generateMetadata` is nuanced I think ~ I have some questions that I've asked the core team.
author: icyJoseph

body:
I think side-effects should be documented more in detail as well.

When I had my `permanentRedirect` in `generateMetadata`, embeds (on Discord) did not work. With `permanentRedirect` in the page component only, it works.

With `permanentRedirect` in the page component, Google Search Console does not recognize the redirect and treats the incorrect (previously indexed) url as canonical despite a different canonical URL being set in the metadata, perhaps due to the meta refresh being in the body instead of the head.

Hi, 

As of React 19, I don't think you need to wrap with head right?

- https://react.dev/reference/react-dom/components/link

> If the <link> has a rel="stylesheet" prop, then it has to also have a precedence prop to get this special behavior. This is because the order of stylesheets within the document is significant, so React needs to know how to order this stylesheet relative to others, which you specify using the precedence prop. If the precedence prop is omitted, there is no special behavior.

Put a precedence prop on it, to any arbitrary string value, and it should be placed in the head.

body:
Thanks for the detailed report 🙌
I was able to reproduce this behavior on next@canary using the provided reproduction link.

Interestingly, the diagnostics channel does fire correctly in Node.js, but fails silently in the edge runtime, even when using instrumentation.ts as expected. This might be due to polyfill limitations or intentional runtime restrictions.

One workaround I tried was to explicitly check for process.emit availability before registering the subscription — didn’t help in edge mode.

Might be worth clarifying in the docs if diagnostics subscriptions are intended to work in edge environments or not. Happy to help test a fix!

body:
We could not detect a valid reproduction link. **Make sure to follow the bug report template carefully.**

### Why was this issue closed?

To be able to investigate, we need access to a reproduction to identify what triggered the issue. We need a link to a **public** GitHub repository ([template for App Router](https://github.com/vercel/next.js/tree/canary/examples/reproduction-template), [template for Pages Router](https://github.com/vercel/next.js/tree/canary/examples/reproduction-template-pages)), but you can also use these templates: [CodeSandbox: App Router](https://codesandbox.io/s/github/vercel/next.js/tree/canary/examples/reproduction-template) or [CodeSandbox: Pages Router](https://codesandbox.io/s/github/vercel/next.js/tree/canary/examples/reproduction-template-pages).

The bug template that you filled out has a section called "Link to the code that reproduces this issue", which is where you should provide the link to the reproduction.

- If you did not provide a link or the link you provided is not valid, we will close the issue.
- If you provide a link to a private repository, we will close the issue.
- If you provide a link to a repository but not in the correct section, we will close the issue.

### What should I do?

Depending on the reason the issue was closed, you can do the following:

- If you did not provide a link, please open a new issue with a link to a reproduction.
- If you provided a link to a private repository, please open a new issue with a link to a public repository.
- If you provided a link to a repository but not in the correct section, please open a new issue with a link to a reproduction in the correct section.

**In general, assume that we should not go through a lengthy onboarding process at your company code only to be able to verify an issue.**

### My repository is private and cannot make it public

In most cases, a private repo will not be a sufficient **minimal reproduction**, as this codebase might contain a lot of unrelated parts that would make our investigation take longer. Please do **not** make it public. Instead, create a new repository using the templates above, adding the relevant code to reproduce the issue. Common things to look out for:

- Remove any code that is not related to the issue. (pages, API routes, components, etc.)
- Remove any dependencies that are not related to the issue.
- Remove any third-party service that would require us to sign up for an account to reproduce the issue.
- Remove any environment variables that are not related to the issue.
- Remove private packages that we do not have access to.
- If the issue is not related to a monorepo specifically, try to reproduce the issue without a complex monorepo setup

### I did not open this issue, but it is relevant to me, what can I do to help?

Anyone experiencing the same issue is welcome to provide a minimal reproduction following the above steps by opening a new issue.

### I think my reproduction is good enough, why aren't you looking into it quickly?

We look into every Next.js issue and constantly monitor open issues for new comments.

However, sometimes we might miss one or two due to the popularity/high traffic of the repository. We apologize, and kindly ask you to refrain from tagging core maintainers, as that will usually not result in increased priority.

Upvoting issues to show your interest will help us prioritize and address them as quickly as possible. That said, every issue is important to us, and if an issue gets closed by accident, we encourage you to open a new one linking to the old issue and we will look into it.

- [How to create a Minimal, Complete, and Verifiable example](https://stackoverflow.com/help/mcve)

body:
I can confirm this issue on v16.2.0 (also tested v16.2.1 — same behavior).

  Environment:
  - OS: Windows 11 (MSYS)
  - Runtime: Bun 1.3.6
  - Node.js: v22.20.0
  - Next.js: 16.2.0
  - Bundler: Turbopack (default)
  - Routes: ~157

  Config (next.config.ts):
  reactCompiler: true, cacheComponents: true, viewTransition: true, authInterrupts: true, staleTimes: { dynamic:
  30, static: 180 }

  Symptoms:
  - .next/ cache grows to 9+ GB over time
  - Node.js process reaches ~15 GB heap then OOM crashes
  - GC trace shows ineffective mark-compacts near heap limit
  - Growth rate: ~650 MB/min while navigating routes

  What I tested:
  - turbopackFileSystemCacheForDev: false — disk growth stops but RAM leak persists
  - turbopackFileSystemCacheForDev: true — disk cache grows without GC
  - reactCompiler: true disabled — still leaks, .next/ reached 1.1 GB in 5 min
  - viewTransition: true disabled — still leaks
  - optimizePackageImports added — no measurable difference
  - serverExternalPackages for heavy deps — no measurable difference
  - NODE_OPTIONS='--max-old-space-size=4096' — crashes earlier, doesn't fix
  - Clearing .next/ — temporarily fixes, leak returns
  - Checked circular dependencies (madge) — none found
  - next dev --webpack — STABLE. Started at 227 MB after clean cache, reached 471 MB after 3 min heavily navigating
   ~157 routes, stayed at 227 MB after 10 min idle on a fresh start (no growth). Compare: Turbopack reached 1.1 GB
  in 2 min under the same usage and kept growing indefinitely until OOM.

  Reproduction:
  My repo is private, but I believe this issue likely reproduces on any medium-to-large App Router project (~150+
  routes) with Turbopack as the default bundler. A minimal reproduction with create-next-app + many routes could
  potentially trigger it.

  Happy to provide a Turbopack trace (NEXT_TURBOPACK_TRACING=1) if helpful.

author: pedro757

body:
Adding a concrete data point on Next.js 16.2.4 / React 19.2.5 / Turbopack, since the original report
   is on 15.3.4 and this still reproduces.

  Symptoms:
  - When .next/dev is small (just-cleaned state), the dev server idles at ~200 MB RSS, similar to what
  OP reports.
  - Once .next/dev reaches ~40 GB on disk, the dev server idles at 8 GB+ RSS — no navigation needed,
  no compilations, just sitting there.
  - From that idle baseline, route visits and HMR push it to 16 GB easily. RAM never recovers.

  So the growth pattern OP describes (each route adds RAM) compounds with a second, more severe
  effect: idle baseline scales with the persistent cache size on disk. The cache appears to be
  loaded/mapped into the Node process at startup.

  Project size for context:
  - ~54 route segments (page.tsx / layout.tsx)
  - ~419 components
  - React Compiler enabled (reactCompiler: true in next.config.ts)
  - No custom webpack config; Turbopack defaults

  Key finding — .next/dev is the smoking gun.

  After a few days of active development, du -sh .next/dev reported 36 GB, almost entirely under
  .next/dev/cache/turbopack/. The persistent dev cache grows unbounded across sessions and is never
  pruned. The on-disk size correlates directly with idle RAM, which strongly suggests Turbopack is
  mmap'ing or hot-loading the cache contents into the Node heap at startup.

  Workaround that fixed it for us:

```bash
  rm -rf .next/dev
  bun run dev   # or npm/pnpm equivalent
```

  After clearing, .next/dev rebuilds to ~1.3 GB and the dev server idles at ~2 GB RSS again. We have
  to repeat this every few days.

  Happy to share a trace / heap snapshot from a bloated state if it would help.
author: RodrigoTomeES

body:
> After a few days of active development, du -sh .next/dev reported 36 GB, almost entirely under .next/dev/cache/turbopack/. The persistent dev cache grows unbounded across sessions and is never pruned.

yes, pruning is currently not implemented. But even without that the cache should only grow if you add more stuff to your application, or access more routes. It's technically unbounded, but only at the scale you do changes in the code.

> The on-disk size correlates directly with idle RAM, which strongly suggests Turbopack is
mmap'ing or hot-loading the cache contents into the Node heap at startup.

That's unexpected. The RAM usage should be mostly unaffected by cache size. We are mmaping the cache, but that only loads the pages when access and the OS can give back pages when under memory pressure.

> Happy to share a trace / heap snapshot from a bloated state if it would help.

A trace `NEXT_TURBOPACK_TRACING=turbo-tasks` of the startup with a large cache, might indeed help here.

body:
### Solution 
Recently after shifting to Next.js 16.*, we’ve been facing a lot of issues with Turbopack.
It’s aggressively eating CPU cores, increasing RAM usage, slowing rebuilds, and making laptops overheat during development. Sometimes crashed next dev sessions also leave zombie node processes running in the background.
Because of this, our workflow became noticeably slower than before.
That’s why nextcool — a open source CLI tool focused on fixing common Next.js/Turbopack development issues automatically.
Why nextcool?

Kill zombie node / next processes
Clean .next, .turbo, .swc, cache bloat
Purge package manager caches
Rebuild projects safely
Run dev/prod server with CPU core limiting
Reduce laptop overheating during development
Diagnose RAM / CPU / Turbopack issues
How to use

Install globally:
`npm i -g nextcoolor` 
or

`bun add -g nextcool`
Then go to your Next.js project and run:
`nextcool`

In NPM : https://www.npmjs.com/package/nextcool

body:
Adding a data point — **high CPU at true idle** (not just during compilation), on Apple Silicon.

### Environment
- Next.js **16.2.7** (Turbopack, default)
- macOS arm64, **M-series** Mac
- Package manager: **bun** (`next dev`), deps installed via **pnpm**
- App Router

### Symptom
The `next-server` dev worker holds **~230–245% CPU sustained while completely idle** — no in-flight requests, no source file changes, and nothing being written to `.next/`. RAM sits around **3–4 GB** (oscillates with GC, not a monotonic leak). The server still responds to requests instantly, so it isn't hung — a background loop just keeps ~2.3 cores busy with no apparent work.

### `sample` profile (2s, idle)
Main thread is stuck in a microtask flood driven by a native threadsafe function:

```
node::SpinEventLoopInternal
  v8impl::ThreadSafeFunction::AsyncCb
    node::InternalCallbackScope::Close
      v8::internal::MicrotaskQueue::PerformCheckpoint / RunMicrotasks
        node::RegisterDestroyHook
        v8::internal::Runtime_JSWeakRefAddToKeptObjects / Heap::KeepDuringJob
```

Deepest self-time frames are inside `next-swc.darwin-arm64.node`. Live threads include **`notify-rs fsevents loop`** and ~11 `tokio-runtime-worker` threads — i.e. the Turbopack/Rust file watcher appears to be firing continuously even though nothing in the project is changing.

### Things ruled out
- **Not** workspace-root misdetection (#92978 / #94432): project has its own `pnpm-workspace.yaml` and there is no stray lockfile in any parent directory.
- **Not** app file churn: `find -newermt '-10 seconds'` over the project is empty across repeated snapshots.
- **Not** initial compilation: CPU stays pegged 4+ minutes after start with zero requests.

### Workaround from #93896 did **not** help here
Adding the suggested flags had no effect on idle CPU in this case (still ~240%):
```js
experimental: {
  webpackMemoryOptimizations: true,
  preloadEntriesOnStart: false,
}
```

So at least on this setup the idle CPU is independent of the preload/memory flags and looks tied to the native fs-watcher loop.

body:
I'm the author of #94915 (auto-closed as `invalid link` because my app repo is private). Posting my data points here since this umbrella issue matches what I'm seeing.

**Environment**
- openSUSE Tumbleweed, 32 GB RAM
- Node 24.5.0, Bun 1.3.14
- `next@16.2.9`, `react@19.2.7`, App Router
- Bun workspace monorepo (`workspaces: ["packages/*"]`, internal `@sdk` package)
- `next-intl`, ~63 route segments, ~496 `.ts`/`.tsx` files
- No stray parent lockfiles (#92978 ruled out on my machine)

**Severe case (16.2.6, stale `.next/dev/cache/turbopack` ~6.5 GB / 6149 files, ~35 min session)**
- `next-server` RSS: **~16 GB**
- Idle growth: **+250 MB / 10 s** (no requests, no file changes)
- Idle CPU: **~310%**
- System swap fully utilized; collateral Cursor SIGKILL + `core.node` coredumps

**16.2.9 + fresh `.next/dev` (same heavy client route, 5× GET, then 90 s idle)**

| Config | Idle baseline (60 s) | Post-compile RSS | +90 s idle CPU |
|--------|---------------------|------------------|----------------|
| Defaults | 434 MB / 6% | 2012 MB | **17.5%** |
| `turbopackServerFastRefresh: false` | 432 MB / 5% | 1828 MB | **25.5%** |
| Both `turbopackServerFastRefresh: false` + `turbopackFileSystemCacheForDev: false` | 419 MB / 3.7% | 1758 MB | **17.6%** (no `cache/turbopack` dir; `.next/dev` = 74 MB) |

**What I learned**
- Upgrading 16.2.6 → 16.2.9 did not fix the underlying behavior
- `turbopackFileSystemCacheForDev: false` stops disk cache bloat but **not** idle CPU
- `turbopackServerFastRefresh: false` did not help me (unlike @tanc in #91396)
- Persistent **~17–25% idle CPU** after compile suggests the FS watcher / cache invalidation loop (#94735) more than server HMR alone

**Current workaround:** both experimental flags above + periodic `rm -rf .next/dev`. Considering `--webpack` for daily dev.

Happy to capture `NEXT_TURBOPACK_TRACING=turbo-tasks` on a bloated `.next/dev` if that would help (@sokra's ask earlier in this thread).

Numbers are from one machine / one session — a concrete data point, not a benchmark.

### Environment
- Next.js **16.2.6** (Turbopack, default)
- React 19.2.4, App Router
- macOS **darwin 25.5.0**, Apple Silicon, 15 logical cores
- Multi-package monorepo with several `package-lock.json` files

### Symptom
`next-server` sits at **~700–770% CPU while completely idle** — no in-flight requests, no file edits, no log output, browser tab closed. It still serves requests instantly, so it isn't hung; a background loop just keeps ~7 cores busy.

```
$ ps -Ao pid,%cpu,command -r | grep next-server
66026 718.5 next-server (v16.2.6)
```

### `sample <pid> 2` (idle)
Hot path is the Rust file watcher + an fstat storm:

```
1106 Thread_..: notify-rs fsevents loop
  ! 65 FSEventsClientProcessMessageCallback (in FSEvents)
  !   65 FSEventsD2F_server (in FSEvents)
... thousands of fstat (in libsystem_kernel.dylib)
```

### Controlled A/B (same app, same machine, idle CPU ~5s after one `GET /`)

| Scenario | Idle CPU |
|---|---|
| `next dev` (Turbopack, default) | **~750%** |
| Turbopack + `SIGSTOP` on all sibling file-writers (a concurrent Vite dev + esbuild) | ~750% (no change) |
| Turbopack + `turbopack.root` pinned to the app dir | ~750% (no change) |
| `next dev --webpack` | **~0.0–0.3%** |

### Takeaways
- **Not external file churn** — pausing other processes writing into the monorepo changed nothing.
- **Not the inferred monorepo root alone** — pinning `turbopack.root` is good hygiene (and helps the memory-pressure case in #94432) but did **not** fix idle CPU here.
- **Not app code / SCSS** — the identical app on webpack idles at ~0%.
- The only variable that fixes it is the **bundler**: the Turbopack dev watcher (`notify-rs`/FSEvents) is the culprit, consistent with the feedback-loop theory in #94915 / #94735.

### Workaround
Defaulting dev to webpack until this is fixed upstream:

```json
{ "scripts": { "dev": "next dev --webpack", "dev:turbo": "next dev" } }
```

Happy to run `NEXT_TURBOPACK_TRACING=1` and attach a trace if that would help narrow it down.

author: gaearon

body:
Ran into this on Next 16.2.7 (Pages Router, M-series Mac) and traced the mechanism (same symptom as the now-locked #93896): `next-server` was pinned at 600–780% CPU while completely idle (no requests, no file changes, 10+ minutes). `experimental.turbopackFileSystemCacheForDev` defaults to true in 16.x, and our persistent cache at `.next/dev/cache/turbopack` had grown to **7.7 GB (~2,000 files) over ~3 weeks** of normal dev use. A native `sample` of the process showed tokio-runtime-workers busy-spinning and heavy napi threadsafe-function traffic, with the cache directory being rewritten continuously at idle.

Deleting `.next` fully resolved it: fresh boot burst ~250% for a few seconds, then flat 0.0% at idle, returning to 0.0% after page compiles. Setting `experimental.turbopackFileSystemCacheForDev: false` prevents recurrence. FWIW the commonly-suggested `preloadEntriesOnStart: false` workaround is a no-op in dev — in 16.2.7 it's only read when `!options.dev`.

So this looks like unbounded persistent-cache growth plus a compaction/persistence loop that never converges once the DB is large.

body:
Hey @roguesherlock. I think it is a bit unrelated question, maybe for discussion rather than issue. 

But there is a great writeup in [request memoization](https://nextjs.org/docs/app/guides/caching#request-memoization) section of the guide. It says it memoize request per rendering pass. 

Just to make it easier for you - it de-duplicates function calls that happen almost at the same time. This allows you to not worry too much about calling the same function/request across different components (and pages). 

The guide literally says: "Memoization only applies to the React Component tree" and "It doesn't apply to fetch requests in Route Handlers as they are not a part of the React component tree."

For you second question - that's more react question. For sure not relevant here. Try to read on this topic in React blogs or docs and then I recommend trying it yourself to see.

body:
Having similar issues with "auth protected" pages.

When navigating to /protected while not authenticated relevant middleware will redirect you to the home page. However, if you then try to login and then navigate to /protected, you will be met with the same redirect to the home page (completely skipping past the middleware). 

This behavior only happens in production and is not solved gracefully with any cache clearing methods:

- `router.refresh()` / `router.prefetch(route)` **WILL** work but you to arbitrarily wait for them to complete (not promises)
- `revalidatePath(route)` will **NOT** work
- Cache busting headers will **NOT** prevent the redirect from being cached
- Alternative redirect status codes will **NOT** prevent the redirect from being cached

Ideally, Next.js would avoid caching route redirects that have specific no-cache headers and we'd have a way to know exactly when the client has cleared the routing cache instead of having to arbitrarily set a delay after calling relevant methods.

btw. this works as a workaround:

```ts
after(async () => await run())
```

So maybe always use `after()` instead of `waitUntil()`?
author: rechenberger

body:
Hi, thanks for the report.

`waitUntil` is a Vercel primitive. To achieve the `waitUntil` behavior in Next.js, you should use `after`, which takes care of some necessary additional plumbing and tracking on the server (for example, it'd tell the framework that it's ok to use `revalidatePath` in the `after` context). Vercel [documentation](https://vercel.com/docs/functions/functions-api-reference/vercel-functions-package#usage-with-next.js) mentions that you should use `after` with Next.js but I will see about getting this documentation updated to more explicitly indicate that it's not just a recommendation, but a requirement.

author: sunpietro

body:
> I believe that's the nature of server actions. You can't abort them.

Why we need an abort method for server actions

When uploading documents, there may be situations where I want to cancel an ongoing request—for example, if I decide to change the upload flow or the selected documents midway. Since server actions typically use POST requests and are executed sequentially, there’s currently no way to interrupt or cancel them once initiated.

As a result, even if I no longer want those documents to be uploaded, the server continues processing the request, causing unnecessary load and delays. Worse, any new request I make remains in a pending state until the previous uploads are completed. This leads to a poor user experience and can cause unexpected behavior in the application. An abort method would help solve this by allowing us to cancel server actions when needed.

body:
Want to add one more use case: as Next.js does not provide WebSocket integration, pretty often Server Actions are used as a "subscribe socket" when the long polling HTTP request produces periodical events in the output.

In such cases, when the client disconnects (or the internet connection is broken on the client side), there is no way to stop this server action and free up the resources for now.

So, hope that the AbortController will allow us to fix this issue too!

```ts
  /**
   * Run the Webpack build in a separate process to optimize memory usage during build.
   * Valid values are:
   * - `false`: Disable the Webpack build worker
   * - `true`: Enable the Webpack build worker
   * - `undefined`: Enable the Webpack build worker only if the webpack config is not customized
   */
  webpackBuildWorker?: boolean

  /**
   * Enables optimizations to reduce memory usage in Webpack. This reduces the max size of the heap
   * but may increase compile times slightly.
   * Valid values are:
   * - `false`: Disable Webpack memory optimizations (default).
   * - `true`: Enables Webpack memory optimizations.
   */
  webpackMemoryOptimizations?: boolean

   /**
   * The amount of pages to export per worker during static generation.
   */
  staticGenerationMaxConcurrency?: number

  /**
   * The minimum number of pages to be chunked into each export worker.
   */
  staticGenerationMinPagesPerWorker?: number
```

By default these are set to:

```ts
    webpackBuildWorker: undefined,
    webpackMemoryOptimizations: false,
    staticGenerationMaxConcurrency: 8,
    staticGenerationMinPagesPerWorker: 25,
```

I guess, maybe activate the first two and see if that helps out.
