Hi @agurtovoy! 
I looked into this and confirmed the issue: when generateStaticParams() produces a path that matches an existing static route, the static route is silently overridden in production builds.
According to the [App Router documentation](https://nextjs.org/docs/app/building-your-application/routing#static-and-dynamic-routes) and [generateStaticParams reference](https://nextjs.org/docs/app/api-reference/functions/generate-static-params), static routes should take priority over dynamic ones with overlapping paths.
I’m setting up a minimal reproduction and can propose a fix to ensure the build either respects static route priority or throws a clear warning for conflicting paths.
Let me know if anyone is already working on this — otherwise I’ll share the repro soon!
Thanks!

body:
Hi this is expected behavior. Please refer to the the the documentation of [understanding cookie's behavior](https://nextjs.org/docs/app/api-reference/functions/cookies#understanding-cookie-behavior-in-server-components)

> - Reading cookies works in Server Components because you're accessing the cookie data that the client's browser sends to the server in the HTTP request headers.
> - Setting cookies cannot be done directly in a Server Component, even when using a Route Handler or Server Action. This is because cookies are actually stored by the browser, not the server.
>
> The server can only send instructions (via Set-Cookie headers) to tell the browser to store cookies - the actual storage happens on the client side. This is why cookie operations that modify state (.set, .delete, .clear) must be performed in a Route Handler or Server Action where the response headers can be properly set.

body:
Please see the documentation on setting a Turbopack root directory: https://nextjs.org/docs/app/api-reference/config/next-config-js/turbopack#root-directory

You should configure the root to match the root of your repository.

All referenced files must live under the configured root, including symlinks. We do this because we want to make the Turbopack cache portable across machines in the future, and that won't work if you have files that reference absolute paths or paths outside of your repository.

We may allow other ways to loosen these constraints further in the future (e.g. by allowing multiple roots), but that's a well-known feature request.

<summary>
Here's my patch for next@14.2.5
</summary>

```diff
diff --git a/dist/build/swc/options.js b/dist/build/swc/options.js
index 59ec8f63b70e69b196d731d5e9253dcb1e358437..70368be4ed16425a4b69ec2e78be9ec47863ce6d 100644
--- a/dist/build/swc/options.js
+++ b/dist/build/swc/options.js
@@ -48,7 +48,7 @@ function getParserOptions({ filename, jsConfig, ...rest }) {
         ...rest,
         syntax: hasTsSyntax ? "typescript" : "ecmascript",

-        decorators: enableDecorators,
+        decorators: true,
         // Exclude regular TypeScript files from React transformation to prevent e.g. generic parameters and angle-bracket type assertion from being interpreted as JSX tags.
         [hasTsSyntax ? "tsx" : "jsx"]: !isTSFile,
         importAssertions: true
@@ -92,6 +92,7 @@ function getBaseSWCOptions({ filename, jest, development, hasReactRefresh, globa
                 } : {},
                 legacyDecorator: enableDecorators,
                 decoratorMetadata: emitDecoratorMetadata,
+                decoratorVersion: "2022-03",
                 useDefineForClassFields: useDefineForClassFields,
                 react: {
                     importSource: (jsConfig == null ? void 0 : (_jsConfig_compilerOptions4 = jsConfig.compilerOptions) == null ? void 0 : _jsConfig_compilerOptions4.jsxImportSource) ?? ((compilerOptions == null ? void 0 : compilerOptions.emotion) && !isReactServerLayer ? "@emotion/react" : "react"),
diff --git a/dist/esm/build/swc/options.js b/dist/esm/build/swc/options.js
index 77981a6143c87c7e4492aa71320cf9dc9dadc6f0..90f088a70a972babfaa9c2f1d7f3e5c2f6c19154 100644
--- a/dist/esm/build/swc/options.js
+++ b/dist/esm/build/swc/options.js
@@ -22,7 +22,7 @@ export function getParserOptions({ filename, jsConfig, ...rest }) {
         ...rest,
         syntax: hasTsSyntax ? "typescript" : "ecmascript",
         dynamicImport: true,
-        decorators: enableDecorators,
+        decorators: true,
         // Exclude regular TypeScript files from React transformation to prevent e.g. generic parameters and angle-bracket type assertion from being interpreted as JSX tags.
         [hasTsSyntax ? "tsx" : "jsx"]: !isTSFile,
         importAssertions: true
@@ -66,6 +66,7 @@ function getBaseSWCOptions({ filename, jest, development, hasReactRefresh, globa
                 } : {},
                 legacyDecorator: enableDecorators,
                 decoratorMetadata: emitDecoratorMetadata,
+                decoratorVersion: "2022-03",
                 useDefineForClassFields: useDefineForClassFields,
                 react: {
                     importSource: (jsConfig == null ? void 0 : (_jsConfig_compilerOptions4 = jsConfig.compilerOptions) == null ? void 0 : _jsConfig_compilerOptions4.jsxImportSource) ?? ((compilerOptions == null ? void 0 : compilerOptions.emotion) && !isReactServerLayer ? "@emotion/react" : "react"),
```
</details>

so you need to start a patch session thing then go to
`dist/build/swc/options.js`
and 
`dist/esm/build/swc/options.js`

and set `decorators: enableDecorators`
and `decoratorVersion: "2022-03"`
in both

body:
👀 You may well be correct, using `flatConfig` instead of `configs` resolves the type errors, though running ESLint does still fail due to the module being CJS, not ESM. You can't even work around this by doing `nextPlugin.flatConfig` though as `flatConfig` is not part of the default `plugin` export.

The documentation, unfortunately, does not clarify either way what is intended; they still recommend using the compact support 🙃 https://nextjs.org/docs/app/api-reference/config/eslint

body:
Thank you for your reply!

I tried installing @vercel/fonts using:

`npm install @vercel/fonts`

But I got the following error:

```
npm error code E404
npm error 404 Not Found - GET https://registry.npmjs.org/@vercel%2ffonts - Not found
npm error 404
npm error 404  '@vercel/fonts@*' is not in this registry.
npm error 404
npm error 404 Note that you can also install from a
npm error 404 tarball, folder, http url, or git url.

Instead, I installed geist with:

`npm install geist`

and imported it like this:

`import { GeistSans } from "geist/font/sans";`

body:
That’s precisely the reason why the documentation is actually pretty explicit that it is absolutely necessary to always check as close as possible to your data source whether the user is still authenticated and authorized, such as before executing the actual logic in a server action or function.

From: [https://nextjs.org/docs/app/guides/authentication#optimistic-checks-with-middleware-optional](https://nextjs.org/docs/app/guides/authentication#optimistic-checks-with-middleware-optional)
> While Middleware can be helpful for initial checks, it shouldn’t be your sole defense against data protection. Most security checks should be performed as close to your data source as possible. For more information, refer to [Data Access Layer](https://nextjs.org/docs/app/guides/authentication#creating-a-data-access-layer-dal).

From: [https://nextjs.org/docs/app/guides/authentication#server-actions](https://nextjs.org/docs/app/guides/authentication#server-actions)
> Treat [Server Actions](https://nextjs.org/docs/app/getting-started/updating-data) with the same security considerations as public-facing API endpoints and verify if the user is authorized to perform a mutation.

It seems quite clear to me. I’m not even sure how this could be interpreted differently. Middleware should never be used for actually securing routes with session management.

body:
I went thru the docs and understood what they are trying to say and taking your issue into consideration, this is all what I have to say (I am not a geek) about it:

1. Regarding "Did this not apply to the examples before it?". It does apply to the above 3 bullet points as well. 

- The first bullet said the following - 

> revalidatePath only invalidates the cache when the included path is next visited. This means calling revalidatePath with a dynamic route segment will not immediately trigger many revalidations at once. The invalidation only happens when the path is next visited.

What this generally means is that when you use the `revalidatePath` the cached data that existed all this time will be considered as "stale" and if anyone (u or me) visits the route that is set to be revalidated (ex: `revalidatePath('/dashboard/products');` ) instead of serving the stale data, it will refetch the data from the DB or wherever it resides and revalidate the cache with fresh data. If the data for example in '/dashboard/products' was 2 products and you could setup a logic in the frontend on how adding a product successfully will trigger `revalidatePath('/dashboard/products)` which results in fetching fresh data when someone visits the url 'dashboard/products' next time only and not immediately like you would find in SSR. revalidatePath is more of ISR oriented since it provides stale data (cached data) initially and then upon trigger of revalidatePath we get fresh data replacing the old cache with new cache.

2. Regarding "In the above three bullets it seems first and last one refer to server side cache (namely full route cache?), in that case, they can be grouped together for more clarity." Yes, you are right. The docs for this part can confuse a lot.

3. Reading the previous issue I am not fully understanding what's going when `deleteItem` is called but to my knowledge with AI assistance I found out that, when you trigger a server action inside the `startTransistion` block, Next Js will automatically refetch the current route's data if it was invalidated by something like `revalidatePath()`. 

_What AI has to say:_

> 1. The server-side cache for the current path (e.g., /search?q=...) is invalidated via revalidatePath().
> 2. Since you're using startTransition() on the client:
>     The router automatically re-fetches the current route’s data without a full page reload.
>     This causes Next.js to re-render the current page with fresh data, even though the user hasn’t navigated.

Do know that using `revalidatePath` in the client side causes all of the routes to revalidate it's data _for now_ and will be solved in the future with updates hopefully.
Using `revalidatePath` in the server side causes only the specific route to be revalidated.

I think you misunderstood. Nextjs has different caching [mechanisms](https://nextjs.org/docs/app/guides/caching#overview). In my first recommendation, I meant the cited three bullets from the docs say nothing about [data cache](https://nextjs.org/docs/app/guides/caching#data-cache). When they say things like "path is next visited" this _suggests (to me at least) they might be not talking about data cache_, because _visiting_ is more associated to a page visit to me and data cache is about results of data fetches. That's why I think in the first and third bullets they mean [full route cache](https://nextjs.org/docs/app/guides/caching#full-route-cache).
Also in that same bullet they say "calling revalidatePath with a dynamic route segment " and dynamic route segments are about pages afaik, so no data cache there. So for better clarity it would be better if they mention which caches they refer to in each bullet.

In my third recommendation I was suggesting they add word _immediately_ to their second bullet - to prevent confusions as in the gh discussion linked in that same recommendation.

I think if you re-read my recommendations with this new info in mind it should be clearer.

body:
I believe the answer to your concerns lies in [this section](https://nextjs.org/docs/app/guides/caching#cache-interactions). In essence, revalidatePath is used to revalidate the Data Cache for a specific path. All other ‘Good to know’s’ essentially convey that the function strictly does not _strictu sensu_ “revalidate” the data but rather clears the data cache, so it gets revalidated on the next request for that data on that route. If no data is ever cached in a route, this route will also not be cached in the Full Route Cache.

In my opinion, it is beneficial to read and comprehend the [general documentation on all caching](https://nextjs.org/docs/app/guides/caching) thoroughly before delving into the documentation pages for specific functions.

body:
Hi,

Thanks for the issue and PR.

I am not sure I fully agree here though. At least not with some claims in this issue, and not with the current PR implementation. That doesn't mean we can't try to make some improvements though.

Your PR does have some weird changes, what's up with that?

When you say:

> request memoization native to React

I have to answer with https://github.com/vercel/next.js/blob/6b35981a80959db80e89a5dff27535c4094e3828/packages/next/src/server/lib/dedupe-fetch.ts#L35 which the fetch dedupe, that memoizes requests. 

Initially yes, React had this, https://github.com/facebook/react/blob/d4e78c42a94be027b4dc7ed2659a5fddfbf9bd4e/packages/react/src/ReactFetch.js but this got dropped, and Next.js implemented its own. 

We should remove this good to know:

```
Request memoization is a React feature, not a Next.js feature. It's included here to show how it interacts with the other caching mechanisms.
```

Yes, request memoization uses React.cache, but in a whole different manner than the section we are joining into the memoization section.

The section you are moving up, used to be the purposed to reflect `memoization/caching` without fetch, for those who use other types of data access, such as ORMs, but would still have liked some kind of memoization/deduplication. 

We have a section that explains this here: https://nextjs.org/docs/app/getting-started/fetching-data#deduplicate-requests-and-cache-data

I don't want to make this caching section all that much more complex though. This caching guide was mostly made to help with confusion around fetch behavior in the server, and what others things Next.js does cache. Let's think a bit more about this.

body:
It's a complex feature with some edge cases not fully ironed out yet. I'll try to convey useful information though.

Today when you don't specify any params for `generateStaticParams` Next.js interprets this as a high cardinality param and produces a fallback shell that is suitable to show users for any param value. In this case the fallback shell says "loading posts..." and if you hit refresh in the browser you would consistently see this.

But the prefetch to the page is producing an ahead of time prefetched response which fills the param values in because of a quirk of PPR that we will be changing soon that makes it so client navigations to dynamic param routes can't use fallback RSC data. This means that the prefetched links end up getting statically prerendered and then the navigation is instant. We will be changing this so it uses the fallback RSC data which will need to "resume" the dynamic portion on navigation.

For a blog this isn't really appropriate, you want to statically prerender the blog content. So you should provide at least one id in `generateStaticParams` that Next.js can use to validate the static shell will have some content in it.

Now for why the "use cache" doesn't make the dynamic renders fast. "use cache" needs an implementation. Right now when you self host it will use a memory cache for dynamic caching. But on vercel there is no memory cache in the serverless function runtime yet so it is effectively a noop cache there. This is probably going to change but you can also use more specific cache implementations such as `"use cache: remote"` which will plug into Vercel's runtime cache when used there. (`"use cache: remote"` is also a memory cache when self hosted). You can also provide your own cache implementation for the default cache handler or create your own named handlers and customize how caching is done in your project.

For a blog the main goal is to use "use cache" to get more stuff into the static prerender. If you have a very static site you might have no dynamic content at all. In these cases you don't really need an additional memory cache because the entire thing is just cached as part of the static HTMl and RSC data.

So basically this is working as expected but with planned changes in the future

body:
Hi folks -

This error message was a bit confusing, so we adjusted it in #82052 to explain how you can silence it. To avoid getting this warning, you'd need to either ensure your application only has 1 lockfile, or alternatively explicitly specify the root of your application in `nextConfig.turbopack.root` ([docs](https://nextjs.org/docs/app/api-reference/config/next-config-js/turbopack#root-directory)). 

As for the implementation details, Turbopack is attempting to locate the root dir of your project and is using lockfiles to do so.  The algorithm recursively looks upward through the filesystem and may catch stray lockfiles in parent directories that don't actually correspond with your application. When you see this warning message, it means that Turbopack inferred the root is the directory of the selected lockfile but we aren't 100% confident that it's the correct root.

We could not detect a valid reproduction link. **Make sure to follow the bug report template carefully.**

### Why was this issue closed?

To be able to investigate, we need access to a reproduction to identify what triggered the issue. We need a link to a **public** GitHub repository ([template for App Router](https://github.com/vercel/next.js/tree/canary/examples/reproduction-template), [template for Pages Router](https://github.com/vercel/next.js/tree/canary/examples/reproduction-template-pages)), but you can also use these templates: [CodeSandbox: App Router](https://codesandbox.io/s/github/vercel/next.js/tree/canary/examples/reproduction-template) or [CodeSandbox: Pages Router](https://codesandbox.io/s/github/vercel/next.js/tree/canary/examples/reproduction-template-pages).

The bug template that you filled out has a section called "Link to the code that reproduces this issue", which is where you should provide the link to the reproduction.

- If you did not provide a link or the link you provided is not valid, we will close the issue.
- If you provide a link to a private repository, we will close the issue.
- If you provide a link to a repository but not in the correct section, we will close the issue.

### What should I do?

Depending on the reason the issue was closed, you can do the following:

- If you did not provide a link, please open a new issue with a link to a reproduction.
- If you provided a link to a private repository, please open a new issue with a link to a public repository.
- If you provided a link to a repository but not in the correct section, please open a new issue with a link to a reproduction in the correct section.

**In general, assume that we should not go through a lengthy onboarding process at your company code only to be able to verify an issue.**

### My repository is private and cannot make it public

In most cases, a private repo will not be a sufficient **minimal reproduction**, as this codebase might contain a lot of unrelated parts that would make our investigation take longer. Please do **not** make it public. Instead, create a new repository using the templates above, adding the relevant code to reproduce the issue. Common things to look out for:

- Remove any code that is not related to the issue. (pages, API routes, components, etc.)
- Remove any dependencies that are not related to the issue.
- Remove any third-party service that would require us to sign up for an account to reproduce the issue.
- Remove any environment variables that are not related to the issue.
- Remove private packages that we do not have access to.
- If the issue is not related to a monorepo specifically, try to reproduce the issue without a complex monorepo setup

### I did not open this issue, but it is relevant to me, what can I do to help?

Anyone experiencing the same issue is welcome to provide a minimal reproduction following the above steps by opening a new issue.

### I think my reproduction is good enough, why aren't you looking into it quickly?

We look into every Next.js issue and constantly monitor open issues for new comments.

However, sometimes we might miss one or two due to the popularity/high traffic of the repository. We apologize, and kindly ask you to refrain from tagging core maintainers, as that will usually not result in increased priority.

Upvoting issues to show your interest will help us prioritize and address them as quickly as possible. That said, every issue is important to us, and if an issue gets closed by accident, we encourage you to open a new one linking to the old issue and we will look into it.

### Useful Resources

- [How to Contribute to Open Source (Next.js)](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=cuoNzXFLitc)
- [How to create a Minimal, Complete, and Verifiable example](https://stackoverflow.com/help/mcve)

body:
I found a workaround for this issue.

Instead of directly re-exporting the type like this:

```ts
export { type FooType } from "./foo.type";
```
You can avoid the error by importing and re-exporting the type like this:
```ts
import type { FooType as _FooType } from "./foo.type";
export type FooType = _FooType;
```
With this approach, the error no longer occurs, even when using Turbopack.

Still hitting this on **Next.js 16.2.3 + Turbopack**.

Our `'use server'` barrel files export server actions and need to also re-export types and non-function values (Zod schemas, constants) from sibling model files:

```ts
'use server';

// server actions — these work fine
export const { createUser, deleteUser } = withContext(userService);

// re-exports from model files — these fail
export { type UserId, type User } from './model';                    // type-only
export { type ApiKey, apiKeyNameSchema } from './api-keys/model';    // types + Zod schema
```

```
Only async functions are allowed to be exported in a "use server" file.
```

This forces us to maintain a separate barrel file that manually re-exports every type and value from every model file, duplicating the list anytime a type is added. Would be great if `'use server'` could allow re-exports of non-function values (or at minimum type-only re-exports), since they don't participate in the server action protocol.

body:
My presumption says the fundamental issue isnt that serve component are over riding the client components, rather how NEXT handle hydration & metadata application order, or you can say a race condition in this case.
SSR flow in somewhat like this: nextjs collects all the meta data from layout page and before any client side code is injected, nextjs injects a <title> tag in the initial HTML response.
And since layout components hydrate first other page components hydrate afterward  and typically there's no coordination between layout/page title updates.

Also if we go by this case then : 
With 50ms timeout: Page's title update happens AFTER layout's hydration
With 1ms timeout: Page's title update happens BEFORE layout's hydration completes.

Maybe a Context function could resolve this.

### Why was this issue closed?

To be able to investigate, we need access to a reproduction to identify what triggered the issue. We need a link to a **public** GitHub repository ([template for App Router](https://github.com/vercel/next.js/tree/canary/examples/reproduction-template), [template for Pages Router](https://github.com/vercel/next.js/tree/canary/examples/reproduction-template-pages)), but you can also use these templates: [CodeSandbox: App Router](https://codesandbox.io/s/github/vercel/next.js/tree/canary/examples/reproduction-template) or [CodeSandbox: Pages Router](https://codesandbox.io/s/github/vercel/next.js/tree/canary/examples/reproduction-template-pages).

The bug template that you filled out has a section called "Link to the code that reproduces this issue", which is where you should provide the link to the reproduction.

- If you did not provide a link or the link you provided is not valid, we will close the issue.
- If you provide a link to a private repository, we will close the issue.
- If you provide a link to a repository but not in the correct section, we will close the issue.

### What should I do?

Depending on the reason the issue was closed, you can do the following:

- If you did not provide a link, please open a new issue with a link to a reproduction.
- If you provided a link to a private repository, please open a new issue with a link to a public repository.
- If you provided a link to a repository but not in the correct section, please open a new issue with a link to a reproduction in the correct section.

**In general, assume that we should not go through a lengthy onboarding process at your company code only to be able to verify an issue.**

### My repository is private and cannot make it public

In most cases, a private repo will not be a sufficient **minimal reproduction**, as this codebase might contain a lot of unrelated parts that would make our investigation take longer. Please do **not** make it public. Instead, create a new repository using the templates above, adding the relevant code to reproduce the issue. Common things to look out for:

- Remove any dependencies that are not related to the issue.

We've documented this as a known unplanned feature [here](https://nextjs.org/docs/app/api-reference/turbopack#unsupported-and-unplanned-features):

> Standalone :local and :global pseudo-classes (only the function variant :global(...) is supported).

Unfortunately to opt-into using Turbopack, you'd have to adjust to use the function variant of global.

author: bgw

body:
Hi @bablukup and @bgw,

Thanks so much for jumping on this issue so quickly and for your clear feedback.

I've looked into `@capsizecss/metrics` as you suggested and confirmed that Cascadia Mono isn't listed there. While we could wait for `@capsizecss/metrics` to add support, having a non-functional component in Next.js isn't ideal for now.

I'd like to propose an alternative solution. It looks like `@capsizecss/unpack` offers a `fromUrl` function, which allows us to extract font metrics directly from a URL. You can find more details about it here: https://github.com/seek-oss/capsize/blob/%40capsizecss/metrics%403.5.0/packages/unpack/README.md#font-metrics.

My idea is to use this `fromUrl` function to fetch the font metrics directly from a URL (e.g., from the official Cascadia Mono font files) and then integrate these metrics into `capsize-font-metrics.json`. This would give us a way to temporarily use Cascadia Mono in our Next.js project until it's officially supported upstream.

What do you both think of this approach?
author: dorapon48

body:
If you need to use `Cascadia Mono` today, you should use it as a local font: https://nextjs.org/docs/pages/getting-started/fonts#local-fonts

I appreciate that you want to help, but we're not going to add a one-off hack to our build scripts for `Cascadia Mono`, and we're certainly not going to fetch and measure every Google Font file during our build process -- that would be very slow. The pre-bundled dependencies need to reproducable, so fetching from a URL would violate that (Google Fonts does ship minor changes without changing the Font name).

If you want this fixed in Next.js:
- Submit a PR to `@capsizecss/metrics`, and work with upstream to update their database.
- Submit a PR to Next.js bumping the dependency and rebuilding the prebundled version.

body:
Thanks a lot @d-mon-  for your investigation!
We were trying to debug this problem until we stumbled upon your issue. The solution for us was to revert to 15.4.0 — even in 16.0.0-beta, the problem is still reproducible.

This issue becomes even worse when a Next.js app is served behind a Cloudflare proxy, since Cloudflare tries to normalize duplicated headers:
```
Location: /redirect
Location: /redirect
```
becomes
```
Location: /redirect, /redirect
```
The resulting redirect in the browser is interpreted as
`https://domain/redirect,%20/redirect`, leading to a 404.

This is a major problem, as it effectively blocks Next.js users from upgrading when they are deploying behind Cloudflare or other proxies that merge duplicate headers.

body:
Hi,

The App Router in Next.js bundles a specific version of React to ensure full support for React Server Components (RSC) and other advanced features. These capabilities often require tight coordination with React internals, so we need to stay in lockstep with React changes to ensure stability and correctness. This behavior has been in place since the App Router was stabilized.

In contrast, the Pages Router continues to rely on the version of React installed in your project’s package.json, since it does not have the same rendering constraints.

We agree this is an important detail to clarify, and I’ve surfaced this internally with our documentation team to improve visibility. Thanks for raising it!

author: kcoulsy

body:
This happens when App Router and Pages Router 404s are mixed (and/or route re‑exports/edge runtime), which can break the clientReferenceManifest in 15.4.x.
Fix:
  - Use a single 404: either app/not-found.tsx (App Router) or pages/404.tsx (Pages Router), not both.
  - Only the root layout should contain ```<html>/<body>;``` nested layouts must not.
  - Avoid re‑exports for routes; return the component directly.
  - Put client‑only UI in client components (no ssr:false inside server components).
  - Use Node 18/20 LTS (avoid 22), clear .next, restart.
  - Upgrade to the latest 15.4.x or canary where manifest handling is more stable.

After these changes, 404 behavior is consistent and the manifest error disappears in dev and prod.

body:
Hi everyone,
﻿
### Root Cause Confirmation
I've identified the core issue lies in React Refresh's component detection logic. The problematic line is in [react-refresh-runtime.development.js](https://github.com/facebook/react/blob/3958d5d84b3d3e6ae5c1caef9c8cf0dc58e862e6/packages/react-refresh/src/ReactFreshRuntime.js#L684):
﻿
```javascript
return typeof name === 'string' && /^[A-Z]/.test(name);
```

(This matches uppercase-starting string)
﻿
### What's happening
This heuristic assumes **any uppercase-starting function is a React component**. While this convention holds for components, it incorrectly classifies utility functions like `FunctionTest()` as components. This causes:
﻿
1. **Incorrect HMR handling**: Utility changes trigger component-level refresh instead of module-level invalidation
2. **Update propagation failure**: Client components depending on these utilities don't re-render
3. **Server/client mismatch**: Server components refresh while client components appear "stale"
﻿
### Quick Validation
To confirm this is the culprit:
1. In repo [client-component-hmr-no-re-render](https://github.com/tmota900/client-component-hmr-no-re-render)
2. Open `node_modules\next\dist\compiled\react-refresh\cjs\react-refresh-runtime.development.js` (or a similar directory)
3. Find `isLikelyComponentType()` (line 621 (approx))
4. **Temporarily add** these 2 lines:
```diff
           var name = type.name || type.displayName;
+
+          if (name === 'FunctionTest')
+            return false // Selectively ignore `FunctionTest`
+
           return typeof name === 'string' && /^[A-Z]/.test(name);
```
5. Restart dev server and verify if client components now update correctly when utility functions change

Notes:
- This is a **diagnostic change only** - not a permanent solution
﻿
### Solution Pathways
I'm still seeking a solution, and currently exploring the following directions:
﻿
1. next.js Handling
  Special handling for `/^[A-Z]/` in Next.js
﻿
2. react-refresh Enhancement
  Heuristic improvements in react-refresh


﻿
Will open a PR once I have a concrete, tested proposal.
﻿

body:
Hi! I looked into your project and found the issue.

The error happens because Next.js expects the root layout (the one with <html> and <body>) to be placed directly at src/app/layout.tsx. In your case, it's inside src/app/(others)/layout.tsx, which is treated as a nested layout, not the root.

Solution:
Move the layout file that contains <html> and <body> to src/app/layout.tsx. Then, remove the <html> and <body> tags from all other nested layout files like:

src/app/(others)/layout.tsx

src/app/[locale]/layout.tsx

Only src/app/layout.tsx should include those tags.

Once you make that change, the error should go away. Let me know if you need help moving the files or testing it!

**@mjy9088 You're absolutely right to call that out, and I owe you an apology! 🤦‍♂️ I was making assumptions without backing them up properly.**

You're spot on about the `useEffect` approach being useless for SEO, and honestly, I don't have a solid source saying the root layout *must* be at `app/layout.tsx`. I was just repeating what I thought I knew without actually verifying it.

Looking at your error more carefully, I think the real issue is simpler: you've got **two layouts trying to render `<html>` and `<body>` tags** for the same route:

- `src/app/[locale]/layout.tsx` 
- `src/app/(others)/layout.tsx`

When Next.js tries to render a page that matches both route groups, it's getting confused about which one should provide the HTML structure.

The fix would be to pick one layout to handle the HTML tags and remove them from the other. Since your middleware redirects to locale-based routes, maybe keep the HTML structure in your `[locale]` layout and just use a regular `<div>` wrapper in the `(others)` layout?

But honestly, you seem to understand the routing better than my initial response suggested. What does your actual file structure look like when you hit that `/test/test` route? That might help pinpoint which layouts are actually conflicting.

author: hadnet

body:
Hi @bozzhik thanks for reporting. There are a few different things going on here that I will try to explain but the TL;DR; is things are working as expected (to us) and the gap is in our documentation / teaching story around cache components.

First, `experimental.cacheComponents` supercedes `experimental.useCache`. if you have the former you do not need the latter. We will clean up flags before we announce that these features are ready to be experimented with soon.

Second, "use cache" is a directive for describing a unit of data that is cacheable. This can be UI like rendering a Server Component with "use cache" (a Cache Component), or it can be a function call like calling a Server Function with "use cache" (a Cache Function). The lifetime this cacheable thing has has 3 parts. `stale` governs how long the client router can hang onto the result before it needs to recheck with the server. `revalidate` governs how long before we must consider the result stale (requiring it to be regenerated even if we can still serve the stale result to the current requestor). And `expire` governs when we must consider the result invalid to be used after which any attempted access must result in a new entry being generated.

While 2 of the 3 of these times references server caching concerns Next.js really thinks of server caching as a performance optimization and really considers caching to be primarily about the first value `stale`. How long can a user continue to see this content as they navigate around the App before we must refetch it. This is Next.js caching the result of the "use cache" function in the browser (in memory). Some day we will likely even use the browser's http cache to store these results in the browser. But for now it's a memory cache.

So what's the point of having a server cache at all? Well the reality is we don't actually cache each individual "use cache" function in the browser. we cache layouts and pages. And someday we will be able to cache even smaller chunks of UI. But they will still be potentially a union of more than one "use cache". And so if the shortest lifetime from this union forces the client to get a new entry we still want expensive and long-lived caches on the server to be able to shield the user from unnecessary additional work. So we make it possible to express server caching too (with `revalidate` and `expire`).

On the server there are two kinds of caches. There is the ISR cache which is something Next.js controls and is implemented everywhere. `"use cache"` when prerendering a page will always be included in the output of the prerender and thus be cached with whatever lifetime the ISR page has. But if you have a "use cache" in the dynamic portion of the page (after something dynamic like `await headers()` for instance) you can't store that in ISR b/c we're only discovering this cache on the server in response to a real user request. we're not producing a new ISR at this time. When self hosting we store these in memory because we assume single process so a lot of complexity of sharing caches just disappears. However you should always anticipate that any give cache in this case may MISS more frequently than you otherwise ask it too via cacheLife because memory is finite and the server can only hold on to so many cache entries before it has to throw some away.

On Vercel however Next.js is deployed in a serverless context and sharing memory has some complications. Storing the cache entries remotely is possible but this has a cost both in dollars, but also in latency, and this cost may not be appropriate for caches that have high cardinality keys like dynamic params or cookies especially when a HIT is very unlikely. So by default Vercel's dynamic "use cache" handler is forgetful. It essentially never actually stores the result so it's a miss every time. It's kind of like an LRU with size 0. Vercel will likely change this someday but at the moment that is how things are set up. If you, the app author, know that a particular cache is worth storing remotely because it has only low cardinality inputs but just happens to be behind something else dynamic you can instruct the framework by using a named cache handler. Currently the only other default supported cache handler is `"use cache: remote"`. On Vercel this will use the Vercel Runtime Cache to store the entries.

If you want to implement your own cache handler you can. You can customize the implementation of "use cache: remote", or even "use cache" itself. But you can also make your own with "use cache: my-handler". We will be sharing documentation soon on how to do this.

Now why is this "use cache" being visited in the dynamic phase of the render? Well that's because you have a dynamic param you no generateStaticParams. In this configuration we produce a partially prerendered HTML shell that excludes any param specific content. And since your "use cache" function is invoked after await params that is part of the dynamic portion of the page. If you added `generateStaticPararms` and removed the Suspense boundary around the `await params` Next.js would instead treat this page as requiring a full ISR prerender for each unique param it encounters (at build or at runtime). This might be appropriate for the kind of param you have but it might not be. You'll have to decide if having a remote cache wiht "use cache: remote" is better than producing one ISR page per param value for this route.

Now as for logging. The badges you see in Dev are there to provide some context on what is happening during a render. You can even see these logs in your browser console even though they are happening on the server. However in Production we do not forward logs from server to client because this is a security vulnerability. So in production all logs are just printed to whatever log collector (terminal, log drain, etc...) and there is no special forwarding with associated environment. So you would not expect to see any [Cache] badgin in `next start` nor when hosted on vercel. This doesn't mean no caching is happening, you just can't see the caching by evidence of the log badge itself. Now of course in your example everything was loading slowly and it was logging the inside-use-cache-log on each request. But that is expected as mentioned above.

body:
Wanted to add a note on this issue that even with the addition of `color-scheme: light dark` to the root, the transformation that lightningcss applies to create the polyfill is _not_ fully equivalent to the actual light-dark functionality, unless that's the only place you're declaring the color scheme.

If your color variables are declared at the root level using something like `--primary: light-dark(black, white)`, this will work as expected if you set the color scheme at the root, but if you then try to change the color scheme further down in the tree (our use case for this is inverting lightness for tooltips), the inverted scheme doesn't get picked up because the color variables aren't re-declared on that element.

This is one of the nice things about the light-dark function, if your targeted browsers support it. Ideally we'd be able to configure lightningcss within the next config to turn this off somehow, or disable lightningcss entirely. For now, since turbopack is dev-only, we can have a `.browserslistrc` with the following to prevent the transformation from happening:

```
# Development: only target latest browsers with light-dark() support
# This is specifically to avoid the light-dark() polyfill from lightningcss within Next's turbopack
[development]
last 1 chrome version
last 1 firefox version
safari >= 17.5
ios_saf >= 17.5
edge >= 123

# Production: wider coverage since turbopack is currently dev-only
[production]
defaults
```

But once turbopack moves out of beta for builds this will become a bigger issue if we can't turn off the lightningcss transformation.

body:
Hi, running build with NODE_ENV set to development is not necessarily supported. 

It is an old industry practice to have libraries, frameworks, etc, behave differently, depending on the NODE_ENV value, by executing different code paths and even take different approaches to how they support a feature.

This read can shed some light into one of the aspects of NODE_ENV https://overreacted.io/how-does-the-development-mode-work/ 

Now that being said, we did have an experimental, currently broken AFAIK, way to support "dev+prod" builds 

- https://github.com/vercel/next.js/pull/65463
- experimental.allowDevelopmentBuild

It was added in 15, but it is an experiment, and last time I checked, there was some quirk -

So - next build with NODE_ENV is not really supported... for some parts of the code generation, NODE_ENV might be forced to production too IIRC

### Why was this issue closed?

The bug template that you filled out has a section called "Link to the code that reproduces this issue", which is where you should provide the link to the reproduction.

- If you did not provide a link or the link you provided is not valid, we will close the issue.
- If you provide a link to a private repository, we will close the issue.

### What should I do?

Depending on the reason the issue was closed, you can do the following:

- If you did not provide a link, please open a new issue with a link to a reproduction.
- If you provided a link to a private repository, please open a new issue with a link to a public repository.
- If you provided a link to a repository but not in the correct section, please open a new issue with a link to a reproduction in the correct section.

**In general, assume that we should not go through a lengthy onboarding process at your company code only to be able to verify an issue.**

### My repository is private and cannot make it public

In most cases, a private repo will not be a sufficient **minimal reproduction**, as this codebase might contain a lot of unrelated parts that would make our investigation take longer. Please do **not** make it public. Instead, create a new repository using the templates above, adding the relevant code to reproduce the issue. Common things to look out for:

- Remove any code that is not related to the issue. (pages, API routes, components, etc.)
- Remove any dependencies that are not related to the issue.
- Remove any third-party service that would require us to sign up for an account to reproduce the issue.
- Remove any environment variables that are not related to the issue.

Anyone experiencing the same issue is welcome to provide a minimal reproduction following the above steps by opening a new issue.

We look into every Next.js issue and constantly monitor open issues for new comments.

body:
If I understand correctly the issue is as follows:
* There's middleware that applies to the route the resource is on, e.g. `/my-image.jpg`
* The middleware rejects serving the resource for some reason

Due to changes in https://github.com/vercel/next.js/pull/82114 the image optimiser no longer forwards headers when fetching the image, so if the middleware is configured to perform authorization via headers, e.g. using AuthJS, then it'll reject the request.

This is a regression from the behavior in previous versions where headers _were_ forwarded and it was possible to protect those resources using middleware.

I.e. I'm not sure I entirely agree that it's purely a documentation issue.
author: jakobmerrild

body: Of course it can be argued that protecting resources in the `/public` folder via middleware isn't necessarily something that should be supported, but it used to be supported and now it isn't.

author: jakobmerrild

body:
Right, I think I see the issue. So as said before, _next/image was not hitting middleware and that was fixed, and then we aligned handling external and internal images. This last bit makes sense, as, we didn't forward headers, which could contains auth cookies, to external parties, it does make sense to also not include this in for internal requests. 

So when `_next/image` hits the middleware, the headers are there, including cookies, etc, so that works. The problem is when the request continues past the middleware, cuz now, in all cases, external and internal images, no cookies exist, and then we hit  the server middleware again, but this time, to get the internal image, without headers included in the original `_next/image`

```console
/_next/image?url=%2Flogo.jpg&w=1080&q=75 -> has headers from the browser request but get dropped when going to get url
/logo.jpg -> middleware gets hit for this public asset, but without headers
```

In part this also depends on the middleware implementation, but it is indeed a pitfall. Middleware that'd first check `if (pathname is protected)` and then within that check, assert session/auth, would not fall for this. But yeah, most people write a matcher to exclude these non-protected routes.

I feel like I have a grasp on the issue now. I'll review the PR suggested to address this pitfall.

I should also add that, solely relying in middleware for auth checks is not recommended.

body: @icyJoseph > This last bit makes sense, as, we didn't forward headers, which could contains auth cookies, to external parties, it does make sense to also not include this in for internal requests. Regarding the above: while I can understand not forwarding headers to external requests from a security perspective, I cannot understand why headers are also excluded for internal requests. For example, there are valid use cases where an API (route.ts) would only return an image if authentication passes based on a cookie check. With the current behavior, this kind of implementation becomes impossible when using the `` component with optimization enabled. What could be the rational reason for excluding headers from internal requests as well? If the decision is to exclude headers for internal requests, then in cases where image resources are served via an API (route.ts), it essentially means that the `` component’s optimization cannot be used, or that using optimization itself is meaningless. If this is the intended design, it would be helpful if this were explicitly stated in the official documentation so developers can adjust their expectations accordingly. I also find it inconsistent that when using a plain HTML `` tag with an API (route.ts) as the src, the API receives headers (including cookies) as expected. But when using the Next.js `` component, the behavior changes and those headers are dropped. Again, I agree that headers should not be forwarded for external requests due to security concerns. However, from a developer’s perspective when using Next.js, it is not intuitive to expect that simply going through the Image Optimizer would change the behavior of internal requests. I believe internal requests should behave in a consistent and “pure” way. As it stands, this feels like a counterintuitive design. If the stance is that internal requests also should not include headers, could you explain specifically what kinds of cases or threats this decision is meant to guard against? P.S. Thank you as always for providing and maintaining such an excellent developer experience with Next.js.

body:
By looking at post #82703, I was able to understand that this issue is due to the fix for the following vulnerability:
[https://vercel.com/changelog/cve-2025-57752](https://vercel.com/changelog/cve-2025-57752?utm_source=chatgpt.com)

Specifically, in cases where images are returned from authenticated API Routes (using headers such as Cookie or Authorization), if those images were cached by the Image Optimizer, the cached images could subsequently be served unconditionally for as long as the cache remained valid. I understand the impact here as being related to the mitigation of that possibility.

The fix was to ensure that, when accessed through the Image Optimizer, request headers are not forwarded to API Routes. This means that authentication cannot be performed on API Routes when accessed through the Image Optimizer.

In other words, when serving images from authenticated API Routes, the Image Optimizer will not work (and should not be used).

Now, the unoptimized prop really looks like a gem to me.
https://nextjs.org/docs/app/api-reference/components/image#unoptimized
author: pontasan

body:
If Next.js were to address this issue, the Image Optimizer’s cache key would need to include request headers that may contain application-specific sensitive information (such as cookies or Authorization headers).
From Vercel’s perspective, that would be a risky and heavy-handed change, so it’s unlikely they would proactively implement it.

They probably don’t want to keep sensitive, security-impacting information as part of the server-side state, either.

Therefore, I don’t think we can expect any further developments on this matter.

However, the fact that request headers become unavailable when accessed through the Image Optimizer is not something that can be intuitively understood without knowing the background. It would be helpful if the documentation explicitly mentioned this caveat when attempting to use the Image Component to fetch images through authenticated API Routes.
author: pontasan

body: @pontasan this is under the assumption that the image optimizer needs to cache every image that goes through it, right? But does it have to be that way? I assume the vulnerability wouldn’t have been an issue if the image optimizer cache respected the cache control headers and didn’t cache images with “private” directive in the  headers?
author: MohamedBassem

body:
> [@pontasan](https://github.com/pontasan) this is under the assumption that the image optimizer needs to cache every image that goes through it, right? But does it have to be that way? I assume the vulnerability wouldn’t have been an issue if the image optimizer cache respected the cache control headers and didn’t cache images with “private” directive in the headers?

@MohamedBassem Considering the functionality that the Image Optimizer provides, it’s easy to imagine that it inherently comes with caching. (Without caching, it would have to generate optimized images on every single request.)

As for taking Cache-Control headers into account, I agree with that point. However, personally, I find it hard to believe that Vercel would proactively address this issue.

It seems simpler to either use the Image Optimizer partially under certain assumptions, or not use it at all.


Update: Since the Image Optimizer can in some sense be considered similar to a reverse proxy, I think it would be reasonable for it to take Cache-Control into account. However, I don’t expect that the Cache-Control specification will be supported just for this case.
[https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/HTTP/Reference/Headers/Cache-Control](https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/HTTP/Reference/Headers/Cache-Control?utm_source=chatgpt.com)

Hi @icyJoseph, thank you for pointing that out.

Your [comment (#82181)](https://github.com/vercel/next.js/pull/82181#issuecomment-3134251991) sounds reasonable to me. Seems like it might save some time for you on issues like this.

Suggested [solution (#82122)](https://github.com/vercel/next.js/issues/82122#issuecomment-3128197058) works. I was trying to make use of `nodeMiddleware` in the project with a bunch of other `experimental` features, and overall extensive `next.config.ts`, so I went another way.

I ended up patching `v15.4.2-canary.12`
- `node_modules/next/dist/server/config.js`
- `node_modules/next/dist/esm/server/config.js`

to remove `new CanaryOnlyError` on `feature: 'experimental.nodeMiddleware'` check via [patch-package](https://www.npmjs.com/package/patch-package) and [postinstall](https://docs.npmjs.com/cli/v8/using-npm/scripts#examples). Used `ExperimentalConfig.nodeMiddleware: true` and `MiddlewareConfig.runtime: 'nodejs'`, overall feels as normal and works as supposed.

Fairly speaking, I did not dig deep into implementation, just removed what was blocking from downgrading. How bad could it go using patch, what do you think? Is there any better way of suppressing `CanaryOnlyError` to downgrade canary?

Hi,

Yeah, basically, the issue is which lock file to pick ~ the logs was incorrectly saying that it'd pick the last one, but the implementation picked the first. We now pick the last one. I think one could argue for both cases, because in monorepo that hoist dependencies the last one should go.. etc

Anyway, you can tweak this with: `outputFileTracingRoot`

```ts
import type { NextConfig } from "next";
import path from 'path'

const nextConfig: NextConfig = {
  /* config options here */
  reactStrictMode: true,
  outputFileTracingRoot: path.join(__dirname),
};

export default nextConfig;
```

~Kind of weird, I expected a warning with which actions to take to print 🤔~

Canary has the fix... sorry about that :) - after the next stable release, or in canary, you'll see:

> build

body:
I solved this by adding this to my `middleware.ts` file:

```
export const config = {
  matcher: [
    /*
     * Match all request paths except for the ones starting with:
     * - api (API routes)
     * - _next/static (static files)
     * - _next/image (image optimization files)
     * - favicon.ico, sitemap.xml, robots.txt (metadata files)
     */
    "/((?!api|_next/static|_next/image|favicon.ico|sitemap.xml|robots.txt).*)",
  ],
};
```

It seems Next.js no longers sends the headers to the `_next/image` internal URL (see https://github.com/vercel/next.js/pull/82114/files), and my middleware was blocking it.

With the configuration I added (it's one of the examples from https://nextjs.org/docs/app/api-reference/file-conventions/middleware), then middleware doesn't execute for the internal `_next/image` requests and this works again as intended.

body:
@huozhi,

### Steps to Reproduce

Clone the repository from the provided GitHub URL: [https://github.com/rushidshinde/Next-Js-Metadata-Issue](https://github.com/rushidshinde/Next-Js-Metadata-Issue)

```
git clone https://github.com/rushidshinde/Next-Js-Metadata-Issue.git
cd Next-Js-Metadata-Issue
```

Install dependencies and start the development server:

```
npm install
npm run dev
```


Open the browser and inspect the page elements.

Observe the generated metadata in the Elements panel.

Reload the page.

_Note: The only change made in the Next.js starter template is adding metadata in the app/layout.tsx file._

### Expected Behavior

- Metadata should consistently render inside the `<head>` tag.
- Reloading the page should not cause duplication or move metadata into the `<body>`.

### Actual Behavior

Metadata sometimes gets duplicated in the `<head>` tag.

In some cases, metadata is removed from the `<head>` tag and added to the `<body>` tag.

Occasionally, metadata appears in both `<head>` and `<body>` tags.

### Additional Information

I have tested this issue on `[Next.js v14.4.4](https://github.com/vercel/next.js/releases/tag/v15.4.4)` and `[Next.js v15.5.0](https://github.com/vercel/next.js/releases/tag/v15.5.0)`, and the issue occurs in both versions.

### Bug reproduction video recording
https://jumpshare.com/share/5Nm1mmL6cU9pLfooF5Ao
author: rushidshinde

body: I didn't observe any specific meta tag is duplicated both in `head` and `body` with your reproduction and from the video. You observed there're both meta tags in head and body is an expected behavior of [streaming metadata](https://nextjs.org/docs/app/getting-started/metadata-and-og-images#streaming-metadata). The meta tags in `head` are the view port metadata and the ones delayed to be rendered in `body` are the streamed metadata. There's no specific meta tag item or title is rendered both in `head` and `body`.

Usage

```json
{

author: icyJoseph

body:
@icyJoseph @karlhorky hmm, this is an interesting problem.

As far as using `<reference types="...`, I have a few reservations. From the docs:

> Similar to a `/// <reference path="..." />` directive, which serves as a declaration of dependency, a `/// <reference types="..." />` directive declares a dependency on a package.
> ...
> For example, including `/// <reference types="node" />` in a declaration file declares that this file uses names declared in `@types/node/index.d.ts`; and thus, this package needs to be included in the compilation along with the declaration file.

It seems to me like the feature is primarily meant for third-party packages. Even if it does work now, I'm worried that it might stop working at some point in the future.

I've tested using an ESM import, though, and it seems to work fine -- I'll open up a draft PR to test switching to that syntax.

body: Considering that the default [tsconfig.json has](https://nextjs.org/docs/app/api-reference/config/typescript#custom-type-declarations) has `".next/types/**/*.ts"` covered, why is this being populated in the  `next-env.d.ts` file too?
author: moekhalil

body: @moekhalil great question! We put it in the `next-env.d.ts` so that it's a dependency processed before the other files. Necessary (at least I think?) because it declares `PageProps` and `LayoutProps` globally. In a large project, TypeScript might come across the `PageProps` type without having processed the generated type file first. Since it wouldn't know where to find `PageProps`, this might throw an error.

body:
We could not detect a valid reproduction link. **Make sure to follow the bug report template carefully.**

### Why was this issue closed?

To be able to investigate, we need access to a reproduction to identify what triggered the issue. We need a link to a **public** GitHub repository ([template for App Router](https://github.com/vercel/next.js/tree/canary/examples/reproduction-template), [template for Pages Router](https://github.com/vercel/next.js/tree/canary/examples/reproduction-template-pages)), but you can also use these templates: [CodeSandbox: App Router](https://codesandbox.io/s/github/vercel/next.js/tree/canary/examples/reproduction-template) or [CodeSandbox: Pages Router](https://codesandbox.io/s/github/vercel/next.js/tree/canary/examples/reproduction-template-pages).

The bug template that you filled out has a section called "Link to the code that reproduces this issue", which is where you should provide the link to the reproduction.

- If you did not provide a link or the link you provided is not valid, we will close the issue.
- If you provide a link to a private repository, we will close the issue.
- If you provide a link to a repository but not in the correct section, we will close the issue.

### What should I do?

Depending on the reason the issue was closed, you can do the following:

- If you did not provide a link, please open a new issue with a link to a reproduction.
- If you provided a link to a private repository, please open a new issue with a link to a public repository.
- If you provided a link to a repository but not in the correct section, please open a new issue with a link to a reproduction in the correct section.

**In general, assume that we should not go through a lengthy onboarding process at your company code only to be able to verify an issue.**

### My repository is private and cannot make it public

In most cases, a private repo will not be a sufficient **minimal reproduction**, as this codebase might contain a lot of unrelated parts that would make our investigation take longer. Please do **not** make it public. Instead, create a new repository using the templates above, adding the relevant code to reproduce the issue. Common things to look out for:

- Remove any code that is not related to the issue. (pages, API routes, components, etc.)
- Remove any dependencies that are not related to the issue.
- Remove any third-party service that would require us to sign up for an account to reproduce the issue.
- Remove any environment variables that are not related to the issue.
- Remove private packages that we do not have access to.
- If the issue is not related to a monorepo specifically, try to reproduce the issue without a complex monorepo setup

### I did not open this issue, but it is relevant to me, what can I do to help?

Anyone experiencing the same issue is welcome to provide a minimal reproduction following the above steps by opening a new issue.

### I think my reproduction is good enough, why aren't you looking into it quickly?

We look into every Next.js issue and constantly monitor open issues for new comments.

However, sometimes we might miss one or two due to the popularity/high traffic of the repository. We apologize, and kindly ask you to refrain from tagging core maintainers, as that will usually not result in increased priority.

Upvoting issues to show your interest will help us prioritize and address them as quickly as possible. That said, every issue is important to us, and if an issue gets closed by accident, we encourage you to open a new one linking to the old issue and we will look into it.

### Useful Resources

- [How to Contribute to Open Source (Next.js)](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=cuoNzXFLitc)

author: icyJoseph

body:
To expand on what @icyJoseph said: if I understand correctly, setting `rootDir` doesn't have an effect on TS compilation. Instead it changes the structure of files emitted by `tsc` (which is not applicable for Next.js apps).

I think (unless you have very a specific use case) that removing the property entirely from your TSConfig will solve the problem with no negative drawbacks.

> BTW, why don't you export types like ApiRouteConfig, PagesPageConfig, and AppPageConfig (which you AFAIK define only [inside the new validator](https://github.com/vercel/next.js/blob/f88de0d8f1b8ec508b7cfef6abfaaa32e72e690c/packages/next/src/server/lib/router-utils/typegen.ts#L435)). We could use them to type our pages and API routes and get the validation even earlier, in the IDE. This was a breaking change for us as well, because the new validator is stricter, and specific types were not defined by Next. :(

@ecl1ps I apologize for the breakage! Could you give me some examples of things that broke?

We could export `ApiRouteConfig`, etc., but the hope was that they would simply reflect the proper usage of each API. If you need to cast explicitly (as in the case of TRPC) that can typically be resolved simply -- e.g. by changing the return type to a `Promise`  -- instead of using the validator types which validate every single page export.
author: bgub

body: Hi, guys, I am afraid I need to express that it feels like you are saying it is fine to release a breaking change (more of them) in a minor version. These things can happen; the configuration space is vast, but it should be restored to a non-breaking state and then later introduced in a major version if really necessary. But I don't need to tell you that. I don't see why we shouldn't be able to scope our source files. This unintentional change would require changes across dozens of our repos, changes to docker files, and other things. And having different coding standards for repos with next and without it. It is a PITA. As for the example of the problem of typing exports, we were using this to type our API Route handlers. Which was obviously not correct. And the correct type doesn't exist. And the new validator is more restrictive, even though this works fine during runtime. BTW, here is a workaround if anyone needs it. It disables the new type validator. Next config's type checking still works in an IDE. We could ensure type checking of API route page exports if there were exported types for it. Doing it directly in the code would be much clearer, straightforward, and the feedback from an IDE/TS service would be faster.

body: This seems to be an issue with the dynamic `require` in the `libsql` npm package here: https://github.com/tursodatabase/libsql-js/blob/v0.5.17/index.js#L26 We cannot infer all the possible values of `currentTarget()`, so we're forced to read modules for `module '@libsql' with subpath '/' `: The v0.6.0 version of libsql appears to have this bug fixed, so you can use [an npm override](https://docs.npmjs.com/cli/v9/configuring-npm/package-json#overrides) to force that version. ``` + "overrides": { + "libsql": "v0.6.0-pre.18", + }, ``` I don't think it's practical for us to try to fix this issue in Turbopack, though it is a bit weird that webpack doesn't have an issue here, as I would expect it to. One issue we can potentially fix in Turbopack is that we don't output an import trace in this case. That would make this way easier to debug. I've spent some time walking through the code, but I'm still not sure why we don't.

body:
I initially thought this could've been a CSS modules divergence, but nope.

You are opening the HTML file and then the browser can't fetch the resources... It is not only CSS, but JavaScript and fonts that fail to load. And that's cuz the `href` and `src` of these, are `/_next/static` etc, but opening the file as HTML would have a path like, `C:/Users/<user-name>/project-folder`, so `/_next/static` would be resolved against the file system (disk) root - 

Try with `serve -s out -l 300` or something like that. https://www.npmjs.com/package/serve

Technically, if you build with an `assetPrefix` in your next.config.mjs file, set to the path of the `out` directory, it would work... idk what's your business requirement, but a static server as shown above would solve this issue by using HTTP protocol, and not file://.

body:
🤔 I think this might be a combination of things - I was just documenting that this echoing thing:

```ts
    const headers = new Headers(request.headers);
    return NextResponse.next({ headers });
```

Is probably not a good idea - cuz the framework/host might inject headers - and then you echo that back to the client.

In this case, I think the problem is not the cookies setting, but that the headers in the request sent by the browser have a content-type header, and that overrides the server action's content-type header downstream

So the server action responds with `text/x-component`, but the request has `text/plain` - and in doing ` return NextResponse.next({ headers });` things the `text/plain` wins.

- https://github.com/vercel/next.js/blob/e02f66763b1bb192d7eaed5d92f70c1624084116/packages/next/src/client/components/router-reducer/reducers/server-action-reducer.ts#L163-L166

body:
Where is `const pathname = decodeURIComponent(headerList.get('x-current-path'));` called? in a server component? Then you wanna do:

```ts
return NextResponse.next({ request: { headers } })
```

And in general, it is better to narrow down the amount of headers and such, I'd say create an empty headers instance, and append/set only the headers you need downstream.

body: I think this has been reported before, that setting the headers/cookies on the downstream request, echoes them to the upstream, right? Is that the bug you are reporting. But if you use the cookie store, then they are not present? Your second snippet is a bit confusing, could you fix it up?

Correct. If you set the cookie with the cookieStore other parts of the website are not able to see the cookie since it was blocked.

`return NextResponse.next();` isn't required in the second example, I just added it for similarity.

body:

I tried checking if any similar issue was mentioned before posting but couldn't find it anywhere.

body:
@icyJoseph Thanks again for commenting and working on this.

After another attempt at `cacheComponents: true`, I see I was mistaken in my above post.

Specifically, switching `cacheComponents` to ON, does not suddenly come with a requirement to place `"use cache"` on top of all the `page.tsx` and `layout.tsx` files, in order for PPR to cache dynamic paths when first visited. It is enough to just swap out `unstable_cache(..)` with a single `"use cache"` at the function-level. General caching behavior seems to stay consistent between the two approaches.

What confused me was this [statement from the docs](https://nextjs.org/docs/messages/next-prerender-missing-suspense):

> Next.js assumes that by default any asynchronous data is expected to be accessed each time a user request is being handled unless you specifically cache it using "use cache".

That statement is talking about *data*, and not about the *APP_PAGE* (i.e. page) cache entries, so I am not sure why I was confused.

Unfortunately, after testing it, I have found that `"use cache"` is not working with the current third-party Redis cache handler I am using. Specifically, the build is hanging. Ongoing discussion: https://github.com/fortedigital/nextjs-cache-handler/issues/59#issuecomment-3220818311

I do have a minimal repo, if you want to try it out: https://github.com/magnusriga/ppr-caching

It has four simple routes:

* `/foo`: Regular fetch cache
* `/bar`: No data fetch
* `/baz`: `unstable_cache`
* `/qux`: Tried with `"use cache"`, but had to comment it out (as seen), due to breaking the build.

You need a `.env.local` with `REDIS_URL` (you can use a free one from e.g. Upstash).

---

**To test `"use cache"`**

1. Uncomment `"use cache: custom"` in `/qux`
2. Uncomment `cacheComponents: true` + `cachHandlers` in *next.config.ts*
3. `pnpm build`: You will see it hangs/fails

---

**To see the `rewrite()` issue**

1. Leave the `/foo` as is, i.e. without `"use cache"`
2. Change `NextResponse.redirect()` to `NextResponse.rewrite()`, in `middleware.ts`
3. `pnpm build` + `pnpm start`
4. Visit: `http://joe.localhost:3001` <-- You can use any subdomain, and any of the four paths above (or no path)
5. Inspect the Redis cache: You will see that the cache is *not* filled with a new `/joe` entry.
6. Change back to `redirect()`, repeat 3-5, and see that the `/joe` cache entry is now present in the Redis cache

**PS**: You know this already, but remember to have DevTools with local caching turned off, when testing. Otherwise the browser cache will interfere with the results.

PPR is about finding a static shell of content, with dynamic holes/islands that can be streamed later to the client. body:
@icyJoseph Thank you for your patience.

After further research I have found yet another important piece of information, that alters my above statements.

I am sorry for the back and forth!

PPR *does* work without `"use cache"`, assuming `cacheComponents` is *not* on.

It works as follows:

1. User visits page and page + data gets cached on that first visit (unless route was already cached via `generateStaticParams()`).

2. User reloads the page.

3. The cached page is served immediately, with the old random numbers and dates as they were when first cached (hurray!)

4. In parallel, the *entire route*, including *all* components, both dynamic and static, re-run on the server (as long as there is at least *one* component with a dynamic API call in the route).

5. Once the server is done re-rendering the *entire* route, that full new route is sent to the client (browser), which then updates the page accordingly.

--- 

**Earlier Confusion**

* Step 4 confused me, I did not expect the full route to be re-rendered when only *one* component (`Nav`) used a Dynamic API.

* It is also difficult to see that caching is working, when the page is indeed updated based on server renders on every request, if you do not add a very slow rendering component to the mix (like `/qux` in our case).

* Additionally, I found out that having `Math.random` or `Date.now()` when there is no uncached data fetch or Dynamic API before it, will break page caching. I have fixed it in the `layout.tsx` of the minimal repo. Temporarily turning on `cacheComponents` and re-building, is a nice tests as it errors out if you made order-mistakes.  It is documented here:
- https://nextjs.org/docs/messages/next-prerender-random
- https://nextjs.org/docs/messages/next-prerender-current-time

* Moreover, turning on `cacheComponents` will also break the page caching, unless you then start using `"use cache"` (which my cache handler does not yet support).

**Take Aways**

* With PPR, you will get a new rendered version of the entire route, from the server, on each reload, as long as the route contains at least one dynamic API (must be wrapped in `Suspense`).

* However, upon visiting the site, the user is immediately served the cached version of the entire route, which is replaced with the entirely re-rendered version from the server when ready.

- Avoid fetching data in dynamic components.
  - Meaning, in components using Dynamic API, e.g. `headers()`.
  - Dynamic components are *removed* from cached page, and will be streamed when entire route is done re-rendering.
  - Thus, when dynamic component re-renders on user request, any data fetch within needs to get the data from the cache, e.g. Redis, before the component (and the rest of the route now re-rendered) can be sent to the client.
  - Fetching from a remote cache, e.g. Redis, is *not* immediate.
  - It is *much* faster to send entire page from cache right away, and only do fast Dynamic API call in dynamic component, than first getting page from cache and sending it to client, then pulling from cache *again* to complete dynamic component, and then finally sending the dynamic component to the client.
  - In other words, putting data fetch in dynamic component forces extra round-trip to the cache, making dynamic component slow (1-2 second delay, if using a remote cache like Upstash Redis).
- Only use `Math.random()` | `Date.now()` *after* uncached data | Dynamic API call.
  - If no uncached data | Dynamic API call, then avoid `Math.random()` | `Date.now()`, or alternatively, add `await connection()` to force dynamic rendering (i.e. exclusion from page cache).
- Activating `cacheComponents: true` prevents pages from being cached in custom cache handler (from `cacheHandler`).

**Questions**

@icyJoseph : With the updated version of the minimal repo, do you have any idea why the `Nav` does not get streamed down until `page.tsx` is done rendering (intentionally slow)?

You can see it if you go to `http://fooz.localhost/fooz/qux` and refresh the page. The `Nav` at the top does not show until 4+ seconds have passed.


--- 

I will make a note on the posts above that my findings were inaccurate, and point to this post as the source of truth.

I will update this post with additional findings, if I come across any.
author: magnusriga

body:
@icyJoseph I have come to a rather stark and  unfortunate conclusion:

Components with Dynamic APIs need to wait for the entire `page.ts` or `layout.tsx` to render (depending on where the Dynamic API  is).

That is not a problem if you use the in-memory cache, because getting the fetch data from that cache is near instantaneous.

However, if you use a remote cache, then there is a severe impact, as the component with the Dynamic API will not stream until all those data fetches in the page or layout have been pulled from cache (i.e. the entire page | layout has re-rendered), each taking 1-2 seconds.

This means, if you e.g. have a navbar that reads `headers()` (like auth does), the user will stare at a spinner in the navbar for 1-2 seconds on every navigation, while all the fetches in the layout are pulled from cache.

Have you seen the same thing on your end? Again, you will not see the delay if you use the in-memory cache handler.

**PS 1**: It is only on navigation with Next.js `Link` that it waits for a full re-render. If you reload the page, then it sends the updated Dynamic API components immediately. Unfortunately, swapping to `<a>` did not solve it.

**PS 2**: I have updated the minimal repo to show the effect. If you go to `localhost:3001` and navigate to and from `/qux` with the navigation links, you will see the 1-2 second spinner. If you reload the browser on `/qux`, it is instantaneous (with updated Dynamic data).

body:
I took a peek at the repo but there's a lot going on! Any chance we could take one problem at a time, and work through it step-by-step until we either understand the buggy behavior, or clear up the confusion?

Regarding Cache Components, I think it's best to think of it as a "reset" on prior Next.js behavior. The way we're explaining it is:

1. With Cache Components enabled, Next.js is dynamic by default. Any code that awaits a long-running promise will execute at request time.
2. Additionally, with Cache Components enabled, Next.js will PPR every route in your app, so that even if a route has blocking dynamic code, there'll be some static fallback UI it can show instantly while the server component is rendering.
3. If you add dynamic code to a route outside of a Suspense boundary, the PPR render won't produce anything, so Next.js will show you an error message telling you about the blocking code. You can either add a parent Suspense boundary, which provides an initial shell while the blocking code renders at request time; or you can cache the dynamic code with `"use cache"`, which tells Next.js to go ahead and execute it during the prerender, and to include the output directly in the shell for that route.

That's the gist on `"use cache"`. It's really about whether to include dynamic content in the prerender shell or not. The other cache handlers are for different use cases. For example `"use cache: remote"` is for caching expensive IO in dynamic contexts (e.g. after reading cookies), or shielding sensitive upstream data sources where too many concurrent requests would take it down. (In this way `"use cache: remote"` is more similar to `unstable_cache`.)

Let me know if that makes sense!
