author: benblank

body:
Right, since you are using `useActionState` in a framework that supports React Server Components, you have to use `use client`, because otherwise the bundler attempts to do Server Components by default. 

The codesandbox fork in the React docs is using `react-scripts` (create-react-app), and AFAIK that never got to support React Server Components.  That being said `useActionState`, just like `useState` and others is not exclusive to React Server Components bundling so to speak, you can just use it. 

To get the progressive enhancement, they do mention: `<form> be rendered by a [Server Component](https://react.dev/reference/rsc/use-client)`
author: icyJoseph

body: Unfortunately that's a mistake in the react docs when they say that `<form>` must be  rendered by a Server Component to get progressive enhancement of error messages - it's been confusing people for a long time (see for example https://github.com/reactjs/react.dev/issues/6601 and https://github.com/reactjs/react.dev/pull/6627). The link actually takes you to the page for a 'use client'.
author: mdj-uk

body:
Aha, so it sounds like the React docs should say something more like "for progressive enhancement, the <form> element needs to be rendered *using* React Server Components, *by* a Client Component" — because the hook can only work on the client, but the "without JavaScript" progressive enhancement requires some level of SSR. Yes?

I had seen that the link was to the `"use client"` page, but assumed that was just because the page also goes over the definition of "Server Component" and "Client Component" and the differences between them. 😅

Thanks so much for helping me get this straight! I'm going to go ahead and close the issue now, since this clearly isn't a Next issue.
author: benblank

body:
> Aha, so it sounds like the React docs should say something more like "for progressive enhancement, the `<form>` element needs to be rendered _using_ React Server Components, _by_ a Client Component" — because the hook can only work on the client, but the "without JavaScript" progressive enhancement requires some level of SSR. Yes?

Yep that's my understanding, in the case where you have error messages to deal with -  though to be clear I'm not on the react or nextjs team I'm just a nobody who got confused by this a while ago :-) 

To get progressive enhancement including error messages you need an SSR'd client component which calls `useActionState(myServerAction, initialState)` and renders the `form` with the resulting action. Then you can submit the form before js has loaded and the html you get back will include the error message. Which is amazing!

If you don't care about the error message and don't need `useActionState` you can render `<form action={myServerAction} >` directly from a server component which will also submit without js.

body:
So I investigated this case, and think that this behaviour might be intentional. In Next.js 15.5.4, when we build, we get the following output:

```
Route (app)
┌ ○ /_not-found
├ ● /[locale]
├   └ /en
└ ƒ /[locale]/stories/[slug]
```

Which is technically wrong, as the route with the `[slug]` is under the `[locale]`, which defines `dynamicParams = false` which applies to the entire route, not just the `[locale]` segment.

Next.js 15.6.0-canary.47 produces the following output:

```
Route (app)
┌ ○ /_not-found
├ ● /[locale]
├   └ /en
└ ● /[locale]/stories/[slug]
    └ /en/stories/[slug]
```

Which I'd argue is actually more accurate, but in this case, still has the same rules of `dynamicParams` getting applied, and as no `slug` was generated, any unknown pages should trigger a 404.
author: wyattjoh
amannn

body:
Thanks for the prompting! I've dove in and identified a few bugs based on your example that should be addressed in a future canary (see https://github.com/vercel/next.js/pull/84889). In this case, there's a few things at play here:

1. **Bug in Next.js**: Due to a bug in Next.js's handling of parallel routes, the presence of one for that particular route was incorrectly marking that route as being static instead of dynamic. My PR mentioned above will ensure that those routes that are marked as dynamic without the parallel route are marked as dynamic with them too. Also found another bug related to redirect loops for 404 pages which was connected, so that'll be fixed soon too!
3. **Absence of `generateStaticParams`**: Your route omitted the `generateStaticParams` in the route with the `[slug]`. As a result, Next.js treated those pages as dynamic, which means they weren't subject to the same `dynamicParams = false` rule that was applied. Adding the `generateStaticParams` will ensure that the generated routes including `[slug]` are treated as static, but as mentioned before, will make them subject to the same `dynamicParams = false` configuration.

Currently within Next.js, there's no way to scope the `dynamicParams` value. Also, although we take suggestions for improvements to this API seriously, we've actually chosen to remove `dynamicParams` in the experimental Cache Components feature. There's no current replacement for this specific API as of yet, as the new API's are centred around suspense boundaries and `"use cache"`, so suggestions on that API would be appreciated (though probably better suited for a GitHub Discussion rather than a GitHub Issue).

{pendingMetadataTags}

{pendingMetadataTags} // No Suspense
) ``` Rebuilt Next.js and tested. **Result:** ✅ All metadata tags now render in `` correctly. ### Verified With Multiple Tests Tested various scenarios: - Layout + page both have metadata - Only layout has metadata - Partial overlap All work correctly with Suspense removed. Used both browser DevTools and curl to verify. ### Questions 1. **What is the Suspense optimizing?** - Is it to stream HTML faster? - For synchronous `export const metadata`, there's nothing async to wait for - For async `generateMetadata()`, resulting metadata needs to be in head anyway 2. **TODO comment:** Lines [149-151](https://github.com/vercel/next.js/blob/canary/packages/next/src/lib/metadata/metadata.tsx#L149-L151) say: ```tsx // TODO: We shouldn't change what we render based on whether we are streaming or not. // If we aren't streaming we should just block the response until we have resolved the // metadata. ``` Is this TODO being worked on? 3. body:
## Root Cause Found: RSC Flight Data vs SSR HTML I've done much more testing and found the root cause of this issue. ### The Problem When `serveStreamingMetadata` is true (the default), metadata is sent via **RSC Flight data** instead of **initial SSR HTML**. React's hoisting only works on SSR HTML, not Flight data. ### Evidence I created multiple test scenarios (relative to my sample): **Test 1: Inline JSX metadata** (bypasses Next.js API) ```tsx export default function Page() { return <>Test
Content
} ``` ✅ **Result:** All tags in `` (React server-side hoisting works) **Test 5/6: Next.js metadata property** ```tsx export const metadata = { title: 'Test', description: '...' } ``` ❌ **Result:** All tags in `` (sent via Flight data, no hoisting) **Test 8: Promise + Suspense** (plain JSX, no Next.js API) ```tsx const metadataPromise = new Promise(resolve => setTimeout(() => resolve(Test), 1000) ) return {metadataPromise} ``` - curl: Tags in `` (server can't hoist delayed content) - Browser: Only `` hoisted, `<meta>` tags stay in body - **Finding:** React's client-side hoisting is incomplete ### The Two Channels **Channel 1 - SSR HTML** (actual HTML tags): ```html <head><title>Test ``` - React's server-side hoisting works ✅ - What bots/crawlers see - Used when content is available during initial render **Channel 2 - RSC Flight data** (serialized in scripts): ```html ``` - For Suspense boundaries that resolve later - Client reconstructs and patches into DOM - React's hoisting **doesn't work** on this ❌ ### Why Metadata Goes Through Flight Data When Suspense wraps metadata ([`metadata.tsx` lines 163-166](https://github.com/vercel/next.js/blob/canary/packages/next/src/lib/metadata/metadata.tsx#L163-L166)): 1. Server starts streaming HTML 2. Encounters Suspense with pending metadata promise 3. Sends placeholder, continues streaming 4. Later: Metadata resolves 5. Sends via Flight data (Channel 2) 6. Client patches it into body 7. No hoisting happens ❌ ### The Fix Remove the Suspense wrapper: ```tsx // Current (broken): return (
// ← Remove {pendingMetadataTags} // ← Remove
) // Fixed: return ( {pendingMetadataTags} // Forces server to wait, uses SSR HTML ) ``` **Testing:** I verified this fix works - all metadata renders in `` correctly with all test scenarios. ### Why This Works Without Suspense: - Server **waits** for metadata promise (even if instant) - Metadata becomes part of initial SSR HTML (Channel 1) - React's server-side hoisting moves tags to `` ✅ - Proper HTML structure for bots, browsers, everyone **Trade-off:** Response delayed by milliseconds, but: - Metadata is invisible anyway - For `export const metadata`, it's instant (already synchronous) - For `async generateMetadata()`, metadata must be in initial HTML for SEO - Correctness matters more than microseconds ### Questions for Team 1. **Why use RSC Flight for metadata?** - Metadata needs to be in initial HTML for SEO/bots - Flight data is for dynamic component updates - These seem incompatible? 2. **Why is `serveStreamingMetadata` true by default?** - What's the performance benefit of streaming invisible metadata? - Breaks functionality (SEO, social sharing, standards) 3. **The TODO comment** ([lines 149-151](https://github.com/vercel/next.js/blob/canary/packages/next/src/lib/metadata/metadata.tsx#L149-L151)) says: ```tsx // TODO: We shouldn't change what we render based on whether we are streaming or not. // If we aren't streaming we should just block the response until we have resolved the // metadata. ``` Is this being worked on? 4. **Would you accept a PR** that: - Removes the Suspense wrapper? - Changes `serveStreamingMetadata` default to `false`? - Or implements the TODO (always block for metadata)? ### Impact Affects **all App Router apps** using `export const metadata` in layout.tsx (the recommended pattern for site-wide defaults). Breaks: - SEO - Social media sharing (Twitter, Facebook, LinkedIn, WhatsApp) - HTML validation - Document structure ### Reproduction https://github.com/robbchar/next-metadata-example Layout metadata renders in ``. With Suspense removed, it renders in ``. --- Happy to provide more details or submit a PR with the fix!

body:
This is also happening with
```ts
htmlLimitedBots: /.*/
```
set in my next configuration file, which sounds strange as it should’ve completely disabled streaming metadata.

UPDATE:
Looking at the code, I see that whether to stream metadata or not is always the product of a runtime evaluation: https://github.com/vercel/next.js/blob/canary/packages/next/src/server/lib/streaming-metadata.ts#L16.

First of all, I don’t see why the absence of a `user-agent` header should make the logic fall back to the streaming option, while IMO it would make sense to opt for the “safest” option when in doubt, which is a blocking render where we avoid streaming stuff for a client which does not guarantee us to be able to handle it.
 
Also, as somebody running a Next.js website in a k8s cluster as a “dynamic” server delegating caching to a CDN put in front of it (I never cache anything at the application level, which to me has never made sense anyway, and I spit out as-static-as-possible payload cached by the CDN), this makes zero sense, as it’s gratuitously making Next.js uncacheable at a CDN level, since the server is changing its rendering behaviour depending on each request's headers. 

I’m totally fine with this feature being opt-in, but `htmlLimitedBots` is not a solution for those of us who would happily opt-out of streaming behaviour completely.

We encountered this same issue deploying Nimiq blockchain integration (uses Web Workers with importScripts).

**Our findings:**
- Turbopack transforms `self.location.origin + '/file.js'` → `'./file.js'` during worker bundling
- This breaks importScripts() since blob URLs can't resolve relative paths
- Webpack version works fine (serves workers via HTTP, not blob URLs)

**Reproduction:** 
- Turbopack starter (broken): https://github.com/onmax/nimiq-starter/tree/main/starters/nextjs-turbopack

body:
One of the changes we've made with cache components is the way that we support high cardinality pages. When you have a high cardinality page (which is a page you haven't prerendered), we'll serve the static fallback shell fast and then stream in the rest of the response. For pages without any other dynamic accesses, this is very fast. This does present a problem though for pages that have some dynamic access, like `await headers()`. On those pages, we can't even completely prerender them because of the dynamic access.

If you're looking for the more traditional ISR-like behaviour where the first visit of the page is the static page, and future visits just get that cached copy, you'll need to remove your suspense boundaries. A suspense boundary signals to Next.js/React that you have a valid intermediate state that can be served. For pages that are listed in the `generateStaticParams`, we'd prerender up to those suspense boundaries if other dynamic accesses occurred inside (or completely if not). You still get the convenience of cache components, but you do lose the ability to provide those loading states.

If you're interested in starting a discussion on this feature and have some suggestions to improve the API, please feel free to start a discussion! As for this issue, I'm going to close it, as it's currently working as designed.

author: Nayeem-XTREME

body:
So, I think the formal explanation here is that `params` is unknown, so this component can't be cached, aka, pre-rendering won't be able to do anything about this. So at dev time, the issue is already surfaced. 

You can wrap this in a Suspense, through loading.tsx yes, but I think, defining a `generateStaticParams`, that returns at least one item, also does the trick,  so that there's at least one route that's not-blocking. Then in production, that route serves instantly, and any other new route, blocks while it generates, and then gets also saved to be served later, instantly too.

I added some more information and the problem is that we are attempting to load a CSS file

webpack fails in a different way, it fails when it tries to parse your `.woff` file as javascript.  If i remove the font file then it does work, but it creates empty modules for your css files.  hmmm

So the problem is that your `import(..)` is too dynamic and we end up trying to include .css dependencies.  A workaround for what you want to do is to rewrite your import to include `/index` 

```
const selectedTheme = await import(`@/styles/themes/theme-${themeName}/index`);
```

That will work with both webpack and turbopack and should be what you want.   

We definitely need a better error message here

Options:
1 create an empty ecmascript module in this case which appears to be what webpack does??
2 filter non-ecmascript modules from dynamic import resolve results, and don't even try to accumulate them (consequence is that you can only dynamic import es modules, not other assets)
3 produce an error if we match non-ecmascript moduels and encourage users to write more specific patterns.

im going to discuss with the team to figure out the best path forward, 3 is the most conservative so we might start there

body:
I understand this can be tricky! To get your route to render using the ISR approach with a dynamic path segment like `[subdomain]`, you'll need to add:

```tsx
export async function generateStaticParams() {
  return []
}
```

This tells Next.js that the page should be statically rendered.

A helpful note: You might think setting `dynamic = "force-static"` would handle this, but it actually works a bit differently than you'd expect. Instead of controlling whether the page renders statically, it changes how functions like `await headers()` behave—they'll return empty objects rather than actual values. I'd generally recommend avoiding `"force-static"` since it's easy to misunderstand what it does, and you might not get the behavior you're looking for.

body:
@timneutkens

> This is expected to fail because the `lib` folder is outside of the project.

I believe this assumption isn’t entirely accurate. When I run `bun install` (or `npm install`), the `lib` package is correctly installed inside `next/node_modules`, just like any other dependency. From Turbopack’s perspective, this should be a standard installed dependency, not an import from outside the project root.

For practical reasons, the source for `lib` happens to live in a sibling directory, but once installed, it exists within the project scope. The difference here is that I’m importing it as a package (`import {libNumber} from "lib"`) rather than using a relative path (`import {libNumber} from "../lib"`). The former should resolve to the installed dependency, which works correctly with Webpack but fails with Turbopack.

So my question is: why can’t Turbopack resolve it the same way Webpack does? I’m not importing a file outside the project, I’m importing an installed dependency.

body:
The problem here is that `withPayload` does already add `drizzle-kit` as external (as it should be). But Turbopack (and Webpack for that matter) doesn't actually make it external but bundles it instead because it's not resolveable from your app folder.
This is necessary because for externals, `path/to/your-app/.next/server/chunks/19238adef9229.js` would contain `require("drizzle-kit")` which means it has to be resolvable from `path/to/your-app/node_modules` (which is only the case if you declare `drizzle-kit` as a dependency in your app package.json).

Turbopack does have a warning for this case:
```
⨯ ./node_modules/.pnpm/@libsql+client@0.6.2/node_modules/@libsql/client/lib-esm/node.js
Package @libsql/client (serverExternalPackages or default list) can't be external
The request @libsql/client matches serverExternalPackages (or the default list), but it can't be external:
The request could not be resolved by Node.js from the project directory.
Packages that should be external need to be installed in the project directory, so they can be resolved from the output files.
Try to install the package into the project directory.
```

However, Payload patches console.warn to silence all of them: https://github.com/payloadcms/payload/blob/8cdb5dc29efbebfe43f9d4171990a38b1ec70b40/packages/next/src/withPayload.js#L18-L33


(For reference, there is a very long thread here about this: https://github.com/vercel/next.js/issues/68805. But that doesn't really help you here.)

body:
All cases mentioned here are caused by Turbopack to performing a kind of tree shaking even for these external files. That is incorrect however, as even unused imports (if you don't use any of the imported bindings, and the file is marked as `sideEffects: false`) are still needed at runtime, since Node.js will execute everything anyway.
Will be fixed by #85722

I think the risk of confusion is valid (it certainly tripped me up when I started using CSS Modules) but I do have two concerns:

body:
I've faced this disappointing and annoying issue too, and here’s a clear explanation of the core problem that I’ve narrowed it down to.

When `cacheComponents: true` is enabled in Next.js 16, any component that renders content using a **React Portal** doesn’t go away after navigation.  
If you navigate with `<Link>` or `router.push()`, the portaled content (like dropdowns, popovers, or modals) stays stuck on the screen and never disappears until you refresh the page.

I’ve tested this in:
- shadcn / Radix UI dropdown
- Headless UI popover
- React Aria popover
- and a manually written component using `ReactDOM.createPortal`

Here’s a minimal reproduction with all four test cases:  
👉 **[github.com/SorooshGb/nextjs-portal-cache-issue-repro](https://github.com/SorooshGb/nextjs-portal-cache-issue-repro)**

It demonstrates the problem clearly across multiple libraries.

body:
For what it's worth I think this is a known limitation called out in the docs.

> [Avoid passing dynamic inputs](https://nextjs.org/docs/app/getting-started/cache-components#avoid-passing-dynamic-inputs)
> You must not pass dynamic or runtime data into use cache functions unless you avoid introspecting them. Passing values from cookies(), headers(), or other runtime APIs as arguments will cause errors, as the cache key cannot be determined at pre-render time.

Can work around with generateStaticParams

> [params prop](https://nextjs.org/docs/app/api-reference/file-conventions/page#params-optional) - This is runtime data unless you provide at least one example value through [generateStaticParams](https://nextjs.org/docs/app/api-reference/functions/generate-static-params). When provided, those specific param values are treated as static for prerendered paths, while other values remain runtime

However being able to "use cache" with dynamic params seems like it would be incredibly helpful and the lack of this feature will stop any attempt at me moving my multi tenant app over to cache components.
author: rshaul

body:
> For what it's worth I think this is a known limitation called out in the docs.
> 
> > [Avoid passing dynamic inputs](https://nextjs.org/docs/app/getting-started/cache-components#avoid-passing-dynamic-inputs)
> > You must not pass dynamic or runtime data into use cache functions unless you avoid introspecting them. Passing values from cookies(), headers(), or other runtime APIs as arguments will cause errors, as the cache key cannot be determined at pre-render time.

I thought only the use of cookies(), headers(), connection(), and searchParams would force / require a dynamic context.

The Next team just updated the [documentation](https://nextjs.org/docs/app/api-reference/directives/use-cache-remote), but it's sill unclear to me if `"use cache"` is supposed to be incompatible with dynamic routes. I've added the `"use cache: remote"` directive [here for testing](https://next16-cache.vercel.app/en-us/remote): it is massively slow compared to 'use cache'.

> 
> Can work around with generateStaticParams
> 
> > [params prop](https://nextjs.org/docs/app/api-reference/file-conventions/page#params-optional) - This is runtime data nless you provide at least one example value through [generateStaticParams](https://nextjs.org/docs/app/api-reference/functions/generate-static-params). When provided, those specific param values are treated as static for prerendered paths, while other values remain runtime

Using `generateStaticParams` is ok when you have a few pages. In real world context (eg e-commerce), you can't really afford to prerender thousands of pages on every single build, and must rely on ISR. Before cacheComponents, we used segment config `export const dynamic = 'force-static'` on dynamic routes to generate on-demand static cache. Segment config not being compatible with cacheComponents, this is no longer an option.

body:
I’ve been wrestling with this problem for days — the page that caches perfectly on local, but not on Vercel. No docs, no examples, and the most confusing part: it worked locally.
I went deep — through canary builds, through PPR, through every experiment with use cache, unstable_cache, and even React’s native request scope `cache()` function (which does not cache in dynamic routes in Vercel). Every result felt magical and random until I finally understood what’s really going on (at least part of it).

There’s one internal doc / deep explanation that changed everything for my understanding:
https://github.com/vercel/next.js/issues/82477#issuecomment-3321468224

**Why ISR Isn’t Always the Right Answer**
ISR sounds like a silver bullet for speed, but it’s not. It rebuilds pages, not shared sub-trees.
If your app has a shared shell that used in hundreds of dynamic slugs, ISR can’t cache that shared tree across routes.
use cache (or use cache: remote) is what actually makes those shared layers reusable and fast.

Once I stopped trying to force ISR everywhere and started thinking in shell caching layers, things clicked.
Now my dynamic routes load fast, hit cached shells instantly, and fetch only minimal live data.

**Why This Feels So Complicated After PPR**
PPR merged with cache components early on — that’s why a lot of the old explanations (from v15) suddenly stopped making sense.
Before, you could think of static vs dynamic routes simply.
Now, PPR means there are nested caching phases inside one route tree — and whether your cache works depends entirely on which phase your component is executed in.

So yes, it’s confusing — but once you realize that **params define the boundary between static and dynamic**, it all becomes consistent.
Think of it as: What am I suspending and partially prerendering in this dynamic route?
Is it the full page? The components it renders? Or just the article name + content data fetched from the DB using the id/slug from the params promise?

**Do we really need to cache the full article page (or a big component that hold shared parts for all articles)?**
Or do I just need to cache the shell (which lives in the CDN) that holds everything except the data itself — which can be cached remotely (or even in CDN if we have magical future) and rendered partially?

I believe ISR has its place, but when dealing with very large numbers of dynamic routes, PPR with carefully designed caching layers can be faster and dramatically cheaper.

Hopefully this helps the next person before they spend a month trying to understand why their dynamic route won’t cache.

body:
Hi @leo-cheron thanks for raising this issue. And thanks everyone else for weighing in.

## TL;DR;
I'll get into a detailed explanation of what is going on in this scenario but I'll start with a TL;DR; The observed behavior is expected with Next.js and Vercel's current capabilities. Next.js's behavior is not likely to change, but Vercel and any other managed host can provide enhanced support for "use cache" to make it better match expectations

## The example
Ok so let's first understand the example.

There is a dynamic param on this page and it is being accessed immediately. This means that nothing else in this page can be prerendered statically because the param value isn't know before a user actually makes a request for this route. If you added a `generateStaticParams` function that provided at least one value for this param then Next.js will treat it like a prerenderable param in some circumstances. But given our test case does not use this API it's simpler to just consider everything after the `await params` as only available when a user navigation occurs (either initial document load or when click a next/link that performs a SPA style navigation)

## Default Cache behavior
Next.js is an open source project and can be deployed in a variety of environments. (Hopefully) understandably it cannot ship with a particularly advanced cache storage engine out of the box because these typically cost money and require specific setup. One thing is can do though is it can cache in memory. In practice this is only useful for simple self-hosted deployments because as soon as you run multi-process you run into issues of cache entry drift between process memory and you have to coordinate tag invalidation across processes. However since some people do deploy single process Next.js projects we do by default enable this memory cache as the storage for both default "use cache" functions as well as "use cache: remote" functions. In the latter case it isn't really remote caching but the point is many instances of `next start` are running production locally and rather than making you configure a remote cache for this case we default to the same in memory cache if a remote cache is not configured for your project.

So, given the default storage engine for "use cache", both `next dev` and `next start` will cache the Page component in the above example. On every user visit the cache entry is retrieved from the memory cache (if warm) and returned immediately.

## Caching behavior on 3rd party hosts
When Next.js runs on a provider host the host has the option to provide implementations of the cache storage engine for all of Next.js's caches. This includes "use cache" and "use cache: remote". This allows you to use these directives and get some platform provided caching behavior that is integrated with the platform. In Vercel's case "use cache" and "use cache: remote" have different implementations.

### Vercel "use cache: remote" handler
When remote cache handler on Vercel is hooked up to Vercel's paid Runtime Cache service. Reading and writing to this cache is managed by the framework and host integration and incurs costs to the Vercel customer. It also allows for the cached Page component in the original example to be read from a cache on every user request assuming the cache was warmed up once. And it works across any number of processes because the Runtime Cache service is a remote service that can respond to any instances of Next.js and is already integrated with time and tag based revalidation so that when you use these APIs within Next.js the cached reads from this remote cache service are managed in a way to be synchronized. (i.e. you won't end up reading stale data occasionally as soon as a new cache entry is produced)

### Vercel "use cache" handler
The default cache handler on Vercel does not actually cache anything in process memory. Vercel is a serverless function host and so your application is running on potentially many different processes simultaneously. Unlike the remote cache there is no way (yet) to inform every function execution about tag invalidations so it can correctly evict caches from local memory. To preserve correctness the default cache handler simply omits saving the entry anywhere on the server.

So in the context of the example code above, when deployed to Vercel (and likely any other managed host that runs more than one process per deploy) the server cache lifetime of "use cache" in a navigation context is generally going to be zero.

## No Cache Cache?!?
At first this might seem a bit extreme. How can you have a feature called "use cache" that doesn't cache. Well one of the tough things about building a very powerful and broad feature is that it can be easy to focus on the user case you currently have in front of you and measure it's capabilities in only that context without considering the other uses of the feature.

"use cache" is about more than server caching dynamic content. It is explicitly not just a better version of `unstable_cache()`. When you use "use cache" you are informing Next.js about a unit of data or UI and how long it can be used and what inputs it has so that Next.js can do a number of things
1. Partial Prerendering: Even without a dynamic runtime cache "use cache" allows Next.js to discover which parts of your application should be prerenderable and prefetched to enable instant navigations.
2. Stale time: Even if the server cache does not actaully cache the entry, the stale time information from that cache function tells the client router how long that part of the Page can be re-used before it must be refetched again.

The stale time features are still underdeveloped but we're actively focussed on making pages prefetchable with content that relies upon runtime only data like dynamic params and cookies and it is going to play a big role in these features very soon.

If you consider "use cache" a client API first and foremost, informing the router in running in your browser about what can be prefetched and how long it can be kept around before getting a  new copy from the server then the addition of server caching feels like an important consideration but not the only consideration for what "use cache" should do.

## Debugging Challenges
Even if you grant my position that it's reasonable to not cache in memory on the server on certain hosts it probably doesn't help that you couldn't have arrived at that conclusion intuitively on your own. We debated whether out of the box Next.js shouldn't memory cache either. We decided not to go this direction because then you can easily get dependent on these caches not actually caching and then if someone figures out how to do memory caching for the default cache handler you program semantics change.

Another idea is to make it configurable. We considered requiring users to register a cache handler implementation for their project so you had to take a step to make a choice about what you wanted the behavior to be. Then platforms could maybe expose their defaults as installable handlers you plug in. Vercel's would of course not do memory caching locally when configured. We did not do this as a requirement because we're trying to reduce config. Though I am coming around to the idea that we warn if no handlers are registered and then you go to your provider to install theirs and the installed version delegates to the host platform when deployed on it.

## Why not just remote cache always on Vercel
Another question many folks likely have is why not just always remotely cache on vercel. There are a number of reasons.
1. It costs money. You should be in control of when you opt into something that has a cost as much as possible. And since this API is not just about server caching it's not obvious that all instances of "use cache" actually are worth storing in a paid service.
2. Many inputs flowing into a "use cache" after something that cannot be prerendered are very high cardinality. Imagine saving a cache entry to a remote cache where the cache key has a user token in it, or the dynamic param is so high cardinality you'd expect near zero reuse. The cache metadata around lifetimes is still important to Next.js but the value proposition of remotely caching by default isn't necessarily there.
3. It means every cache lookup requires a network hop. Not every cacheable value is worth the network latency to check for a miss, especially if a miss is likely. Often it's just cheaper / easier to generate a fresh entry. A good example of this is Vercel's edge-config package. On Vercel you can read from this store in under a millisecond in many cases. To make the value read cacheable in say a prerender you wouldn't want to also have to introduce a network hop too.
4. You might be using "use cache" to do CPU caching. Some things are expensive to compute but don't require IO. there is React.cache but that has some challenge with respect to argument identify for cache keying. Using "use cache" is a nice way inside Next.js to get an in-request cache that has no network overhead and can still save you CPU time.

It's a tricky balance to strike but we decided that the extra information you encode when you choose to use "use cache: remote" to opt into remote caching makes sense because you are then in control of where the entry is stored and you are making a claim that all the above mentioned reasons for not remote caching don't apply in this case.

## Taking Control
"use cache" can be customized. You can provide a [cache handler implementation](https://nextjs.org/docs/app/api-reference/config/next-config-js/cacheHandlers) to `cacheHandlers.<name>` in `next.config.js` to take control of where `"use cache: <name>"` is cached on the server. `"use cache"` is equivalent to `"use cache: default"` which can be customized with `cacheHandlers.default`. You can also invent your own named handlers like `"use cache: foo"` and `cachenHandlers.foo: ...`.

One thing we'd caution though is to consider the reasons to not exclusively use a remote cache before turning all your "use cache" functions into remotely stored caches through default handler customization. You might find it's worth it to leave `"use cache"` for prerendered content and defining what is prefetchable and save `"use cache: remote"` for places where you have very slow upstream data services that have reasonable likeliehood of being re-used across multiple user requests or repeated request from the same user.

## Future Plans
Vercel will likely pursue a version of memory caching. So someday the expected behavior of this project is likely to be the actual behavior when deployed to vercel. However it is quite hard to integrate this with tag invalidation and so we expect it will take a while and we might have a few goes at it before we settle on something we feel comfortable shipping to users.

## Feedback
We really appreciate feedback. In particular I'd like to know if the explanation above makes sense and if messaging from Next.js itself could better convey this without you having to have discovered all these concepts in doc already.

body:
@leo-cheron those vercel.app links have deployment protection on so I requested access but cannot yet actually see the 
behavior you are describing. However I think I can imagine it and I can explain.


## Prefetching and Instant UI
When you have a link to some page Next.js will prefetch the link. What is returned from that prefetch depends on the nature of the destination. Before Cache Components you could use `loading.js` to define a prefetchable loading state. If you didn't use this however then only fully static pages would be prefetched and anything dynamic would render on navigation.

With Cache Components the model is slightly different. Every route is a partially prerendered. In this world the prefetch contains the statically prerenderable content and then on user navigation the rest of the page will render. Since your param is dynamic the `"use cache: remote"` function after the `await params` is not part of the static prerender so it must be fetched on user navigation. The remote caching should make this fast but it won't be prefetched so it will still take some time and the Suspense boundary around this page will show it's loading state.

We recognize that this is still somewhat limiting. You went through the effort to indicate the page could be cached and yet we still don't cache it in the client even after you have navigated to it the first time. Solving this problem is what the team is actively working on right now. While prefetching static content is great it should also be possible to instruct Next.js to prefetch content that does rely on request time data like cookies, headers, params, etc.... But even if you don't want to prefetch every link in this way there is a special case for the page you just navigated to. When we respond to a navigation that contains some or only `"use cache"` components we will start to treat this response as filling the prefetch cache so that if you navigate away and come back (within the same SPA session) we can instantly render the cached portions while any dynamic slots stream in. In your case the entire page is marked as cached so in effect this page would start to act like it was cached in the browser until the stale time occurs and then another navigation would lead to a fresh navigation.

The reason we don't just ship prefetching of request-time content all the time has to do with cost control. For some apps this may be desirable but for others it might be infeasible for all prefetches to incur actual compute wherease prefetching a prerendered static asset is fine. We need a way to express your preference for cost tolerance and ensure that the prefetch will actually result in something visible to the user. For instance if you instructed Next.js to prefetch the page with runtime data but you didn't use Suspense and you didn't use `"use cache"` then we cannot actually return any of that from the prefetch and we've wasted time responding to the prefetch with nothing of user value. So when you configure Next.js to do this more expensive form of prefetching you will also be configuring it to assert at build time (and in dev) that the prefetch led to something actually visible to the user. There are other challenges here b/c to do this at build time we don't have access to some actual request data, for instance if you depend on a session token from cookies we won't have a valid token to use for our assertions and may be unable to actually deliver on the goal of ensuring the prefetch was contentful.

## Static Params
Now params are sort of a special case because unlike other request time data Next.js can sometimes make params available to static prerenders. We have a `generateStaticParams` API that let's you specify during the build some set of params that you want to prerender ahead of time. Prior to Cache Components this point that route into ISR mode where any newly discovered param value when the server was running would be prerendered before being served to the user. This can help in some sites because you might not want to prerender the entire world on every build but you have a page that is largely static and you don't want to render dynamically on every visit.

With Cache Components we have partial prerendering so using static params has slightly different implications. Any prerendered-at-build-time params will end up largely the same. But we also produce what we call a "fallback shell". This is a version of the page where the param is considered dynamic (just like if you didn't have generateStaticParams at all). When a new param value is encountered at runtime Next.js decides whether to do the ISR thing or just resume the fallback shell with dynamic data depending on whether the fallback shell has any visible content in it. If the shell is empty it will do what Next.js does without Cache Components and just prerender the page and serve it to this user and any other requests to this path.

In the future we will be looking at making the version where the new param is treated as a resumable partial prerender into an upgrade heuristic. If a page with a particular param value is only visited a handful of times it will be treated as resumable. But if it is visited often it will "upgrade" to a static route because we have evidence it is low enough cardinality the static page is likely to be worth the cost of storage and revalidation.

## Your empty fallback work around
Now as for your removal of the fallback changing the behavior of the page on navigation, this is surprising. I'd like to see the code and also get access to the deployment. In general Next.js does not introspect the fallback so whether it is null or full of something interesting to look at it shouldn't change whether it is rendered or not. If it is, then it might be a weird interaction with a bug in React. We'll have to look into it.

I hope that helps clarify what is going on here. LMK if anything doesn't make sense

body:
@mdj-uk @leo-cheron 

without cache components if you have a dynamic param and you don't have `generateStaticParams` for that param then those routes will always just be dynamic. You may or may not see a loading state depending on how fast cached content resolves when you load those pages and if they are prefetched but generally I'd guess you would see a loading state

with `generateStaticParams` all new values for that param will trigger static generation. On first visit this can be slow b/c the whole page needs to prerender before anything is shown but then subsequent visits including client navs via link click should feel instant b/c the entire page is just available statically. This **can** be desirable but for many use cases it is not b/c if you have very high cardinality params you wouldn't want to pay the cost of prerendering and storing a page that is unlikely to be visited a second time.

With cache components the heuristic is different.

Any params availalbe during build via `generateStaticParams` are available statically. Any values discovered at runtime as considered high cardinality and will always be resolved on navigation. So even if you remote cache the page it still isn't prefetched b/c the param itself is considered dynamic so you need to click the link before it starts fetching anything. We know this is limiting which is why we are working on "runtime prefetching". This will allow you to opt into prefetching even dynamic things like params not known at build time. This won't help with the initial page load b/c that isn't prefetched but clicking a link that is prefetched with runtime values means you can now prefetch dynamic params or even data that relies on cookies.

body:
I believe that in middleware, errors thrown inside were surfaced through the request lifecycle, meaning onRequestError would report them. 

However, proxy is intended to act as a network boundary and routing layer and is executed outside the request instrumentation pipeline used by onRequestError.

Correct me if im wrong, but I believe this is totally expected behavior and you shouldn't be doing anything outside "rewriting, redirecting, modifying the request or response headers, or responding directly" as stated in the documentation for proxy.

body:
Just ran into this.  It's specific to Next.js 16+ projects using turbopack.

The issue isn't the logs.  It's that something gets triggered in the host server and CPU usage spikes.  It's a runtime issue - NOT A LOGGING ISSUE - (it will display 404 correctly in the log on the entered route).  You need to look at system resources spiking for this one - e.g. Activity Monitor on Mac.

**Work around** is to use webpack: `next dev --webpack`

## 문제 분석

문서에서 `proxy.ts`의 runtime 정보가 일관되지 않음:

1. **v16 블로그 포스트**: "runs on the Node.js runtime"

4. **Proxy docs**: 언급 없음

## 해결 방안

실제 동작을 확인한 결과, `proxy.ts`는:
- **Edge Runtime**을 사용합니다 (기본적으로 middleware와 동일)
- `export const runtime = 'nodejs'`로 명시하면 Node.js runtime 사용 가능

## 권장 문서 수정

다음 위치의 문서를 다음과 같이 수정하는 것을 제안합니다:

### 1. Proxy 문서 (app/api-reference/file-conventions/proxy)
추가:
```markdown
## Runtime

By default, `proxy.ts` runs on the **Edge Runtime**, similar to middleware.

If you need to use Node.js APIs, you can specify the runtime:

```typescript
export const runtime = 'nodejs'

export default function(request: Request) {
  // Your proxy logic
}
```
```

### 2. Migration Guide 일관성 유지
현재 설명이 맞음 (Edge Runtime) - 변경 불필요

### 3. Auth Docs 확인
"Edge Runtime" 설명이 맞음

### 4. V16 블로그 포스트
다음과 같이 수정 권장:
> `proxy.ts` runs on the **Edge Runtime** by default (for consistency with middleware), but you can opt into Node.js runtime if needed by setting `export const runtime = 'nodejs'`.

## 확인이 필요한 부분

이 수정 사항은 TypeScript 타입 정의와 실제 구현에서 확인해야 할 부분:
- `proxy.ts`의 기본 runtime 설정
- `export const runtime` 설정 지원 여부
- 실제 동작 테스트 필요

## 제안하는 다음 단계

1. 실제 코드베이스에서 `proxy.ts`의 runtime 설정 확인
2. 위 문서 위치에서 일관성 있게 설명 수정
3. Migration guide와 Auth docs는 이미 정확함 (변경 불필요)

body:
Reproduced the issue
Can confirm that the RangeError occurs when rendering a code frame [here](https://github.com/vercel/next.js/blob/17c65509535a2d19f5fbf99f273a91f531993364/packages/next/src/shared/lib/turbopack/utils.ts#L139)

The issue is that babel is matching a regex again a line that is 11Mb long inside of `opencv.js`  on that line which contains a `require('fs')` call, so we are trying to highlight it and blow the stack.

This doesn't fail during webpack because of the alias configuration, however if you remove that it also doesn't fail since webpack simply fails to report line/column information for this error message and thus we don't try to render a codeframe.

So a simple workaround for next is to be defensive when rendering codeframes.  I think disabling highlighting on long lines for `codeframe` is very reasonable.  (vscode does this) and in fact we perhaps shouldn't even be attempting to render a 11mb long line.

body:
looks like this is a known issue inside of the tokenizer library: https://github.com/lydell/js-tokens?tab=readme-ov-file#known-failures

in the case of opencv the issue is the large inline base64 wasm binary.  the tokenizer blows up on it (which is exactly the sort of thing called out in that readme)

The solution here for next is simply to be defensive against overly large inputs, this isn't ideal but with that in place we render a useful error message

```
 ⨯ ./node_modules/.pnpm/@techstark+opencv-js@4.11.0-release.1/node_modules/@techstark/opencv-js/dist/opencv.js:31:643
Module not found: Can't resolve 'fs'


Import trace:
  Browser:
    ./node_modules/.pnpm/@techstark+opencv-js@4.11.0-release.1/node_modules/@techstark/opencv-js/dist/opencv.js
    ./pages/index.ts

https://nextjs.org/docs/messages/module-not-found
```

Which would hopefully make it clear that the problem is missing alias config

I am also investigating how to make `code-frame` itself handle this more gracefully

Adding a data point: we're hitting this on `next@16.1.6` in a **non-static, non-export** app — standalone-mode SSR behind an Nginx reverse proxy — so the bug is not limited to `output: 'export'`.

### Setup
- `next@16.1.6`, `react@19`, App Router
- `next.config.ts`: `basePath: '/roadmap-generator'`, `output: 'standalone'` (no `output: 'export'`)
- Deployed in Docker, behind Nginx that serves `https://host/roadmap-generator/*` and forwards upstream
- No `generateStaticParams`, no `output: 'export'`

### Symptom
Dynamic route `/edit/[id]` (a client component — `'use client'` at the top of `page.tsx`) gets stuck on its loading state indefinitely. Opening devtools shows a mix of correctly-prefixed and **unprefixed** `_next/` URLs in the SSR HTML for this route:

| Page | URLs with `/roadmap-generator/` prefix | URLs without prefix |
|------|----------------------------------------|---------------------|
| `/` (static prerendered) | All chunks + fonts | — |
| `/edit/[id]` (dynamic SSR, `'use client'` page) | Some chunks | CSS bundle, several JS chunks, turbopack runtime chunk, both fonts |

The unprefixed URLs return 404 through the proxy (since the app is mounted at `/roadmap-generator/*`), the page never hydrates, and the user sees a permanent "Loading…".

Interestingly the dashboard `/` route emits all URLs correctly prefixed — so it's specifically the dynamic + client-component route shape that's affected.

### Workaround
Until this is fixed we're using an Nginx `sub_filter` to rewrite unprefixed `/_next/` URLs to `/roadmap-generator/_next/` in both HTML and RSC payloads:

\`\`\`nginx
proxy_set_header Accept-Encoding 'identity';
proxy_buffering on;
sub_filter_once off;
sub_filter_types text/html application/json text/x-component;
sub_filter '"/_next/'  '"/roadmap-generator/_next/';
sub_filter '\"/_next/' '\"/roadmap-generator/_next/';
\`\`\`

(The `Accept-Encoding: identity` and `proxy_buffering on` are required, otherwise `sub_filter` silently no-ops on gzipped/streamed responses.)

This restores the app but we'd love to drop it once the upstream fix lands. Happy to put together a minimal repro if it would help — my attempt at a trivial scaffold (basePath + CSS + `next/font` + client-component dynamic route) didn't reproduce, so the trigger is subtler than it first looked and I'd want guidance on which direction to push before spending more time on a repro.

@ceolinwill  Thanks for taking this seriously and for submitting an issue on the React repo.

It’s clear now that the core issue comes from React’s side.  
Either React needs to address this directly, or if that’s not possible, UI libraries need to be made aware of this scenario and start accounting for it by cleaning up their portals manually.

I always understood that the whole idea behind `cacheComponents`, `"use cache"` and the earlier "dynamicIO" was to remove all the implicit caching behavior from Next.js and make it fully opt-in + PPR — that was my expectation when enabling it, not to introduce new, unexpected behavior like route wrapping with `<Activity>`.

author: carlos-dubon

body:
@ijjk @timneutkens @sokra @huozhi @icyJoseph

This issue has now been open for ~3 months and it’s clearly affecting many production apps, not just edge cases.

Yes, we understand that the increased number of requests in Next.js 16 is _“working as intended”_ per the blog post and related issues.
But **“working as intended” does not equal “optimal”** when the real-world outcome is:

- 4× more requests
- Higher CPU usage
- Increased latency in some cases
- Significantly higher cloud bills

Many of us are seeing **real money impacts** here, hundreds to thousands of dollars per month, with no proportional, user-visible performance gains...

This effectively shifts cost from bandwidth to request count, and while that may look neutral on paper, **cloud providers bill per request**. We are the ones paying for that trade-off.

Staying on v15 is not a real solution.
Disabling prefetch entirely is not a real solution either (users do notice the navigation delay)

The fact that the community is forced to apply bandaid fixes (like wrapping `Link` to disable prefetch globally, or patching Next.js internals) should be a strong signal that something here is off.

I’ve been a long-term Next.js supporter, but this is exactly the kind of change that makes teams seriously reconsider their stack for new projects. I know I’m not the only one actively evaluating alternatives like Astro because of this.

We’re not asking for blame.
We’re asking for acknowledgment that:

- The current behavior is causing serious performance and cost regressions
- The trade-off is not acceptable for many production workloads
- This needs either smarter batching, fewer duplicate prefetches, or an opt-out that doesn’t punish UX

Please treat this as a real production concern, not just expected behavior.
This is impacting businesses, not benchmarks.

We need a fix!

author: AndreMaz

body:
This is a complete upgrade blocker for us. There is another issue here that has not really been called out.

In Next 16+ it looks like `generateMetadata` and the page render are now being served via separate `?_rsc=` requests. We make the same upstream API call in `generateMetadata` and in the RSC tree, and we rely on per-request dedupe to avoid doubling that work, either via Next’s `fetch` request collapsing or using `React.cache` wrappers.

Once those two pieces run in different RSC requests, that dedupe no longer applies because it only works within a single request context. In practice we now get two near-simultaneous calls hitting different instances, missing our downstream caches, and multiplying load on our API. This is not a small regression. It increases origin traffic, CPU, latency, and cost, and it is hard to mitigate without restructuring data flow or introducing heavier cross-request caching.

I'm working on moving routes back to Pages - we're part way through an incremental App Router migration but that very much looks on hold.

author: rodsotdia

body:
Apologies for the slow response here.

In Next.js 16, we changed prefetching so that shared layouts are deduplicated across routes. If two links share a layout segment, that segment is only fetched once. Previously, every `<Link>` prefetch would re-fetch the full route tree from the root, even layouts that were already cached from prefetching a different link. This was a frequent source of complaints — people reported redundant prefetch requests consuming significant bandwidth, especially on pages with many links. The deduplication addressed that feedback, but the tradeoff is more individual HTTP requests per route (one per segment rather than one for the whole route). For sites where you pay per request, or that have many links on a page, this is a real problem — and this had real cost implications for many of you. We should have addressed this sooner.

We always intended to follow up with a mechanism to bundle those per-segment requests back into fewer requests while preserving the deduplication benefits. The reason we didn't just bundle everything from the start is that we think the right long-term answer is a size-based heuristic, not a blanket "always bundle." Small segments benefit most from individual requests (where deduplication saves the most), while larger groups of segments benefit from being bundled together (where reducing request count saves the most). Getting that heuristic right takes iteration — but shipping the deduplication without the bundling meant the interim cost fell on users, and that wasn't an acceptable tradeoff to push out without warning. We should have told people about this before the release — at minimum, been upfront that this optimization was planned and advised people to evaluate the request volume impact before upgrading.

On the Vercel pricing question: I understand why this looks bad. Vercel charges per request, Next.js increased the number of requests, and Vercel makes Next.js. The technical decision was motivated by performance — layout deduplication eliminates redundant data transfer — not by pricing. But that distinction doesn't matter much when the result is a higher bill and no one told you it was coming. The lack of communication made the optics worse, and more importantly, it left people without the information they needed to make informed upgrade decisions. That's on us.

We've now implemented an initial fix as `experimental.prefetchInlining` ([#90555](https://github.com/vercel/next.js/pull/90555)). When enabled, all segment data for a route is bundled into a single response instead of individual per-segment requests. This brings the request count back down to roughly 2 per route in the common case — one for the route tree, one for all segment data. (More complex setups like parallel routes or intercepted routes may see slightly more, but still far fewer than the per-segment approach.) This works regardless of hosting platform — self-hosted, Vercel, or otherwise. It'll be available in the next canary release after the PR lands, and we'll follow with a stable maintenance release.

We expect some form of request bundling to become the default in a future release — but likely controlled by a size-based heuristic rather than a blanket on/off switch. The idea is that segments below a certain size threshold would still be fetched individually (maximizing deduplication), while larger groups would be bundled (minimizing request count). The experimental flag is there so the API can evolve toward that without a breaking change.

A note on the `experimental` label: this is production-ready and fully supported by the team. The only reason it's behind an experimental flag is that we may refine the API surface later — for example, changing from a boolean to a bytes threshold. Any such change would be simple and mechanical to migrate. Don't let the `experimental` namespace deter you from using this in production.

### Relevant Pull Request

- https://github.com/vercel/next.js/pull/90555

```js
// next.config.js
module.exports = {
  experimental: {
    prefetchInlining: true,
  },
}
```

We also saw a **3x increase in CPU and traffic to our app** after upgrading from Next.js v15 to v16. We further observed massive spikes in STALE cache responses and our full route cache hit ratio plummeting. 

After debugging of the Next.js internals, we discovered that **fresh pods are discarding perfectly valid, fresh cache entries for dynamic routes**. This is happening because critical TTL information (revalidate) relies on a "pod-local" memory state that only recovers the TTL *after* an unnecessary background render is forced. Combined with our aggressive prefetching, this missing TTL causes a thundering herd of concurrent renders.

**With this patch applied our render volume and resource usage returned to v15 levels**.

---
### Deep Dive
When using a custom cache handler with the App Router, if you export `revalidate = 600` on a dynamic route (e.g., `app/[locale]/page.tsx`), the first request to any specific path (like `/de`) on a fresh pod will **always** trigger a background revalidation, even if the cache returns a completely fresh payload.

#### 1. Exact String Matching at Runtime
When a request comes in for a dynamic path like `/de`, `IncrementalCache.get` asks `SharedCacheControls` for the TTL for that specific path.
```typescript
// packages/next/src/server/lib/incremental-cache/shared-cache-controls.external.ts
public get(route: string): CacheControl | undefined {
  // 1. Check in-memory map
  let cacheControl = SharedCacheControls.cacheControls.get(route)
  if (cacheControl) return cacheControl
  
  // 2. Exact match against dynamic routes manifest (fails route != pattern)
  const dynamicPrerenderData = this.prerenderManifest.dynamicRoutes[route]
  if (dynamicPrerenderData) { ... }
  
  return undefined
}
```

The `route` argument here is the *resolved concrete path* (e.g., `"/de"`). But the prerender manifest only contains the *route pattern* (e.g., `"/[locale]"`). Because it does a direct object key lookup instead of a Regex match. The lookup returns `undefined`. 

#### 2. The 1-Second Fallback & Concurrent Render Storms
Because the runtime fails to match the route pattern, `IncrementalCache` falls back to its hardcoded default of **1 second**.
*(`calculateRevalidate` in `packages/next/src/server/lib/incremental-cache/index.ts`)*

Here is how this completely breaks down under aggressive prefetching in a Kubernetes cluster:

1. A fresh pod spins up (e.g., during a deployment or scaling event).
2. Due to our aggressive prefetching and the v16 RSC request volume, a flood of requests for `/de` hits the fresh pod.
3. The custom cache handler returns perfectly fresh entries from the cache (e.g., it is 45 seconds old, out of a 600s TTL).
4. Next.js fails to find the TTL in the pod's memory or the manifest, and defaults to 1 second.
5. Because 45s > 1s, Next.js marks the perfectly good cache as `isStale = true`.
6. **The Thundering Herd:** Because the prefetch requests are arriving concurrently, Next.js fires off multiple unnecessary background renders for the exact same page (`/de`) at the exact same time.
7. **The "Copy-on-Write" Recovery:** Once the *first* of these background renders finishes, Next.js executes the React tree, *finally* extracts the `revalidate = 600`, and saves it to the pod-local in-memory map: `SharedCacheControls.cacheControls.set('/de', { revalidate: 600 })`.
8. Subsequent requests to `/de` on *that specific pod* work perfectly.
9. But a request to `/fr` on that pod, or `/de` on *any other fresh pod*, will suffer the exact same 1-second penalty

This pod-local "copy-on-write" state means our shared cache is practically useless for dynamic routes immediately following a deployment. Every unique path requires a background render on every unique pod just to learn the TTL.

*(Note: Data Cache (`fetch`) works fine because `IncrementalCache` trusts the `revalidate` value stored *inside* the cached payload itself. Pages actively ignore this payload TTL and rely strictly on the `SharedCacheControls` lookup).*

---
### Our Workaround
To prevent our backend from being hammered with concurrent renders on every unique dynamic path after a deploy, we had to patch `SharedCacheControls.get` to return a sensible fallback TTL instead of `undefined`.
```javascript
return {
  revalidate: process.env.NEXT_SHARED_CACHE_CONTROLS_REVALIDATE_FALLBACK
    ? Number(process.env.NEXT_SHARED_CACHE_CONTROLS_REVALIDATE_FALLBACK)
    : 60,
  expire: undefined,
};
```
This ensures that valid data loaded from the cache is treated as fresh for at least 60 seconds. When it finally *does* expire and trigger a render it saves the correct TTL to the pod-local memory safely without the initial thundering herd.

---
### Expected Behavior
How we would actually like to have handled this: We are already successfully storing metadata (including the correct `revalidate` time) alongside our cache entries. **The TTL staleness check in `IncrementalCache` should be able to use this payload information** (just as it already does for Data Cache `fetch` entries) instead of relying entirely on the brittle `SharedCacheControls` in-memory + manifest mechanism. 

Unfortunately, we cannot simply patch this staleness logic ourselves. The `IncrementalCache` class for App Router pages is heavily precompiled and inlined, making any direct patches to `isStale` calculations unmaintainable. 

Allowing the Full Route Cache to trust TTL data returned from the `cacheHandler` payload would completely eliminate the reliance on pod-local state, permanently fixing this issue for distributed deployments.

body:
I think the docs should explain more clearly how prefetching works for PPR routes. They explain PPR, but not how prefetching works on those routes (the default rendering behavior when Cache Components is enabled btw): https://nextjs.org/docs/app/guides/prefetching#partial-prerendering-ppr

My expectation is that if multiple links share the same route shell, Next should prefetch that shared shell once and cache it on the client, so navigation feels instant when the user clicks one of those links.

For example, on a grid of `/products/[slug]` links, I would expect a single prefetch for the shared product-page shell, not separate prefetch requests for each visible product link.

What I’m seeing instead is up to 5 prefetch requests per link. On a page with 20 product links, that can easily become around 100 requests. That seems hard to reconcile with the idea of prefetching as a way to prepare the client for instant navigation to the shared shell.

author: icyJoseph

body:
@icyJoseph I'd like to add a use case where supporting `"use cache"` in proxy/middleware would make a lot of sense — at least for self-hosted environments.

**Our setup:**

We self-host Next.js on our own Node.js server. Our middleware/proxy handles two key things:

1. **URL resolution from CMS** — every incoming request is resolved in middleware to an internal route via a CMS API (headless e-commerce). The CMS determines which page should be rendered based on the URL.

2. **Redirects from CMS** — users configure their own redirects in the CMS. Middleware needs to evaluate them on every request.

Both of these operations are ideal candidates for caching — CMS data changes on the order of hours/days, yet middleware calls them on **every request**. When CMS data changes, we revalidate via a revalidation hook (`cacheTag`), so Next.js cache semantics would be a perfect fit here.

**The code sharing problem:**

We use the same functions (e.g. `locationResolve()`) in server components, where `"use cache"` works without issues. But as soon as we call the same function from middleware/proxy, it fails. This forces us to either:
- duplicate the logic without `"use cache"` for middleware, or
- implement our own caching layer outside of Next.js cache semantics.

Both are unnecessary complexity when the same function works everywhere else in the application.

**Question:**

Is there a way to detect at runtime that a function is being called from a middleware/proxy context? That would at least allow us to conditionally skip the `"use cache"` directive and fall back to our own cache.

Alternatively — is there any plan to support `"use cache"` in middleware/proxy for the self-hosted Node.js runtime, where middleware runs on the same server as the rest of the application and there's no architectural reason why caching shouldn't work?

This is actually working as intended. If you inspect the network requests going to the Next.js server, they send different values for the request headers. These request different files/parts/segments from Next.js, and do not represent duplicate requests.

This is due to Next.js 16 making the Client Segment Cache the new mechanism that we use to request/store segment data for prefetching. These prefetch requests made to routes that are static or partially static will not trigger an invocation, and instead will be served out of the cache.

body: I can confirm this issue and would like to add an important detail about the severity: **prefetch requests are blocking user navigation**. ### Additional Impact: Navigation Blocking In our production application, we're experiencing the same duplicate prefetch behavior, but with a critical UX issue: - **Navigation is blocked** when users click a link before the prefetch request completes - Multiple prefetch requests for `/c/brands?_rsc=` can take **5+ seconds** to complete - If a user clicks the brands link during this time, navigation is delayed until all prefetch requests finish - This creates a very poor user experience where the site feels unresponsive ### Our Setup - **Next.js**: 16.0.1 - **React**: 19.2.0 - **Navigation**: Using `next-intl`'s Link component wrapped in custom components - **Affected Route**: `/c/brands` (complex server component with multiple Suspense boundaries) ### Reproduction 1. Build: `pnpm build` 2. Start: `pnpm start` 3. Navigate to home page 4. Open DevTools Network tab, filter for `_rsc=` 5. Observe multiple prefetch requests for the same route 6. **Click the link before prefetch completes** ← Navigation is blocked here 7. Notice the delay until prefetch finishes ### Network Behavior We see multiple requests like: ``` GET /c/brands?_rsc=abc123 GET /c/brands?_rsc=def456 GET /c/brands?_rsc=ghi789 ```
author: arfa123

body:
The reason that you're seeing different values for the `?_rsc=` query parameter is that request headers like `Next-Router-State-Tree`, `Next-URL`, `RSC`, `Next-Router-Prefetch` and `Next-Router-Segment-Prefetch` are different! These requests are loading small files, and the client deduplicates requests for the same layout shared between different links. For example, if you had 10 links to different "products" that all shared the same layout, we'd only fetch the shared layouts once, reducing the total bandwidth transferred over the network.

We'll definitely take a look at any strange navigation behaviours though!

author: eps1lon

body:
Hi @eps1lon,

I understand that this particular GitHub issue about multiple prefetch requests is considered working as intended, in the sense that these are distinct prefetches rather than duplicated ones. In that context, closing this specific issue makes sense.

That said, there are several other reports focusing on the infrastructure impact of these multiple requests on Vercel and similar platforms (see #85470), including:

* increased CPU usage
* increased CDN costs due to per-request billing
* increased deployment times from generating and transferring more files

Our main concern is to ensure that these cost implications are not themselves considered working as intended, even if the underlying prefetch behavior is.

body:
https://react.dev/reference/rsc/use-client#serializable-types
> Functions that are **not** exported from **client-marked** module

I could fix this issue by creating custom `next/link` component like below:

```tsx
// ./CustomNextLink.tsx
'use client'

export { default as CustomLink } from 'next/link'
```

```tsx
import { CustomLink } from './CustomNextLink';

<Header linkComponent={CustomLink} />
```

However, since [next/link is already marked as 'use client'](https://github.com/vercel/next.js/blob/55ef0e3ebc1d43e1a4a191341dc2a415e12124d4/packages/next/src/client/link.tsx#L1), so I'm wondering why this workaround is necessary. 🤔
author: ktmouk

body:
Hi, I was able to reproduce the issue. 

I observed that you can unblock with a "pass through re-export" file:

```tsx
'use client'

import Link from 'next/link'

export { Link }
```

NOT saying you should do that - I've asked the team to look into this. Thanks for the report. 

I think the issue was introduced when this module was included https://github.com/vercel/next.js/blob/ad93e452a458a27110e7cf5e8272e40d4741b756/packages/next/src/client/app-dir/link.react-server.tsx#L4 - hopefully we'll have time to loop back on this soon.

body:
Fix submitted in #93246 — the root cause is that `file_stem()` (Rust/Turbopack) and `path.parse().name` (JS/webpack) only strip the last extension, so `proxy.page.ts` yields `"proxy.page"` instead of `"proxy"` and proxy detection fails silently.

The fix uses `file_name().split('.').next()` (Rust) / `base.split('.')[0]` (JS) to extract the base name before the first dot. Covers all 5 detection sites (3 Rust, 2 JS) and includes an e2e test. Verified in all 4 modes (dev/prod × turbopack/webpack).

### Why was this issue closed?

To be able to investigate, we need access to a reproduction to identify what triggered the issue. body: I’d like to share what I’ve found so far. I discovered that references to the objects that persist after a request remain in a variable with the distinctive name pendingOperations. This implementation does not exist in the Next.js source code but is present in the React react-server implementation. I assume that this code is used internally by the Next.js server runtime. https://github.com/facebook/react/blob/edd05f181b72272fb87b77bd84d2c048a4613955/packages/react-server/src/ReactFlightServerConfigDebugNode.js#L62 It’s also been confirmed that the difference between production and development — where the issue occurs only in development mode — is due to differences in the runtime. A memory leak occurs when using "next/dist/compiled/next-server/app-page-turbo.runtime.dev.js". https://github.com/vercel/next.js/blob/684d11bfc9fd491102c4f13168ff681df6001952/packages/next/src/server/route-modules/app-route/module.compiled.js#L21 I understand that this issue is related to the tracing implementation using async_hooks, but I don’t yet know why the references continue to be retained. In app-page-turbo-runtime.dev.js, which includes the previously mentioned react-server implementation, I confirmed that simply replacing the async_hooks callbacks with dummy implementations allows garbage collection to work properly even in an infinite loop. However, I still don’t know whether the issue of references not being released even after a request has completed is a potential problem on the Next.js side or on the React side.

body:
We're experiencing a severe memory leak in our Next.js 16.1.6 + React 19.2.4 application. Memory grows continuously with each request, eventually causing OOM crashes in production (Docker/Kubernetes) and the dev server.

Observed Behavior
- Memory growth: ~4-6 MB per page load in development, much faster under production load
- Production impact: Container crashes with OOM (exit code 137) after ~8 minutes of traffic
- Memory pattern: Both heap and external memory grow continuously without plateau
- Memory Growth Under Load (Production Container)
- 
```json
{"type":"MEMORY","timestamp":"...","rss_mb":92,"heap_total_mb":33,"heap_used_mb":21,"external_mb":4}
// ... 8 minutes of traffic ...
{"type":"MEMORY","timestamp":"...","rss_mb":4664,"heap_total_mb":3155,"heap_used_mb":3037,"external_mb":1090}
```
We already tried and it not fixed the issue:
❌ Custom cache handler with bounded maps
❌ Setting revalidate: false on all fetch calls
❌ Setting dynamic = 'force-dynamic' on pages
❌ Setting httpAgentOptions.keepAlive: false
❌ Setting experimental.preloadEntriesOnStart: false
❌ Replacing native fetch with node-fetch v2

After analyzing the memory usage we identify the next item that is consuming more:
- WeakRef (+42,433 instances): These are used by React's reconciler. They should be garbage collected when targets are unreachable, but they're growing - meaning their targets are being retained somewhere.
- ReactPromise (+4,584 instances): This is React's internal promise type for RSC. The accumulation suggests streaming promises aren't being cleaned up after resolution.
- CallSiteInfo/StackFrameInfo: V8 retention of stack trace information, possibly from Error objects or performance tracking.
author: tigraqwerty

body:
@tigraqwerty I'm facing the same issue. I've even tried the node-fetch v2 [#85914](https://github.com/vercel/next.js/issues/85914#issuecomment-3811283072).

What "helped" as a work around was to set a memory limit on the container running the application. Shitty? Yes. It works? Kinda. It will reach the maximum memory allocation and the the process will try to force reusing memory.

Another thing we did was to create a cron that every once and a while, it wipes clean the `.cache` folder. Brute force? Yes, totally. But it helped a lot.

**The problem still persists**, but it takes a lot longer to appear. Previously the leak would cause the site to go down in about 30min-1h. Now it takes around 16h or so.

Another work around was to pick the least amount of traffic hour of the day, drop the running container and switch to another one, clean. It works like """fast restart""" your server.

author: djjrip

body:
I hit the exact same `pendingOperations` leak described above — great detective work @pontasan.

In my case the immediate trigger was the Turbopack hot-reloader: `hot-reloader-turbopack.js` creates one `subscribe()` call (an async generator) per compiled server chunk, running as an infinite `for await…of` loop. The async generator produces **3–4 async hook IDs per HMR event** (the generator object itself, a step-Promise per `.next()`, the yielded inner-Promise, and a `Promise.resolve()` wrapper from `for await…of`). All of these end up in `pendingOperations` with captured stack traces.

With many subscriptions × many events the Map grows faster than V8's GC can drain it, ultimately throwing:

```
RangeError: Map maximum size exceeded
    at Map.set (<anonymous>)
    at AsyncHook.init (…/app-page-turbo.runtime.dev.js:53:268561)
    at promiseInitHookWithDestroyTracking (node:internal/async_hooks:336:3)
    at createIterator (…/next/dist/build/swc/index.js:512:31)
    at …/next/dist/server/dev/hot-reloader-turbopack.js:127:30
```

I've opened a PR that replaces the async generator in `subscribe()` with a manual `AsyncIterableIterator` that returns one `Promise<IteratorResult<T>>` per `next()` call — reducing async-resource creation from O(events × 3–4) to O(events × 1):

**https://github.com/vercel/next.js/pull/91704**

The `pendingOperations` leak in request handling (the original case in this issue) may have a separate cause, but reducing the hot-reloader's async-resource pressure should at least help the dev-server-crash variant.

body:
I wish the docs were clearer, but nothing is cached client side unless it's prefetched. (Unless you alter [`experimental.staleTimes.dynamic`](https://nextjs.org/docs/app/api-reference/config/next-config-js/staleTimes) to be non-zero)

By default anything static or marked 'use cache' is prerendered and prefetched. But not 'use cache: private'. So we need to set `prefetch={true}` on link (as opposed to `'auto'`/`null`), or call `router.prefetch`.

I think the plan is that in future we can configure 'runtime prefetching' for a page, which means that content marked 'use cache: private' will also be prefetched and cached by default. But that's not yet documented/recommended.

body:
I investigated this issue and opened **#95710**.

The root cause was that the codemod assumed `@eslint/migrate-config` always generates `eslint.config.mjs`. For `.eslintrc.js` and `.eslintrc.cjs`, it actually generates `.js`/`.cjs`, causing the reported failure.
