body:
This looks related to a broader Turbopack server chunking issue.

There is another Turbopack bug where component-level CSS Modules are over-shared across unrelated routes, causing render-blocking CSS to load where the component is never rendered. In this issue, the opposite problem appears: server dependencies are under-shared, and the same class is duplicated per route, breaking `instanceof` checks.

In both cases, #89252 Turbopack seems to be compiling each route as an isolated server bundle without a stable shared module graph for server code. Webpack does not exhibit either behavior.

This suggests a systemic issue with how Turbopack deduplicates (or fails to deduplicate) server-side dependencies across routes.

If this issue is not already being worked on, I’d be happy to take it and help work on a fix.
author: Shanmukha27-web

body:
bundling the module into multiple different output chunks is expected.  the different routes may end up in different lambdas in production and so need to be self contained.  The heuristics for shared chunks are complex and so it doesn't always happen especially when the sharable dependencies are small.

however if both chunks are loaded in the same runtime the actual module should be deduplicated by our runtime.    

Can you clarify the error case in the repro?  simply bundling the module twice is not considered an error
author: lukesandberg

body: At iFixit we ran into a similar Turbopack issue that resulted in duplicating a module that provides `useContext()` and `<Provider>`. The duplication results in two separate Context objects (also separate Providers) resulting in the Context not being able to use the value from the Provider up the tree.

body:
Adding a corroborating data point from a production Next.js 14 → 16 (Turbopack) migration, since this matches the maintainer's explanation above almost exactly, plus a related crash we hit while investigating a config-level workaround.

**Context**: after migrating a Pages Router app off webpack to Turbopack (Next 16.2.10), we saw a +26% overall First Load JS regression, with transactional pages up 45–56%. Using `next experimental-analyze` and manual gzip/module-ID diffing of `.next/static/chunks/*.js`, we found the same shared-module-duplication pattern described here, just for plain ESM classes/functions pulled in via static imports (not dynamic `import()`), across Pages Router routes rather than App Router lambdas.

Concretely: our `/home`'s own ~86 KB gzip chunk shares 27 of its 42 module IDs with an ~86 KB gzip chunk also loaded by other routes, plus ~15 more modules unique to home. Instead of the 27 shared modules being extracted once and home loading a small delta chunk on top, Turbopack recompiled all 27 into a second, near-full-size chunk. The same ~53 KB/~86 KB chunk-size pairing repeats across other page routes. This lines up with the "heuristics for shared chunks are complex and so it doesn't always happen especially when the sharable dependencies are small" explanation above: in our case the "small" shared dependency graph is a 3rd-party SDK client/auth module imported from `_app`.

We also tried `experimental.turbopackTreeShaking: true` (advanced module-fragment tree shaking) hoping finer-grained shaking would shrink these duplicated chunks. It crashed our production build outright:

```
thread 'tokio-runtime-worker' panicked at turbopack/crates/turbopack-ecmascript/src/tree_shake/graph.rs:743:16:
index out of bounds: the len is 8 but the index is 10
Error [TurbopackInternalError]: index out of bounds: the len is 8 but the index is 10
  ... Execution of MiddlewareEndpoint::edge_chunk_group failed
  ... Execution of EcmascriptModulePartAsset::select_part failed
  ... Execution of split_module failed
```

This looks like the same index-desyncing bug class fixed in #95516, just hit via our `middleware.ts` module graph rather than the reported repro. Happy to share a minimal repro if useful, since PR #95516 mentioned there may be other cases in the advanced tree-shaking codepath still panicking.

Is there a tracking issue (or is this issue the tracking issue) for exposing a user-facing knob analogous to webpack's `optimization.splitChunks.cacheGroups`/`minChunks`, so apps with this shape of shared-dependency-across-many-routes can opt into more aggressive extraction even at the cost of Turbopack's default per-route self-containment? Happy to provide our route-bundle-stats and chunk diffs if that would help prioritize.

Turbopack appears to be doing a strict **string comparison** between the Next.js version and the @next/swc version.

In cases where Next.js is **15.5.11** and **@next/swc is 15.5.7** (which is currently the latest published SWC version), Turbopack reports a version mismatch, even though this setup is fully valid and installed automatically by Next.js itself.

This is a false-positive warning: the versions are semver-compatible (same minor), and there is no real incompatibility.

Thanks for looking into this.

I can confirm this is reproducible consistently and appears to be Turbopack-specific:
- Does not reproduce when Turbopack is disabled (`experimental.turbo = false`)
- Webpack scopes the CSS correctly to only the routes where the component is rendered
- With Turbopack, component-level CSS Modules are included in unrelated route chunks and block render

This has a significant production impact in larger apps (multiple seconds of render-blocking CSS).

If this issue is not already being worked on, I’d be happy to take it and work on a fix. Please let me know if that’s okay.
author: Shanmukha27-web

body:
Hi! I’ve been investigating this CSS behavior and wanted to confirm intent before prototyping a fix.

After testing production builds with **both Turbopack and Webpack**, this is not Turbopack-only. CSS from universal routes (specifically `app/not-found`) is promoted into a shared chunk and preloaded globally.

This creates a scaling issue in large apps:

- fallback CSS is render-blocking even on unrelated routes
- unused styles block paint
- Lighthouse blocking time grows with app size

Additionally, the preload for universal CSS appears before route-critical CSS, effectively prioritizing fallback styles over active route styles.

This looks like an architectural side effect of universal route hoisting rather than a bundler bug.

---

## Evidence

Production dashboard route loading `not-found` CSS:

![universal-css-preload](https://github.com/user-attachments/assets/f8014883-2b64-402b-8383-969da994f22d)

---

Is this preload behavior intentional for error/not-found safety, or unintended?  
If intentional, would there be interest in a lower-priority or deferred loading strategy so route CSS remains unblocked?

Happy to investigate or prototype once direction is clarified.

body:
I confirmed that this is currently expected behaviour (architecture trade off) of next.js 
In the App Router model, app/not-found and app/error are treated as part of the Global Shell availability. Since any route segment can potentially throw a 404 or an Error during streaming or navigation, Next.js eagerly preloads these fallback UI styles to ensure an instant, layout-shift-free transition to the error state.
Currently,What we can do is try keep not-found ultra lightweight, use tailwind utility class instead of other heavy libraries

body:
Hey I've been investigating this and I have found that this is WAI prefetching. My setup is to do a production build like

`pnpm build && pnpm start`

We need to [Disable Prefetch](https://nextjs.org/docs/app/guides/prefetching#disabled-prefetch) in order to stop the importing of the button component and the index page. There are two places the index page is linked to where we need to disable prefetch.

Firstly, the `not-found.tsx` route is being pre-loaded in this application, so we need to replace the `<Button>` with `<Link prefetch={false} ...>`.  

Secondly the `<Header>` component has a `<LInk>` to `/` that also needs to have prefetch disabled.

I wrote the code that demonstrates this as a PR to the reproduction repo: https://github.com/t18n/next-js-app-router-css-bundle-repro/pull/1

Let me know if I misunderstood or missed something. I hope this explains it but if not I'm happy to dig deeper.
author: robert-j-webb

body:
@robert-j-webb thanks for testing and sharing the PR appreciate the investigation 

I tried your changes locally, but unfortunately the issue still persists on my side.

Disabling `<Link prefetch={false}>` does reduce some extra page prefetching, but the CSS from unrelated routes is still being bundled and loaded even when there is no navigation or prefetch happening.

So it doesn’t seem to be only a prefetch problem.

From my testing, this looks more like an architectural behavior:

• `not-found` / `error` routes are treated as globally reachable  
• their CSS is hoisted to shared chunks  
• which makes it render-blocking  

@t18n Removing `not-found` technically “fixes” the CSS load, but that hurts UX (blank/unstyled fallback), so it’s not really a practical solution.

For now, the only safe workarounds I’ve found are:

1. (Recommended) Use Tailwind utility classes in `not-found`  
   → already global, zero extra CSS, no CLS

2. Dynamically import CSS modules  
   → avoids hoisting but causes layout shift (CLS), so not production friendly

3. styled-jsx  
   → similar behavior, still loaded at render time

So realistically the best approach today is just keeping `not-found` extremely lightweight and avoiding heavy component/library imports.

A proper fix probably needs a framework-level change (like lower-priority loading or optional CSS isolation), which feels more like a feature request than something we can fully solve at the app level.

Happy to keep experimenting if we find more clues 🙂

author: robert-j-webb

body:
We were investigating this issue in the source and wanted to share what we found in case it helps narrow things down.

There seem to be two layers to this. The first is the one most discussed in this thread (error/not-found CSS), but we think the second one is what explains @t18n's case where removing not-found.tsx didn't help.

## Layer 1: Shared layout module graph walks pull CSS from all transitive imports

This is likely the bigger factor and the one that explains why the issue persists even without not-found pages.

Each server entry (e.g., `app/[locale]/blog/[slug]/page`) is built by `next-app-loader`, which recursively resolves convention files (layout, error, loading, not-found, etc.) at every segment level. Each resolved file becomes an eager import:

`packages/next/src/build/webpack/loaders/next-app-loader/index.ts:1113`
```js
const ${varName} = () => import(/* webpackMode: "eager" */ ${JSON.stringify(modulePath)});
```

Then `FlightClientEntryPlugin.collectComponentInfoFromServerEntryDependency` (line 729) does a **recursive walk of every module reference** from each entry dependency. Any CSS module reachable anywhere in that walk gets collected:

`packages/next/src/build/webpack/plugins/flight-client-entry-plugin.ts:792-804`
```js
if (isCSSMod(mod)) {
  // ...
  CSSImports.add(modResource)
}
```

Since layouts are shared across all child routes, any CSS reachable from the layout's import graph gets collected into every route entry that shares that layout. So if `[locale]/layout.tsx` imports a `<Header>` that imports a `<Navigation>` that references route-specific components, all their CSS ends up in every route under that layout, even routes that never render those components.

The walk stops cleanly at client component boundaries (line 817) — it does not recurse into a client component's own CSS imports. Client-component CSS arrives separately through the injected client entry loader (`next-flight-client-entry-loader.ts:53-55`), which eagerly imports the client modules and their CSS.

## Layer 2: Error/not-found/global-error CSS compounds the problem

On top of the layout walk, several mechanisms add more CSS that bypasses deduplication:

### `global-error` is added to all tree layers

`packages/next/src/build/webpack/loaders/next-app-loader/index.ts:360-362`
```js
// Add global-error to ALL layers' filePaths, so that it's always available.
filePaths.set(GLOBAL_ERROR_FILE_TYPE, globalError)
```

This runs for every segment layer, not just root, which makes global-error CSS a dependency of every route entry.

### CSS deduplication doesn't cover error/not-found

`packages/next/src/build/webpack/plugins/flight-client-entry-plugin.ts:134`
```js
const POSSIBLE_SHARED_CONVENTIONS = ['template', 'layout']
```

`deduplicateCSSImportsForEntry` (line 137) only tracks CSS inheritance through template and layout. Error and not-found conventions aren't in this list, so their CSS ends up in every route's client entry without dedup.

### Shared chunk promotion via CssChunkingPlugin

`packages/next/src/build/webpack/plugins/css-chunking-plugin.ts:306`

When `chunk.split(newChunk)` creates shared CSS chunks, CSS that appears across multiple entries gets merged into chunks visible to all entrypoints.

### No deferred loading path for boundary CSS

`packages/next/src/server/app-render/render-css-resource.tsx`

All CSS is rendered as `<link rel="stylesheet" precedence="next">`. There's no mechanism to lazy-load styles that are only needed when an error boundary activates.

---

We looked at a few possible fix directions but each has tradeoffs we're not sure about:

- **Adding error/not-found to `POSSIBLE_SHARED_CONVENTIONS`** would change the CSS dedup inheritance model. Template/layout CSS is designed to cascade down the route tree, but error CSS probably shouldn't follow the same inheritance rules. Could cause missing styles when error boundaries actually activate in nested routes.
- **`STANDALONE_BUNDLE_CONVENTION`** (currently `global-not-found`) looked promising at first, but on closer reading it ensures standalone entries get their *own* copy of CSS. It doesn't prevent that CSS from appearing in other entries, so extending it wouldn't solve the promotion.
- **Deferring error/not-found CSS loading** would reduce blocking time, but risks a flash of unstyled content when error boundaries actually trigger. The eager loading at line 360 seems to be an intentional tradeoff ("so that it's always available"), so changing it would need careful consideration.
- **Scoping the layout module graph walk** so it doesn't collect CSS from components that aren't rendered on the current route would address the root cause, but it's a fundamental change to how the bundler determines CSS dependencies per entry.

Restricting `global-error` CSS injection to the root layer only might be the least risky starting point. It already only renders at root level, so its CSS arguably doesn't need to be in every layer's entry. But we don't know the full picture on Turbopack parity or edge cases there either.

Hope the code pointers are useful. The maintainers here will know which tradeoff fits best.

author: vtamara

body:
thanks for confirming that this works 👍 

in the long run we plan on supporting the long tail of platforms using wasm but we are not yet ready to commit to doing that work (in theory this becomes easier when we update to NapiV3.... but also non trivial).  Natively supporting openbsd is also an option but it would be a lot of overhead and expose us to some non trivial costs (even rust only supports openbsd as tier 3), so i don't forsee us doing it.

body: I'm still testing but i have a fix for this issue in https://github.com/vercel/next.js/pull/89615, but i have confirmed that it fixes the repro case and I have an understanding of the root cause.  Shared chunk heuristics could violate dependency ordering if you were unlucky.  This wouldn't happen in dev because we don't do global shared chunk analysis, and because it was sensitive to shared chunks, adding/removing a dependency could trigger/fix it since it would change the set of shared chunks.

author: jonas-is-coding

body:
Correction with exact package names:

This is an ESLint 10 compatibility issue rather than a project-specific configuration problem. In the current state, `eslint-config-next` still depends on `eslint-plugin-react` behavior that assumes APIs changed in ESLint 10, which is why errors move between rules like `react/display-name`, `react/no-direct-mutation-state`, and then other internals. For stable CI, the reliable option today is to pin ESLint to v9 when using `eslint-config-next`. If ESLint 10 is required, the only consistent path is a fully custom flat config that does not depend on `eslint-config-next` until upstream compatibility is complete.

Ok after much research, I realized that including the devtools _only happens in the reproduction_ when `package.json.browserlist` includes the `Last 2 X versions`, where X is any browser. 

```json
  "browserslist": [
    "last 2 Chrome versions", // Any of these lines will cause the bug to happen
    "last 2 Firefox versions", // Any of these lines will cause the bug to happen
    "last 2 Safari versions", // Any of these lines will cause the bug to happen
    "last 2 Edge versions", // Any of these lines will cause the bug to happen
    "not dead"
  ],
```

I'm not sure why this is impacting Webpack's ability to tree shake, but at least there is a work around for those that want to avoid adding this to their production bundles.

body:
The problem is that Turbopack creates relative symlinks in `.next/node_modules/` based on the build-time directory depth, and these break when you copy .next to a different path depth in a multi-stage Docker build.

Build stage: `/workspace/app/.next/node_modules/pino-<hash>` -> `../../../node_modules/pino` (resolves correctly)
Runtime stage: `/app/.next/node_modules/pino-<hash>` -> `../../../node_modules/pino` (goes to `/../node_modules/pino` which doesnt exist)

Two workarounds:

Match directory depths in your Dockerfile:
```dockerfile
WORKDIR /workspace/app
COPY --from=builder /workspace/app/.next ./.next
COPY --from=builder /workspace/node_modules ../node_modules
```

Or use cp -rL to dereference symlinks:
```dockerfile
RUN cp -rL .next/node_modules /tmp/resolved_node_modules
COPY --from=builder /tmp/resolved_node_modules .next/node_modules
```

The long-term fix on Turbopack's side should probably be to either use absolute symlinks, or just copy the actual files into .next/node_modules/ instead of symlinking, since standalone output is meant to be self-contained.

body:
The root cause is how Next.js re-serializes the internal request URL after a middleware rewrite. When your `url` search param contains a literal `&` character (as part of the image URL's own query string), it needs to stay percent-encoded as `%26` in the outer URL's query string. But somewhere in the internal URL processing the value gets decoded and then re-serialized without proper encoding, so the `&` becomes a literal separator and splits your `url` param into two separate params.

So your rewrite URL goes from something like:
```
/_next/image?url=http://...?timestamp%26secret=xxx&w=3840&q=75
```
to:
```
/_next/image?url=http://...?timestamp&secret=xxx&w=3840&q=75
```

Now `secret` is a top-level param on the image endpoint instead of being part of the `url` value. Classic double-encoding/decoding issue.

As a workaround you could double-encode the url param value before setting it:

```ts
// instead of
rewriteUrl.searchParams.set("url", imageUrl.toString());

// double-encode
rewriteUrl.searchParams.set("url", encodeURIComponent(imageUrl.toString()));
```

You'd need to decodeURIComponent on the receiving end though. Alternatively you could base64-encode the URL param value to avoid special characters entirely.

body:
This is a documentation gap in how default.tsx interacts with layout.tsx in parallel route slots.

With your structure:

```
app/
  @slot/
    default.tsx
    layout.tsx
  layout.tsx
  page.tsx
```

When you navigate to `/`, the `@slot/default.tsx` renders as the fallback for the slot, but it's not wrapped by `@slot/layout.tsx`. This is actually the current designed behavior (not a bug), but its not documented clearly.

The reason: default.tsx is a special file that provides fallback content for a parallel slot when no matching route segment exists. Its treated differently from page.tsx in the rendering pipeline. A layout wraps route segments (pages), but default.tsx sits outside the normal route segment tree.

If you want the layout to always wrap the slot content, move the layout logic into the default file itself:

```tsx
// app/@slot/default.tsx
import SlotLayout from './layout';

export default function Default() {
  return (
    <SlotLayout>
      {/* your default content */}
    </SlotLayout>
  );
}
```

Or use a route group to force all entry points through the layout:

```
app/
  @slot/
    (wrapped)/
      layout.tsx
      page.tsx
      default.tsx
```

This definitely should be documented more explicitly since the mental model of "layouts always wrap sibling entry points" is intuitive and the exception for default.tsx is surprising.

body:
Nice debugging on this. The root cause is:

AUTO prefetch creates a cache entry keyed by `/listings` (no search params). When the response comes back as prerendered: true, the entry gets upgraded to FULL, but the cache key never gets updated to include search params. So when you navigate to `/listings?tab=board`, the lookup misses because the key doesnt match. The fallback finds the `/listings` entry but marks it as aliased, which forces a full RSC fetch.

Your workaround of using `prefetch={true}` works because it forces a FULL prefetch from the start which creates the cache entry with the full URL including search params.

Another option if you dont want to change prefetch behavior: manage the tab param as client-side state instead of in the URL.

```tsx
<Link href="/listings">Listings</Link>
```

And in the listings page:
```tsx
const searchParams = useSearchParams();
const tab = searchParams.get("tab") || "board";
```

Not ideal if you need the tab to be shareable via URL, but it sidesteps the cache key mismatch entirely.

body:
# Security Analysis: Why `return null` is the Right Fix

@vinassefranche's concern about this being "too loose" is understandable given the CVE hardening context, but the fix is actually sound. Let me trace through why:

## What Changed

```diff
- if (!areAllActionIdsValid(formData, serverModuleMap)) {
-   throw new Error("Failed to find Server Action")
- }
+ const validAction = areAllActionIdsValid(formData, serverModuleMap)
+ if (validAction === false) return null
```

## Code Flow Analysis

### Before (throws):
1. POST to non-existent server action
2. `areAllActionIdsValid()` returns `false` (no valid action IDs in formData)
3. `throw` → uncaught exception → 500 error
4. Monitoring alerts on 500
5. Developer confused (this looks like a server bug, not a client error)

### After (returns null):
1. POST to non-existent server action  
2. `areAllActionIdsValid()` returns `false`
3. `return null` → falls through to normal routing
4. Router can't find a handler for POST → 404
5. Clean client error, no false monitoring alert

## Security Implications

**The CVE hardening is fully preserved.** Here's why:

- `areAllActionIdsValid()` still validates every action ID against `serverModuleMap` before ANY decoding happens
- If the check fails, we NEVER reach `decodeAction()` — the validation gate is intact
- `return null` doesn't bypass security, it just changes what happens AFTER validation fails
- Returning `null` is already the established pattern in `handleAction()` for non-server-action requests (see lines handling `!isPossibleServerAction`, URL-encoded MPA actions, etc.)

**The throw was actually creating security UX debt:**
- It leaked information ("Failed to find Server Action" in error logs)
- It produced 500s that pollute production monitoring (real bugs get lost)
- It treated a client error (invalid request) like a server bug (threw an exception)

## Consistency with Existing Code

This fix doesn't introduce a new pattern—it standardizes existing behavior:

```ts
// Line ~800: already returns null for non-POST requests
if (method !== "POST") return null

// Line ~813: already returns null for URL-encoded (non-FormData) actions
if (contentType?.includes("application/x-www-form-urlencoded")) return null

// Line ~1021: already returns null for missing/invalid next-action header
if (!actionId || actionId === "") return null
```

Our change makes `areAllActionIdsValid` returning `false` consistent with these: "This doesn't match the server action pattern, let normal routing handle it."

## Test Coverage

The PR's test updates verify:
- MPA POST with no valid action IDs → 404 (not 500)
- Test still passes (fixture was already expecting 500, but marked with FIXME: "should be 404")
- Removes assertions for the old error log (no longer thrown)

## Edge Case: Version Skew

One scenario to consider: deployed app A has action XYZ, but app B (old deployment) tries to invoke it. 

- **Before**: 500 + error log
- **After**: 404 for MPA, proper error for fetch

For fetch actions (with `Next-Action` header), the code path still goes through `handleUnrecognizedFetchAction()` which returns a proper error with `NEXT_ACTION_NOT_FOUND_HEADER`. Only MPA form POSTs get a generic 404, which is reasonable for a mismatched deployment.

## Conclusion

[This is](https://github.com/vercel/next.js/pull/90101) a safe fix that:
- ✅ Preserves all security validation (actions still checked before decode)
- ✅ Fixes operational issues (500→404 for invalid requests)
- ✅ Uses the established pattern for non-server-action requests
- ✅ Has test coverage

The concern about being "too loose" doesn't apply here because we're not loosening what gets *executed*—we're only changing the error response for requests that are already rejected by validation.

Thank you for the detailed breakdown of the regression in Next.js 15.4/15.5
regarding locale detection and the domains array.

On Wed, Apr 1, 2026, 4:30 AM Eduard ***@***.***> wrote:

> *EKjs* left a comment (vercel/next.js#90131)
> <https://github.com/vercel/next.js/issues/90131#issuecomment-4168770793>
>
> This is a regression in how Next.js 15.4/15.5 resolves the default locale
> when a domains array is present in the i18n config.
>
> The behavior change: in v15.3, when browsing on the default domain, locale
> detection uses the main defaultLocale from the i18n config. In v15.4+, if a
> locale also appears in a domain's config (e.g. "fr" exists in both the
> default domain and "example.fr"), Next.js incorrectly picks up the
> domain's defaultLocale instead.
>
> You mentioned the correct value is still present in
> req[Symbol.for("NextInternalRequestMeta")] but its not being used. So the
> locale resolution logic changed to prefer the domain-level default over the
> request-level detection.
>
> Workaround: handle this in your middleware by checking the actual host and
> overriding the locale:
>
> export function middleware(request) {
> const host = request.headers.get("host");
> const isDefaultDomain = host === "yourdomain.com";
>
> if (isDefaultDomain) {
> const url = request.nextUrl.clone();
> // force correct locale for default domain
> return NextResponse.rewrite(url);
> }
> }
> Or if you dont actually need domain-based locale routing (i.e. you support
> all locales on all domains), consider removing the domains array from the
> i18n config and handling domain routing separately. That avoids the
> matching issue entirely.

body:
I've submitted a fix in PR #93151.

**Root cause:** In `RouteModule.prepare()` (introduced during the 15.4 Pages Router handler refactoring), the `defaultLocale` fallback chain used `domainLocale?.defaultLocale` — but `domainLocale` was matched using the detected locale (not just hostname). So visiting `/fr` on the default domain would match the `example.fr` domain entry and incorrectly use its `defaultLocale` instead of the main config value.

**Fix:** Removed `domainLocale?.defaultLocale` from the fallback chain since `base-server.ts` already sets the correct `defaultLocale` in request metadata via hostname-only matching. The locale-based domain matching is preserved for `isLocaleDomain` (needed for link domain prefixing).

Thanks for rebasing and for the offer to collaborate!  I reached the same
root cause and the identical fix, so #93151 looks correct to me.

One complementary addition: your test covers locales equal to a domain's
`defaultLocale` (`/go`, `/do`), but `detectDomainLocale` also matches via a
domain's `locales` array — so `/go-BE` on the default host hits a different
branch. I verified this case locally:

```ts
const res = await fetchViaHTTP(ctx.appPort, `${ctx.basePath}/go-BE`)
const $ = cheerio.load(await res.text())
expect($('#router-locale').text()).toBe('go-BE')
expect($('#router-default-locale').text()).toBe('en-US')
expect(JSON.parse($('#props').text()).defaultLocale).toBe('en-US')

body:
Interesting, I do think that unblocks me as it works if I add it to the reproduction demo. Thanks so much for a quick response on that!

However, I still think this is a pretty major documentation bug, at a minimum, due to the difference in behavior:

* In App Router, all you have to do is `response.cookies.set()`, and the SSR logic that runs after `proxy.ts` will see the new cookie in the list returned from `cookies()`.
* In Pages Router, you must _additionally_ do `request.cookies.set()` for `ctx.req.cookies` to be updated.

Additionally, I think the App Router and Pages Router documentation for interacting with cookies is generally a bit confusing:

* https://nextjs.org/docs/app/api-reference/file-conventions/proxy#using-cookies
* https://nextjs.org/docs/pages/api-reference/file-conventions/proxy#using-cookies

Neither of these explain the differences in behavior between the `request` and `response` cookie objects. Crucially, the Pages Router documentation doesn't mention anything about having to pass the updated `request` object into `NextResponse.next()` **for cookies.** This _is_ directly mentioned as required **for headers** here: https://nextjs.org/docs/app/api-reference/file-conventions/proxy#using-cookies

Honestly, I don't understand _why_ in either case you'd be required to do this - is the `request` object passed to `proxy()` supposed to be treated as read-only?

Either way, I'd be happy to contribute to the docs now that I've had some clarifications on the expected behavior, I don't think it'd take much to clean up that section. It looks like both the Pages Router doc and App Router doc are generated from the same source, so can probably just document setting the response cookie for App Router and then add a caveat that you must also set the `request` for Pages Router.

body:
I encountered a similar problem： Turbopack Memory Regression in 16.1.x Compared to 16.0.11 (Large App Router Project)

---

## Summary

We are experiencing a significant memory usage regression in Turbopack between Next.js 16.0.11 and 16.1.x during production builds.

The issue appears during the **optimized production build phase**, before SSG execution. The JavaScript heap remains low and stable, while RSS memory increases substantially, suggesting the issue originates from Turbopack's Rust layer or module graph handling rather than application-level code.

---

## Environment

* Next.js: 16.0.11 vs 16.1.6
* Turbopack enabled (`next build --turbopack`)
* React: 19.2.x
* App Router
* ~6,700 routes (large-scale project)
* Windows environment
* 19 workers (default parallelism)

Command used:

```bash
next build --turbopack --experimental-debug-memory-usage
```

---

## Observed Behavior

### ✅ Next.js 16.0.11

Peak memory during graph build phase:

* Peak RSS: ~8.1 GB
* JS Heap: ~52 MB
* After compilation completes, RSS drops to ~2.4 GB
* Build completes successfully

Memory usage appears proportional to worker count and project size.

---

### ❌ Next.js 16.1.6

Peak memory during graph build phase:

* Peak RSS: ~12.9 GB
* JS Heap: ~50–150 MB
* No corresponding increase in JS heap
* Significant memory spike compared to 16.0.11

This suggests a regression in Turbopack memory handling in 16.1.x.

---

## Important Observations

1. JS heap remains low (<150MB) in all cases.
2. The spike occurs during the **"Creating optimized production build"** stage.
3. Memory drops after compilation, indicating no long-term leak.
4. SSG phase memory is stable (~2.5GB RSS).
5. Limiting workers reduces memory proportionally.

This strongly suggests the issue is related to Turbopack module graph construction or worker-level memory duplication introduced in 16.1.x.

body:
Did some digging into this. There's two important changes to make when looking at memory leaks.

First, adding `--expose-gc` so that the garbage collector can be manually forced to run:

```
CMD ["node", "--expose-gc", "server.js"]
```

Then, adding `global.gc()` to the page component to force garbage collection on each request.

After adding those changes I built the app and run 10,000 requests:

```
ab -n 5000 -c 100 http://127.0.0.1:3000/
# leaving some time to have it settle. Then triggering again
ab -n 5000 -c 100 http://127.0.0.1:3000/
```

Running it shows memory going up, sure, but that's not unusual when you trigger 100 concurrent requests that have to be rendered. It stops at about 295MiB in this case.

```
f67dfbd5f1d3   next-demo   0.00%     295.3MiB / 7.653GiB   3.77%     129MB / 1.08GB   0B / 0B     11 
```

After the requests letting the server settle with no new requests shows it goes down to about 150MiB.


There's a level of "leak" (intentionally quoted) in undici (Node.js's fetch library) in which it creates performance entries which "leak" but are limited to a set number of entries, so it won't go back down to 0 but also won't exceed a limited number of entries, causing memory to go up after the first few requests and not back down to the original number.


I've also opened #90771 which does reduce memory usage overall but as far as I can tell was only leaking 2 objects and those got overwritten by every incoming request, so it's not growing in size, just consistently keeping one request. That's a bug and the PR fixes it, I'm not expecting it'll have a big impact, though on the test app I did measure it around 210MiB after the changes.

This shows what that number is:

```
CMD ["node", "-e", "console.log(require('v8').getHeapStatistics().heap_size_limit / 1024 / 1024 + ' MB')"]

Reducing the heap size will cause more garbage collection.

body:
Working through this, and I am seeing the correct `filepaths` (i.e., it has reference css) returned by the `postcss/tailwind` plugin, but then they are only read here, in [webpack.rs](https://github.com/vercel/next.js/blob/canary/turbopack/crates/turbopack-node/src/transforms/webpack.rs#L578-L581)

```
   let file_subscriptions = file_paths
                        .iter()
                        .map(|p| async move { self.cwd.join(p)?.read().await })
                        .try_join();
```

Since `read()` does return a `Vc<FileContent>` it should be simple enough to turn the `info` function into a `#[turbo_tasks::function]` in order to include these files in tracking, however I suspect there's a reason why this isn't done.  **It makes me question why the reads are here?** The result is joined together but, as far as I can tell, it's not used at all. 

Alternatively, the file paths could be passed all the way to `postcss.rs` in the [process](https://github.com/vercel/next.js/blob/canary/turbopack/crates/turbopack-node/src/transforms/postcss.rs#L491) function, so that we can add these file paths as reads here to trigger revalidation of the postcss task when they change. This makes the most sense to me, but I don't see a simple way of adding this to `turbopack-node` crate. 

I'd like to get some maintainer input beforehand to decide on which path to take since I'm not clear on which approach is favorable.

body:
## Analysis

This appears to be a cache key mismatch issue in the RSC prefetch mechanism. The root cause:

1. When \`<Link href="/test">\` prefetches, it caches the RSC response keyed by the **visible URL** (\`/test\`)
2. The proxy adds \`testParam=testValue\`, so the actual fetch hits \`/dynamicPages/filtered?testParam=testValue\`
3. When you navigate to \`/test\` (no params), the router finds a cached prefetch for \`/test\` and serves it
4. The cache hit bypasses the RSC fetch entirely — even though the searchParams have changed

**Why removing the hidden param fixes it:** Without the hidden param, the visible URL and actual URL match, so the cache key accurately represents the page state.

**Why \`prefetch={false}\` fixes it:** No prefetch = no stale cache to serve on navigation.

### Potential workarounds until fixed:

**1. Disable prefetch for proxy-rewritten routes:**
\`\`\`tsx
<Link href="/test" prefetch={false}>Test page</Link>
\`\`\`

**2. Use router.push instead of Link for these routes:**
\`\`\`tsx
const router = useRouter()
<button onClick={() => router.push("/test")}>Test page</button>
\`\`\`

**3. Add a dummy param to force cache misses:**
\`\`\`tsx
// In the page, add a timestamp or random value to the Link
<Link href={\`/test?_=${Date.now()}\`}>Test page</Link>
\`\`\`
(Ugly but forces fresh fetches)

### Suggested fix direction:

The prefetch cache key should account for the **rewritten URL** (including hidden params), not just the visible URL. This likely requires the router to store rewrite metadata alongside cached responses, or to invalidate prefetch entries when the rewrite adds params that affect \`searchParams\`.

cc @vercel/next-server-components — this seems related to the prefetch cache invalidation logic.
author: xXMrNidaXx

body:
## Analysis: Prefetch Cache Key Collision

This is a cache key collision in the prefetch/RSC cache. The bug occurs because:

1. **Prefetch phase**: `<Link href="/test">` prefetches `/test` (no params)
2. **Cache key**: The prefetch result is cached under the *source* URL (`/test`), not the *rewritten* URL
3. **The rewrite adds hidden params**: `testParam=testValue` — but the cache doesn't know about this
4. **Navigation**: When you navigate to `/test` with no visible params, it uses the cached prefetch
5. **Subsequent navigations**: The RSC cache thinks it already has `/test` data, so it doesn't re-fetch

### Why it works when you load with params initially

Loading `/test?page=2` creates a cache entry for `/test?page=2`. When you click `+`, the new URL `/test?page=3` is a cache miss → RSC fetch fires → works.

But `reset` navigates to bare `/test` → cache hit on the stale prefetch → no fetch.

### Why `prefetch={false}` fixes it

No prefetch = no stale cache entry. Every navigation is a cache miss → fresh RSC fetch.

### Suggested fix directions

**Option A — Include rewrite destination in cache key:**

The prefetch cache key should incorporate the actual rewritten URL (after middleware), not just the source URL. This would require middleware to communicate the final URL back.

**Option B — Invalidate prefetch cache on param change:**

When `searchParams` change (including going from params → no params), treat it as a cache miss even if the pathname matches.

**Option C — Timestamp or version the prefetch:**

Add a TTL or version to prefetch cache entries so they expire. This is less precise but simpler.

### Workaround

For now, you can work around this by making the `testParam` visible in the URL (not hidden by rewrite), or by using `router.refresh()` after navigation:

```tsx
const router = useRouter();

const handleFilterChange = () => {
  router.push(newUrl);
  router.refresh(); // Force RSC re-fetch
};
```

Ugly, but works until this is fixed.

---
*Corey Nida — [RevolutionAI](https://revolutionai.io) | Next.js & AI Infrastructure*

Great investigation — this is a subtle caching/prefetch interaction bug.

**Root cause analysis:**

The prefetch for `/test` runs before any user interaction. When the proxy adds `testParam=testValue`, the prefetch caches an RSC response keyed to `/dynamicPages/filtered?testParam=testValue` (the rewritten URL).

When you navigate to `/test` with **no params**, the client has a "fresh" prefetch for the param-less URL. But internally, the cached RSC payload was for the *rewritten* URL which includes the hidden param. This creates a mismatch:

1. When URL has no searchParams → client thinks "cache is valid" (no params = no staleness)
2. But the cache was keyed to a URL with `testParam=testValue` 
3. On subsequent navigations, the cache validator compares against the wrong baseline
4. The client skips `_rsc` fetches because it believes nothing changed

**Why `page=2` works initially:**
- Loading with a param forces a fresh server request (cache miss)
- RSC is fetched and properly keyed

**Why reset breaks it:**
- Navigating to param-less state matches the "stale" prefetch cache entry
- From that point, the client uses the param-less baseline for staleness checks
- Any new param addition appears unchanged against the empty-param baseline

**Workarounds:**

1. `prefetch={false}` — as you noted, avoids caching the poisoned entry
2. `revalidate` header in the rewrite response — forces cache invalidation
3. Add a visible search param in the original URL instead of hiding it in proxy
4. Use server actions instead of URL state for the filter controls

**Fix suggestion:**
The prefetch cache key should probably include a hash of the *final rewritten URL* after middleware, not just the source URL. This would prevent the cache mismatch since `/test` and `/test?testParam=testValue` would have different keys.

Alternatively, middleware that adds hidden params could set a header indicating cache should key on the rewritten URL.

> during next.config.ts resolution poisons the AsyncLocalStorage context.

> In Next.js 16, the next/headers module eagerly initializes internal
> stores when imported. When this happens during config resolution (which
> runs outside the normal request lifecycle), the stores get set up in the
> wrong context. Later, when actual page renders run, they find a
> stale/mismatched store and throw the Expected workUnitAsyncStorage to
> have a store invariant.
>
> This worked in Next.js 15 because the headers module initialization was
> lazier, or config resolution was more isolated from the runtime module
> graph.
>
> The fact that you can't reproduce it in minimal setups suggests the issue
> depends on pnpm workspace module resolution hoisting. In complex monorepos,
> pnpm might resolve next/headers to a shared instance that gets loaded
> once and persists across both config and runtime contexts. In simpler
> setups, module resolution might hit different instances.
>
> Workarounds:
>
>    1.
>
>    *The one you already found*: avoid importing modules that transitively
>    depend on next/headers in next.config.ts. Keep config imports separate
>    from runtime imports.
>    2.

>    a module that imports next/headers, use import type for types and await

We could not detect a valid reproduction link. **Make sure to follow the bug report template carefully.**

### Why was this issue closed?

To be able to investigate, we need access to a reproduction to identify what triggered the issue. We need a link to a **public** GitHub repository ([template for App Router](https://github.com/vercel/next.js/tree/canary/examples/reproduction-template), [template for Pages Router](https://github.com/vercel/next.js/tree/canary/examples/reproduction-template-pages)), but you can also use these templates: [CodeSandbox: App Router](https://codesandbox.io/s/github/vercel/next.js/tree/canary/examples/reproduction-template) or [CodeSandbox: Pages Router](https://codesandbox.io/s/github/vercel/next.js/tree/canary/examples/reproduction-template-pages).

The bug template that you filled out has a section called "Link to the code that reproduces this issue", which is where you should provide the link to the reproduction.

- If you did not provide a link or the link you provided is not valid, we will close the issue.
- If you provide a link to a private repository, we will close the issue.
- If you provide a link to a repository but not in the correct section, we will close the issue.

### What should I do?

Depending on the reason the issue was closed, you can do the following:

- If you did not provide a link, please open a new issue with a link to a reproduction.
- If you provided a link to a private repository, please open a new issue with a link to a public repository.
- If you provided a link to a repository but not in the correct section, please open a new issue with a link to a reproduction in the correct section.

**In general, assume that we should not go through a lengthy onboarding process at your company code only to be able to verify an issue.**

### My repository is private and cannot make it public

In most cases, a private repo will not be a sufficient **minimal reproduction**, as this codebase might contain a lot of unrelated parts that would make our investigation take longer. Please do **not** make it public. Instead, create a new repository using the templates above, adding the relevant code to reproduce the issue. Common things to look out for:

- Remove any code that is not related to the issue. (pages, API routes, components, etc.)
- Remove any dependencies that are not related to the issue.
- Remove any third-party service that would require us to sign up for an account to reproduce the issue.
- Remove any environment variables that are not related to the issue.
- Remove private packages that we do not have access to.
- If the issue is not related to a monorepo specifically, try to reproduce the issue without a complex monorepo setup

### I did not open this issue, but it is relevant to me, what can I do to help?

Anyone experiencing the same issue is welcome to provide a minimal reproduction following the above steps by opening a new issue.

### I think my reproduction is good enough, why aren't you looking into it quickly?

We look into every Next.js issue and constantly monitor open issues for new comments.

However, sometimes we might miss one or two due to the popularity/high traffic of the repository. We apologize, and kindly ask you to refrain from tagging core maintainers, as that will usually not result in increased priority.

Upvoting issues to show your interest will help us prioritize and address them as quickly as possible. That said, every issue is important to us, and if an issue gets closed by accident, we encourage you to open a new one linking to the old issue and we will look into it.

### Useful Resources

- [How to create a Minimal, Complete, and Verifiable example](https://stackoverflow.com/help/mcve)

body:
Hiyo, we spend some time investigating this. We can tell that there's no memory leak. Tests done in canary.

The problem is that several requests, prevent Garbage Collection from cleaning up. If one lets GC kick in, then memory stays bounded.  If GC can't run, the server will run out of memory. We haven't pinpointed what changed the threshold between versions, but we confirmed memory is properly reclaimed when GC gets a chance to run.

I'll go ahead and close for now.

body:
## Update: Unable to reproduce after further investigation

After more thorough testing, I can no longer reproduce this issue reliably. Here's what I found:

### Isolation Testing
I systematically tested Turbopack with progressively more complex CSS:
1. **`@import "tailwindcss"` only** — ✅ works
2. **+ `@import "tw-animate-css"`** — ✅ works
3. **+ `@import "shadcn/tailwind.css"`** — ✅ works
4. **Full `globals.css`** (all imports + `@theme inline` + custom CSS) — ✅ works
5. **Hot-reload** (editing CSS while server runs) — ✅ works

All tests used `rm -rf .next` before starting, same package versions (next 16.1.6, @tailwindcss/postcss 4.2.1, tailwindcss 4.2.1).

### Root Cause Hypothesis

Looking at the panic logs more carefully, all crashes occurred within a ~21 minute window. The error chain is:

```
PostCssTransformedAsset::process → evaluate_webpack_loader → DiskFileSystem::read 
→ reading file C:\...\flow2code\nul → os error 1 (ERROR_INVALID_FUNCTION)
```

On Windows, `nul` is a reserved device name (equivalent to `/dev/null`). OS error 1 (`ERROR_INVALID_FUNCTION`) occurs when standard file I/O is attempted on a device name.

**Most likely cause**: A corrupted `.next` cache contained a source map reference that resolved to `nul` (possibly from a `/dev/null` POSIX path in a PostCSS source map). Once the cache was cleared and the server restarted cleanly, the issue didn't recur.

### Recommendation

While I can't reproduce this anymore, there's still a potential underlying issue: **Turbopack's `DiskFileSystem::read` should gracefully handle Windows reserved device names** (`NUL`, `CON`, `PRN`, `AUX`, `COM1`–`COM9`, `LPT1`–`LPT9`) instead of panicking. These can appear in source maps or file references from Unix-oriented tooling.

Feel free to close this if it's not actionable without a reliable reproduction. I'll reopen if I hit it again.

body:
I did some more digging, since i encoutered the same error and wanted to share what I found — though I'm not deeply familiar with the internals here, so happy to be corrected.

Looking at the two compiled files in `node_modules/next/dist/compiled/react-server-dom-turbopack/cjs/`, there seems to be an asymmetry in `reportGlobalError` between the server and client versions.

The server version (`react-server-dom-turbopack-server.node.development.js`) has a defensive `typeof` check:

```javascript
((chunk = chunk.reason),
"function" === typeof chunk.error && chunk.error(error));
```

But the client version (`react-server-dom-turbopack-client.node.development.js`) — which is where the crash occurs according to the stacktrace — does not:

```javascript
chunk.reason.error(error); // no typeof check
```

I understand that the server and client versions of `reportGlobalError` may intentionally differ for good reasons I'm not aware of (consumer and producer). But could this missing guard on the client side be contributing to the crash? If the asymmetry is unintentional, it might be worth bringing the client version in line with the server version:

```javascript
((chunk = chunk.reason),
"function" === typeof chunk.error && chunk.error(error));
```

Would love to hear if anyone has more context!

### Why was this issue closed?

To be able to investigate, we need access to a reproduction to identify what triggered the issue. We need a link to a **public** GitHub repository ([template for App Router](https://github.com/vercel/next.js/tree/canary/examples/reproduction-template), [template for Pages Router](https://github.com/vercel/next.js/tree/canary/examples/reproduction-template-pages)), but you can also use these templates: [CodeSandbox: App Router](https://codesandbox.io/s/github/vercel/next.js/tree/canary/examples/reproduction-template) or [CodeSandbox: Pages Router](https://codesandbox.io/s/github/vercel/next.js/tree/canary/examples/reproduction-template-pages).

The bug template that you filled out has a section called "Link to the code that reproduces this issue", which is where you should provide the link to the reproduction.

- If you did not provide a link or the link you provided is not valid, we will close the issue.
- If you provide a link to a private repository, we will close the issue.
- If you provide a link to a repository but not in the correct section, we will close the issue.

### What should I do?

Depending on the reason the issue was closed, you can do the following:

- If you did not provide a link, please open a new issue with a link to a reproduction.
- If you provided a link to a private repository, please open a new issue with a link to a public repository.
- If you provided a link to a repository but not in the correct section, please open a new issue with a link to a reproduction in the correct section.

**In general, assume that we should not go through a lengthy onboarding process at your company code only to be able to verify an issue.**

### My repository is private and cannot make it public

In most cases, a private repo will not be a sufficient **minimal reproduction**, as this codebase might contain a lot of unrelated parts that would make our investigation take longer. Please do **not** make it public. Instead, create a new repository using the templates above, adding the relevant code to reproduce the issue. Common things to look out for:

- Remove any code that is not related to the issue. (pages, API routes, components, etc.)
- Remove any dependencies that are not related to the issue.
- Remove any third-party service that would require us to sign up for an account to reproduce the issue.
- Remove any environment variables that are not related to the issue.
- Remove private packages that we do not have access to.
- If the issue is not related to a monorepo specifically, try to reproduce the issue without a complex monorepo setup

### I did not open this issue, but it is relevant to me, what can I do to help?

Anyone experiencing the same issue is welcome to provide a minimal reproduction following the above steps by opening a new issue.

We look into every Next.js issue and constantly monitor open issues for new comments.

However, sometimes we might miss one or two due to the popularity/high traffic of the repository. We apologize, and kindly ask you to refrain from tagging core maintainers, as that will usually not result in increased priority.

Upvoting issues to show your interest will help us prioritize and address them as quickly as possible. That said, every issue is important to us, and if an issue gets closed by accident, we encourage you to open a new one linking to the old issue and we will look into it.

The assessment (seemingly written by AI) is wrong. The difference between `as: '*.js'` and `as: '*.tsx'` is at most milliseconds

Stuff like this seems pure guessing / hallucination:

> the redundant source-map merging alone adds ~50 s of compilation time.

It won't be resolved by changing `as`.

I had a look at a trace from the provided application and switching to `as: '.js'` did not help much. It's just a lot of code being generated that then needs to be parsed. Most of the time is spent running the loader.

body:
Confirming this is **not Turbopack-exclusive** — same root cause reproduces on **webpack dev** in Next.js 16.2.6, with a different trigger.

**Stack:**
- `next@16.2.6`
- `next dev --webpack` (Turbopack explicitly disabled)
- App Router with `@drawer/(.)[id]/page.tsx` parallel + intercept route over a list page

**Trigger (different from the OP's HMR-save scenario):**
Clicking a row in the list fires an RSC fetch `GET /<list>/<uuid>?_rsc=...` → **500** → retry **200** to the full detail page (hard navigation, drawer never opens).

**Server log:**
```
⨯ Error: Invalid interception route: /<list>/(.)(.)(.)...(.)<uuid>.
Must be in the format /<intercepting route>/(..|...|..)(..)/<intercepted route>
GET /<list>/<uuid> 500 in ~800ms
GET /<list>/<uuid> 200 in ~3s
```

**Network signature (same as OP):**
Response header on the failing RSC fetch:
```
x-nextjs-rewritten-path: /<list>/(.)(.){uuid}
```

**What this adds to #91265:**
- Bug is **not exclusive to Turbopack** — webpack dev is affected too.
- Trigger is **not exclusive to HMR saves** — a plain RSC fetch to a UUID-segment intercept route reproduces it from a cold dev start (no save loop required).
- This is consistent with the OP's root-cause analysis pointing at `setup-dev-bundler.js` — that module is shared between webpack and Turbopack dev pipelines, so the same `beforeFiles.push(...interceptionRoutes)` without prior filter affects both.

**Production unaffected** (matches OP) — `next build && next start` resolves the intercept route correctly. Bug is dev-runtime only.

Would help if a maintainer could trigger CI on #91364 — the fix looks targeted and the PR has been waiting on first-time-contributor approval since March 14.

body:
Hey so I put your reproduction into a github repo so it's easier to see the differences: https://github.com/robert-j-webb/pokemon-cache-repo

I changed a lot of the code so that I could more clearly understand when caching is happening - I recommend cloning it, installing, and then running dev and e2e tests. You can see some pretty interesting behavior, look at the logs to see when the cache code actually runs.

If you run the `pokemonDetele.tsx` with `onPokemonDeleteSucceeds` then you can see the cache actually _never_ updates after the first test. If you change it to `onPokemonDeleteFails`, then after the `delete` is called, the cache updates. 

Chronologically, with `onPokemonDeleteFails`: 

Test 1
1. View Bulbasaur
2. Delete Bulbasaur (which refreshes cache, where bulbasaur is gone)

Test 2
1. Reset database (this has no effect on the cache)
2. Go to Bulbasaur in other browser, views cached pokemon which is deleted

Whereas with `onPokemonDeleteSuceeds`

Test 1
1. View Bulbasaur
2. Delete Bulbasaur (which **DOES NOT** refresh cache)

Test 2
1. View cached bulbasaur
2. Delete cached bulbasaur (no effect)


I do think that the way the router cache is working is confusing, thanks for clarifying it, specifically when you say:

> This is what I think happens: when you call router.push to navigate away from a page, the page you navigated from is somehow cached.

HOWEVER, if you modify `pokemonDelete.tsx` to not have `router.push` in `pokemonDeleteFails`, the tests still fail, ie:

```ts
  async function onPokemonDeleteFails() {
    await deletePokemon(pokemon);

    await clearPokemonFromCache(pokemon.id);

    // router.push("/pokemon");
  }
```

Has the same result. 


But you are right, it is really confusing why this doesn't clear the cache:

```ts
  async function onPokemonDeleteSucceeds() {
    await deletePokemon(pokemon);

    router.push("/pokemon");

    await clearPokemonFromCache(pokemon.id);
  }
```

Since the only difference is the `router.push` which should have no effect on the cache. 

I'll look into this more and see if I can make sense of it.

body:
Hare Krishna 🙏

I cloned the reproduction repo and tested the behavior locally.

I can confirm that after navigating from **page A → page B**, page A remains in the DOM with `display: none`, so `body:has([data-page="a"])` still evaluates to `true`.

Using a selector similar to what @Thakisis suggested (filtering out hidden elements) also worked for me:

```css
body:has([data-page="a"]:not([style*="display: none"]))
```

https://github.com/user-attachments/assets/e953ae00-33fb-488a-92d4-0efbd463124c

I cloned the [[next-activity-has-repro](https://github.com/binarystride/next-activity-has-repro)]  repo to reproduce the issue and verify the behavior locally.

This prevents the stale match when navigating from A → B in the reproduction project.

However, relying on checking inline styles feels a bit fragile. Having a stable attribute like `hidden` or something like `data-router-hidden` for inactive segments might make selectors more reliable.

Just sharing my findings while testing the reproduction repo. 😇

I found that between `16.2.1` and `16.2.2` with the introduction of a config option called `turbopackServerFastRefresh` a previously opt-in option became opt-out. In our install this option needs to be turned off otherwise in dev mode (does not occur in production builds) the memory and CPU grow until the system is overwhelmed. The 'fix' is to add to `next.config.ts` in the `experimental` section:

```
  experimental: {
    turbopackServerFastRefresh: false
  }
```

I'm not sure if it is circular dependencies that cause this when turbopack fast refresh is on but debugging it cost me a lot of time so I'm happy to leave this option turned off.

body:
Thanks for the explanation. I understand the current implementation, but I don't think this should be framed as documentation-only.

The core concern here is not merely that `generateMetadata()` re-runs on navigation. The concern is that, in practice, App Router presents preserved layouts as a reusable part of the rendered route tree, while metadata resolution for those same preserved ancestors is effectively treated as fully invalidated on sibling navigation.

That creates a mismatch in behavior:

- the shared layout UI is preserved
- the shared layout component does not re-render
- but the root layout metadata path can still trigger the same shared data read again

In real applications, root-layout data and root-layout metadata are very often derived from the same source of truth: site settings, tenant config, branding, SEO defaults, navigation context, etc. From that perspective, this is not just a docs discoverability issue. It is at least a framework-level optimization gap, because preserved ancestor state in the render tree does not translate into preserved ancestor metadata/data reuse.

I agree that `React.cache()` is request-scoped, and I agree that metadata is route-wide. But those facts alone do not fully address the ergonomics/perf issue exposed by this repro. The current behavior may be "working as implemented", yet still be a suboptimal behavior at the framework boundary.

So I think this issue should remain open either as:

1. an optimization request for preserved-ancestor metadata/data reuse during sibling navigation, or
2. a design limitation that needs an explicit framework-level escape hatch beyond "use lower-level caching yourself".

Documentation clarification is helpful, but it does not resolve the underlying inconsistency between preserved layout rendering and non-preserved metadata-dependent data reads.

If full metadata reuse is not feasible, it would still be useful to explain why preserved layout segments cannot provide any reuse signal to ancestor metadata resolution.
author: Innei

body:
Fair point—the inconsistency is real. Layout rendering skips re-rendering preserved ancestor segments via `flightRouterState`, but metadata resolution has no equivalent; it always walks the full tree from scratch. So the render tree can short-circuit work on sibling navigations, but metadata resolution cannot, even for ancestors with unchanged params.

Agreed this should stay open as a framework optimization/design request rather than a docs issue. The docs PR (#91427) still clarifies current behavior and the `fetch`/`unstable_cache` workaround in the meantime.

body:
Thank you for the whole clarification and RP

On Mon, Mar 16, 2026, 7:51 AM Hammad Khan ***@***.***> wrote:

> *hammadxcm* left a comment (vercel/next.js#91410)
> <https://github.com/vercel/next.js/issues/91410#issuecomment-4067438681>
>
> Spent more time digging into the metadata pipeline to see if there's a
> viable path here. Wanted to share what I found since @Innei
> <https://github.com/Innei> raised a good question about why preserved
> segments can't provide a reuse signal.
>
> The fundamental problem is how accumulateMetadata() works — it
> shallow-merges metadata from every segment in the tree on each navigation.
> Root layout typically provides the title template (%s | My Site), OG
> defaults, icons, etc., and the page provides page-specific overrides. If we
> skip calling collectMetadata() for the root layout because it's a
> "preserved" segment, we simply have no value to merge. The final <head>
> would be missing the layout's contributions entirely.
>
> So to skip the call, we'd need to cache the previous result somewhere. I
> looked at a few angles:
>
>    -
>
>    *unstable_cache around the metadata call itself*: breaks if
>    generateMetadata() reads cookies() or headers() (which is common for
>    auth-dependent metadata). unstable_cache throws on dynamic data
>    access. Also, it writes to the shared incrementalCache, so you'd risk
>    serving one user's personalized metadata to another unless you key on the
>    full request context — at which point you're not really caching.
>    -
>
>    *Per-segment in-memory cache keyed by segment + params*: still
>    cross-request, still has the privacy issue for anything that reads
>    cookies/headers. And there's no way to know ahead of time whether a given
>    generateMetadata() will access dynamic data before you actually call
>    it.
>    -
>
>    *Using the existing flightRouterState to filter*: this controls which
>    child subtrees to walk, but the issue is the *current* segment's own
>    metadata call. The root layout is the starting point of the walk, not
>    something that gets filtered by router state.
>
> So yeah — the render tree can skip preserved ancestors because React
> components are stateful on the client and the server just doesn't send new
> RSC payload for them. But metadata is stateless and computed fresh each
> time on the server side. Making it stateful across requests opens up
> correctness/privacy issues that are hard to solve generically.
>
> For now the best workarounds depending on your setup:
>
> // If you're on Next.js 15+ with the experimental flag:export async function generateMetadata() {
>   'use cache'
>   const data = await db.query('site-metadata')
>   return { title: data.title }}
> // fetch with revalidate (works today):export async function generateMetadata() {
>   const res = await fetch('https://...', { next: { revalidate: 3600 } })
>   return { title: (await res.json()).title }}
> // unstable_cache for non-fetch data sources:import { unstable_cache } from 'next/cache'const getCachedConfig = unstable_cache(
>   async () => db.query('site-metadata'),
>   ['site-config'],
>   { revalidate: 3600 })export async function generateMetadata() {
>   return { title: (await getCachedConfig()).title }}
>
> I think keeping this open as a long-term optimization request makes sense
> — 'use cache' on generateMetadata is probably the closest thing to a real
> solution here once it stabilizes. Labeling as something like linear: next
> or area: metadata might help it get triaged by the core team.

body:
The `cookies()` / `headers()` privacy concern doesn't fully address the issue. When the framework decides to preserve a layout segment — skipping its re-render — it has already implicitly determined that the request context for that segment is stable enough to reuse. Arguing that metadata resolution for that same segment must re-run due to dynamic request data is contradictory.

This feels less like a deliberate design decision and more like an architectural gap: the metadata pipeline simply has no awareness of the render pipeline's preservation state. If it is intentional, it would help to have an explicit explanation of why these two pipelines are designed to be fully decoupled.

Could someone from the core team clarify: is there an active plan to address this, or is this expected to remain a gap indefinitely? A "long-term optimization" label without a concrete owner tends to mean it won't be revisited.
author: Innei

body:
Taking a step back, I think there's a cleaner way to think about this.

On initial page load, full server-side metadata generation is correct and necessary. But on subsequent client-side navigations, the current model forces a full metadata re-evaluation as part of the RSC request — even when the layout that owns that metadata is being preserved. I'd argue that's the wrong default.

An alternative model worth considering: for preserved layout segments, their metadata contributions could be considered stable on client navigations and not re-evaluated as part of the RSC request — unless the segment itself is explicitly invalidated.

The `cookies()` / `headers()` concern doesn't really hold up here either. If the framework has already decided that a layout segment is preserved — meaning it's not re-rendering, not re-fetching — it has implicitly determined that the request context for that segment hasn't meaningfully changed. Claiming that metadata resolution for that same segment must re-run because of dynamic request data is contradictory: you can't simultaneously say "this layout's render is stable enough to skip" and "this layout's metadata is too dynamic to reuse."

The current behavior feels like a consequence of metadata resolution being a separate, context-unaware pipeline rather than a deliberate design choice. It'd be worth the core team explicitly addressing whether this split is intentional and whether treating preserved segments as metadata-stable on client navigations is a direction being considered.
author: Innei

body:
@Innei I want to push back a bit on one specific claim because I think it's the crux of the disagreement:

> If the framework has already decided that a layout segment is preserved — meaning it's not re-rendering, not re-fetching — it has implicitly determined that the request context for that segment is stable enough to reuse.

This isn't quite how preservation works under the hood. When the client navigates, it sends the current `flightRouterState` to the server. The server then walks the loader tree and calls `matchSegment()` at each level — that function just checks whether the segment identifier (the string or `[paramName, paramValue]` tuple) matches what the client already has. If it matches, the server skips `createComponentTree()` for that segment and doesn't include `seedData` in the response.

That's a structural identity check: "does the client already have a rendered version of this segment?" It's not evaluating whether cookies changed, whether headers differ, or whether the request context is still valid for that layout. A user could navigate from /alpha to /beta right after a session cookie changes, and the root layout would still be "preserved" because the segment name hasn't changed. So preservation is a rendering/payload optimization, not a freshness or context-stability guarantee.

Metadata resolution is a separate pipeline that walks the full `loaderTree` every time, with no access to `flightRouterState` at all. It has to produce a complete merged `<head>` for the new route — root layout contributes title templates, OG defaults, icons, etc. that get shallow-merged with page-level metadata. You can't assemble the final `<head>` without running every segment's contribution.

That said, I do agree with the broader point that these two pipelines could theoretically be made more aware of each other. If the framework knew that a preserved segment's `generateMetadata()` doesn't depend on child params or dynamic request data, it could skip re-evaluation. But that kind of static analysis doesn't exist today, and getting it wrong silently serves stale metadata — which is arguably worse than the perf hit.

I think this is solidly in "framework optimization request" territory, and probably worth core team input on whether making the metadata pipeline preservation-aware is something they'd consider. The `'use cache'` directive on `generateMetadata` seems like it could cover this use case once it's stable, since it lets users opt in to caching explicitly rather than the framework guessing.

author: robert-j-webb

body:
Hello @robert-j-webb,

Thank you for looking into this.

The observed issues (CSS ordering problems, hydration errors, etc.) are only symptoms of an underlying bug at the Turbopack level.

This problem can be reasoned about without any knowledge of Emotion, tss-react, or MUI. It is fundamentally a module resolution issue related to package conditions.

In short:

Different builds of `@emotion/react` end up being included in the same server graph, which leads to cascading issues.

This falls into a well-known class of problems commonly referred to as the "dual package issue" in the bundler ecosystem.

A very similar issue was previously encountered in Vite and fixed by @Andarist in this PR:
https://github.com/vitejs/vite/pull/13370

To clarify, the actual situation here is more complex. However, to illustrate the class of problem, here is a simplified example:

- Dependency A is published only as CJS (`a.cjs`) and depends on B as a peer dependency.
- Dependency B is published in both CJS and ESM (`b.cjs` and `b.mjs`).

The user installs both and writes:

```ts
import "a";
import "b";
```

If the bundler ends up including `a.cjs`, `b.cjs`, and `b.mjs`, this creates a dual package situation, which is a bug.

Valid outcomes would be:
- `a.cjs` + `b.mjs`
- `a.cjs` + `b.cjs`

As long as there is only one instance of B in the final graph.

Again, this example is only meant to illustrate the general class of issue. The real-world case here involves a more complex set of conditions (exports, environments, runtimes, etc.), but the underlying problem is the same.

The root issue is that Turbopack does not resolve package conditions in the same way as other bundlers like Vite, Webpack, Rollup (with `@rollup/plugin-node-resolve`), Bun, or esbuild.

All of these bundlers correctly avoid including multiple instances of `@emotion/react` in the final build.

Sorry for pinging you on this @Andarist. If you have a moment to confirm whether this analysis is accurate, it would help validate the issue.
author: garronej

body:
Without digging too much into this - if the bundler ends up *bundling* 2 duplicates of a single Emotion version, this is a bug in the bundler. The `package.json#exports` in Emotion are structured in such a way that the bundler should always pick up the `"module"` condition, regardless of the CJS/ESM rules of the importer. 

If the bundling process *bundles* Emotion and externalizes it too at the same time, that also can lead to similar issues but that's a situation that should just be avoided and, ideally, not created in the first place.

The bundler shouldn't "prefer" any condition - it should specify what condition it supports for any given request and just pick the first matching one from `package.json#exports`. That's how the algorithm is supposed to work and that's the rule we guide ourselves when authoring those maps. 

I believe that whenever the bundler configures the conditions they support, they should just include `"module"` (unless a specific user override is specified or something). See:
https://github.com/rollup/plugins/blob/5cc7fc5cb1b7fbff42130a4cd798f709cd6f3158/packages/node-resolve/src/index.js#L31

body:
GlebKodrik, this appears to be a known limitation documented in the Next.js Turbopack documentation.

According to the [Turbopack docs on CSS ordering](https://github.com/vercel/next.js/blob/canary/docs/01-app/03-api-reference/08-turbopack.mdx#known-gaps-with-webpack):

> "Turbopack will ensure that CSS files appear in the same order as their corresponding JS imports, following the import order... This can lead to subtle rendering changes when adopting Turbopack, if applications have come to rely on an arbitrary ordering."

The docs also explicitly note on the [CSS page](https://github.com/vercel/next.js/blob/canary/docs/01-app/01-getting-started/11-css.mdx#development-vs-production):
> "CSS ordering can behave differently in development, always ensure to check the build (`next build`) to verify the final CSS order."

**Suggested workarounds from the documentation:**
1. Use `@import` in CSS files to force explicit ordering
2. Identify conflicting CSS rules that target the same properties and make them more specific
3. The non-deterministic behavior you're seeing (disappearing when removing files) is related to how Turbopack infers side-effect-free modules - this is expected but can be frustrating

Since this is documented as a known gap, a fix would require changes to Turbopack itself. If the workarounds don't resolve your issue, you may want to file a feature request or check if there are existing GitHub issues tracking CSS ordering improvements in Turbopack.

body:
## Updated findings — Turbopack shared chunk issue

The minimal repro works, so this is NOT a framework-level bug. Closing this issue. The problem is project-specific.

**Root cause identified:** When a Next.js 16 app has source files that import heavy packages (Clerk, Sanity, Inngest, Supabase), Turbopack creates shared chunks that are loaded by ALL serverless functions — even a zero-import `/api/ping` route. Something in those shared chunks hangs during initialization on Vercel.

**Evidence:**
- Minimal repro with same deps *installed* but not *imported by source files* → works
- Full project where source files import those deps → ALL API routes hang, including zero-import routes

This appears to be a Turbopack function bundling behavior where shared chunks bleed across unrelated function boundaries. Will continue investigating which specific import causes the hang.

body:
To add a little more background:
document.currentScript is a pretty old API, to the point that it existed before Pale Moon forked from Firefox.
The specification is vague on how it should be have in async contexts, and it was written before the concept of microtasks.
For a while, Webkit/Blink browsers showed the originating script tag, while FF showed `null` in microtasks and async contexts.
This bug was filed for FF: https://bugzilla.mozilla.org/show_bug.cgi?id=1620505 and eventually resolved to make Gecko match the Blink behavior.

Resolved. Vercel support identified the root cause: conflicting dynamic route parameter names at the same path level (`[eventId]` and `[id]` under `api/calendar/admin/events/`).

Renamed to use consistent `[id]` and all API routes work now.

Suggestion for the Next.js team: this conflict produces zero output in build logs or runtime logs — the build succeeds and the function silently fails to initialize. A build-time validation that checks for conflicting parameter names at the same path level would save developers significant debugging time. The error message exists internally (`You cannot use different slug names for the same dynamic path`) but is only visible in Vercel's internal platform logs.

Closing this issue. Thank you.

Great reproduction, very handy. 

I found that the place where page props are being cached is in [`shared/lib/router.ts` in `sdc`](https://github.com/vercel/next.js/blob/canary/packages/next/src/shared/lib/router/router.ts#L701) which doesn't have any cache eviction logic.

I added this code to [this line](https://github.com/vercel/next.js/blob/canary/packages/next/src/shared/lib/router/router.ts#L1609) after `getRouteInfo`

```js
      if (Object.keys(this.sdc).length > 10) {
        const firstKey = Object.keys(this.sdc)[0]
        console.log('deleted', firstKey)
        delete this.sdc[firstKey]
      }

body:
From my understanding, a version of the team's position here may be that you can always undo persistence, but you can't undo non-persistence. So persistence is the right default. I'm not sure I agree or represent that correctly though.

Another way to think about it is that, in native apps, there's "tab switches" and "push nav" behaviors for buttons. And here we seem to be classifying everything as a "tab switch", with `key={bfcacheid}` as an opt-in for "push nav".

If we think this should be configurable, I wonder where this configuration belongs. Usually composable configuration that works somewhere down the tree is better than top level only. Which again speaks in favor of `key={bfcacheid}` as opt-out because it can be more granular. Whereas if opt-out is default or top-level, you can't opt in somewhere deeper below.

Curious to hear which cases you consider making the strongest case for why this behavior is bad.
