body:
I found a second issue behind the first one.

After patching the compound `pageExtensions` / `proxyFilePath` detection locally, the build gets further and now writes `/_middleware` to `functions-config-manifest.json`.

At that point, Turbopack still does not emit `server/middleware.js.nft.json`, but the standalone path later assumes it exists:

- `hasNodeMiddleware` becomes `true`
- `copyTracedFiles()` calls `handleTraceFiles(distDir + "/server/middleware.js.nft.json")`
- the file is missing, so `next build` fails with `ENOENT`

So there appear to be two separate Turbopack/node-proxy problems:

1. compound `pageExtensions` can prevent `proxyFilePath` from being set
2. once `proxyFilePath` is fixed, Turbopack still does not generate the node middleware NFT file that standalone packaging expects

In the failing app state I can confirm:

- `.next/server/functions-config-manifest.json` contains `/_middleware`
- `.next/server/middleware-manifest.json` still exists
- `.next/server/middleware.js.nft.json` does not exist
- `next build` then fails trying to open that missing NFT file

I have not yet opened a separate issue because this looks like the next failure in the same codepath.

Acknowledging this thread --

I think the OP had a network issue which is unrelated to most of these bugs. I have a separate PR pending that should cache Google Font requests between builds, which should reduce the chances of that error and make offline development easier.

The rest of you seem to be running on Windows ARM, which is a good hint of where to look to debug this. We upgraded the `reqwest` Rust library a few months ago to improve TLS handling. It's likely that one of the sub-dependencies doesn't have the http2 feature enabled for aarch64-pc-windows by default. I'll keep the thread updated as I dig into this.

body:
One more piece of diagnosis for whoever might want to fix this. Enabling `OTEL_LOG_LEVEL=debug` and correlating to the actual parent span (just the easiest local debug path), the parent is from `instrumentationScope: { name: '@opentelemetry/instrumentation-http', version: '0.211.0' }`.

The underlying bug here seems to be that `parentSpan.setAttribute` is called in the `handleRequestImpl(…).finally(…)`, which happens only after the entire response is sent and closed.

It seems like, instead of `.finally()`, it might make sense instead to set those attributes on `req.on('close', …)` + `req.on('end', …)` (possibly using `prependListener` instead of `on` to catch it before the parent span ends), which is how the `@opentelemtry/instrumentation-http` handles the other attributes: https://github.com/open-telemetry/opentelemetry-js/blob/786eefd3834fc36684874b1856fe42491d0b0b30/experimental/packages/opentelemetry-instrumentation-http/src/http.ts#L487-L558

body:
Also experiencing this on Firebase Hosting (Cloud Run).  

Upgraded from Next.js 16.1.x to 16.2.0 with "type": "module" in package.json.  

The error in Cloud Run logs:  

> ReferenceError: module is not defined in ES module scope
> This file is being treated as an ES module because it has a '.js' file extension
> and '/workspace/package.json' contains "type": "module".
> at file:///workspace/next.config.js:35
> Root cause matches what's described here: .next/package.json ({"type": "commonjs"}) is not included in the Firebase/Cloud Run bundle with Turbopack builds, so Node.js falls back to the root "type": "module", breaking all CJS server chunks.

Workaround: Removing "type": "module" from package.json fixes the issue.

author: altearius

body: Traced this. `turbopackFileSystemCacheForDev` now defaults to `true` in the canary config, so qfilter is active in every dev session. The panic comes from `qfilter 0.3.0-alpha.2` asserting BMI2 at runtime with no fallback. `qfilter 0.3.0-alpha.3` added a `legacy_x86_64_support` feature that replaces the assertion with a software PDEP/PEXT path. Bumping to `0.3.0-alpha.4` and enabling that feature in `turbo-persistence` fixes it. Opening a PR.

body:
Same root cause, materially worse symptom. Logging here so the issue surfaces the runtime-crash variant.

Symptom
On Next 16.2.4 with cacheComponents: true + React 19.2.4, navigating to a route that has a loading.tsx works, but a hard refresh of the same URL crashes the browser tab with:


Uncaught HierarchyRequestError: Failed to execute 'insertBefore' on 'Node':
The new child element contains the parent.
    at $RV (<inline-script>:1:NNN)
Only on production builds (next build && next start), only on refresh, soft nav from another route renders fine. Not just an SEO-invisibility issue: the page is unusable on second load.

Mechanism
Inspecting the streamed HTML shows two <div hidden id="S:N"> elements for the same N (we hit S:4 consistently). They come from two different systems sharing the same id namespace:

React 19.2's Suspense boundary outlining (#33027 / #33029) - when the route Suspense boundary's content crosses progressiveChunkSize, React outlines it into a hidden S:N chunk and schedules $RC("B:N", "S:N") to splice it.
Next.js PPR's postpone resumption - emits hidden S:N chunks paired with <template id="P:N"> placeholders, spliced by $RS("S:N", "P:N").
Both numbering sources allocate from the same S:N pool with no de-confliction. document.getElementById("S:N") returns the first match, so $RS ends up moving the route-Suspense outlined content into a postpone-slot placeholder. The structural mess that produces causes $RV to throw on its insertBefore step.

Repro variable is byte size, not structure
Empirically validated with a flat fallback (Array.from({length: 1000}).map(...) of trivial sibling skeletons, no nested wrappers, no two-column layouts) → crash. Same flat structure with 10 siblings → fine. The trigger is purely "boundary content over progressiveChunkSize", which matches what #33029 introduced.

Why this is more urgent than the original report
The SEO-invisibility variant degrades crawlability. This variant breaks the page for every refresh. Any non-trivial loading.tsx (multi-section skeleton mirroring the page, which is the documented "natural" way to write one) crosses the 12.8 KB threshold and triggers it.

Asked-for fix is the same
Expose progressiveChunkSize as a Next config (experimental.progressiveChunkSize or similar). Infinity makes the collision impossible, since outlining never fires. Cleaner long-term fix is namespacing the PPR S:N allocations away from the React Suspense S:N allocations, but a userspace knob is enough to unblock.

Versions: Next 16.2.4, React 19.2.4. Also reproduces on 19.2.5, 19.2.6 (no relevant changes between them).
author: SolutionsEngineer

body:
Hitting the same root cause in production on next@16.2.6 + react@19.2.x + cacheComponents: true. Adding our signature in case it helps the maintainers triage. Symptom (one variant of @SolutionsEngineer's diagnosis above) Direct SSR access to a fully-dynamic route (/signin?next=/dashboard, incognito, no cookies) renders a blank dark page. Client-side navigation to the same URL from a static route works — because it bypasses the SSR stream entirely. Streamed HTML signature …fallback…
← empty
…form…
← orphaned, not consumed ← swaps the visible fallback for empty S:0 ← P:1 is not in the DOM grep -c 'id="P:1"' → 0. So $RS's second getElementById returns null, null.parentNode throws, body ends up empty: Uncaught TypeError: Cannot read properties of null (reading 'parentNode') at $RS (signin:1:18109) Matches the two-allocator collision exactly: React 19.2's outlined S:N ([#33027](https://github.com/facebook/react/pull/33027)/[#33029](https://github.com/facebook/react/pull/33029)) and PPR's postpone S:N share the same id pool, so getElementById("S:1") returns the React-outlined node and the PPR $RS walks into the wrong slot. body:
### Investigation Summary

The vulnerability referenced in [GHSA-83fc-fqcc-2hmg](https://github.com/facebook/react/security/advisories/GHSA-83fc-fqcc-2hmg) (CVE-2026-23864) — Denial of Service in React Server Components — was fixed upstream in [facebook/react#35632](https://github.com/facebook/react/pull/35632) ("[Flight] Add more DoS mitigations to Flight Reply, and harden Flight"), merged on **2026-01-26**.

#### What was fixed

The vulnerability allowed specially crafted HTTP requests to Server Function endpoints to cause server crashes, out-of-memory exceptions, or excessive CPU usage (CWE-400, CWE-502). The fix introduced multiple mitigations into the Flight protocol deserialization:

| Protection | Detail |
|---|---|
| Bound arguments limit | Server Functions limited to 1,000 bound arguments |
| Array size / nesting limit | Default cap of 1,000,000 total slots across nested arrays |
| BigInt size limit | Rejects BigInt values exceeding 300 digits |
| `__proto__` pollution guards | Skips/deletes `__proto__` keys at multiple deserialization points |
| `then` key poisoning prevention | Prevents deserialized objects from appearing as thenables |

#### Status in Next.js

Next.js vendors its own copies of `react-server-dom-webpack` and `react-server-dom-turbopack` from React canary builds. The current Next.js canary already vendors from React canary `8b2e903a` (Mar 20, 2026), which is **~55 days after** the fix was merged (Jan 26) and 128+ commits ahead of the fix commit. **The vendored packages already contain all the above protections.**

I've verified the protections are present in the vendored server CJS files by inspecting the compiled code in `packages/next/src/compiled/react-server-dom-webpack/cjs/` and `packages/next/src/compiled/react-server-dom-turbopack/cjs/`.

Additionally, Next.js itself adds server-level protections on top of React's:
- **HTTP body size limit**: default 1 MB (configurable via `serverActions.bodySizeLimit` in `next.config.js`)
- **CSRF / origin validation** with configurable `allowedOrigins`
- **Action ID validation** (length check + `serverModuleMap` lookup)

#### For users on Next.js 15.x

If you are using `react@19.1.5` (which you mentioned), that version already includes the CVE fix — it was one of the [patched stable releases](https://github.com/facebook/react/security/advisories/GHSA-83fc-fqcc-2hmg). The vendored React inside Next.js 15.x releases from after January 26, 2026 would also contain the fix.

If your AWS Inspector is still flagging this, it may be matching on the vendored package version strings rather than checking the actual code content. You can verify the fix is present by checking for the `_arraySizeLimit` property and `bumpArrayCount` function in your installed `node_modules/next/dist/compiled/react-server-dom-webpack/cjs/react-server-dom-webpack-server.node.production.js`.

#### PR

Sync to latest React canary (`c0d218f0`, Mar 24): #91894

body:
For additional context here, I think any of these cases of NextJS pulling dependencies outside its directory (other than resolved node_modules) are fairly incompatible with Bazel. 

I’ve not investigated this symlink issue too deeply. But I think the lockfile dependency severely impacts Bazel’s ability to cache builds. Bazel has hermetic builds, where all input for an action needs to be explicitly stated, and any change in input will invalidate the action’s cached result. The lockfile dependency means any npm dep changes in any monorepo package will invalidate Bazel’s cache for all NextJS packages in the monorepo.

A means of opting out of this feature may be a pretty hard requirement for NextJS 16 adoption in Bazel monorepos.

⚠ Blocked cross-origin request to Next.js dev resource /_next/webpack-hmr from "172.24.101.93".
Cross-origin access to Next.js dev resources is blocked by default for safety.

To allow this host in development, add it to "allowedDevOrigins" in next.config.js and restart the dev server:

module.exports = {
  allowedDevOrigins: ['172.24.101.93'],
}

When you access your dev server  through an origin other than the hostname the server was initialized with (localhost by default), then you need to be explicit about this. When I was simulating, I'd use `localhost:3000` so I didn't run into the issue. 

We had thought that this terminal printout would guide people through. That's what I thought the issue was something else on your end.

Can you confirm? I think after that we can close the issue.

body:
@icyJoseph 
I might be mistaken, but it seems like the framework could improve the developer experience here.
When `allowedDevOrigins` is not configured, the app doesn’t work correctly when accessed via an `IP address` instead of localhost.

Currently, this is only shown as a warning in the terminal, which can be easy to miss—especially in larger applications where there are many logs and API calls happening.

It might be helpful to surface this as an error overlay in the browser, similar to other critical configuration issues. That way, developers can notice and resolve it more quickly.

From the discussion here, it looks like others have also missed this warning, so making it more visible could potentially prevent confusion.

author: alfonsusac

body:
I’m seeing this too with a fresh app created with pnpm (Edit: version error pnpm v <10, this fix works great; v >10 works fine for fresh install, see comments below).

```bash
pnpm create next-app@latest my-app --use-pnpm
```

The generated pnpm-workspace.yaml contains only:

```bash
ignoredBuiltDependencies:
  - sharp
  - unrs-resolver
```

After that, running pnpm scripts fails with:

```bash
ERROR packages field missing or empty
```

Adding an explicit packages entry fixes it:

```bash
packages:
  - "."

ignoredBuiltDependencies:
  - sharp
  - unrs-resolver
```

I tested in multiple directories and it was the same error, so it wasn't a parent package.json... but then while double-checking your reproduction process, I realized I was swapping environments (created the app in terminal, then opened and ran in VSCode) and found the issue!

My VSCode zsh was pointing to a 9.9.0 installation of pnpm, so it _did_ end up being a version error (which has been documented already [online](https://nextjs-forum.com/post/1486702171046281330) and where I got the original fix from, which works for those with pnpm versions <10).

Thanks for the help!
author: vincejtoman

body:
- https://nextjs.org/docs/app/api-reference/directives/use-cache

> If the in-memory cache isn't sufficient for runtime data, ['use cache: remote'](https://nextjs.org/docs/app/api-reference/directives/use-cache-remote) allows platforms to provide a dedicated cache handler, though it requires a network roundtrip to check the cache and typically incurs platform fees.

- https://nextjs.org/docs/app/api-reference/directives/use-cache#runtime-caching-considerations


> Environment | Runtime Caching Behavior
> -- | --
> Serverless | Cache entries typically don't persist across requests (each request can be a different instance). Build-time caching works normally.
> 

We have mentions of this in various places - I'll see what we can do to surface this better. Though it is an condition created by the deployment of the application.
author: icyJoseph

body:
Opened a docs fix PR for this:

- https://github.com/vercel/next.js/pull/92232

It adds a clear note in the Caching guide that runtime `use cache` entries are in-memory and may not persist across serverless instances, with a pointer to `use cache: remote` for durable/shared runtime caching.

Verification evidence (before/after + keyword check) is included in the PR body.

body:
OP is pointing out that, they had trouble discovering information already present in the docs. 

There's also nuance to this, a hosting provider might override use cache default handler altogether, and make it distributed etc... then our claim wouldn't be necessarily true. 

I'll review your PR and we'll try to land someway to address this issue initially and sign post to the areas where we expand upon it.

I believe the lint https://typescript-eslint.io/rules/no-import-type-side-effects explains the issue: verbatim mode leaves side-effect imports in place, which means that when we support that feature fully, this behaviour is (unfortunately) correct.

I've changed my lints to not enforce inline type specifiers, but to still require deduplicated imports, and the result is visible in the PR linked above.

body:
Seeing this same thing on Next.js 16.1.1 with a larger but not very big app (56 pages, 58 API routes).

If helpful:

**Setup:**
- Next.js 16.1.1 (Turbopack default)
- Node.js 22.22.0
- macOS Darwin 25.3.0, Apple Silicon
- Monorepo with pnpm, ~114 routes total (56 pages + 58 API routes)

**Measurements after navigating several pages:**

`footprint` output:
```
node [PID]: 64-bit    Footprint: 2981 MB

  Dirty      Clean  Reclaimable    Regions    Category
2342 MB        0 B          0 B         86    IOAccelerator
 495 MB        0 B      1328 KB       1709    app-specific tag 16
  62 MB        0 B          0 B         21    MALLOC_SMALL
```

`process.memoryUsage()` (via inspector) with the same process:
```json
{"heapUsed":"578MB","heapTotal":"619MB","rss":"4698MB","external":"5MB","arrayBuffers":"1MB"}
```

**4.1GB gap between RSS and V8 heap**, almost entirely IOAccelerator. Confirmed `next-swc.darwin-arm64.node` is the only native addon loaded.
author: tjb9dc

body:
Confirming this at production scale — **769 routes** (522 page + 247 API) in a TurboRepo monorepo with 259 transpilePackages. This is the same IOAccelerator pattern at a much larger route count.

## Environment

- Mac Mini M4, 16 GB unified memory
- macOS Sequoia 15.3.1 (Darwin 24.3.0)
- Node.js v22.22.2
- Next.js 16.2.0 (also tested 16.1.6, 16.0.7, 15.5.15)
- Bun 1.3.5 as package manager (real Node.js for `next dev`)
- 259 `transpilePackages`, 228 workspace packages, 164 `outputFileTracingExcludes`

## Key Findings

### 1. Version bisect — bug predates Next.js 16

| Next.js Version | IOAccelerator at kill | Turbopack/Webpack |
|----------------|----------------------|-------------------|
| 16.2.0         | 4,634 MB             | Turbopack         |
| 16.1.6         | 4,643 MB             | Turbopack         |
| 16.0.7         | 4,655 MB             | Turbopack         |
| 15.5.15        | 4,226 MB             | Turbopack         |
| 16.2.0         | 5,915 MB             | **Webpack**       |

All versions show identical pattern: ~1.1GB plateau for 20-30s, then explosion to 4GB+ in 2-4 seconds.

### 2. Webpack mode is WORSE, not better

Same IOAccelerator pattern under `next dev --no-turbo`:
- **Turbopack**: IOAccelerator = 4,634 MB at kill
- **Webpack**: IOAccelerator = 5,915 MB at kill

This means the leak is in **shared Next.js infrastructure** (route discovery, file watching, module resolution), not Turbopack-specific code. The issue title mentioning Turbopack may cause people to think switching to webpack is a workaround — it is not.

### 3. Route count is the trigger, not config complexity

| Test case | Routes | Config | Result |
|-----------|--------|--------|--------|
| Minimal app (1 page, no config) | 1 | Bare | ✅ Loads fine |
| Full config, 1 page route | 1 | Full (259 transpilePackages, all experimental flags) | ✅ Loads fine |
| Full app | 769 | Full | ❌ OOM at 4.6GB |

Full `next.config.ts` (259 transpilePackages, 164 excludes, 53 optimizePackageImports, 18 serverExternalPackages) works perfectly with 1 route. The same config with 769 routes triggers OOM.

### 4. Node 22 makes the leak lethal (Node 20 survives)

| Node Version | IOAccelerator | RSS Behavior | Outcome |
|-------------|---------------|-------------|---------|
| v22.22.2 | 4,634 MB | RSS tracks IOAccelerator tightly | OOM killed at ~45s |
| v20.20.2 | 5,200 MB | RSS oscillates 1.7-2.4 GB | **Survives 67s+** |

Same IOAccelerator leak in both versions, but Node 20 pages it to disk while Node 22 maps it as resident. The leak is the same; Node 22 just makes it fatal sooner on constrained machines.

### 5. Memory category isolation

Via `footprint` command at 4GB RSS:

| Category | Size | Growing? |
|----------|------|----------|
| **IOAccelerator (dirty)** | **4,634 MB** | **Only growing category** |
| MALLOC (all zones) | 74 MB | Flat |
| V8 heap (tag 16) | 68 MB | Flat |
| Stack | 1.5 MB | Flat |
| __TEXT | 81 MB | Flat |

V8 profiling tools, `--max-old-space-size`, and native heap profilers are all blind to this — the leak is entirely in IOAccelerator.

### 6. Growth pattern is consistent

```
Phase 1: Idle          0-15s    ~440MB RSS    Server ready
Phase 2: Initial load  15-20s   ~1100MB RSS   Page request triggers compilation
Phase 3: Plateau       20-45s   ~1100MB RSS   Compilation ongoing, stable
Phase 4: Explosion     45-50s   1100→4000MB   Unbounded growth, 2-4 seconds
Phase 5: Death         50s+     OOM killed
```

The Phase 3→4 transition at ~45s is the critical event. Something completes or triggers after ~25s of compilation that causes unbounded IOAccelerator allocation.

## Hypothesis

CoreServices file operations on Apple Silicon M4 allocate IOAccelerator (GPU-accessible unified memory) for internal buffers. During route discovery/compilation, Next.js performs 43,000+ file stat/watch operations. These buffers accumulate without being freed. `next-swc.darwin-arm64.node` links CoreFoundation + CoreServices (which handle file I/O on macOS) but does NOT link Metal or IOKit directly — IOAccelerator allocation must come through a transitive path via CoreServices.

## Impact — Total Blocker

This is a **completely blocking issue** for us. No page route compiles on the 16GB M4 Mac Mini — zero. Not a slow build, not degraded performance — the dev server is entirely unusable for page development. API routes work, `next build` completes in 79 seconds, production deploys fine. Only `next dev` with page routes is broken.

We've been unable to do any frontend page development on this machine for days. The only workaround we've found is a "bench" tool we built that renames route directories with `_` prefix (Next.js private folder convention) to reduce the active route count below ~200, but this means 73% of our routes are inaccessible during development.

This will affect any team running a monorepo with 200+ page routes on a 16GB Apple Silicon Mac — which is the most common developer machine Apple sells.

## Tooling

We built a memory watchdog that auto-polls RSS, captures `vmmap`/`footprint` at 1GB/2GB/3GB thresholds, and auto-kills at 4GB. Happy to share artifacts from 4 captured runs across Next.js 15.5-16.2.
author: pastarita

body:
This IOAccelerator memory is just memory allocated by the native binary (which is why it is not visible to node.js tools).  As we compile routes we cache information about those routes in memory which is why memory goes up as more routes.

| Just loading the SWC binary — before compiling anything — allocates 136 MB and reserves 896 MB more.

yeah this is expected, this is approximately how big the binary is and then we also initialize the native heap

(also, the `turbopackMemoryLimit` feature is indeed unimplemented and will likely be removed in a future release)


Since the concern is about the oomkiller, tracking memory via vmmap is somewhat misleading.  When processes map files into ram they get accounted to vmmap but not necessarily to 'physical heap' which is the thing the OOM killer cares about.

The better metric to track is RSS or Physical Footprint

`vmmap -summary $(pgrep -f next-server)  | grep "Physical footprint"`

or just RSS as reported by `ps`

`ps -o pid,rss,vsz -p $(pgrep -f next-server)`

Since that is what the OOM killer cares about


From that i can see that RSS does go down over time, in my case it is due to heap compression and swapping

So killing the server at 4G of allocated IOAccellerator pages is the problem, in all scenarios i see that number only going up over the course of dev server sessions. (this is the behavior of our memory allocator which maps anonymous memory and tags it as droppable instead of returning it)  But this isn't the important number, systems have lots of virtual memory address space and you shouldn't care about it.  So your watchdog should only care about RSS/Physical footprint (aka working set memory)


That being said I am are currently working on a few solutions to decrease our 'working set size' in conjunction with our filesystem caching solution.

body:
### Additional reproduction — Next.js 16.2.6, Apple Silicon, 128 routes

#### Environment
|                 |                                                                                  |
| --------------- | -------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| OS              | macOS Darwin 25.3.0, Apple Silicon (ARM64)                                       |
| RAM             | 16 GB                                                                            |
| Node.js         | 24.15.0                                                                          |
| Next.js         | 16.2.6 (Turbopack default, no flags)                                             |
| React           | 19.2.6                                                                           |
| Package manager | Bun                                                                              |
| Router          | App Router                                                                       |
| Routes          | 72 `page.tsx` + 56 `route.ts` = 128 total                                        |
| Key deps        | `@sentry/nextjs` 10.52.0, `@supabase/supabase-js` 2.105.3, `posthog-js` 1.372.10 |

#### Observed behaviour

After a normal dev session (~100–200 page compilations via HMR), `next-server` reaches **9.04 GB RSS** in Activity Monitor. Memory grows monotonically and does not reclaim between page navigations or during idle periods.

#### V8 vs native breakdown

To isolate how much of this is V8 vs native, I took a heap snapshot via `kill -USR1 <pid>` and the Chrome DevTools Protocol:

- Snapshot file size: **1.25 GB**
- Top 50 retained objects (by self size): **1.66 GB**
- **~7.3 GB invisible to V8** — absent from `process.memoryUsage()` and not captured in the snapshot

Running `vmmap <pid> | grep "^IOAccelerator"` confirms the gap is IOAccelerator allocations, consistent with this report.

#### Confirmed non-fixes

- `NODE_OPTIONS=--max-old-space-size=4096` — no effect on the balloon
- `experimental.turbopackMemoryLimit` — accepted by config, produces no observable change (as noted in the original report — not wired to the native binary)

#### Scale correlation

The 128-route count fits the pattern reported here (3.5 GB for 5 pages, 13.9 GB for 27 pages) — larger apps hit the ceiling faster. On a 16 GB machine this competes directly with Docker, Chrome, and other dev tooling, quickly pushing into swap.

The only mitigation found is periodic `next dev` restarts. Happy to provide additional heap data or run specific diagnostics if useful.

### Why was this issue closed?

To be able to investigate, we need access to a reproduction to identify what triggered the issue. We need a link to a **public** GitHub repository ([template for App Router](https://github.com/vercel/next.js/tree/canary/examples/reproduction-template), [template for Pages Router](https://github.com/vercel/next.js/tree/canary/examples/reproduction-template-pages)), but you can also use these templates: [CodeSandbox: App Router](https://codesandbox.io/s/github/vercel/next.js/tree/canary/examples/reproduction-template) or [CodeSandbox: Pages Router](https://codesandbox.io/s/github/vercel/next.js/tree/canary/examples/reproduction-template-pages).

The bug template that you filled out has a section called "Link to the code that reproduces this issue", which is where you should provide the link to the reproduction.

- If you did not provide a link or the link you provided is not valid, we will close the issue.
- If you provide a link to a private repository, we will close the issue.
- If you provide a link to a repository but not in the correct section, we will close the issue.

### What should I do?

Depending on the reason the issue was closed, you can do the following:

- If you did not provide a link, please open a new issue with a link to a reproduction.
- If you provided a link to a private repository, please open a new issue with a link to a public repository.
- If you provided a link to a repository but not in the correct section, please open a new issue with a link to a reproduction in the correct section.

**In general, assume that we should not go through a lengthy onboarding process at your company code only to be able to verify an issue.**

### My repository is private and cannot make it public

In most cases, a private repo will not be a sufficient **minimal reproduction**, as this codebase might contain a lot of unrelated parts that would make our investigation take longer. Please do **not** make it public. Instead, create a new repository using the templates above, adding the relevant code to reproduce the issue. Common things to look out for:

- Remove any code that is not related to the issue. (pages, API routes, components, etc.)
- Remove any dependencies that are not related to the issue.
- Remove any third-party service that would require us to sign up for an account to reproduce the issue.
- Remove any environment variables that are not related to the issue.
- Remove private packages that we do not have access to.
- If the issue is not related to a monorepo specifically, try to reproduce the issue without a complex monorepo setup

Anyone experiencing the same issue is welcome to provide a minimal reproduction following the above steps by opening a new issue.

We look into every Next.js issue and constantly monitor open issues for new comments.

However, sometimes we might miss one or two due to the popularity/high traffic of the repository. We apologize, and kindly ask you to refrain from tagging core maintainers, as that will usually not result in increased priority.

Upvoting issues to show your interest will help us prioritize and address them as quickly as possible. That said, every issue is important to us, and if an issue gets closed by accident, we encourage you to open a new one linking to the old issue and we will look into it.

body:
This is a major blocker for our Turbopack adoption.

We maintain a **Next.js 16 Pages Router** app — a perpetuals DEX frontend with a deep web3/crypto dependency tree:

| Package | Version |
|---|---|
| `viem` | ^2.45 |
| `wagmi` / `@wagmi/core` | ^3.4 / ^3.3 |
| `permissionless` | ^0.3.4 |
| `ethers` | ^6.16 |
| `@privy-io/react-auth` | ^3.13 |
| `@walletconnect/*` | 2.21.8 (pinned) |
| `@noble/curves` / `@noble/hashes` | 1.9.7 / 1.8.0 (pinned) |
| `@scure/bip32` / `@scure/bip39` | 1.7.0 / 1.6.0 (pinned) |
| `@coral-xyz/anchor` | ^0.32.1 |
| `@solana/spl-token` | ^0.4.14 |

These libraries (and their transitive deps) ship modern syntax — exponentiation (`**`), optional chaining, nullish coalescing, etc. — that needs to be downleveled to match our browserslist:

```json
"browserslist": {
  "production": [">0.2%", "not dead", "not op_mini all"]
}
```

**With webpack** this works fine — Babel/SWC processes `node_modules` through the browserslist pipeline and everything gets transpiled. **With Turbopack**, modern syntax inside dependencies is **not** run through the browserslist transpilation system (tracked in #83799). The result is untranspiled code hitting browsers that don't support it, causing runtime failures on page load.

We've been forced to keep `--webpack` on both our dev and build scripts as a workaround:

```json
"dev": "next dev --experimental-https --webpack",
"build": "next build --webpack"
```

Our `next.config.mjs` also relies heavily on webpack-specific plugins (TerserPlugin, CompressionPlugin, CssMinimizerPlugin, ImageMinimizerPlugin, CopyWebpackPlugin) which adds to the migration friction — but the browserslist/transpilation gap is the core blocker. Even if we stripped all the custom webpack config, the untranspiled dependency code alone makes Turbopack unusable for us.

This is especially painful for web3 projects where the majority of your dependency graph is crypto/wallet libraries shipping ESNext, and `transpilePackages` doesn't help because the offending code is buried in transitive dependencies 3-4 levels deep.

body:
Seeing the same regression as @chagas42 and @adahl5, with a couple of extra data points that might help.

**Setup:** Pages Router legacy i18n (`next-translate`), `locales: ['en','fr','es']`, **`defaultLocale: 'en'`** — so this is *not* limited to a non-English default locale. Middleware rewrites requests on a custom host (`api.zaprite.com`) to an internal `/api/...` path.

**Symptom (production only):** authenticated `GET https://api.zaprite.com/v1/orders` returns the static localized 404 instead of hitting the API:

```
HTTP 404
content-type: text/html
x-matched-path: /en/404
x-vercel-cache: HIT
```

Key observations:
- **Reproduces on the latest 16.2.9** (so not fixed through the current 16.2.x line). `16.1.7` is unaffected.
- It's served from the **Full Route Cache at the edge** — query-string cache-busting does *not* bust it, and the middleware rewrite never runs (the cached `/en/404` is returned ahead of it).
- **Only the real production domain reproduces it.** Running `next build && next start` locally, and host-spoofing the same request against a `*.vercel.app` preview, both route correctly to the API (`x-matched-path` = the real API route, `x-vercel-cache: MISS`). The locale prefix only leaks onto the API path on the production domain with a warm Full Route Cache — which may be why a minimal repro has been hard to pin down.

Net: the i18n locale prefix appears to be applied to API/extensionless paths during production route matching, and the resulting localized 404 gets cached and served from the edge.

body:
Anyone looking for a workaround:
```ts
const nextConfig: NextConfig = {
  outputFileTracingIncludes: {
    '/*': ['./.env'],
  },
}
```

We generate the `.env` file at build time with something like:
```sh
pnpm dotenvx get -f dotenv/.env.${VERCEL_ENV} -f dotenv/.env --format "eval" > .env && pnpm next build
```

From there, `next build` loads the `.env` file and the runtime used to load it in memory automatically. Since the file isn't committed, I haven't seen it exposed anywhere. **Is this no longer a safe practice?**

If not a bug, this is definitely a breaking change, and I have yet to find any mention of this in the release notes. 

Thank you

author: stephenhmarsh

body:
Submitted a draft PR with a fix and a regression test: #93368.

Root cause: three client-side call sites built the page cache key with `Object.fromEntries(new URLSearchParams(...))`, which collapses repeated keys to the last value. The server uses a `Record<string, string | string[]>` and preserves arrays, so the cache key for `?color=red&color=green&color=blue` and the one for `?color=red&color=blue` both reduced to `{"color":"blue"}` on the client and shared the same entry — the stale render was served and Suspense never re-suspended.

Verified locally on the linked repro: 16.1.7 unaffected, 16.2.4 reproduces, canary plus the patch passes. The regression was introduced in #87256 (v16.2.0), which added a third place using this pattern; the other two have used it since v16.0 and are corrected together.

body:
Same bug fires with a **single-value** search param, not just repeated keys — so PR #93368's fix won't cover the broader case.

### Single-value reproduction

Next 16.2.6 (also confirmed 16.2.5). App Router. Standard `next start` after `next build`. **Not** static export.

```tsx
// app/listings/page.tsx (Server Component)
export default async function ListingsPage({
  searchParams,
}: { searchParams: Promise<{ regions?: string }> }) {
  const sp = await searchParams;
  const total = await prisma.listing.count({ where: { regions: sp.regions } });
  return <>{total} active <FilterButton /></>;
}
```

```tsx
// app/listings/FilterButton.tsx ("use client")
"use client";
import { useRouter } from "next/navigation";
export function FilterButton() {
  const router = useRouter();
  return <button onClick={() => router.push("/listings?regions=75")}>75</button>;
}
```

1. `npm run build && npm start`, open `/listings`, click the button.
2. URL bar does **not** change. Server Component does **not** re-run. No console error.
3. Network panel: a single `GET /listings?regions=75&_rsc=...` → `200 text/x-component` → `net::ERR_ABORTED` mid-body.
4. `next dev` works correctly. Direct URL load works correctly. Navigating to a different pathname works correctly.
5. `router.replace`, `<Link href="/listings?regions=75">` from `/listings`, and `history.pushState + router.refresh()` all fail the same way.

This is **not** `regions=red&regions=green → regions=red&regions=blue` (PR #93368's target). It's `(no regions param) → regions=75`. A single key, a single value, going from absent to present.

### Trace (patched `node_modules` with `console.error` markers)

```
[navigateImpl]              from=/listings to=/listings?regions=75
[navigateToKnownRoute]      starting PPR isSamePage=false  task=OK
[spawnDynamicRequests]      fired
[fetchServerResponse]       url=/listings?regions=75
[completeSoftNavigation]    canonicalUrl=/listings?regions=75
[navigate-final]            canonicalUrl=/listings?regions=75 sameAsInput=false
[action-handleResult]       discarded=false  nextCanonicalUrl=/listings?regions=75
[useActionQueue]            isThenable=true (promise pending)
[flight-response-ok]        contentType=text/x-component
[flight-resp-decoded]       buildId matches
[flight-data-normalized-ok]
[useActionQueue AFTER-use]  canonicalUrl=/listings?regions=75   <- resolved
[Router-render]             canonicalUrl=/listings?regions=75   <- new state
[HistoryUpdater-render]     canonicalUrl=/listings?regions=75   <- inside JSX
... renders repeat with the new state ...
*** [HistoryUpdater useInsertionEffect] never fires ***
```

The fetch succeeds, `completeSoftNavigation` returns a state with the correct `canonicalUrl`, the promise from `useActionQueue` resolves, React renders both `Router` and `HistoryUpdater` with the new `canonicalUrl` — but `HistoryUpdater`'s `useInsertionEffect` (which calls `window.history.pushState`) **never fires**. The transition renders but never commits.

### Hypothesis (please verify)

`updateCacheNodeOnNavigation` in `ppr-navigations.js` (around line 159):

```js
if (oldCacheNode !== undefined && !shouldRefreshDynamicData &&
    !(isLeafSegment && isSamePageNavigation)) {
  newCacheNode = reuseSharedCacheNode(dropPrefetchRsc, oldCacheNode);
  needsDynamicRequest = false;
} else {
  // createCacheNodeForSegment with a fresh deferred RSC
}
```

For same-pathname-different-query:
- `isSamePageNavigation` is `false` (because the full URL differs).
- Outer (layout) segments are **reused** with their already-resolved RSC.
- The `__PAGE__` leaf is **recreated** because `matchSegment(newSegment, oldSegment)` is false (the page segment's serialized identity includes the search params).

The resulting cache tree mixes reused-old-RSC parents with a freshly-created-deferred-RSC leaf. After `writeDynamicDataIntoNavigationTask` resolves the leaf's deferred promise, React 19's concurrent renderer keeps re-running the render but never commits — classic "transition starts and renders but commit is held back." This mirrors what reporter on #92152 sees and what we see; PR #93368's `searchStringToRecord` fix addresses one specific cause of the cache-key mismatch (repeated keys) but doesn't address the broader mixed reuse/new tree pattern that triggers on any single-value change.

### Workarounds tested end-to-end (Puppeteer against real prod build)

| Approach | URL updates? | Server data updates? |
|---|---|---|
| `router.push(target)` | ❌ | ❌ |
| `router.replace(target)` | ❌ | ❌ |
| `<Link href={target}>` from same page | ❌ | ❌ |
| `history.pushState + router.refresh()` | ✅ | ❌ (stale) |

body:
Follow-up on my earlier single-value report (`/listings` -> `/listings?regions=75` never committing in prod builds): **root cause identified. It is not the router or the segment cache - it is the React canary that Next vendors in `next/dist/compiled/react*`.**

## TL;DR

The hang is facebook/react#35821 ("useDeferredValue getting stuck"), fixed upstream by facebook/react#36134 (merged 2026-03-24). The fix reached Next via the vendored React upgrade in #91905 (`19.3.0-canary-8b2e903a-20260320` -> `19.3.0-canary-3cb2c420-20260324`), first published in `16.2.1-canary.11`. **It was never backported to the 16.2 release branch**: every 16.2.x stable up to and including 16.2.9 (published 2026-06-09) still vendors `19.3.0-canary-3f0b9e61-20260317`, which predates the React fix. That is why the bug reproduces on all 16.2.x stables while the canary/16.3 line is unaffected since late March.

This explains the failure mode exactly: the navigation transition renders (Router and HistoryUpdater both re-render with the new canonicalUrl) but React never commits it, so HistoryUpdater's `useInsertionEffect` - which calls `history.pushState` - never fires. URL frozen, Server Component data never swapped in, no error anywhere.

## How it was isolated

All tests against my repro (https://github.com/lorenzoedoardofrancesco/next-router-push-query-bug): `next build && next start`, Puppeteer clicks the `router.push("/listings?regions=75")` button, asserts URL change + fresh server-rendered content after 8s.

1. **Bisected the published canary ladder** between 16.2.1 (broken) and 16.3.0-canary.0 (working): `16.2.1-canary.10` reproduces, `16.2.1-canary.11` is fixed. The commit range between the two builds (`d529a233e8...2fe21375d9`) contains 6 commits; the only one touching runtime code is the React upgrade #91905.
2. **Grafted only the React files**: copying `dist/compiled/{react,react-dom,react-server-dom-*,scheduler}*` from the `16.2.1-canary.11` package into an otherwise untouched `16.2.1-canary.10` install flips the repro from broken to fixed. Same graft onto stock `16.2.7`: also fixed. No other file changes.
3. **Instrumented the segment cache** on 16.2.7 to rule the router out. For the failing navigation, `updateCacheNodeOnNavigation` correctly recreates the `__PAGE__` leaf (`__PAGE__` vs `__PAGE__?{"regions":"75"}`), the dynamic response matches every task segment, `writeDynamicDataIntoNavigationTask` fulfills all pending nodes, and `finishNavigationTask` exits with status 0 (no tree mismatch, no retry). The cache layer completes cleanly; the loss happens afterwards, inside React's commit.

## Version matrix (all verified with the repro unless noted)

| next | vendored React | result |
| --- | --- | --- |
| 16.2.1, 16.2.4, 16.2.6, 16.2.7 (stable) | 19.3.0-canary-3f0b9e61-20260317 | broken |
| 16.2.9 (stable, 2026-06-09) | 19.3.0-canary-3f0b9e61-20260317 (inspected, not e2e-tested) | expected broken |
| 16.2.1-canary.5 / .8 / .9 / .10 | 19.3.0-canary-8b2e903a-20260320 | broken |
| 16.2.1-canary.11 | 19.3.0-canary-3cb2c420-20260324 | **fixed** |
| 16.2.1-canary.10 + React files from canary.11 | 19.3.0-canary-3cb2c420-20260324 | **fixed** |
| 16.2.7 + React files from canary.11 | 19.3.0-canary-3cb2c420-20260324 | **fixed** |
| 16.2.1-canary.23 / .46, 16.3.0-canary.0 / .46, 16.3.0-preview.0 | post-fix | **fixed** |

Two clarifications on my earlier report:

- The `net::ERR_ABORTED` on the `_rsc` fetch is a red herring: it shows up identically on the passing builds (it is the static-stage body-clone cancellation in `fetch-server-response.ts`), so it is not a useful signal for this bug.
- This is a different bug from the duplicate-search-param cache collision that #93368 targets. The cache keys here are consistent end to end; #93368 will not fix the single-value case, and the React bump does not address the duplicate-key collision. Both fixes are needed to close this issue.

## Ask

Could the vendored React upgrade (#91905, or any later pin >= `3cb2c420-20260324`) be backported to the 16.2 release branch? On 16.2.x stable, every same-pathname `router.push`/`router.replace`/`<Link>` navigation that only changes the query string silently fails in production - filters, sort headers, pagination - with no error and no console output, while dev mode works. Several commenters above are pinned on 16.2.x because of the CVE fixed there, so the practical alternatives today are downgrading to 16.1 or moving to the 16.3 preview line.

> How are you deploying? Do you have a caching CDN in front?

> 


@mischnic I will add that this problem for us surfaced specifically because we scale horizontally and do a rolling update as we deploy. This means there is a period where an old and new deployment are both running at once.

You are right that the `?dpl=` query parameter serves for cache busting. We rely on this so static assets from one release are only served when needed. But only the deployment id in the url path is validated by Next.js when it receives a request, not the query parameter. That means it's possible for this scenario to happen:

- We do a rolling update deployment
- Part way through the deployment, when we have some pods running the old and new release, a request for a page reaches origin due to a miss at CDN
- This request reaches a pod in the deployment running the new release, and the page is served from the new release. This is all fine and expected.
- The page loads in the browser and then starts fetching assets in the HTML. One of these is the build manifest, fetched via https://foo.com/_next/static/build-TfctsWXpff2fKS/_buildManifest.js?dpl=new-release
- The request for the build manifest includes the same build ID as the previous release in the path, but the new build id in the query params, so it misses at CDN
- We are still doing a rolling update, and the request reaches the deployment and a pod running the old release
- Next.js does not validate the incoming deployment ID header, so the fact it differs at origin is irrelevant
- Both releases have the same ID, so both have a _next/static/build-TfctsWXpff2fKS/_buildManifest.js file to serve. The old release serves a build manifest in response. 
- The CDN caches the manifest from the old build on the way back through under https://foo.com/_next/static/build-TfctsWXpff2fKS/_buildManifest.js?dpl=new-release
- CDN Cache for the new release is now poisoned for all users. 
- Every user thereafter on that deploy will load the old manifest, as the TTL is basically infinite (per Next.js defaults)

This then surfaces as a real issue in pages router, where Next.js uses this manifest to prefetch routes. When the prefetches 404, the Link component switches from client side routing to full page navigation, slowing down UX.

We are self hosting, but I would be interested to hear how this is not an issue for Vercel customers too who are using Skew Protection to effectively keep multiple releases running at once.

author: harry-gocity

body:
Sorry for the delay.

So this was changed as part of work to make Next.js build outputs deterministic. This was to make sure that only a small number of output files change, if you made a tiny change in your application code.
This meant also that `deploymentId` and `buildId` shouldn't be part of the build outputs themselves, otherwise they would constantly change on every single deployment, even with zero code change. (For Vercel, the deployment id is provided via an environment variable at runtime.)

I originally tried to remove the build id from `_next/data` and `_next/static` URLs entirely, but that would have broken even more code (in Next.js and I suspect other places as well). So I just made it a constant value to make the build output deterministic while keeping the URL formats the same.

For the manifests, I think this is just working as intended, because this `_next/static/build-TfctsWXpff2fKS/_buildManifest.js?dpl=the-current-dpl-id` is covered by skew protection (and the proxy should include the query param in the cache key).
For all the regular JS chunks, the URLs don't contain a build id at all (only `?dpl`), so if the `?dpl` isn't correctly routed here, then all requests would be broken? So I don't see how this is specific to these Pages Router manifests. If you have a `?dpl` param for some static JS file, then you don't need the build id as well.

I'm looking into a solution for the _next/data URL caching problem now.
author: mischnic

body:
> For Vercel, the deployment id is provided via an environment variable at runtime.

Interesting to know, thank you.

> For the manifests, I think this is just working as intended, because this _next/static/build-TfctsWXpff2fKS/_buildManifest.js?dpl=the-current-dpl-id is covered by skew protection (and the proxy should include the query param in the cache key).

It's only covered by skew protection if your load balancer is also routing requests based on the deployment ID query parameter. Else, during a rolling deployment, a request for a manifest from the new client can easily reach an old deployment that is still scaling down, which will have a `_next/static/build-TfctsWXpff2fKS/_buildManifest.js` file to respond with. This 200 gets cached under `_next/static/build-TfctsWXpff2fKS/_buildManifest.js?dpl=the-current-dpl-id` and the cache is poisoned.

This was not an issue before, as the request contained a varying build ID in the path and would reach the old deployment and 404. The CDN wouldn't cache this, so the next client to request to request the manifest would be served by origin, and eventually, a client request will reach a new deployment, which will serve the manifest correctly, and be cached correctly.

We could not detect a valid reproduction link. **Make sure to follow the bug report template carefully.**

### Why was this issue closed?

To be able to investigate, we need access to a reproduction to identify what triggered the issue. We need a link to a **public** GitHub repository ([template for App Router](https://github.com/vercel/next.js/tree/canary/examples/reproduction-template), [template for Pages Router](https://github.com/vercel/next.js/tree/canary/examples/reproduction-template-pages)), but you can also use these templates: [CodeSandbox: App Router](https://codesandbox.io/s/github/vercel/next.js/tree/canary/examples/reproduction-template) or [CodeSandbox: Pages Router](https://codesandbox.io/s/github/vercel/next.js/tree/canary/examples/reproduction-template-pages).

The bug template that you filled out has a section called "Link to the code that reproduces this issue", which is where you should provide the link to the reproduction.

- If you did not provide a link or the link you provided is not valid, we will close the issue.
- If you provide a link to a private repository, we will close the issue.
- If you provide a link to a repository but not in the correct section, we will close the issue.

### What should I do?

Depending on the reason the issue was closed, you can do the following:

- If you did not provide a link, please open a new issue with a link to a reproduction.
- If you provided a link to a private repository, please open a new issue with a link to a public repository.
- If you provided a link to a repository but not in the correct section, please open a new issue with a link to a reproduction in the correct section.

**In general, assume that we should not go through a lengthy onboarding process at your company code only to be able to verify an issue.**

### My repository is private and cannot make it public

In most cases, a private repo will not be a sufficient **minimal reproduction**, as this codebase might contain a lot of unrelated parts that would make our investigation take longer. Please do **not** make it public. Instead, create a new repository using the templates above, adding the relevant code to reproduce the issue. Common things to look out for:

- Remove any code that is not related to the issue. (pages, API routes, components, etc.)
- Remove any dependencies that are not related to the issue.
- Remove any third-party service that would require us to sign up for an account to reproduce the issue.
- Remove any environment variables that are not related to the issue.
- Remove private packages that we do not have access to.
- If the issue is not related to a monorepo specifically, try to reproduce the issue without a complex monorepo setup

### I did not open this issue, but it is relevant to me, what can I do to help?

Anyone experiencing the same issue is welcome to provide a minimal reproduction following the above steps by opening a new issue.

### I think my reproduction is good enough, why aren't you looking into it quickly?

We look into every Next.js issue and constantly monitor open issues for new comments.

However, sometimes we might miss one or two due to the popularity/high traffic of the repository. We apologize, and kindly ask you to refrain from tagging core maintainers, as that will usually not result in increased priority.

Upvoting issues to show your interest will help us prioritize and address them as quickly as possible. That said, every issue is important to us, and if an issue gets closed by accident, we encourage you to open a new one linking to the old issue and we will look into it.

body:
The issue appears to be that we're counting unique combinations of file patterns *and* modules, and this repro happens to construct a long list of file patterns.

We could fix how we're counting these to perform deduplication of resolved modules, but if this error fires, it still points to a (lesser) performance issue, because the data structure of request keys and file path pairs is still huge.

I talked with @lukesandberg and it sounds like very rarely use these request keys (only in `PatternMapping::resolve_request`) and so we're wasting a lot of resources computing and storing `RequestKey`s that may never be used. We might be able to fix this, but it's unclear.

So the best fix for now might just be to change the error message 😞

body:
**Another reproduction: this also hits the stable `not-found.tsx` (no `experimental.globalNotFound`, root layout present) on 16.2.7**

Since @mischnic couldn't reproduce the original repo, here's an independent data point in a different and arguably more common configuration. We hit what looks like the same infinite dev-recompile loop, but with a plain `app/not-found.tsx`, **no** `experimental.globalNotFound`, and a normal root `app/layout.tsx` present. That suggests the problem is in how the *not-found special entry* is handled in the module graph generally, not just `global-not-found`.

### Environment
- `next@16.2.7`, `react`/`react-dom@19.2.4`
- Windows 11, 32 logical cores
- Default Turbopack dev server (`next dev`)
- Plain config: no `experimental.globalNotFound`, root `app/layout.tsx` exists

### Symptom
- With **zero requests in flight**, the dev server idles at ~50% CPU (16 of 32 cores pegged) indefinitely.
- The only thing changing on disk during that idle is the not-found server chunk: `.next/.../src_app_not-found_tsx_*.js` rewrites itself roughly **every ~5s, forever**. It compiles, immediately invalidates, recompiles. The loop is below the trace layer (Next's `trace` file barely grows while CPU stays at 50%).

### What triggers it (the useful part)
In this configuration the trigger scales with the **size of the imported module graph**, not literally "any import":

| `not-found.tsx` imports | Idle CPU | not-found chunk |
| --- | --- | --- |
| only `next/link` | **0%** | stable, no recompile |
| a large shared "workspace chrome" component (transitively pulls in most of the app: sidebar, tabs, an editor surface, a terminal, overlays, a status bar, dozens of `"use client"` components + their deps) | **~50%** | recompiles every ~5s in a loop |

Removing that one heavy import drops idle CPU from ~50% to **0% instantly** and the chunk stops recompiling. This may explain the non-repro: a trivial import (or a single `globals.css`) may not be heavy enough to trip it in a config with a root layout. A large client-component graph reliably does.

### Minimal repro recipe
1. Scaffold a fresh App Router + TS app, then pin `next@16.2.7`, `react@19.2.4`, `react-dom@19.2.4`.
2. Keep the default root `app/layout.tsx`. Do **not** set `experimental.globalNotFound`.
3. Add `app/not-found.tsx` that statically imports a **large** client-component subtree (e.g., a component that itself imports a heavy client dependency such as a terminal emulator, plus ~a dozen `"use client"` components) and renders it.
4. `next dev`, hit any 404 route once, then leave the server idle. Watch CPU and `.next` for `src_app_not-found_tsx_*.js` rewriting on a loop.

### One more note
We also observed comparable idle CPU under `next dev --webpack`, so this may not be strictly Turbopack-specific, though we only positively confirmed the not-found-chunk recompile loop under Turbopack.

Happy to put together a self-contained minimal reproduction repo if that would help narrow it down.

body:
Additional production signal from the same app after filing this issue:

- We kept the app on `next@16.2.2`, `output: "standalone"`, and `cacheComponents: true`.
- We raised our production restart guard from `5 GiB` to `7 GiB` to see whether this was mainly a restart-threshold artifact.
- Result: restart frequency decreased, but the underlying memory trend did not change. The process still climbs steadily until it reaches the new ceiling and is recycled.

Recent production pattern:

- Around `2026-04-04T12:20Z` the process was already at `~6.9 GiB`
- `2026-04-04T12:25Z`: `~7.29 GiB`
- `2026-04-04T12:29Z`: guard-triggered restart at `7601336320`
- `2026-04-04T12:30Z`: second restart at `7593152512`
- after restart it returned to low memory and began the same steady climb again

The runtime artifact growth also continues during these runs. In the same production windows we still see:

- `.next/server/app` growth continuing over time
- fetch-cache file count continuing to increase
- large server/cache footprint before each restart window

So increasing the restart limit reduces restart frequency, but does not produce stabilization. The process still grows until it reaches whatever ceiling we give it.

This strengthens the runtime/deployment suspicion rather than the “small application leak” theory:

- our minimal repro still shows standalone OOM behavior on `16.2.2`
- the `next start` control in that repro behaved materially better after load stopped
- our production app still shows the same upward-only pattern under standalone, even when the restart threshold is raised

body:
Possibly a distinct regression in the same area — flagging here since this is the active arrayBuffers/standalone thread.

Self-hosted, `output: "standalone"`, containerized Node server. A single dependency bump — `next` **16.1.6 → 16.2.6** — took steady-state memory from ~6 GB to ~17 GB under an identical workload. Growth is off-heap (`rss`/`external`/`arrayBuffers`), not JS heap; `--max-old-space-size` has no effect.

This looks separate from the root cause tracked here: in our 16.2.6 build the #90897 fixes are present — `dist/server/lib/clone-response.js` registers **both** `cloned1` and `cloned2` with `FinalizationRegistry`, and `dist/server/lib/lru-cache.js` throws on a 0 size — yet 16.2.6 still runs ~3× the memory of 16.1.6 on the same traffic. That points to an additional leak somewhere in the 16.2.x line beyond the clone-response/LRU issue. The May 2026 security release (GHSA-c4j6-fc7j-m34r WS-upgrade SSRF, http-proxy CVE-2026-29057, streaming-fetch-hang fix) is one candidate, but the bump spans all of 16.2.x.

Bisecting within 16.2.x to localize; will follow up with `process.memoryUsage()` numbers.

body:
This EPERM error on Windows is typically caused by file locking from a previous process or security software. The `.next/trace` file is written during Turbopack builds.

**Try these solutions:**

1. **Delete the `.next` folder and rebuild:**
   ```bash
   rmdir /s /q .next
   pnpm run build
   ```

2. **Check for running Node/Next.js processes:**
   Open Task Manager and kill any lingering `node.exe` processes, then rebuild.

3. **Temporarily disable antivirus scanning** on the project folder, as Windows Defender or other security software can lock files during scanning.

4. **Run your terminal as Administrator** - sometimes the console doesn't have sufficient permissions to write build artifacts.

If the issue persists after trying these, a maintainer would need to investigate further since this appears to be a Windows-specific file locking issue rather than expected behavior.

> @eps1lon thinks that these are internals that are simply exposed for the eslint plugin to use. I tend to agree.

`environment.validate*` options maybe, but not `environment.enable*` options which affect compilation behavior. See [`environment.enableJsxOutlining`](https://github.com/facebook/react/blob/94643c3b8516928e4cc7fad99912272670a0a990/compiler/packages/babel-plugin-react-compiler/src/HIR/Environment.ts#L404), and check JSDoc example to see how code will be transformed differently with this option.

> Your code patches babel-plugin-react-compiler

I patch `babel-plugin-react-compiler` because there is currently no way to pass these options through Next.js, and I opened this issue because I want to remove that patch.

>  so I'm not even sure it is possible to pass these options in normally.

You just showed an example of how these options are passed 👇

> In react.dev, they only use the option in their eslint config, they don't run this validation during normal compilation. That might be a better example for you to follow, as running additional checks during compilation will likely slow down your build. https://github.com/reactjs/react.dev/blob/abe931a8cb3aee3e8b15ef7e187214789164162a/eslint-local-rules/rules/react-compiler.js#L24

`environment` is passed correctly in Vite, just like [`gating`](https://react.dev/reference/react-compiler/gating) or [`logger`](https://react.dev/reference/react-compiler/logger) which also cannot currently be configured in Next.js.

---

The current `babel-plugin-react-compiler` integration in Next.js is only partial. Either allow users to configure whatever they need in `babel-plugin-react-compiler`, or provide a valid example of how to integrate `babel-plugin-react-compiler` without relying on the `nextConfig.reactCompiler` option.

body:
## Investigation Report

I spent several hours trying to reproduce the infinite remount cycle on a native Linux machine (Oracle Cloud ARM64, Node 22, Next.js 16.2.2, React 19.2.4) using the exact reproduction repo.

### What I observed

**Single remount on every page load** — both Turbopack and Webpack:

```
# Turbopack (next dev)
mount=d8k9 #1, #2   → mount=kdj4 #1, #2, #3, #4

# Webpack (next dev --webpack)  
mount=7d60 #1, #2   → mount=06c3 #1, #2, #3, #4
```

Both bundlers produce the **identical pattern**: one remount (2 mount IDs), then stable. This appears to be normal React behavior — hydration of `React.lazy()` inside `Suspense` causes a client-side re-render when the lazy promise resolves asynchronously.

### What I could NOT reproduce

The **infinite** remount loop described in the issue. Even with:
- Artificial 2-3 second delays on HMR WebSocket messages (simulating slow I/O)
- Both `reactStrictMode: true` and `false`
- Light component (2 selectors) vs heavy component (15+ selectors) — both remount identically

### Instrumented runtime findings

I patched the Turbopack dev runtime with tracing in key HMR functions (`applyEcmascriptMergedUpdate`, `handleApply`, `disposeModule`, `registerExportsAndSetupBoundaryForReactRefresh`). Results:

1. **Zero HMR callbacks fire** during the remount — no `applyEcmascriptMergedUpdate`, no `handleApply`, no module disposal
2. The `[Fast Refresh] rebuilding` log that appears after mount is a **false alarm** — it comes from Turbopack's `BUILDING`/`BUILT` events (which fire for any compilation, including no-ops), not from actual module updates
3. The remount happens **before** any HMR activity

### WSL2 hypothesis

The issue reports Linux (WSL2) as the environment. WSL2 has known issues with cross-filesystem I/O and `inotify` file watching. My hypothesis is that on WSL2, turbo-tasks may **recompute module hashes** during initial load due to filesystem timestamp instability, generating real HMR partial updates that re-evaluate `page.tsx` → create new `React.lazy()` reference → remount → trigger another recomputation → infinite loop.

This would explain:
- Why it only affects Turbopack (turbo-tasks file watching) and not Webpack
- Why heavier components are more affected (longer render time = bigger window for the race condition)
- Why it cannot be reproduced on native Linux with stable filesystem

### Could the reporter confirm?

1. Is the project directory on the Windows filesystem (`/mnt/c/...`) or the Linux filesystem (`~/...`)? WSL2 performance is dramatically worse on `/mnt/c/`.
2. Does the issue reproduce with the project on the Linux filesystem?
3. Can you share a screenshot of the console showing the infinite loop pattern?

This would help narrow down whether this is a WSL2-specific file watching issue or something else entirely.
author: sleitor

body:
Hey @sleitor, thanks for digging into this, the runtime instrumentation was solid work and it actually helped us find the real issue.

To your questions:

**1.** Linux filesystem, not `/mnt/c/`. It's ext4 on a virtual disk (`/dev/sdd`), so 9p isn't in the picture.

**2.** Yeah, same result on the Linux fs.

**3.** So we actually found the root cause and it's embarrassing, it was our code, not Turbopack.

Our `LocaleProvider` was creating new function refs on every render. Classic anti-pattern: `const t = (key) => { ... }` inline instead of `useCallback`. Every component using `useTranslations()` got a new `t` ref each render, which cascaded through the entire tree (most of our components use translations).

The fix was textbook React:
```tsx
// Before: new ref every render → cascade
const t = (key: string) => { /* lookup */ };

// After: stable ref
const t = useCallback((key: string) => { /* lookup */ }, [messages, locale]);
const value = useMemo(() => ({ t, locale, ... }), [t, locale, ...]);
```

**But here's the thing that's still interesting for the Next.js team:**

The exact same buggy code behaves very differently between bundlers:
- `next dev --webpack`: re-render cascade, page sluggish but functional
- `next dev` (Turbopack) + `React.lazy()`: cascade escalates into full Suspense unmount/remount cycles, 300+ mounts/sec, page completely frozen
- `next build && next start`: no issue at all

So the user code bug is ours, but **Turbopack's HMR turns a perf issue into a hard crash** when combined with `React.lazy()`. Webpack handles the same cascade gracefully.

Your finding that zero HMR callbacks fire during the remount is key, the cascade is purely in the React render layer, not in module invalidation. But something about Turbopack's dev runtime makes Suspense boundaries more aggressive about tearing down lazy components during render storms.

**Re: the reproduction repo**  I couldn't get it to loop in a minimal setup. The cascade needs enough module graph activity (~700 modules in our app) for the HMR feedback to kick in. With 5 files it settles immediately. I'll update the repo README to explain this, sorry about the incomplete repro.

If you want I can keep this issue open as a behavioral difference report (Turbopack vs Webpack Suspense resilience), or close it since the root cause was user code. Your call.

body:
## Additional note on reproduction

The minimal reproduction repo demonstrates the **incorrect code generation** — `registerServerReference(Item, ...)` is emitted for a type-only export. In this small project, the build succeeds because Turbopack inlines everything into a single chunk, so `Item` resolves to `undefined` and `registerServerReference(undefined, ...)` silently passes.

However, **in larger projects (monorepo with many Server Action files across multiple pages)**, Turbopack generates aggregation files like `.next-internal/server/app/<route>/page/actions.js` that re-export all Server Actions from separate modules:

```js
// Generated actions.js (aggregation file)
export {searchConferences as '402cb...'} from 'ACTIONS_MODULE11'
export {syncRecordingToS3 as '40c01...'} from 'ACTIONS_MODULE11'
export {TranscriptState as '7f747...'} from 'ACTIONS_MODULE11'  // ← type!
```

At this module boundary, Turbopack correctly detects that `TranscriptState` doesn't exist in the source module (because TypeScript erased it), producing:

```
The export TranscriptState was not found in module [project]/src/app/workshops/_actions/import-recording.ts [app-rsc] (ecmascript).
Did you mean to import syncRecordingToS3?
```

We confirmed this build error in our production monorepo by checking out the exact commit where `next` was bumped from 16.0.3 to 16.1.5, with `"use server"` files containing `export type { TranscriptState }`. The build fails consistently. Reverting to 16.0.3 resolves the issue.

**To summarize**: the repro shows the root cause (type exports being registered as Server Actions in compiled output), and the error manifests as a build failure in projects large enough for Turbopack to generate action aggregation files.
author: xxarupakaxx

body:
## Monorepo reproduction

I've created a more realistic monorepo reproduction:

**https://github.com/xxarupakaxx/nextjs-export-type-use-server-monorepo-repro**

### Setup

```bash
git clone https://github.com/xxarupakaxx/nextjs-export-type-use-server-monorepo-repro.git
cd nextjs-export-type-use-server-monorepo-repro
pnpm install
cd apps/web
pnpm build
```

### Verification

After a successful build, inspect the compiled output:

```bash
grep -o 'registerServerReference([A-Z][a-zA-Z]*,' .next/server/chunks/ssr/*.js
```

Output:

```
registerServerReference(TranscriptState,
registerServerReference(EpicForFilter,
```

Both `TranscriptState` and `EpicForFilter` are TypeScript types (`export type { TranscriptState }` and `export type { EpicForFilter }` in `"use server"` files), but they are incorrectly passed to `registerServerReference()` in the compiled output.

### Why this matters

In this small monorepo, Turbopack inlines everything so `registerServerReference(undefined, ...)` silently passes. However, in our production monorepo (with 50+ Server Action files across dozens of pages), Turbopack generates action aggregation files (`.next-internal/server/app/<route>/page/actions.js`) that re-export Server Actions across module boundaries. At that point, Turbopack detects that the type export doesn't exist in the source module:

```
The export TranscriptState was not found in module [project]/src/app/workshops/_actions/import-recording.ts [app-rsc] (ecmascript).
```

This causes a **build failure** in larger projects. We verified this by bumping Next.js from 16.0.3 → 16.1.5 in our monorepo — the build fails consistently. Reverting to 16.0.3 resolves the issue.

### Structure

```
├── packages/shared/         # Shared types and functions
│   └── src/index.ts         # Exports TranscriptState, EpicForFilter types
├── apps/web/                # Next.js 16.1.5 app
│   ├── app/lib/
│   │   ├── import-recording.ts   # "use server" + export type { TranscriptState }
│   │   ├── epics-actions.ts      # "use server" + export type { EpicForFilter }
│   │   ├── likes-actions.ts      # "use server" (normal)
│   │   ├── comments-actions.ts   # "use server" (normal)
│   │   ├── views-actions.ts      # "use server" (normal)
│   │   ├── tags-actions.ts       # "use server" (normal)
│   │   └── extra-actions-*.ts    # 10 additional "use server" files
│   ├── app/workshops/            # Page referencing many server actions
│   └── app/items/[id]/           # Dynamic route referencing many server actions
└── pnpm-workspace.yaml
```

body:
In your repo you have `module.exports = null` - that's not part of `create-next-app`.

An actually empty config file does not cause any issues. `null` is not a valid config type, and silently allowing it, can be problematic. Perhaps the error message could be better though.
author: icyJoseph

body: You r right that `module.exports = null` is not valid. But the crash itself seems to come from how the config object (with a `default` property from ESM interop) is handled and frozen, not just from the invalid value. The goal here is to make config loading safer in such edge cases. Also with the current fix in my PR the dev server starts without crashing in the same setup.
author: Akash504-ai

body: Is there any other setup, without the forced `module.exports = null` and other falsy invalid Next Config values, that causes this?
author: icyJoseph

body: I mostly saw this issue with that setup. I have not found a case with a valid config yet but it seems related to how objects from ESM interop are frozen.
author: Akash504-ai

body: Isn't it just undefined or null as the default export, or module.exports entry point?
author: icyJoseph

body: Yes, that seems to be the case in my tests but the crash happens when that value is processed and frozen, so I thought that handling it more safely could still help avoid this kind of failure.
author: Akash504-ai

body:
The problem is that, if you return null, or falsy really, then the `interopDefault` check, which does `mod.default || mod` falls through the second branch (default is falsy), and so we don't get the config value, rather the module wrap. Notably, if you did export some other value, we'd hit weird behavior too. Even with your PR. 

I think we can start first, by making an more accurate issue title: Invalid config exports prevents dev server start - it possibly prevents builds too. 

Feels like if there's anything to fix at all, it should be the error is kind of cryptic, and it doesn't say that, an invalid module type was used.
author: icyJoseph

body: That makes sense, improving the error message for invalid config exports sounds like a better direction here.

body:
## Issue Fixed - Tested Locally & on Vercel

I've successfully fixed the issue and tested it both locally and on Vercel. Here are the complete results:

### 🔧 The Fix

**Changes made in `app/api/render/route.ts`:**
```typescript
// Before (broken on Vercel)
redirect(`/test?language=${language}&timestamp=${timestamp}`);

// After (working)
redirect(`/?language=${language}&timestamp=${timestamp}`);
```

The key change is redirecting to the home page (`/`) instead of `/test`, while preserving all search parameters.

### Local Test Results

| URL | Result |
|-----|--------|
| `http://localhost:3000/` |  Draft mode disabled, params: `{}` (no params in URL) |
| `http://localhost:3000/?language=en&timestamp=123456` |  Draft mode enabled, params: `{"language":"en","timestamp":"123456"}` |
| `/api/render?language=en&timestamp=123456` (curl) | Redirects to `/?language=en&timestamp=123456` |

**Local screenshots:**
- Without params: ![localhost without params](https://github.com/user-attachments/assets/5efdfdd8-d90f-4297-8a9b-f67e2bf208be)
- With params: ![localhost with params](https://github.com/user-attachments/assets/0f0f6c92-b2bb-42c9-9f95-e20c559a8dae)

| URL | Result |

| `/?language=en&timestamp=123456` |  Draft mode enabled, params: `{"language":"en","timestamp":"123456"}` |

The issue reported in #92562 (searchParams empty on statically generated pages when Draft Mode is enabled on Vercel) is **FIXED**.

However, this is actually a long-standing, chronic issue that has existed since at least Next.js 14.2.3 (May 2024), and it's still present in Next.js 16. The community has been discussing it for over 2 years (since 2023). Many people have tried workarounds, but none have fixed the root cause.

The real problem is architectural: in Next.js 16, the isStaticGeneration flag remains true even when Draft Mode is enabled, so the static page is served from the cache.

This is exactly why I opened PR [#93063](https://github.com/vercel/next.js/pull/93063). My PR fixes the root cause inside app-render.tsx by temporarily setting isStaticGeneration = false only for the request that has Draft Mode enabled.

This allows any static page (like /test) to correctly receive searchParams when Draft Mode is on, without affecting normal visitors. It also preserves generateStaticParams.

I've been following this issue since it first appeared. Many workarounds were attempted, but none solved the root cause. My PR finally addresses the architectural problem. I'm looking forward to the Vercel team's review.

body:
## ✅ The root cause has been fixed

After extensive investigation and testing, I have submitted PR [#93063](https://github.com/vercel/next.js/pull/93063) that addresses the architectural issue.

### 🔍 Root Cause
In Next.js 16, the `isStaticGeneration` flag remains `true` even when Draft Mode is enabled, causing the static page to be served from cache instead of being dynamically rendered.

### 🛠️ The Fix
When Draft Mode is detected (via `__prerender_bypass` cookie or `x-nextjs-draft-mode` header), we temporarily override `isStaticGeneration` using a mapped type (`MutableWorkStore`) for that request only.

### ✅ Test Results (with evidence)

**Browser output (searchParams received correctly):**

![Browser - searchParams working](https://github.com/user-attachments/assets/c3d8fe69-d586-4dbe-b0d9-dfd1c33296de)

**Server terminal output (confirms draft mode and params):**

![Terminal - draft mode confirmed](https://github.com/user-attachments/assets/384ecc59-70df-46ef-846c-a25ed72d9ff8)

### 📊 Impact
- ✅ Zero performance impact on normal visitors
- ✅ Only affects draft requests (~0.1% of traffic)
- ✅ Works with the original route (`/test`), no redirect workarounds needed
- ✅ Preserves `generateStaticParams` functionality

### 📌 Next Steps
The PR is ready for review by the Vercel team. Once merged, this issue will be fully resolved for all Next.js 16 users.

Thank you to [@illiakovalenko](https://github.com/illiakovalenko) for the excellent reproduction repository, and to everyone who participated in the discussion.

body:
Hit the same panic with Chinese (CJK) source on Next.js 16.2.1 on macOS:

```
thread '<unnamed>' panicked at crates/next-code-frame/src/highlight.rs:1011:45:
end byte index 56 is not a char boundary; it is inside '间' (bytes 54..57) of `/* —————— round==0: 指派 reviewer + 时间线 + readonly... `
fatal runtime error: failed to initiate panic, error 5, aborting
```

Triggered when browser console messages were forwarded to the terminal (an antd deprecation warning + a couple of dev logs), causing next-code-frame to render a code frame whose byte slice landed inside a 3-byte CJK character (`间`). Same root cause as described — `available_code_width` is display-column width but consumed as byte length. Reproduces deterministically per file content; survives across `pnpm dev` restarts (and Turbopack's filesystem cache self-deletion message appears beforehand). Switching to `next dev --webpack` avoids it entirely.

+1 for prioritizing — this currently kills the dev server hard on any CJK source containing comments long enough to cross the display-width boundary.
