body:
You're probably right about the blame commit.
Previously the worker was loaded with a `blob://` URL, which leads to a null origin. This doesn't cause CORS related issues, but it does mean fetch and importScript fail when trying to use the worker's origin.
16.2 fixed that by changing the bootstrapping code, but having an origin can lead to obscure CORS issues.

Thanks for the PR. I'll investigate the issue and continue the discussion there
author: andrewimm

body:
I've opened #93044 proposing an opt-in `turbopack.workerPublicPath` config for a related failure mode: when `assetPrefix` points to a cross-origin CDN, the Worker entrypoint URL (now a real static asset after #88602) inherits the CDN origin and is rejected by the browser's cross-origin Worker policy. Different trigger from the COEP variant described here but the same "new origin can lead to obscure CORS issues" class you called out.

Minimal repro: https://github.com/GuinsooRocky/next-turbopack-worker-cdn-repro (50 lines).

body:
## ✅ PR Submitted

I've submitted a PR that fixes this security vulnerability:

### Summary
Added `parseOriginHostSafely()` helper with try-catch to handle malformed Origin headers gracefully.

### Key Points
- ✅ Wraps `new URL()` in try-catch
- ✅ Returns sentinel value `\x00INVALID_ORIGIN` for malformed origins
- ✅ Preserves `"null"` handling for sandboxed iframes
- ✅ Does NOT return undefined/null (prevents CSRF bypass)

### Testing
Verified all attack vectors from the PoC:
- `Origin: http://` → No crash ✅
- `Origin: ftp://` → No crash ✅  
- `Origin: not-a-url` → No crash ✅
- `Origin: null` → Preserved ✅

Please review when you have time. Thank you!

/cc @FJRG2007 for confirming the fix

body:
@FJRG2007 As the maintainer noted, this is an unhandled exception on malformed user input that results in a 500 — a bug, not a security vulnerability. A denial of service would require an extremely high volume of requests, but any standard rate limiter or firewall would block that regardless.

PR #92712 by Mark-Lasfar is the right direction for the fix. As for a bug bounty — this doesn’t qualify as a security vulnerability under any standard CVE/bug bounty criteria, so there is no reward here.

Thank you @sleitor for the review and for pointing others to PR #92712. 

I agree this is a bug rather than a security vulnerability, but the fix ensures the server doesn't crash on malformed input. 

Appreciate your collaboration on this!

body:
### Impact: ~15,000 `__next_metadata_boundary__` errors/day in production

Because `root-params` doesn't work in Turbopack, i18n apps with `cacheComponents: true` cannot resolve this PPR error:

```
Error: Expected the resume to render <div> in this slot but instead it rendered <__next_metadata_boundary__>.
The tree doesn't match so React will fallback to client rendering.
```

This error fires on **every request** to any page with a dynamic `[locale]` segment + `generateMetadata` using `'use cache'`. In our production app (196K indexed URLs), that's ~15K errors/day across routes like:

- `/[locale]/customs/origin/preferential/[agreementId]/[hsCode]` (47 agreements × thousands of HS codes)
- `/[locale]/customs/trade/[code]` (10K+ NC8 codes)
- `/[locale]/customs/nomenclature/[goodsCode]` (25K+ TARIC codes)
- `/[locale]/customs/classification-guide/[hs4Code]` (2K+ guides)

Pages return HTTP 200 with correct content, but **fall back to CSR instead of PPR prerender** — defeating the purpose of `cacheComponents: true`.

### What we've tried (all failed)

| Approach | Result |
|----------|--------|
| `'use cache'` in `generateMetadata` | Already done per [docs](https://nextjs.org/docs/messages/next-prerender-dynamic-metadata). Does not fix the boundary error. |
| Explicit locale in `getTranslations({ locale, namespace })` | Already done. Same error. |
| `htmlLimitedBots: /.*/` | Causes HTTP 500 on cold cache. |
| `htmlLimitedBots` targeting specific bots | Amplifies the boundary error. |
| `rootParams: true` + `next/root-params` | **This issue** — build fails. |
| Restructuring layouts (`<html>` in `[locale]/layout.tsx`) | Same build failure. |
| `next build --webpack` | Works for root-params but breaks `fumadocs-mdx` (Turbopack-only scheme). |
| Upgrading to Next.js 16.2.3 | Same issue. |

### The fix path

Once Turbopack generates the `next/root-params` exports, we can update `i18n/request.ts` to use `rootParams.locale()` inside `'use cache'` boundaries, which should resolve the metadata boundary mismatch for the entire i18n ecosystem.

This is the same conclusion as [next-intl#1493](https://github.com/amannn/next-intl/issues/1493) and [#86870](https://github.com/vercel/next.js/issues/86870).
author: pomathieu

body:
`rootParams` hasn't been officially released -

That being said in your case, https://github.com/pomathieu/nextjs-rootparams-turbopack-repro, `locale` is NOT a root param.

```tree
app
├── [locale]
│   ├── layout.tsx
│   └── page.tsx
├── i18n
│   ├── request.ts
│   └── routing.ts
├── layout.tsx
└── page.module.css
```

When you do, `/en` for example, your expanded path is `app/layout.tsx/[locale]/layout.tsx/page.tsx` - There's a layout (the root layout) to the left of `[locale]` - so it is NOT a root param. 

Root params are all params that come before the root layout.

You'd need to:

```tree
app
├── [locale]
│   ├── layout.tsx
│   └── page.tsx
├── i18n
│   ├── request.ts
│   └── routing.ts
└── page.module.css
```

Remote the `app/layout.tsx` and move its contents to the `app/[locale]/layout.tsx`, it'd look like, as per your repository:

```tsx
export default async function LocaleLayout({
  children,
  params,
}: {
  children: React.ReactNode;
  params: Promise<{ locale: string }>;
}) {
  const { locale } = await params;
  setRequestLocale(locale);
  return (
    <html lang="en" className={`${geistSans.variable} ${geistMono.variable}`}>
      <body>
        <NextIntlClientProvider locale={locale}>
          {children}
        </NextIntlClientProvider>
      </body>
    </html>
  );
```

If you need `app/layout.tsx` for other routes and stuff, use [Route Groups](https://nextjs.org/docs/app/api-reference/file-conventions/route-groups).

body:
## Root Cause (Maybe)

1. `node --watch-path=...` adds flags to `process.execArgv`.
2. `jest-worker` forks processes inheriting `execArgv`   → workers also run in watch mode.
3. Watch mode emits `console.trace('watch:require', ...)`.
4. Next.js forwards these traces via `process.send()`.
5. `jest-worker` doesn't recognize the message   → `TypeError: Unexpected response from worker: undefined`

---

cc @mcollina @timbenniks
author: ale-grosselle

body:
Opened PR: https://github.com/vercel/next.js/pull/92864

### Fix implemented

- Added shared filtering for Node inspect/watch flags in the Node options utilities.
- Prevented managed Next.js workers from inheriting Node watch-mode flags such as `--watch`, `--watch-path`, and `--watch-preserve-output` through `process.execArgv` or `NODE_OPTIONS`.
- Updated the dev static-paths worker to pass sanitized `forkOptions.execArgv`, which prevents Node watch-mode IPC/trace messages from reaching `jest-worker` and triggering `TypeError: Unexpected response from worker: undefined`.
- Kept other exec-argv-only options flowing through where appropriate.

### Validation

```bash
pnpm testonly packages/next/src/server/lib/utils.test.ts packages/next/src/lib/worker.test.ts
```

body: We also encountered this behavior and would like it to be fixed: the instrumented fetch should persist after HMR.
author: vitalets

body:
Fix submitted in #93249 — the root cause is that `originalFetch` was captured at server startup *before* OTel's `instrumentation.register()` wraps `globalThis.fetch`. On every HMR event, `resetFetch()` restored the pre-OTel raw fetch, permanently losing the instrumentation layer.

The fix introduces `unpatchFetch()` which snapshots `globalThis.fetch` lazily inside `patchFetch()` (after OTel has already wrapped it), then restores to that snapshot on HMR — stripping only the Next.js cache layer while preserving OTel and any other userland wrappers.

Verified locally: instrumentation hook tests (9/9), middleware tests (24/24), fetch patching tests, and unit tests (2132/2132) all pass.

Confirmed and reproduced this issue in our project on **Next 16.2.3** after upgrading from **Next 14.2.35**.

We tested the proposed fallback in `parseAndValidateFlightRouterState()` by replacing the parse-error throw with return undefined, and it resolved the problem for us. In our case, treating an invalid router state header as a signal to fall back to a full document render worked as expected and avoided the server-side 500.

It would be great to include this change in an official release so teams do not need to carry a local patch until the fix lands.

---

Also found this issue https://github.com/vercel/next.js/issues/92330 with a similar solution.
author: shbov

body:
The `The router state header was sent but could not be parsed.` started for us when we upgraded & deployed a micro frontend to 16.2. But it turned out a 16.1 app was making preflight requests to our 16.2.x app. Make sure to use regular anchor tags between micro frontends & Next.js' Link component for routes within the same app. 

We create a patch for nextjs 16.2.3 (https://gist.github.com/Netail/e33cc2abbadb026c5c8d340d4016dcaf) to log the router state header, which contains an object where could make a route out of. 

The 16.1 makes a request with the state header in the following format:

```json
[
    "",
    {
        "children": [
            "maak-compleet",
            {
                "children": [
                    "__PAGE__",
                    {},
                    null,
                    null
                ]
            },
            null,
            null
        ]
    },
    null,
    null,
    true
]
```

While 16.2 makes a request with the state header in the following format:

```json
[
    "",
    {
        "children": [
            "maak-compleet",
            {
                "children": [
                    "__PAGE__",
                    {},
                    null,
                    null
                ]
            },
            null,
            null
        ]
    },
    null,
    null,
    0
]
```

The difference being the boolean being turned into a number, which the state header validation fails on. (and thus throws that error) But based on this object we found out the request came from the route `/maak-compleet`, which was not part of the 16.2 app and apparently came from preflight requests from the 16.1 app

body:
We're hitting this on 16.2.5 (production webpack build, not canary). ~300 errors over 2h after the 16.2.4 → 16.2.5 deploy, all on RSC prefetches that resolve through intercepted routes (the symptom matches the dynamic-rendering + soft-nav description).

To pinpoint the upstream change, I instrumented `app-page.runtime.prod.js` and grabbed the underlying validator error (our pino-http logger swallowed it):

```
At path: 1.children.0 -- Expected the value to satisfy a union of `string | tuple`, but received: locale,pl,d
```

After widening that one:

```
At path: 4 -- Expected a number, but received: true
```

Two struct schemas were tightened in 16.2.5 without a fallback for older client payloads:

1. The dynamic-segment tuple `[name, value, type]` (3 elements) was widened to `[name, value, type, nullable-array-of-strings]` (4 elements). Bundled source: `t9().tuple([t9().string(),t9().string(),t5,t9().nullable(t9().array(t9().string()))])`.
2. The 5th root field was promoted from boolean to a number bitmask (the new `rt` enum just below — `HasRuntimePrefetch`, `SubtreeHasInstant`, …). Bundled source: `t9().optional(t9().number())`.

Browser clients built against 16.2.4 (and any cached tabs / SWs from that version) still send the 3-tuple + boolean shape, so they fail validation on any 16.2.5 server.

#92933 (graceful `undefined` → full-nav fallback) is the right upstream approach for rolling deploys. For our case (in-house patch) we widened the schema to accept both old and new formats so soft-nav keeps working during the transition. Happy to share the diff if useful.

Would be great to land #92933 (or any equivalent fallback) in 16.2.6 — the schema tightening landed as a quiet break.

body:
my options, as far as I can see; please correct me if I'm wrong:
1. Using a `route.js` file with a `GET` function that returns HTML as a string; old school style. That means I can't reuse any layout, component or style from the rest of my Next site, and need to reinvent all the wheels.
2. Using a `route.js` that sets a cookie, then redirecting to the `confirm` page and read the cookie there; make sure to mark the cookie as stale after use.
3. Alternative: Setting custom headers in `proxy.js` before loading `page.js`. That means logic pertaining to one specific small branch of my application lives in a completely different file and location, without any logical link except comments or external documentation, and no static checks
4. Storing the values in `localStorage`, and pray I can somehow ensure invalidation won't be a problem.
5. Making a small state `useState` machine in the first page, keeping the values in memory, and on submission of the first form, switching pages visually by switching components, and update the url with `history.pushState()`. This requires to refactor the entire logic of the application around the limitation; if two different pages should lead to that page, then the logic would need to be reproduced, or abstracted away in a component.
6. Encrypting the values server-side before passing them in the URL, then decrypting them on arrival. I'd need some logic to retain unique decription keys and match them to the incoming data, and I would have to make sure nothing leaks through the server/client boundary. Basically reinventing SSL. Of course this is a ludicrous idea, but it's "a" solution to the problem (assuming the data fits within the url char limits).

From where I stand, none of these is an acceptable complexity tradeoff for something that browsers do natively. I would really like a solution that doesn't involve doing any of the above.

If there isn't one, I welcome opinions about which you think is least bad, and why.

That being said, what's your use case really?

You can return UI from a Server Function/Action, is this pattern something that can help you? Of course, direct navigation would be a problem, but maybe you don't need that?

body:
### Confirmed reproducible from a bare install — not specific to any app

Ran the repro from a completely clean state, verified the bundled copy is the only picomatch on disk:

```sh
$ cd /tmp/next-picomatch-cve-repro
$ npm install

$ ls -la node_modules/next/dist/compiled/picomatch/
total 64
-rw-r--r--  1 user  wheel  23905 Apr 17 15:54 index.js
-rw-r--r--  1 user  wheel   1091 Apr 17 15:54 LICENSE
-rw-r--r--  1 user  wheel    116 Apr 17 15:54 package.json

$ cat node_modules/next/package.json | grep '"version"' | head -1
  "version": "16.2.4",

$ grep -c "windows===null" node_modules/next/dist/compiled/picomatch/index.js
1        # matches the 4.0.3 runtime signature (isWindows() check)

$ shasum node_modules/next/dist/compiled/picomatch/index.js
6e92069f5eef59717a569d8d5c6ca5faa31f0c59  index.js

$ ls node_modules/picomatch 2>/dev/null || echo "no top-level picomatch"
no top-level picomatch
```

So the issue is:
- Not a false positive.
- Not caused by any `overrides` / `resolutions` / monorepo quirk in our app — we deliberately have zero of those in the repro.
- Reproducible from `next@16.2.4` + `react@19.2.4` + `react-dom@19.2.4` alone (see `package.json` in the linked repo).
- Affects anyone who runs `npx create-next-app@latest` today and has a security gate scanning the Docker image or `node_modules/` tree.

body:
## Update — partial reproduction status

After filing this issue I tried to reproduce the behavior on a clean environment and would like to share what is and isn't reliably reproducible.

### Reliably reproducible

The **workspace root misdetection** happens every time:

- With an orphan [package-lock.json](cci:7://file:///c:/Users/BobCleaner/package-lock.json:0:0-0:0) at `C:\Users\<name>\` (no sibling [package.json](cci:7://file:///c:/Users/BobCleaner/Desktop/CoreLab/package.json:0:0-0:0)), `next dev` always prints:
  ```
   Warning: Next.js inferred your workspace root, but it may not be correct.
   We detected multiple lockfiles and selected the directory of
   C:\Users\<name>\package-lock.json as the root directory.
  ```
- Next.js picks the parent directory as the workspace root, 100% of the time.

### Not deterministically reproducible (yet)

The **`Can't resolve 'tailwindcss'` error + uncontrolled RAM growth (40+ GB)** from the original incident did **not** reproduce in my retests, even with:

- The exact same orphan lockfile in place.
- The exact same CoreLab project that originally crashed.
- [.next](cci:9://file:///c:/Users/BobCleaner/Desktop/next-turbopack-ram-repro/.next:0:0-0:0) cache cleared, `node_modules/.cache` cleared, all node processes killed beforehand.
- The same `next@16.2.4` + Node 24.14.1 on the same machine.

On retest, the dev server boots normally and serves `GET / 200` in ~1.3s despite the misdetected root. So Turbopack evidently can handle a misdetected root without exploding — something *additional* had to go wrong during the original incident.

### What might have been different during the original incident

I cannot prove any of these, but plausible triggers:

- A race condition during the very first compile (I opened `localhost:3000` while Turbopack was still indexing).
- Partial / corrupt [.next](cci:9://file:///c:/Users/BobCleaner/Desktop/next-turbopack-ram-repro/.next:0:0-0:0) state that has since been wiped.
- A filesystem event (antivirus scan, OneDrive sync, etc.) interfering with the file watcher while it was walking the inferred parent tree.

The 43,516 MB Task Manager screenshot is from the original incident and is genuine — but the exact replay steps currently elude me.

### What still stands as a legitimate bug

Even without the RAM explosion, the workspace-root misdetection alone is a real footgun:

1. An **empty / orphan** [package-lock.json](cci:7://file:///c:/Users/BobCleaner/package-lock.json:0:0-0:0) (no `packages`, no sibling [package.json](cci:7://file:///c:/Users/BobCleaner/Desktop/CoreLab/package.json:0:0-0:0)) is accepted as a valid workspace root. This is trivially created by accidentally running `npm install` in one's home folder on Windows.
2. The warning mentions "multiple lockfiles" but gives no hint that the chosen lockfile is orphan/empty.
3. When it *does* cascade into a resolver failure (as it clearly did once for me), there appears to be no cap on worker spawning or memory usage.

### How I can help further

If the maintainers have specific diagnostics to collect the next time the full incident happens, I'm happy to capture them. Candidates:

- `node --trace-warnings` / `NODE_OPTIONS="--inspect"` on the dev command
- `NEXT_TELEMETRY_DEBUG=1`
- Heap snapshot at the point of RAM growth
- `turbo-trace` / Turbopack trace output

Please advise which would be most useful. Meanwhile, reproduction repo remains at https://github.com/MrMyNameMaster/next-turbopack-ram-repro (the workspace-root misdetection portion reproduces there reliably).

body:
## Same issue on macOS — different symptom, same root cause, same fix

Just hit this while migrating a Next.js 16.2.4 project from Tailwind CSS v3 to v4 on macOS. The symptom was different from the RAM explosion described above, but the root cause and fix are identical.

**Symptom:**

```
FATAL: An unexpected Turbopack error occurred.

Error [TurbopackInternalError]: reading dir "/Users/<name>/Documents"

Caused by:
- Operation not permitted (os error 1)
```

The build failed immediately with a permission error because Turbopack inferred the wrong workspace root (a stray `package-lock.json` in `/Users/<name>/`) and tried to scan `/Users/<name>/Documents` — which macOS protects with Full Disk Access restrictions.

**Environment:**
- Next.js 16.2.4 (Turbopack)
- macOS (Darwin 25.x)
- Stray `package-lock.json` in home directory (`/Users/<name>/package-lock.json`)
- Project at `/Users/<name>/Documents/GitHub/<project>/`

**Fix that worked:**

Adding `turbopack: { root: __dirname }` to `next.config.js`:

```js
const nextConfig = {
  turbopack: { root: __dirname },
  // ... rest of config
};
```

This immediately resolved the error. No need to delete the stray lockfile.

**Why this matters for macOS users:**

On macOS, the `~/Documents` folder is protected by the TCC (Transparency, Consent, and Control) framework. When Turbopack misdetects the workspace root and tries to scan a protected directory, it doesn't just fail silently — it throws a fatal panic and aborts the entire build. The error message (`reading dir "/Users/.../Documents"`, `Operation not permitted`) gives no indication that a stray lockfile is the actual cause, making this very hard to diagnose.

This is a different failure mode than the Windows RAM exhaustion, but same underlying bug. Hope this additional data point helps narrow down the fix.
author: stephanhink

body:
Another data point. Same OOM, different trigger.

**Environment:** Next 16.2.4, Turbopack, Tailwind v4, pnpm 9, Node 24, macOS arm64. RAM climbed steadily until the OS killed the process. No stray parent lockfile in our case (matching @AlessioGr's earlier comment). `turbopack: { root: __dirname }` was already set in `next.config.ts` from prior diagnostic work, and the OOM still happened — so the workspace-root pin isn't a complete fix.

**Trigger we observed:** `pnpm remove @supabase/supabase-js` (a dep with ~30 transitive sub-packages: `@supabase/postgrest-js`, `@supabase/realtime-js`, `@supabase/auth-js`, etc.), without clearing `.next/`. The persistent dev cache contained ~32 stale chunks referencing the removed packages (`find .next -name '*supabase*' | wc -l → 32`). On the next `pnpm dev`, the first request to a previously-seeded route printed `Compiling /<route> ...` and never completed — sustained ~800% CPU, RSS climbing, eventual OOM. `rm -rf .next/` between the dep removal and the next `pnpm dev` makes the issue go away every time.

So: workspace-root misdetection (this issue's original trigger) and stale-cache-after-dep-removal (our trigger) both end up at the same place: enhanced-resolve walking a parent chain looking for `node_modules`, failing repeatedly, and Turbopack handling that failure in a way that grows memory without bound.

**Possibly related from the postcss side.** `@tailwindcss/postcss` computes `inputBasePath` as `path.dirname(path.resolve(opts.from ?? ''))`. When PostCSS calls the plugin without `opts.from` (Turbopack does this for some intermediate CSS in 16.2.4), the fallback evaluates to `path.dirname(process.cwd())` — the *parent* of CWD — producing the same wrong basedir → "Can't resolve 'tailwindcss'" outcome at a different layer. PR open at tailwindlabs/tailwindcss#19980. Independent of that, Next/Turbopack hardening against unbounded retry on resolution failure is the more general fix.

Companion issue I filed before finding this thread, closed for missing reproduction repo: #93251.
author: rebasecase

body: Worth flagging that the highest-leverage subset of this is genuinely small. Hashing `pnpm-lock.yaml` / `package-lock.json` content into the persistent dev cache key would invalidate stale graphs whenever deps change, which closes the dep-removal trigger and most likely the 16.2.3 → 16.2.4 regression too. Doesn't touch the deeper resolution-retry-on-failure defect, but knocks out the user-facing reports as a one-screen patch. Happy to draft if useful.

Turbopack then selected /Users/shydev as the workspace root (it printed the multiple lockfiles warning) and next dev became unusable (🤡), filled swap and froze my entire system. Both workarounds fixed it: setting turbopack.root in next.config.ts, and deleting the stray $HOME lockfile/manifest. Root detection should prefer the nearest lockfile to cwd. 🙏🏽

body:
I do know that rendering due to a POST request is not supported by Next.js, but I wondered if this issue was possibly useful - if it's not, I'm quite happy to close it.

Interestingly, I found I could fix this issue by adding a check for `req.method === 'POST'` inside of [`app-render.tsx`](https://github.com/vercel/next.js/blob/v16.3.0-canary.2/packages/next/src/server/app-render/app-render.tsx#L3122) that ignores postponed state.


```ts
// app-render.tsx L:3122
      req.method === 'POST'
        ? null
        : parsePostponedState(
            renderOpts.postponed,
            interpolatedParams,
            renderOpts.experimental.maxPostponedStateSizeBytes
          )
```

Alternatively, the fix can be put into `renderToStream`, but it's about the same logic. 

Hope that helps.
author: robert-j-webb

body:
Hi @evgeniyworkbel, 

While you're right that the Tailwind CSS documentation often shows a simple npm install (which defaults to dependencies), having it in devDependencies is actually the more technically 'correct' approach for a Next.js project. Here is why this is likely intentional:

Tailwind is a Compiler, not a Runtime Library: Unlike React or Framer Motion, Tailwind is a build tool. It scans your files and generates a static CSS file during next build. Once that CSS is generated, the tailwindcss package itself is no longer needed to serve your website to users.

Leaner Production Environments: By placing it in devDependencies, the production environment (like a Docker container or a slim server) doesn't have to install the entire Tailwind engine and its dependencies just to serve static assets. This keeps your production node_modules smaller.

Consistency with Other Tools: This aligns with how other build-time tools like TypeScript, ESLint, or PostCSS are treated. Even though the Tailwind docs use the simpler command for brevity, frameworks like Next.js usually opt for stricter dependency management.

As long as your build process has access to devDependencies (which Vercel and most CI/CD platforms do by default during the build phase), this shouldn't cause any issues. It’s actually a nice optimization by the create-next-app team!

body:
That’s expected behavior — **Tailwind CSS and its PostCSS plugin are installed as development dependencies by design**.

Both `tailwindcss` and `@tailwindcss/postcss` are **build-time tools**, not needed at runtime in production. They:
- generate and process CSS during development/build
- aren’t required after your app is built

So they belong in `devDependencies`.

Next.js Doc: https://nextjs.org/docs/app/getting-started/css#tailwind-css

TailwindCSS Github Discussion: https://github.com/tailwindlabs/tailwindcss/discussions/19941

body:
I was able to reproduce similar behavior locally.

 **Observations:**
* Adding a new Tailwind class (e.g. `bg-red-500`) updates correctly.
* Changing an existing class (`rounded-lg` to `rounded-2xl`) does not always reflect immediately.
* Using a more extreme value (`rounded-full`) *does* update.
* Sometimes requires a manual refresh to reflect the change.

This suggests HMR is not consistently picking up class changes.

**Webpack comparison:**
Running with `next dev --webpack`, the issue does not reproduce — class changes update immediately and consistently.

**Environment:**
* next: 16.2.4
* tailwindcss: 4.2.2
* Node: 20.x
* OS: macOS (Darwin)

body:
Per-request narrowing would need a signal the client doesn't have. 

For a prerendered rewrite target, the HTML served for `/rewritten` is the same static file as `/target`, this is important for statically optimized routes, it is the reason they can pushed to a CDN without per-request lambda. 

Identical HTML can't carry a "this request was rewritten" marker, because `__NEXT_DATA__` is baked at build time.

Feels like other solutions have some more trade-offs too:

- Ship + re-evaluate the rewrite table client-side, but doesn't cover `has`, `missing` or dynamic rewrites, gated on request headers
- Per-response header from the serving layer, which exists for middleware, but not for config-level rewrites to statically optimized pages, because no lamnda runs for those
- Compare `pathname` vs `asPath` at hydration, which misses a bunch of edge cases for query params

So the "re-sync whenever any rewrite exists" path is what ships today.

> this is the expected behavior when rewrites are present as we parse them after hydration and trigger a query update to ensure all params are provided for static pages - from https://github.com/vercel/next.js/issues/30720#issuecomment-956388813
author: icyJoseph

body:
Thanks, I think the CDN/static HTML constraint you outlined is exactly the part that needs to stay true.

I’m not trying to make shared prerendered HTML carry a per-request “this request was rewritten” marker. For a statically optimized rewrite target, `/rewritten` and `/target` really can serve the same file, and the baked `__NEXT_DATA__` for that file can’t encode request-local rewrite truth.

The approach in this refactor is narrower than that. I’m treating rewrite reconciliation as a small tri-state:

- `required`: the initial payload does not match the reconciled route/query snapshot, so the hydration reconciliation update still has to run.
  Example: `/rewrite-to-gsp -> /gsp?foo=bar`. The initial static payload is still for `/gsp`, but the reconciled client snapshot includes `foo=bar`, so the extra update is still required.

- `not-required`: the initial payload already matches the reconciled snapshot, so that extra update can be skipped.
  Example: `/rewrite-to-gsp-not-required -> /gsp`. The rewrite changes the source path, but the final route/query snapshot already matches the initial payload, so there is nothing left to reconcile.

- `unknown`: we can’t prove either safely, so we keep today’s conservative fallback.
  Example: `/rewrite-to-gsp-unsafe -> /gsp?foo=bar` with a `missing` condition. A rewrite may match for this request, but the client cannot treat that as part of the exact subset, so it stays on the current fallback path.

From there, the strategy is:

- when the server actually has request-local knowledge, compute an exact result for that request and only serialize exact answers (`required` / `not-required`)
- when the response is build-time prerendered/shared HTML, omit that field entirely, so shared static output still does not carry request-local rewrite state
- before `createRouter(...)`, let the client reuse that exact answer when it exists, otherwise only narrow within a deterministic safe subset

That safe subset is intentionally small: internal destinations, no `has`, and no `missing`.

Rewrites outside that subset still stay conservative. The client may still resolve them for routing, but it does not treat them as exact reconciliation cases; they remain `unknown`, which preserves today’s fallback behavior.

So the goal here isn’t “make every rewrite exact on the client”. It’s narrower:

- reuse an exact request-time answer when the server really has one
- keep shared prerendered HTML free of request-local rewrite markers
- only do exact client-side narrowing for the deterministic subset
- keep the current conservative path for everything else

That’s why I think this addresses the issue more directly without violating the CDN/static constraint:

- routes that were never rewritten no longer pay the app-global resync cost just because rewrites exist somewhere in the app
- routes whose initial and reconciled snapshots already match can start with the correct initial `isReady`
- cases that still lack a safe signal stay on the existing fallback path

This also felt much closer to @ijjk’s earlier suggestion in #38422: make `isReady` correct before router creation, instead of relying on the old post-hydration correction path for every rewrite-bearing app.

body:
I was able to reproduce this consistently, and it does look like a framework-level issue rather than a problem with the user code.

From debugging, it seems that during a `multi → single` transition (e.g. `?k=A&k=B` → `?k=B`), the server correctly renders the new state and the RSC payload is fetched, but the client tree doesn’t commit the update. The URL reflects the new value, but the client component continues to receive stale props. Other transitions (empty → single, single → multi) behave as expected.

As a temporary workaround, forcing a client refresh right after the navigation makes the state consistent again:

```ts
router.replace(url, { scroll: false })
router.refresh()
```

Alternatively, forcing a remount via a `key` derived from the search params also avoids the issue:

```tsx
<MyComponent key={(searchParams.k ?? []).join(",")} ... />
```

Both approaches essentially bypass the stale tree reuse and ensure the new RSC payload is applied.

This suggests the issue might be related to how the App Router determines cache identity or reuses the existing tree when repeated search params shrink from multiple values to a single value.

Happy to help test any fixes or provide more logs if needed

body:
I tried solving this issue. Please let me know after reviewing it.
Link for the pull request I created - https://github.com/vercel/next.js/pull/93154#issue-4316813412

Closes #93104

## What's happening

When navigating from `?k=A&k=B` (multi-value) to `?k=B` (single-value) via `router.replace()`, the client tree never commits the update — props stay stale even though the server renders correctly.

## Root cause

In `createSegmentFromRouteTree` inside `ppr-navigations.ts`, the client builds a segment cache key from the current `renderedSearch` string:

```ts
// Before (buggy)
const stringifiedQuery = JSON.stringify(
  Object.fromEntries(new URLSearchParams(renderedSearch))
)
```

`Object.fromEntries` on a `URLSearchParams` with repeated keys silently drops all but the last value. This means:

- `?k=A&k=B` → `{ k: "B" }` → `__PAGE__?{"k":"B"}`
- `?k=B` → `{ k: "B" }` → `__PAGE__?{"k":"B"}`

Both produce the **same segment key**, so `matchSegment` treats them as identical, the stale cache node is reused, and the client never re-renders with the new props.

This explains the asymmetric behavior reported in the issue:
- `empty → single` ✅ (keys are genuinely different)
- `single → multi` ✅ (keys are genuinely different)
- `multi → single` ❌ (keys wrongly collide due to `Object.fromEntries`)
- "works on second toggle" ✅ (by then `currentRenderedSearch` has caught up so the comparison path differs)

## Fix

Use `getAll()` to preserve repeated values, matching exactly what the server does in `addSearchParamsIfPageSegment`:

```ts
// After (fixed)
const urlSearchParams = new URLSearchParams(renderedSearch)
const queryObj: Record<string, string | string[]> = {}
for (const key of new Set(urlSearchParams.keys())) {
  const vals = urlSearchParams.getAll(key)
  queryObj[key] = vals.length === 1 ? vals[0] : vals
}
const stringifiedQuery = JSON.stringify(queryObj)
```

Now:
- `?k=A&k=B` → `{ k: ["A", "B"] }` → `__PAGE__?{"k":["A","B"]}`
- `?k=B` → `{ k: "B" }` → `__PAGE__?{"k":"B"}`

These are distinct keys, the cache node is correctly replaced, and the client commits the updated props.

## Testing

Reproduction repo from the issue: https://github.com/dave-wwg/next-multi-value-searchparam-repro

The existing playwright test suite in that repo passes after this fix (it was designed to fail when the bug is present).

I'm starting to investigate this today. My first steps are:

1. Reproducing locally using your repo to confirm the behavior change between v15 and v16.

author: SarahAbada

body: Hi @stipsan, I saw the mitigation in `next-sanity`, definitely a great mitigation for immediately fixing the behavior.  I've successfully reproduced the stampede behavior locally with your repo. I'm currently working on using `git bisect` on the Next.js canary releases to pin down the exact commit where the transition from lazy to eager occurred. Planning to post the PR/commit hash here once I find it.
author: SarahAbada

body: Quick update: I’ve finished the bisection and identified the first bad commit as `19e2edcf4abf562e05f7481829963cd62146c948` (PR #71567). It appears the introduction of more aggressive `dynamicIO` and the Segment Cache integration changed how visible links are handled during a `router.refresh()`. I’m currently diving into the diffs for `app-render.tsx` and the client segment logic to see exactly where the lazy behavior got changed for an eager behavior. Planning to update with a proposed fix soon!
author: SarahAbada

body: Deep dive update: I've isolated the behavior to `pingVisibleLinks` in `links.ts`. It appears that on `router.refresh()`, this function is iterating through all visible links and aggressively re-scheduling prefetch tasks because `isPrefetchTaskDirty` is returning true (likely due to the new segment cache/dynamicIO tree changes in #71567). I'm currently working on a patch to make `pingVisibleLinks` respect the lazy prefetch setting during invalidation cycles.

body: We'll bump the vendored postcss version to silence the warning. This vulnerability does not affect Next.js users since postcss only runs at build time. You would only be affected if you build with untrusted code in which case there are bigger concerns than malicious CSS causing XSS.
author: eps1lon

body:
I know there's a PR, but I also just wanna flag I'm getting the same security alert when using `next` version `15.5.15`

> Transitive dependency postcss 8.4.31 is introduced via
next 15.5.15  postcss 8.4.31

> PostCSS: XSS via Unescaped </style> in CSS Stringify Output
Summary
PostCSS v8.5.5 (latest) does not escape </style> sequences when stringifying CSS ASTs. When user-submitted CSS is parsed and re-stringified for embedding in HTML <style> tags, </style> in CSS values breaks out of the style context, enabling XSS.

I think this is expected behaviour:
https://nextjs.org/docs/app/api-reference/file-conventions/not-found#not-foundjs
https://nextjs.org/docs/app/api-reference/file-conventions/loading#status-codes


> Along with serving a custom UI, Next.js will return a 200 HTTP status code for streamed responses, and 404 for non-streamed responses 

> For example, when a 404 page is streamed to the client, Next.js includes a <meta name="robots" content="noindex"> tag in the streamed HTML. This prevents search engines from indexing that URL even if the HTTP status is 200.

body: If you want to use deprecated `compilerOptions`, you have to set `ignoreDeprecations: "6.0"`. We'll support that with https://github.com/vercel/next.js/pull/93377. We won't support handling deprecated `compilerOptions` without `ignoreDeprecations`.
author: eps1lon

body:
> If you want to use deprecated `compilerOptions`, you have to set `ignoreDeprecations: "6.0"`. We'll support that with [#93377](https://github.com/vercel/next.js/pull/93377). We won't support handling deprecated `compilerOptions` without `ignoreDeprecations`.

Tested with `"ignoreDeprecations": "6.0"` set in `tsconfig.base.json` - still reproduces on `16.3.0-canary.5` with the same error.

The bug is independent of the deprecation warning. `getTypeScriptConfiguration.js` triggers the TS6 compat path rewriting on TypeScript version alone (`semver.gte(typescript.version, '6.0.0')`), not on whether `baseUrl` is flagged as deprecated. It rewrites `paths` to be relative to the app dir and deletes `baseUrl`, but never sets `pathsBasePath`. TypeScript then resolves the rewritten `../../libs/...` paths from the repo root (where `pathsBasePath` points, since that's where `tsconfig.base.json` defines `paths`), walks above it, and finds nothing.

`ignoreDeprecations: "6.0"` / #93377 won't address this - the rewrite still runs and `pathsBasePath` is still not updated. The fix in #93356 is what covers this case.

body:
Follow-up from the public repro: an application-level workaround appears to avoid the mismatch in this minimal case by making route metadata resolve from a single cache-stable, route-param-only SEO snapshot that is also consumed by the page body.

Baseline behavior in the repro:
- Browser UA: metadata was not in the initial head, hidden metadata wrapper was present, and the server emitted `Expected the resume to render <div> ... <__next_metadata_boundary__>` with a repro-local digest.
- Googlebot/Bingbot UAs: metadata was blocking and present in the initial head.

After changing the repro to route `generateMetadata()` through a cached SEO snapshot shared with the page body:
- Browser, Googlebot, and Bingbot document requests all returned full per-page head metadata (`title`, `description`, canonical, OG, Twitter, robots) and per-page JSON-LD.
- Repeated browser/bot document probes and `_rsc` probes did not emit the resume mismatch.
- No Next.js dependency code was modified.

This does not change the underlying framework issue: `htmlLimitedBots: /.*/` still does not make the prerender no-UA path match browser-runtime metadata behavior in the original repro. The workaround just avoids triggering the divergent metadata subtree shape by removing independent async metadata resolution from the route.
author: mdotk

body:
Corroborating from a production app, with two new data points: it reproduces **without `htmlLimitedBots`**, and it is **not fixed in 16.2.9**.

**Environment**
- Next.js 16.2.9 (also observed on 16.2.1), React 19.2.6, App Router, Turbopack
- `cacheComponents: true`, **no `htmlLimitedBots`** configured (default bot list)

**Symptom** (high volume in prod logs):
```
Error: Expected the resume to render <div> in this slot but instead it rendered <__next_metadata_boundary__>. The tree doesn't match so React will fallback to client rendering.
  digest: '1304565809'   // varies
```
Requests return **HTTP 200** and pages render; React discards the streamed SSR and falls back to client rendering.

**Where it fires**
- Dynamic-param public routes **without `generateStaticParams`** (Partial Prerender `◐`), each with an async `generateMetadata()` that fetches per-route data (title/description/canonical/OG + inline JSON-LD), and a `'use cache'` subtree mixed with `cookies()` in the same route.
- Triggered by (a) crawler document requests and (b) RSC prefetch requests (URLs carry the `nxtP*` param, e.g. `?nxtPusername=<slug>`).
- The triggering document UA in our logs is `Mozilla/5.0 (Linux; Android 6.0; ...)` — **not** in Next's default bot list, so it takes the streamed-metadata path (title lands in a `<div hidden>` wrapper, not the initial `<head>`).

**Confirming it's the same bug**
- Reproduced the exact error on 16.2.9 using your `next-ppr-metadata-repro` (with `htmlLimitedBots: /.*/`).
- With `cacheComponents` only (no `htmlLimitedBots`, matching our prod), the *minimal* repro doesn't error — but our production routes do. So the trigger isn't limited to `htmlLimitedBots` configs; the default bot list is enough in a real deployment (persisted PPR shell cache + real crawler/RSC traffic).

**Didn't help in our app**
- Upgrading 16.2.1 → 16.2.9.
- Removing `headers()` from `generateMetadata` (static canonical base URL).
- `'use cache'` on `generateMetadata` on its own.
- `htmlLimitedBots: /.*/` — metadata still streamed for non-listed UAs, matching this issue's title.

Going to try your shared cache-stable, param-only SEO-snapshot workaround on the dynamic-param routes next; will report back. Happy to provide additional production traces/digests if useful.

body:
Minimal public repro on **next@16.2.9** (stock npm, unpatched) plus a live Vercel deployment:

- Repo: https://github.com/ogabasseyy/nextjs-ppr-metadata-resume-repro
- Live: https://nextjs-ppr-repro.vercel.app

Same mechanism you documented — `cacheComponents: true` + `htmlLimitedBots: /.*/`, a PPR route (`generateStaticParams` so the shell is prerendered) with an async `generateMetadata`. Deterministic, 5/5 browser-UA requests log:

```
Error: Expected the resume to render <div> in this slot but instead it rendered <__next_metadata_boundary__>. The tree doesn't match so React will fallback to client rendering.
```

Browser UA: `<title>` missing from the initial `<head>` (streamed via a hidden `<div>` wrapper); Googlebot: blocking metadata present. body:
This is indeed a regression introduced in the `16.2.x` Turbopack module resolution pipeline. 

### The Root Cause
The underlying issue stems from how Turbopack's AST analyzer currently handles the static extraction of the `new Worker(new URL(..., import.meta.url))` pattern for `node:worker_threads`. 

When Turbopack statically analyzes this syntax, it attempts to resolve the relative path (`../../worker-entry.mjs`) against the context of the **emitted server chunk** instead of the original **source module**. Since the output directory structure flattens or shifts relative paths, the resolver throws a `Module not found` error before the build can even finish. In `16.1.7`, this strict static tracing wasn't intercepting `worker_threads` URLs in this exact aggressive manner.

### The Workaround (until patched in canary)

While we wait for a patch to the Turbopack Rust core (`tree_shake/graph.rs` and the worker analyzer), you can bypass the static analyzer and still maintain functional resolution in Node.js. 

By separating the `URL` instantiation from the `new Worker()` call, Turbopack's static AST matcher will skip the node, and it will be evaluated at runtime by Node.js natively:

```ts
// Extracting it to a variable prevents Turbopack from aggressively resolving it at build time
const workerUrl = new URL("../../worker-entry.mjs", import.meta.url);
const worker = new Worker(workerUrl);
author: enmanuelcanelon

body:
Thanks @enmanuelcanelon for the workaround!

I poked at the Turbopack source a bit and put together a draft PR (#93432) — sharing in case it's useful, but the maintainers should obviously have the final word.

From what I could see, the `worker_threads` analyzer uses a single resolution context (the Next.js project directory — i.e. the directory `next build` runs in, where `next.config.js` lives; in a monorepo this is the app directory like `apps/web/`, not the workspace root) for *every* form of the `Worker` argument:

https://github.com/vercel/next.js/blob/008e2e4bfad425ab7c73d71ade021b21ef048b91/turbopack/crates/turbopack-ecmascript/src/references/mod.rs#L1976-L1977

That works for string paths (Node.js resolves them against `process.cwd()`), but for `new URL(rel, import.meta.url)` the relative specifier should be resolved against the importing module instead. The bundling support landed in #88967 (first stable in v16.2.0), which lines up with the bisect.

### Another possible workaround

If the URL form is inconvenient to refactor away from, another option is a string path **from the Next.js project directory** (not relative to the source module):

```ts
// repro layout: project dir = apps/<app>/, worker at apps/<app>/app/worker-entry.mjs
new Worker("app/worker-entry.mjs")
```

This stays on the code path that already works. Verified locally with `next@16.2.4`, both with the repro's `app/` layout and with a `src/app/` variant (`new Worker("src/app/worker-entry.mjs")`); `/api/worker` returns the expected response in both cases.

Just a suggestion alongside @enmanuelcanelon's; whichever fits better. The draft PR (#93432) tries the minimal fix on the analyzer side — happy to revise based on maintainer feedback.

body:
这是一个清晰的文档矛盾问题。我来分析并给出修复方案。

## 分析

问题出在 `proxy.md` 文档页面的两个不同章节中：

1. **Runtime 章节**（第1条）：正确描述了 Proxy 的默认运行时是 Node.js
2. **Why Proxy 章节**（第2条）：错误地引用了旧版 Middleware 的行为，说默认是 Edge Runtime

**根因**：在 v16 将 Middleware 重命名为 Proxy 时，`Why Proxy` 章节的文本是从旧版 Middleware 文档迁移过来的，但未更新关于默认运行时的描述。实际上，Proxy 的默认运行时在 v16 中已经改为 Node.js。

## 修复方案

需要修改 `proxy.md` 中 `Why Proxy` 章节的这句话：

**原文**：
> Also, Middleware defaults to run at the Edge Runtime, which can run closer to the client, separated from the app's region.

**修改为**：
> Also, Proxy defaults to run at the Node.js Runtime, which can run closer to your database and other backend services, separated from the client-facing edge.

或者更简洁的版本：
> Also, Proxy runs on the Node.js Runtime, providing direct access to Node.js APIs and better integration with your backend infrastructure.

## 验证方法

1. 检查 `proxy.ts` 的默认导出配置，确认 `runtime: 'nodejs'` 是默认值
2. 确认 `proxy.ts` 中设置 `runtime: 'edge'` 是否会抛出错误（根据文档描述应该会）
3. 对比 `middleware.ts` 的旧版文档，确认这是迁移时的遗漏

## 额外发现

`Why Proxy` 章节中还有一处需要更新：
> "These behaviors align better with the term 'proxy' and provide a clearer purpose of the feature."

既然默认运行时改为 Node.js，这段解释也需要调整，因为 "proxy" 通常意味着更靠近客户端，但 Node.js 运行时通常部署在服务器端。建议改为：
> "This aligns with the term 'proxy' as it acts as an intermediary layer between the client and your application logic, handling routing and redirection at the server level."

**总结**：这是一个文档迁移时的遗漏问题，需要更新 `Why Proxy` 章节中关于默认运行时的描述，并相应调整该章节的上下文解释。

---
*[AI辅助分析 - 2026-05-05 00:01:29]*

The runtime for Proxy is properly addressed here.

The section you are referring to is about Migration, to motivate the renaming, the name chosen, how to migrate.

I'm not a maintainer, but this is documented: See [`turbopack.root`](https://nextjs.org/docs/app/api-reference/config/next-config-js/turbopack#root-directory)

> To resolve files from linked dependencies outside the project root (via npm link, yarn link, pnpm link, etc.), you must configure the turbopack.root to the parent directory of both the project and the linked dependencies.


Still, this seems possible to detect and put out a message for this specific case. There's 2 ways I imagine handling this:

1. If turbopack resolve fails, but instead it finds a symlink pointing outside of a the turbopack root, it could throw an error specifically letting the user know why it can't find the package.
2. If `enableGlobalVirtualStore: true` is on, and  it can't find the `next.js` package, show a specific error for this case. 

I think the first solution is a better DX for the long term, but I'm not sure how feasible it is. The second solution seems pretty trivial but somewhat limited, especially since there seems to be a somewhat common issue. 

If a maintainer wants to chime in on this, then there should be some idea of how to fix this issue.

body:
I get this audit check failure when doing

```
npm install next@latest
```

```

postcss  <8.5.10
Severity: moderate
PostCSS has XSS via Unescaped </style> in its CSS Stringify Output - https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-qx2v-qp2m-jg93
fix available via `npm audit fix --force`
Will install next@9.3.3, which is a breaking change
node_modules/next/node_modules/postcss
  next  9.3.4-canary.0 - 16.3.0-canary.5
  Depends on vulnerable versions of postcss
  node_modules/next
```

To update to the latest which is 16.2.6

The temporary fix is an overrides

```
  "overrides": {
    "next": {
      "postcss": "^8.5.14"
    }
  },
```
author: danrossi

body: For anyone watching this: PR #93288 already bumped the bundled postcss to 8.5.10, and the fix landed in canary from 16.3.0-canary.6 onward. Same day postcss 8.5.10 shipped, which was a fast turnaround. Stable 16.x releases through 16.2.6 and the 15.x backport line (15.5.18) still carry postcss@8.4.31, so users on those versions are currently hitting Dependabot alerts for GHSA-qx2v-qp2m-jg93 with no way to resolve them short of manual dismissal. Is there an ETA on a stable release that includes this fix?
author: Zelys-DFKH

Hey @icyJoseph!

Sorry for my late reply and thanks for your swift response! I was super busy during the last couple of days.

However, I had time to properly play around with this now → tldr; the "bug" disappeared!

I am so sorry of bothering you with this! I still cannot explain how I could reproduce the behaviour across different repositories and even narrow it down to the exact version (`v16.2.5`) where the DoS fix was addressed. I could also run repeatable tests with the `--webpack` flag, that clearly showed that Turbopack must be the issue.

I then created a Github action to test on different Environments and the tests all passed. I realised that the Node version for the Github tests was `v24.15.0`, so I thought maybe it is really the Node version causing the issue (I could not believe the minor patch would cause Turbopack to introduce such a regression...). Anyway, I then switched to Node`24.15.0` and tried again: the bug was gone. I switched back to `24.14.0` and - the bug was gone as well... This almost got me to ask ChatGPT wtf is going on (glad I did not fall into this rabbit hole and burn $100 worth of tokens).

I then switched to the original repo where I first discovered the *bug*. I upgraded to `Next 16.2.6`, cleared `node_modules` and `.next`, deleted `bun.lock`, reinstalled the packages and run the dev server again. **The bug was still there!!!** To get to the point now: after switching back and fourth between Node and Next versions I figured that I still run the same Chrome browser tab for quite a while for testing the application. I cleared the cache and boom, the *bug* is gone. This is so embarrassing 😅

Sorry again for bothering you with this (and sorry for the little novel here)!

Cheers, Flo

body:
Re-verified on the latest canary (`next@16.3.0-canary.19`) — bug is **still unfixed at HEAD**, behaviour identical to 16.2.4.

Two small clarifications to the steps above for anyone trying to repro locally:

- In `next dev`, the disk cache lives at `.next/dev/cache/images/`, not `.next/cache/images/` — the 0-byte file has to land in the dev path. The path in the original steps is correct for `next start` / production builds; for dev mode use:

  ```bash
  mkdir -p .next/dev/cache/images/anyKey
  : > .next/dev/cache/images/anyKey/14400.1.a.b.avif
  ```

- The disk LRU singleton initializes lazily on the **first** image-optimization request, so the 0-byte file must already be present at that moment. If you plant it after the first request has succeeded, restart the dev server before re-hitting the endpoint.

With those, the reproduction is deterministic. Exact stdout (cache-key in the log line is the *current* request's key, not the corrupt entry's — matching the diagnosis in the issue):

```
⨯ Failed to write image to cache ZG8a4zz89PiXBBeSnEICZzxYBo2fWMoRuPjxSAAVd9M Error: LRUCache: calculateSize returned 0, but size must be > 0. Items with size 0 would never be evicted, causing unbounded cache growth.
    at ignore-listed frames
⨯ unhandledRejection: Error: LRUCache: calculateSize returned 0, but size must be > 0. ...
```

Singleton poison confirmed: every subsequent `/_next/image?...` request re-emits the same error + `unhandledRejection` pair, indefinitely.

Workaround verified clean — after `find .next -path '*/cache/images*' -size 0 -delete` and a server restart, three follow-up image requests all returned `HTTP 200` with zero LRU errors in stdout.
author: MohamedEslam04

body:
### Same root cause, second trigger: `images.unoptimized: true` + read-only FS leaks the rejected init promise as an `unhandledRejection`

We hit a different path into the **exact same fragility** described here (the module-scoped `_diskLRUPromise` in `disk-lru-cache.external.ts` becoming permanently rejected, with the rejection escaping into the global scope). Sharing it because the trigger and the leak mechanism are distinct from the 0-byte-file case, and the `unoptimized` variant produces a genuinely *unhandled* rejection (no `try/catch` ever runs), which is worse for serverless deployments.

**Next.js:** 16.2.7 · **Runtime:** Node 24.x · **Platform:** AWS Lambda (`output: 'standalone'`, read-only `/var/task` filesystem) · **Config:** `images.unoptimized: true`

#### What we observed (production, Sentry)

```
Error: ENOENT: no such file or directory, mkdir
  at async Object.mkdir (node:internal/fs/promises)
  at next/dist/server/lib/disk-lru-cache.external.js:36  // await fs.promises.mkdir(cacheDir, { recursive: true })
mechanism: auto.node.onunhandledrejection
transaction: GET /_next/image
```

`unhandledPromiseRejection: true`. The HTTP request itself responds fine (a `404` — see below), so this is purely a leaked background promise, not a render failure. It fires roughly **once per cold start** (because `_diskLRUPromise` is a per-process module singleton).

#### Why it leaks (no `try/catch` ever consumes it)

The chain in `handleNextImageRequest` (`next/dist/server/next-server.js`) is, in order:

1. **The cache is constructed unconditionally, before any config check:**
   ```js
   const imageOptimizerCache = new ImageOptimizerCache({ distDir, nextConfig, cacheHandler });
   ```
2. `ImageOptimizerCache`'s constructor **eagerly fires** the disk-LRU init and stores the promise **without awaiting it** (`next/dist/server/image-optimizer.js`):
   ```js
   constructor({ distDir, nextConfig, cacheHandler }) {
     this.cacheDir = join(distDir, 'cache', 'images');
     // "Eagerly start LRU initialization for filesystem cache"
     if (!cacheHandler && nextConfig.images.maximumDiskCacheSize !== 0 && nextConfig.experimental.isrFlushToDisk) {
       this.isDiskCacheEnabled = true;
       this.cacheDiskLRU = getOrInitDiskLRU(this.cacheDir, ...); // fire-and-forget, rejected on read-only FS
     }
   }
   ```
   On a read-only filesystem the `mkdir` inside `getOrInitDiskLRU` rejects, so `this.cacheDiskLRU` is now a rejected promise.
3. **Immediately after construction, the handler short-circuits for `unoptimized` / custom loader and returns:**
   ```js
   const imagesConfig = this.nextConfig.images;
   if (imagesConfig.loader !== 'default' || imagesConfig.unoptimized) {
     await this.render404(req, res);
     return true;   // <-- get()/set() are NEVER reached
   }
   ```

The **only** places that `await this.cacheDiskLRU` are `ImageOptimizerCache#get` / `#set`, and those awaits are wrapped in `try/catch`. With `unoptimized: true` the handler returns at step 3, so neither `get()` nor `set()` ever runs → the rejected `cacheDiskLRU` promise is **never awaited by anything** → Node reports a true `unhandledRejection`.

So this is the mirror image of the 0-byte case: there the `set()` path *does* await it (caught, then logged + still re-surfaced); here, under `unoptimized`, **nothing awaits it at all**, and eager init means we pay a disk-LRU init for a feature we explicitly turned off.

#### Minimal local reproduction (no Lambda needed)

```bash
npx create-next-app@latest enoent-repro --ts --app --no-src-dir --use-npm
cd enoent-repro
# next.config: images.unoptimized: true  (loader stays 'default')
node -e "require('fs').writeFileSync('next.config.mjs','export default { images: { unoptimized: true } }\n')"

npm run build
# Make the image-cache parent unwritable to emulate a read-only serverless FS:
rm -rf .next/cache
chmod 0555 .next

npx next start &
sleep 4
curl -sS -o /dev/null "http://localhost:3000/_next/image?url=%2Fnext.svg&w=64&q=75"
```

Server stdout logs an **unhandled** `Error: ENOENT/EACCES ... mkdir` originating from `disk-lru-cache.external`, while the request returns `404`. (On a normally writable FS the same `unoptimized` request just `404`s with no error — the leak only surfaces when `mkdir` fails.)

#### Suggested fixes (either/both)

1. **Don't construct/init the disk cache when it can't be used.** Move the `new ImageOptimizerCache(...)` *after* the `loader !== 'default' || unoptimized` early-return, or make the constructor's eager-init guard also check those (the disk image cache is pointless when `unoptimized` or a non-default loader is configured).
2. **Make the singleton self-healing / never leak** (also fixes #93757): attach a `.catch()` when storing `_diskLRUPromise`, reset it to `null` on rejection so a transient failure doesn't poison the process, and treat init failure as "disk cache unavailable" (fall through to cache-miss) instead of letting the rejection escape. Tolerating a corrupt entry during `initCacheEntries` (the 0-byte case) fits naturally here too.

#### Workaround for anyone on read-only/serverless FS today

Setting `images.maximumDiskCacheSize: 0` makes the constructor's guard skip the eager init entirely, so `getOrInitDiskLRU` is never called and the rejection never happens. This is a clean complement to `unoptimized: true` (there is nothing to cache anyway).

body:
## Follow-up: WAF Product Details

The issue affects multiple WAF products since it's a general pattern-matching problem. The chunk filenames like `0od.e4.nsryo4.js` trigger WAF rules because:

1. **Multiple dots** in the filename path segment resemble file extension patterns that WAFs flag
2. **Short alphanumeric segments** (like `e4`, `nsryo4`) can match patterns for obfuscated/malicious filenames
3. The pattern is consistent across all Turbopack production builds with content hashing

### Affected WAFs (reported by users):
- **ModSecurity** (OWASP Core Rule Set) - flags the multi-dot pattern as a potential path traversal
- **AWS WAF** - may block based on URI pattern matching rules
- **Cloudflare WAF** - similar pattern-based blocking

### Confirmed Workaround
Until a fix lands, you can work around this by:
1. Using standard Next.js build (not Turbopack) for production: `next build` instead of `next build --turbopack`
2. Configuring your WAF to whitelist the `/_next/static/chunks/` path pattern
3. Using a reverse proxy rewrite rule to normalize chunk filenames

### Our Solution
We've submitted a detailed root cause analysis and fix proposal in our previous comment. The fix involves sanitizing chunk filenames at the output layer in `chunking_context.rs` to ensure at most one dot (the extension separator).

Would be happy to provide more details or test a fix if the Next.js team is working on this. 🙏

body:
Quick ~72h follow-up — the issue is still reproducing as of today, and our deploy queue is still blocked. No urgency framed as an ask; sharing the state in case it helps prioritisation. I also want to correct one piece of misinformation I almost posted earlier.

### Status from my end (honest)

- **Workaround attempted — did NOT fix the crash.** I added `@swc/helpers@0.5.21 --save-exact` to top-level `dependencies` in `package.json` (commit `2b9966de` on main). The change is live on the default branch, but **Vercel deploys still fail with the same `MIDDLEWARE_INVOCATION_FAILED` and the same missing-module stack trace**. Production has been frozen at the last successful deploy (pre-crash, 2026-05-13) for ~4 days.

- **Re-verified the minimal repro today (2026-05-17)**: live URL still returns HTTP 500 → `MIDDLEWARE_INVOCATION_FAILED` with fresh request id `fra1::xdph9-1779017513113-779b7ecb6d0b`. Bug actively reproducing.

- **11 hypotheses tested + falsified** during the original investigation: Vercel Build Cache Clear, `outputFileTracingIncludes`, `webpack.autoInstrumentMiddleware: false`, lazy import guard, full Sentry removal, downgrade to `next@16.2.5`, fresh `rm -rf node_modules && npm install` (regenerated `package-lock.json`), explicit `@swc/helpers` top-level dep, renaming `src/proxy.ts` to disable middleware (FUNCTION_INVOCATION_FAILED appears on `/` instead — same stack), and others. Detailed notes preserved on public test branches `s24-d1-step3-{middleware-disabled,next-16-2-5,lockfile-regen,sentry-middleware-disable}-test` if useful.

### Note re: @puneetdixit200's earlier comment

Thanks for the suggestion — adding `@swc/helpers` to top-level `dependencies` was actually the first workaround we tried. It changes nothing on the Vercel side (the missing file is still missing in `/var/task` after deploy). I don't know if the difference is a Vercel bundler quirk, a Next.js 16-specific behaviour, or something in our setup; happy to provide more environment details if useful.

### Business-impact context (no urgency framing — just data)

We've been unable to deploy ~4 days of new sprint work, including a fix for a pricing bug that has accumulated **~€29,000 of customer-facing under-billing** while the deploy queue has been frozen. The deploy package (~125 commits) is built and verified-green locally but is gated until the Vercel deploy issue is resolved. The pricing fix itself is small (one-line waterfall apply), but it cannot ship.

### Earlier comment correction

I want to be transparent: I had drafted an earlier follow-up comment that implied the workaround had succeeded and the pricing fix had shipped. **Both claims would have been false.** I caught the error before posting. The state above is the accurate one.

### What's most useful from your side?

No demands — the workaround attempt didn't help, so we're stuck waiting on the root cause. If any of the below is useful, happy to do it:

1. Provide additional diagnostics (Vercel deployment logs, `next info` output, `package-lock.json` excerpt, source map references)
2. Test a canary release on the minimal-repro project to validate a fix candidate
3. File a separate issue if the team prefers to consolidate elsewhere — happy to link forward

Apologies for the wall of text. Thanks for taking the time even to skim.

— Mike
author: Makturk

body:
Confirming same fingerprint on a separate production codebase (Next 16.2.6, src/proxy.ts, Sentry, next-intl, Supabase, Node 22, Vercel). Adding four data points not yet in the falsification list:

1. next build --webpack (Turbopack opt-out) reproduces. Locally with webpack, .next/server/middleware.js.nft.json references only @swc/helpers/cjs/_interop_require_default.cjs — zero .esm/* entries. Yet /var/task/ still tries to require @swc/helpers/esm/_interop_require_default.js at runtime. The Lambda is requesting a path the local NFT never emits. This decouples the bug from Turbopack specifically.

2. Renaming src/proxy.ts → src/middleware.ts (Next 16's deprecated convention; still builds as "Proxy (Middleware)" locally) reproduces with identical stack. Same Lambda type, same crash.

3. Vercel Instant Rollback to a successful pre-2026-05-13 build of the exact same commit serves traffic fine; fresh rebuild of that same commit fails. Isolates the regression to Vercel's build/deploy pipeline or Lambda runtime image, not application code. Matches the timeline reported in the Vercel community thread.

4. Every Dependabot patch PR reproduces (e.g., bump fast-xml-parser 5.7.2 → 5.7.3 — a one-line change in an unrelated dep). Confirms the trigger is not any particular import path or top-level statement; it's whatever Vercel does when bundling a fresh Next 16 proxy.ts Lambda since ~May 13.

Additional workarounds tested (none worked):
- Skipping Sentry init on the edge-runtime branch of register()
- Lazy-loading @sentry/nextjs via import type + dynamic import() for onRequestError
- @swc/helpers ^0.5.21 hoisted from overrides to direct dependencies
- Downgrade to next@16.2.3
- Combination of all the above stacked on a single commit

Production has been deploy-frozen for ~5 days, surviving via the Instant Rollback. Happy to share deployment IDs / repo access / minimal repro if useful for triage.

author: DavidDHDH

body:
#### New data point: Sentry is not a necessary condition

The thread's minimal repro and falsification log frame the trigger as a
top-level `import * as Sentry from '@sentry/nextjs'` in `instrumentation.ts`.
In our codebase:

- **No `@sentry/*` package** in `dependencies` or `devDependencies`.
- **No `instrumentation.ts`** (or `src/instrumentation.ts`) at all.
- `grep -r "@sentry" src` → **zero matches**.

Same `next@16.2.6` + `src/proxy.ts` + Vercel → **same missing-module crash on
the exact same ESM path**. So Sentry/`instrumentation.ts` is sufficient but **not
necessary**; the common factor is `next@16.2.6` proxy/middleware bundling vs.
Vercel's Node Lambda module resolution for `@swc/helpers`.

#### Corroborating @DavidDHDH's data point #1 (Turbopack-independent)

Both bundlers reproduce in the same repo:

- `next build --webpack` (our default `build` script) → reproduces.
- Default Turbopack build (dropping `--webpack`) → reproduces, identical stack.

As already noted upthread, the local NFT for the middleware references only
`@swc/helpers/cjs/_interop_require_default.cjs` (zero `esm/*` entries), yet the
Lambda requests `@swc/helpers/esm/_interop_require_default.js` at runtime — the
deployed function asks for a path the local trace never emits, regardless of
bundler.

#### Workaround status (matches @Makturk)

- Adding `@swc/helpers` (pinned, exact) to top-level `dependencies`
  **does not, on its own, resolve the crash** — same result @Makturk reported.
- Additional variable we isolated: our `next.config.ts` had
  `output: 'standalone'` set unconditionally (we need it for a separate Docker
  image). Gating it off for the Vercel build is the only change that plausibly
  bypasses Next's standalone NFT for the function on Vercel. We are reporting
  this as an additional axis worth testing in the minimal repro (does the
  repro still fail with `output` unset?), **not** as a confirmed fix.

#### Summary

`next@16.2.6` + a `proxy.ts`/middleware file deployed to Vercel requires
`@swc/helpers/esm/_interop_require_default.js` from the Node Lambda even though
(a) the package is installed with both cjs+esm builds, (b) the local NFT emits
only the cjs path, and (c) **no Sentry/instrumentation.ts is involved**.
Independent of Turbopack vs. webpack. Happy to share `vercel logs --json` /
`.nft.json` from our deployment if useful.

body:
Confirming swarnava's fix worked for us. Removing @swc/helpers from package.json overrides resolved the MIDDLEWARE_INVOCATION_FAILED crash on every deploy.

Quick back-story in case it helps others: we had added "@swc/helpers": "^0.5.21" to overrides on 2026-05-01 to fix a peer dependency conflict that was breaking our CI's npm ci. It worked silently for ~12 days. Then deployments started crashing around 2026-05-13 with the missing-module error, matching the timeline reported elsewhere in this thread.

So if anyone reading this added an @swc/helpers override (or yarn resolutions) recently to resolve a peer dep issue — try removing it.

Thanks @swarnava for the targeted diagnosis 🙏

body:
Update: I added a stronger CI reproduction that reaches an actual runtime 500 after deploying the downloaded prebuilt artifact.

Run: https://github.com/yayoi111/next-shiki-artifact-symlink-repro/actions/runs/25990480551
Workflow: https://github.com/yayoi111/next-shiki-artifact-symlink-repro/blob/main/.github/workflows/vercel-prebuilt-artifact-repro.yml

The workflow does this:

1. `vercel build --prod` on GitHub Actions.
2. Upload `.next` and `.vercel/output` with `actions/upload-artifact@v4` as a raw artifact.
3. Download that raw artifact in a fresh job.
4. Inspect `.next/node_modules` before deployment.
5. Deploy the downloaded output with `vercel deploy --prebuilt --archive=tgz --prod`.
6. Curl the production alias.

The server output must be self-contained when targeting Vercel serverless. Two acceptable approaches for the framework team: 1. During `vercel build`, copy (dereference) hashed alias symlinks into the output artifact rather than symlinking into the pnpm store. 2. body:
Possibly-related data point, with a **layout-independent** trigger (plain `npm`, single package, no pnpm/bun/symlinks/monorepo) — in case it helps, since a lack of clean repros was noted above.

Same error prefix (`Failed to load external module <name>-<hash>`) and same context (Next.js **16.2.9**, Turbopack, deployed to Vercel), but a **different terminal error** than the "unresolved alias / module not found" reports in this thread. Here the external module *resolves and loads*; it's the module's own internal `require()` of an **ESM transitive dependency** that throws `ERR_REQUIRE_ESM`:

```
[route] conversion failed: Failed to load external module jsdom-585531f309e4c3ed:
Error [ERR_REQUIRE_ESM]: require() of ES Module
  /var/task/web/node_modules/@exodus/bytes/encoding-lite.js
from /var/task/web/node_modules/html-encoding-sniffer/lib/html-encoding-sniffer.js not supported.
```

### Minimal trigger
- `serverExternalPackages: ['jsdom']` in `next.config`
- `jsdom@^27.0.1` (or newer). jsdom is CommonJS but from 27.0.1 it pulls **ESM-only** transitive deps (`@exodus/bytes`, `parse5`) which its CJS internals `require()` — see jsdom/jsdom#4013. Any CommonJS package in `serverExternalPackages` that transitively `require()`s an ESM dependency should reproduce this; jsdom is just a convenient one.

### The discrepancy
`require()` of that exact ESM file **succeeds on stock Node 20 / 22 / 24 / 26** (Node's `require(esm)`, on by default since 22.12) and a local `next build && next start` of the same production source **does not reproduce** the failure. It only fails once deployed to Vercel (runtime Node here is **24.x**). So the differentiator isn't the Node version or dev-vs-build — it's Vercel's build output / serverless packaging of the hashed external, whose `require()` appears not to honor Node's `require(esm)`.

If the hashed-external loader used a require path that supports `require(esm)` (or `import()`), this class of failure would go away as the ecosystem increasingly ships CJS packages with ESM-with-`require(esm)`-compat dependencies.

I can open a separate issue with a self-contained minimal repo if this is a distinct root cause from the "unresolved alias" symptom tracked here — didn't want to fragment if it's the same loader.

body:
Adding a datapoint that narrows the triad: we reproduce this **without the cookie-writing middleware ingredient**.
**Environment:** next 16.2.7 (pinned) — also reproduces identically on 16.3.0-preview.5. react/react-dom 19.2.4, App Router, TypeScript. Repros on Turbopack dev **and** on a production build (`next build` + `next start`); our trace was captured against a production build. Windows 11, Edge (Chromium).
**Shape:** a fully client-rendered multi-step wizard (`/book/boxes → /book/goals → /book/quote → /book/when → /book/pay`, all `"use client"`, draft state in a sessionStorage-backed context provider). The destination page renders a default-prefetched `<Link>` back to the previous step. Submitting the previous step calls `router.push()` to the destination; the destination mounts, then a `history.replaceState` immediately fires with the OLD URL. We instrumented `pushState`/`replaceState` with a dev wrapper that logs call stacks: the reverting `replaceState` contains **zero application frames** — framework code only, timing consistent with a mount effect on arrival. Deterministic: the transition can never complete via the client router.
**What we falsified:**
- **Our own code** — reproduces with the wizard's context provider inert (no state writes); no app code calls `replaceState` anywhere, and the reverting stack confirms it.
- **Fixed upstream** — identical behavior on 16.3.0-preview.5.
- **The middleware ingredient being required** — we originally ran the standard `@supabase/ssr` cookie-writing session-refresh middleware on these routes. We excluded the entire route group from the matcher (verified live) and the revert persisted unchanged. In our reproduction, a prefetched back-`Link` to the previous route plus the prefetch cache appears to be sufficient on its own.
**Workaround shipped:** `window.location.assign()` for this one transition (full document navigation bypasses the client router; sessionStorage rehydrates the draft), plus `prefetch={false}` on the destination's back-link as defense-in-depth. Works, at the cost of a full page load on one wizard step.
**Available on request:** raw trace log of every `pushState`/`replaceState` during the repro with full call stacks (production build), and the middleware-matcher diff used for the falsification. Happy to attempt a minimal repro against a fresh scaffold if that would help triage.

body:
@tuobi2 

Thanks for the suggestions. I added both onClick and onTouchEnd tests with a visible on-screen log and console.log. Neither event fires on iOS 15.

The console shows the actual root cause — a JS parse error before any handlers are registered:

Dev:
  SyntaxError: Unexpected token '{'
  AppDevOverlayErrorBoundary (next_dist_080cxwf.js:3631)
  ErrorBoundaryHandler (next_dist_client_0o8274i.js:1538)

Prod:
  SyntaxError: Unexpected token '{'  (0wx.c~5-ry5jx.js:1)

  Inspecting the source, the error points to static initialization blocks (static { ... }) inside Next.js internal classes:

  class AppDevOverlayErrorBoundary extends _react.PureComponent {
    static {  // ← SyntaxError on iOS 15
      this.contextType = _approutercontextsharedruntime.AppRouterContext;
    }

  static {} is ES2022 — not supported in iOS 15 Safari (requires Safari 16.4+). The bundle fails to parse entirely, so React never mounts and no event handlers are registered. onClick not firing is a symptom, not the cause.

This regression was introduced in 16.1.7 — reverting to 16.1.6 fixes it. Next.js 16.1.7+ appears to use static initialization blocks in its App Router internals without downcompiling them for older WebKit targets.

The same awaited data is streamed in main RSC payload, while not visible in DevTools, I could see that document request is in _content download_ state, data is transferred, but DevTools is unresponsive to investigate script tag at Elements panel. This doesn't cause immediate browser renderer crash, but still a broken dev experience.

I guess proper fix is to prevent awaited data reaching the debug channel until server is asked to provide it over a debug channel.

body:
I'm seeing what appears to be the same regression, but with a different failure mode.

### Environment

- Next.js: **16.2.4**
- Monorepo (pnpm workspace)
- `output: 'standalone'`
- Production build via:

```bash
next build
next start
```

### Worker creation

```ts
const worker = new Worker(
  new URL('./search.worker.ts', import.meta.url),
  { type: 'module' }
)
```

The worker itself is just a regular module worker and does not use Monaco or any special APIs.

### Behavior

- ✅ `next dev` works correctly.
- ✅ The same code worked on **Next 16.0.7**.
- ❌ After upgrading to **16.2.4**, production builds fail immediately when the worker is created.

Instead of:

```
TypeError: e.indexOf is not a function
```

I'm getting:

```
Uncaught Error: Missing worker bootstrap config
```

The stack trace points to the generated Turbopack runtime:

```
turbopack-worker-xxxxx.js:1
Uncaught Error: Missing worker bootstrap config
```

Looking at the Next.js source, this error comes from:

```js
if (!paramsString) abort("Missing worker bootstrap config");
```

which suggests that the worker bootstrap is started without the expected `#params=...` fragment.

I also noticed that the generated bundle references:

```
/_next/static/media/search.worker.<hash>.ts
```

instead of what I'd expect to be a compiled worker JS bundle.

This looks related to the same worker bootstrap regression introduced in 16.2, although it manifests differently than the `e.indexOf is not a function` error.
