body: Confirmed fixed on `next@16.3.0-canary.28` against this exact repro — page hydrates after back-nav even though Chrome serves the document from cache (`deliveryType: "cache"`, `transferSize: 0`). The fix is https://github.com/vercel/next.js/pull/92892 + https://github.com/vercel/next.js/pull/93486. cc @unstubbable
author: gaojude

body:
@gaojude This fix appears to target App Router only (app/layout.tsx pattern). Our app uses Pages Router, and the issue is still reproducible: using browser Back restores the page from history/bfcache and SSR does not run again.

**Expected:**
Back/forward navigation should trigger a full refresh path (or equivalent) so server-side data is re-fetched in Pages Router flows.

**Actual:**
Back returns a restored client snapshot, and SSR-dependent state/data is stale.

Can you confirm one of the following:
- A Pages Router equivalent fix is planned.
- This is now expected behavior, with official workaround guidance for Pages Router apps (for example, an approach similar to the App Router fix but implemented in `_document.tsx` instead of `app/layout.tsx`).

We currently use a dev-only pageshow + back_forward/bfcache reload workaround, but this is only a local mitigation, not a framework-level fix.

body:
> This is intentionally not a PR because the previous stability fix in https://github.com/vercel/next.js/pull/88428 was reverted in https://github.com/vercel/next.js/pull/90384 after causing generated type correctness issues.

IIRC the initial fix, make other things break...

What is it that you are after here? We already recommend ignoring the file, short of expecting it to be ignored to be honest. It has been some weeks since I looked at this.
author: icyJoseph

body:
Yeah, that makes sense. I am not asking to bring #88428 back as-is, especially given the type correctness issues that led to #90384.

What I was after is mostly a clearer contract for `next-env.d.ts`.

If the intended answer is "this file is generated, command-specific, and should not be tracked", then I think this can be closed as expected behavior.

The part that confused me in an existing repo was the command-order churn:

- `next dev` rewrites it to `.next/dev/types/...`
- `next typegen` / build rewrites it to `.next/types/...`
- standalone `tsc --noEmit` needs `next typegen` first if it relies on generated route types

The docs already say to ignore `next-env.d.ts`, but I did not understand from the docs that the file can legitimately switch between those import targets depending on the command.

A small docs note would have been enough for me. A warning when Next rewrites a tracked `next-env.d.ts` would also help existing repos, but I am not blocked on that if the contract is simply that tracked `next-env.d.ts` is unsupported.
author: IFAKA

body:
No worries. I think around v12, the wording around next-env.d.ts was like, we reserve the right to write, and output changes to it, so it is better to have it outside version control. I am thinking changing the https://nextjs.org/docs/app/api-reference/config/typescript#next-envdts to:

```md
## `next-env.d.ts`

Next.js generates a `next-env.d.ts` file in your project root. This file references Next.js type definitions, allowing TypeScript to recognize non-code imports (images, stylesheets, etc.) and Next.js-specific types.

Running `next dev`, `next build`, or [`next typegen`](/docs/app/api-reference/cli/next#next-typegen-options) regenerates this file.

> **Good to know**:
>
> - `next-env.d.ts` is a file managed by Next.js. Its contents are an implementation detail and may change over time. To avoid unnecessary diffs, we recommend excluding it from version control. Do not edit this file manually.
> - The file must be in your `tsconfig.json` `include` array (`create-next-app` does this automatically).
```

Something like that... it should be good enough I think - we want to just cover this scenario, `I see this next-env.d.ts file producing git diffs - what does the docs say about this?`
author: icyJoseph

body:
No worries, that makes sense.

I think that docs wording would cover the confusing case I hit. The key bit for me is just making it clear that `next-env.d.ts` is managed by Next.js, can be regenerated by different commands, and should stay out of version control.

I’m good with treating this as expected behavior / docs clarification. 
I’ll leave the issue open for you folks to close or retag however makes sense.

Thanks!

body:
This is the same root cause as #93905 and is fixed by PR #94139.

**Root cause:** Three deferral layers delay React's fiber commit after `popstate` (browser back/forward):

1. `app-router.tsx` — `startTransition` wrapping the popstate dispatch defers the entire restore as a low-priority React transition
2. `use-action-queue.ts` — dev-mode `appDevRenderingIndicator` wraps ALL dispatches in another `startTransition`, re-introducing deferral even after layer 1 is fixed
3. `app-router-instance.ts` — `async` keyword on `runAction` and `action` functions forces synchronous reducer results through `.then()` microtask, deferring `setState`

The combination means React's `useEffect`, `useLayoutEffect`, ref callbacks, and event handlers all fire late (or appear to never fire) after bfcache restore. The page visually restores but JS execution appears frozen — exactly as described in this issue.

**Fix (PR #94139):** Removes all three deferral layers:
- Popstate and `applyUrlFromHistoryPushReplace` dispatch synchronously (no `startTransition`)
- Dev-mode dispatch skips `appDevRenderingIndicator` for `ACTION_RESTORE`
- `runAction` and `action` functions are synchronous (no `async` keyword)

The `ACTION_RESTORE` fast-path in `dispatchAction` (lines 156-171) was specifically designed for synchronous dispatch but was defeated by these outer wrappers. The TODO at the original `app-router.tsx:391` (Tim Neutkens, 2022-09-06) acknowledges this was always intended to be temporary.

Test suite added: `test/e2e/app-dir/popstate-useeffect-timing/` with MutationObserver-based timing assertions.

Related data point (also posted on #81161): https://github.com/vercel/next.js/issues/81161#issuecomment-4831893448

On Next.js **16.2.6**, Apple Silicon, macOS darwin 25.5.0, multi-lockfile monorepo: pinning `turbopack.root` to the app directory is good hygiene here (guards against the broad-root memory pressure described in this issue), but it did **not** fix a separate problem — Turbopack dev still idles at **~750% CPU** with `notify-rs fsevents loop` + fstat storm. Same app on `next dev --webpack` idles at **~0%**.

So broad-root inference and the idle watcher feedback loop appear to be distinct failure modes on macOS; both may need addressing.

body:
Sorry for the confusion — my earlier link was about caching patterns and not relevant to your bug. After reading the repro more carefully: this is clearly a Turbopack chunk graph emission bug, not a user-land config issue. Turbopack's page entry fails to register the SSR chunk for the next/dynamic-imported 'use client' component when experimental.cacheComponents is active, so the Turbopack runtime can't find the factory at prerender time. Workarounds until Vercel fixes it: 1. Drop experimental.cacheComponents and use "use cache" with the --turbopack flag only (no cacheComponents) The flag is what triggers the broken code path. If you need caching, you can still use "use cache" without enabling cacheComponents. 2. Replace next/dynamic with a regular import + React.lazy or just a direct import Since the bug only fires when a 'use cache' server component renders a next/dynamic() client component, switching the dynamic import to a normal static import (with ssr: false via a wrapper if needed) avoids the broken path. 3. Build with webpack (npm run build:webpack) for now Already noted in your README — it just works. 4. Extract the 'use cache' logic into a separate server component that does NOT contain the next/dynamic call, and pass the dynamic component as a children prop This breaks the direct import chain that triggers the bug: ```tsx// CachedWrapper.tsx ← has 'use cache', no dynamic import 'use cache' export async function CachedWrapper({ children }: { children: React.ReactNode }) { const data = await fetchSomething(); return
{children}
; } // page.tsx ← does the dynamic import, passes it in const DynamicBlock = dynamic(() => import('../components/Block')); ``` This is a known Turbopack issue — worth filing at https://github.com/vercel/next.js/issues with your repo as the repro.

body:
The default setting hasn't landed in stable (which the PR you linked shows). The config is a behavior toggle for something that'll end up being part of how the router just works.

- https://nextjs.org/blog/next-16-2#experimentalprefetchinlining

Explanations about that will be available when it lands, although some of these internals and flags, might be mentioned in architecture docs or blog posts detailing the behavioral changes. It is part of the optimizations and choices, that the framework takes ownership of, so that you can focus on your business code, with everything that ownership implies.

For a bit of background, Next 16 introduced these changes: https://nextjs.org/blog/next-16#core-features--architecture - which lead to a large number of requests being issued agains the server.

The PR that introduced `prefetchInlining` here, https://github.com/vercel/next.js/pull/90555#issue-3992914103, explains it like this:

> A route with N segments now produces N prefetch requests instead of one. Users upgrading from older versions notice significantly more network activity in their devtools, even though the total bytes transferred may be similar or lower due to deduplication.

Arguably closer to what one would expect, rather than fan out N requests, many can be inlined into a single one.

> When enabled, the server bundles all segment data for a route into a single /_inlined response rather than serving each segment individually.

This and other flags are stepping stones towards some new feature set that'll land in the router area. **_I'll keep the issue open_** though, I have a draft somewhere talking about it. I'll update the issue as we near a release that'll include the flag active by default. 

Once again, this behavior is expected to be the way the router works, and the flag mostly exists only for triage/debugging purposes, in other words, apps should not need to ever turn this flag to false. Yet, another way to frame it, it landed on 16.2 for projects to enable and verify that it drives costs down, without causing any other side-effect issues.

body:
Great issue — and the legal framing is spot on.

**One thing worth noting:** I checked the [webmail repo](https://github.com/bulwarkmail/webmail) and they already have `NEXT_TELEMETRY_DISABLED=1` set in their env, which does suppress the warning. So the opt-out mechanism works — but that’s precisely the problem. Under EU ePrivacy and GDPR, **opt-out is not a valid substitute for consent**. The data collection and the warning should never appear in the first place without the developer actively choosing to participate.

**Why "anonymous" may not be enough legally:**
Next.js generates a persistent UUID stored on the machine (`~/.nextjs/`) to correlate telemetry events over time. Under GDPR Article 4(1), persistent pseudonymous identifiers are generally still considered personal data. The "anonymous" label doesn’t automatically make this GDPR-safe.

**What a fully compliant fix would look like:**
1. No data sent on first run — show an interactive consent prompt instead
2. Default answer to the prompt should be **No**
3. Persistent UUID generated and stored only *after* explicit consent
4. Auto-disable in non-interactive/CI environments (detect `CI=true`)
5. A `telemetry: false` option in `next.config.js` for version-controlled, auditable opt-out

Angular CLI and .NET SDK both went through similar controversies and landed on opt-in prompts — that’s the right model here too.

---

**I’d like to help fix this.** I’m happy to work on changing the telemetry behaviour to opt-in by default — specifically:
- Adding an interactive consent prompt on first run (nothing sent before the developer says yes)
- Skipping the prompt and defaulting to disabled in CI/non-interactive environments
- Only generating and persisting the machine UUID after explicit consent

author: RiteshWanave

body:
> **One thing worth noting:** I checked the [webmail repo](https://github.com/bulwarkmail/webmail) and they already have `NEXT_TELEMETRY_DISABLED=1` set in their env, which does suppress the warning. 

Yes, but only in the docker file, not in the example .env files.

But there’s one more thing: The so-called “data subject” (the identifiable natural person) is not the developer of an application, but rather the person whose data is being collected. In other words, this includes not only the developers of the application but also everyone who installs and runs it.


> Next.js generates a persistent UUID stored on the machine

Hmmm, when NEXT_TELEMETRY_DISABLED is set to 1, then next.js claims, that there is no UUID. If they were to transmit such an UUID nonetheless, it would constitute a significant violation of the GDPR. (I haven't checked it.)

> **Why "anonymous" may not be enough legally:** Next.js generates a persistent UUID stored on the machine (`~/.nextjs/`) to correlate telemetry events over time. Under GDPR Article 4(1), persistent pseudonymous identifiers are generally still considered personal data. The "anonymous" label doesn’t automatically make this GDPR-safe.

Yes, that's right. And even for data without an ID, it is not allowed to send non personal data because of the ePrivacy regulation (see links above in the bug report) without consent.


> **What a fully compliant fix would look like:**
> 
> 1. No data sent on first run — show an interactive consent prompt instead
> 2. Default answer to the prompt should be **No**
> 3. Persistent UUID generated and stored only _after_ explicit consent
> 4. Auto-disable in non-interactive/CI environments (detect `CI=true`)
> 5. A `telemetry: false` option in `next.config.js` for version-controlled, auditable opt-out

Exactly!
However, it should be noted that consent must be given entirely voluntarily (e.g., without nudging or deceptive design patterns). It must also be informed, which means that the data subject must know what data is being transferred, what will happen to it, and what that implies. If the data subject is aware of all this and then voluntarily decides to really **want** the processing to take place, then it is legally permitted.

author: sculli-net

body:
I've traced several call sites in `app-render.tsx` and found that `onInstrumentationRequestError` is consistently invoked with a `DigestedError`, which is defined as:
type DigestedError = Error & {
  digest: string
  environmentName?: string
}
Examples include `onHTMLRenderRSCError`, `onFlightDataRenderError`, and `onHTMLRenderSSRError`. This appears to align with the documented API (`Error & { digest: string }`) more closely than the current `unknown` type declaration in `InstrumentationOnRequestError`.

I'm continuing to check the remaining call sites to see whether there are any paths that pass a non-Error value.
author: Yyash64

body:
I did some tracing through the source code.

I found several App Router call sites in `app-render.tsx` where `onInstrumentationRequestError` is invoked with a `DigestedError` (`Error & { digest: string; environmentName?: string }`), which aligns with the documentation.

However, I also found a Pages Router path in `pages-handler.ts` where a raw `catch (err: unknown)` value is forwarded directly to `routeModule.onRequestError(...)` and ultimately to the instrumentation handler.

Because of that path, it seems the handler can receive values that are not guaranteed to be `Error` instances. This makes me think the current `unknown` type may be intentional, and the docs/example (which access `err.message` without narrowing) may need to be updated instead.

I'm continuing to check whether there are any normalization steps elsewhere that guarantee an Error before the user-facing callback is invoked.
author: Yyash64

body:
I traced the flow through several call sites.

For App Router rendering paths, `onInstrumentationRequestError` is often called with a `DigestedError` (`Error & { digest: string; environmentName?: string }`).

However, I also found a Pages Router path in `pages-handler.ts` that forwards a raw `catch (err: unknown)` value directly to `routeModule.onRequestError(...)`, and the value is ultimately passed through `instrumentationOnRequestError(...)` to the user handler without any normalization.

Because of that path, it seems the callback can receive values that are not guaranteed to be `Error` instances. Based on the current implementation, the `unknown` type appears intentional, and the documentation/example may need to be updated to narrow the type before accessing properties like `err.message`.
author: Yyash64

body:
Changing the public type to `Error & { digest: string }` is not a good idea unless all call sites normalize the caught value first.

`pages-handler.ts` still forwards a raw `catch (err: unknown)` through `routeModule.onRequestError(...)`, and `RouteModule.onRequestError` passes that value into the instrumentation callback unchanged.

Based on the current implementation, `unknown` looks correct. The docs/example should probably be updated to narrow before reading `err.message` or `digest`.

body:
Update: the bypass also reproduces with `@vercel/otel` as the delegate provider — so this is not Sentry-specific.

In the repro ([0ed1fe7](https://github.com/pnodet/next-prerender-random-repro/commit/0ed1fe7)):

```bash
REPRO_MODE=vercel-otel pnpm dev
curl -s http://localhost:3000/early-span   # still fails with next-prerender-random
curl -s http://localhost:3000/late-span    # still fine
```

Plain `registerOTel('next-app')` by itself is unaffected — Next's internal spans and `@vercel/otel`'s built-in fetch instrumentation acquire their tracers through the patched path (consistent with #72024 being fixed by #82350). But the documented custom-instrumentation pattern,

```ts
registerOTel({ instrumentations: [new PgInstrumentation()] })
```

constructs the instrumentation in user code before registration (`InstrumentationAbstract`'s constructor calls `trace.getTracer()`), which yields a `ProxyTracer` and hits the same `getDelegateTracer()` bypass.

author: icyJoseph

body:
Hi,

I am using the HeroUI template (v2) with Next.js and after upgrading to Next.js 16.2.9, I started experiencing a random routing issue.

After the application runs for some time, all routes suddenly begin returning 404 responses, including routes that were previously working correctly.

Additional details:

Next.js version: 16.2.9
HeroUI version: v2
Using App Router
No custom proxy configuration
No middleware
No rewrites or redirects configured
Restarting the application temporarily fixes the issue
The problem did not occur before upgrading to 16.2.9

Expected behavior:

Routes should continue working normally during the application's lifetime.

Actual behavior:

After some time, routes randomly start returning 404 responses until the application is restarted.

If needed, I can provide a minimal reproduction repository.

Hi, I'd like to try working on this one.

I read through the issue and the reproduction. The evidence matrix makes the problem clear: the 404 only happens when proxy.ts and --experimental-build-mode compile are combined. A full build works fine, and compile mode without proxy.ts works fine too. So the bug looks specific to how compile mode builds and wires up the proxy/middleware layer, and the runtime then cannot resolve the server action.

This also matches #86753, where proxy.js is not handled correctly in compile mode output, so the fix might be in the same area.

I'll start by looking into how compile mode generates the standalone output for middleware and where action resolution happens at runtime. If a maintainer could point me to the relevant files, that would help me move faster. Happy to open a PR once I have a working fix.

body:
## Feasibility Analysis

Investigated implementing this as an external contributor. Sharing findings for context:

**Root cause:** The build error originates from an intentional invariant in the Rust SWC transform (`react_server_components.rs`) that uniformly rejects **all** route-segment configs (`dynamicParams`, `dynamic`, `fetchCache`, `revalidate`, `experimental_ppr`) when `cacheComponents` is active. This isn't an accidental omission — it's a deliberate guard.

**Why a drive-by PR won't work:** The desired behavior (SSG-only routes with `dynamicParams: false` serving a static 404 rather than triggering a serverless invocation under `cacheComponents`) requires changes deep in the runtime — specifically how cache-component routes resolve dynamic segments at request time. That's architecture-level work spanning the SWC transform, the route manifest, and the runtime handler.

**Verdict:** This is core-team territory. `cacheComponents` is under active Vercel development, so the right fix will likely come as part of that work rather than from an outside PR.

Not planning to open a PR on this one. Hope the analysis is useful!

body: Apologies — this is not a Next.js bug. Root cause was a global export NODE_ENV="development" in my shell profile, overriding the NODE_ENV=production that next build sets. That left React's dev/prod resolution inconsistent, so react resolved to null in the /_global-error SSR chunk during prerender (the tell was the ⚠️ non-standard NODE_ENV value warning on every build). Removing the global export — or running NODE_ENV=production next build — makes the build pass cleanly. --debug-prerender masked it because it forces a consistent NODE_ENV. Closing as environment misconfiguration. Thanks for the pointers!

body:
Confirming this on the served-page side (not just build output), with fresh numbers from a production e-commerce storefront.

**Versions:** next 16.3.0-preview.5 (also observed on 16.2.9), react 19.2.x.
**Setup:** `cacheComponents: true` + `experimental.inlineCss: true`, App Router, one Tailwind global stylesheet imported in the root layout, pages composed of several PPR segments (static shell + multiple Suspense-streamed islands), deployed-style `next build` + `next start`.

Observed on the served documents (decompressed, measured by counting a unique stylesheet substring per document):

| Page | Stylesheet copies | Document size |
|---|---|---|
| Homepage | 4 = 1 inline `<style>` + 3 serialized into `__next_f` | 801,776 B (~390 KB of that is duplicated CSS text, ~49% of the document) |
| Product page | 3 = 1 + 2 | 576,741 B |

The stylesheet is 128,566 B. The number of `__next_f` copies tracks the page's PPR segment count, so heavier pages duplicate more. Gzip hides some of it on the wire (repetition compresses well: homepage 130 KB gzip) but the decompressed cost is paid in parse/memory on every load, and cache-partitioned CDNs/proxies store the full duplication.

With `inlineCss: false` and nothing else changed: homepage document drops to 282,875 B (40 KB gzip) + two immutable-cached external CSS files (128.3 KB total, 21.7 KB gzip) shared across all routes; local prod cold-cache FCP/LCP medians were within noise of the inlined config (home 92/92 ms both ways). So the duplication currently erases the flag's benefit for Cache Components apps - same conclusion as the OP: keep the initial-HTML inline, reference/dedupe the stylesheet in the RSC/segment payloads.

body:
I've opened #95369 with a fix and a regression test for this.

**Root cause:** in `buildAppStaticPaths`, when a nested `generateStaticParams` returns `[]` for one parent value (e.g. `fr`) but a non-empty array for another (`en`), the incomplete `{ lang: 'fr' }` combination made `hadAllParamsGenerated` `false`, which gated off prerendering for the **entire** route — dropping the valid `en` pages too.

**Fix:** in non-PPR mode, drop the incomplete combinations before prerendering so the complete ones (`/en/thing/a`, `/en/thing/b`) are still statically generated while the empty branches fall back to on-demand rendering. The PPR path is unchanged. Verified against the reproduction plus the existing empty-`generateStaticParams` and optional-catch-all suites.

body:
**Hi there! @xJayLee**

First, just to give you some peace of mind: for a massive monorepo like FastGPT, using ~1.5GB to 2GB of RAM during `next dev` startup is actually **expected behavior**. Next.js has to parse, compile, and build source maps for thousands of files in the workspace. 

However, if it's causing your system to lag, freeze, or crash, here are the best ways to optimize it locally on Windows 11:

**1. Use Turbopack (Highly Recommended)**
Since you are on Next.js 15/16, you should be using Turbopack for local dev. It is significantly faster and handles memory much better than the legacy Webpack bundler. 
Update your `package.json` dev script to: 
```json
"dev": "next dev --turbo"
```
*(Reference: [Next.js Turbopack Documentation](https://nextjs.org/docs/architecture/turbopack))*

**2. Increase the Node.js Memory Limit (Prevents Crashes)**
While this won't lower the baseline 2GB usage, it increases the memory ceiling to prevent "Out of Memory" (OOM) crashes during heavy compilation. In PowerShell, run:
```powershell
$env:NODE_OPTIONS="--max-old-space-size=8192"
pnpm dev
```
*(This allocates up to 8GB of RAM to the Node.js V8 heap).*

**3. Add Windows Defender Exclusions (Crucial for Windows)**
Windows Defender constantly scans files Next.js and pnpm create in `.next` and `node_modules`. This causes massive I/O bottlenecks, CPU spikes, and inflates memory usage. 
* Go to **Windows Security > Virus & threat protection > Manage settings > Exclusions**.
* Add **Folder** exclusions for:
  * Your FastGPT project root.
  * Your pnpm global store (usually `%LOCALAPPDATA%\pnpm-store`).
* Add **Process** exclusions for:
  * `node.exe`
  * `pnpm.exe`
*(Reference: [Microsoft Docs on Antivirus exclusions for Node.js](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/windows/security/application-security/application-control/windows-defender-application-control/design/applications-that-need-to-be-allowed) / [Next.js Windows Troubleshooting](https://nextjs.org/docs/app/api-reference/config/next-config-js))*

**4. Close Memory-Heavy Background Apps**
Since 2GB is the baseline for a monorepo this size, ensure browsers with many tabs, Docker Desktop, or other heavy IDEs aren't competing for RAM while running the dev server.

Hope this helps smooth out your local development experience!
